items.title: EvoViM: Recursively Self-Evolving Visual Agents for Exploration with Deferred Queries
items.content: Multimodal large language model (MLLM) agents have shown promising capabilities in task-oriented environments. However, they still struggle when queries are deferred until after exploration, requiring them to retain visual evidence before knowing which details will matter. We introduce EvoViM, a recursively self-evolving framework in which a frozen multimodal model turns its own interaction experience into one visual program for memory and skills. The program retains images and computes directly on pixels, and its operations decide how this evidence is used in each task. During memory evolution, the same model traces failures in its visual trajectories to the operations that lost or misused evidence and revises them. It also rewrites the notes and analysis tools that guide later revisions, which then build on earlier findings and skip changes that have already failed. We evaluate EvoViM with three multimodal models on six tasks covering visual matching, spatial recall, and sequential decision-making, including three tasks with deferred queries. Across the six tasks, EvoViM improves the average score over AutoMem, the strongest baseline in the main comparison, by 31.3-47.6 points on held-out episodes. Programs written once from the initial environment instructions perform substantially worse, highlighting the value of interaction experience in shaping how visual evidence is retained and used. Code and dataset are available at https://evovim.github.io/.

items.title: DRAM: Memory-Efficient Muon via Rank Reallocation in Principal-Random Subspaces
items.content: Memory-efficient Muon methods aim to reduce storage overhead while preserving strong performance, yet existing approaches compromise either convergence guarantees or practical efficiency. In this paper, we focus on subspace optimization for Muon, where the choice of subspace determines the gradient information retained for updating. To preserve dominant information while providing the coverage needed for stochastic convergence guarantees, we construct a principal-random subspace that combines leading singular directions of the stochastic gradient with random directions sampled from their orthogonal complement. Under a fixed rank budget, there is a trade-off between principal exploitation and complementary coverage, making rank allocation important for practical optimization. Our key observation is that the preferred balance shifts from principal-heavy early in training to random-heavy later. Motivated by this shift, we propose \dram, a memory-efficient Muon optimizer that reallocates principal and random ranks across stages while maintaining momentum and performing matrix-sign normalization entirely in the subspace. Theoretically, we establish convergence guarantees for general rank-allocation schedules with nondecreasing coverage factors, obtaining rates of $O(T^{-1/4})$ in the stochastic setting and $O(T^{-1/2})$ in the deterministic setting, with fixed allocation as a special case. Using a simple linear reallocation schedule, \dram achieves the best low-memory performance across three pre-training scales and nine fine-tuning settings.

items.title: VeriLadder: A Multi-Agent Specification Refinement System for Tool-Verified Verilog Datasets
items.content: Training data is a bottleneck in AI, especially for large language models (LLMs) that write Verilog, because register-transfer-level (RTL) code is rarely published and existing datasets mostly check code for syntax, not instruction correctness. This paper presents VeriLadder, a five-level Verilog dataset, and the multi-agent framework that builds it, in which LLM agents write and revise specifications, and EDA tools (a synthesizer and a formal equivalence checker) decide what is accepted. Its levels follow an engineer's checks. Level 1 labels designs from two large Verilog corpora, namely RTLCoder and PyraNet, with synthesis results, failure causes, critical warnings and post-synthesis metrics. 28% of RTLCoder designs fail synthesis and are kept as negatives. Level 2 grades each instruction on four specification qualities, and low grades predict failed rebuilds. Level 3 rewrites each instruction into a refined specification and accepts it only if an LLM from another model family, reading only that specification, writes a circuit formally equivalent to the original. This raises the share of rebuildable designs from 26.1% to 78.2%, keeping every failed specification with its counterexample. Levels 4 and 5 add verified paraphrases and one-fact variants, hard negatives that differ only in one behavior from the verified design. VeriLadder labels the synthesizability of 716,627 designs and, from RTLCoder, provides 11,247 refined specifications, 32,393 paraphrases and 8,397 one-fact variants. Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct on VeriLadder raises functional pass@1 from 31.7% to 50.0% on VerilogEval v2 and from 35.0% to 45.2% on RTLLM v2. The dataset and fine-tuned models are publicly available.

The tool-verified construction approach is significant for hardware code generation where correctness verification is automatable.

items.title: Doing More with Less: Complex Manipulation with a Contact-Adaptive Robotic Hand
items.content: Anthropomorphic robotic hands offer the potential to manipulate objects designed for human hands in environments adapted to human use. However, developing a robotic hand that replicates the human hand in terms of morphology, degrees of freedom, force output, durability, and sensing capabilities remains a formidable challenge, as these requirements inherently involve trade-offs. Here, we propose a robotic hand mechanism designed to address several of these trade-offs by enabling contact-adaptive finger motion, slender fingers, a wide grasping range, and sustained gripping force. We also introduce a motion glove based on quaternion swing-twist decomposition to extract human manipulation intentions and translate them into robotic hand commands, along with a forearm-mounted interface designed to enhance the operator's sense of embodiment. Experimental demonstrations show that a robotic hand with limited active degrees of freedom and no tactile sensing can perform complex tasks, including smartphone pickup and charging, in-hand manipulation, object unboxing and repackaging, and cutting and tying cords, through the combination of the proposed mechanism and effective bimanual coordination.

items.title: Multimodal LLMs Know the Game but Assume the Real World
items.content: Multimodal large language models can state the rules of a video game, but do they apply them when they only see the game? We introduce RuleCraft, 1,240 image questions over 155 Minecraft rules with outcomes verified in the game engine, each asked in text, on the image with the game named, and on the bare image. Six widely used models know the rules and recognize the game, yet answer the bare image by real-world physics: naming the game raises their accuracy on rules where the game departs from reality by 8.2-19.8 points on a main set and by 33.8-52.7 on a hard stress-test set. Their errors pick the real-world outcome, the gap is largest where the game leaves a scene unchanged, and reasoning traces state the game's rule, then answer by reality. On the main set, naming the game mostly swaps the real-world default for the game's. The pattern holds with reasoning, recurs in two more games, and persists on questions the models themselves take to be about the game; one neutral sentence asking for the rules of the world shown recovers much of the gap. Evaluations that name the game measure knowledge of its rules, not world selection.

We introduce RuleCraft, 1,240 image questions over 155 Minecraft rules with outcomes verified in the game engine, each asked in text, on the image with the game named, and on the bare image. Six widely used models know the rules and recognize the game, yet answer the bare image by real-world physics: naming the game raises their accuracy on rules where the game departs from reality by 8.2-19.8 points on a main set and by 33.8-52.7 on a hard stress-test set. On the main set, naming the game mostly swaps the real-world default for the game's. The pattern holds with reasoning, recurs in two more games, and persists on questions the models themselves take to be about the game; one neutral sentence asking for the rules of the world shown recovers much of the gap. Evaluations that name the game measure knowledge of its rules, not world selection.

items.title: RadAG: Reward-Adversarial Attention Guidance for Efficient Inference-Time Alignment of Diffusion Models
items.content: Diffusion and flow-based models have achieved remarkable success in generation, yet their samples often remain suboptimal in fidelity and text alignment. Two lines of inference-time methods address this: extrapolation guidance, such as classifier-free guidance (CFG) and its variants, and reward guidance, which aligns samples with reward models of human preference. Extrapolation guidance needs only forward passes, but it builds its reference by heuristic rules unrelated to the reward and therefore cannot steer sampling toward a given reward. Gradient-based reward guidance steers sampling directly toward a higher reward, but backpropagates through the entire generator at every step. This trade-off raises the question of whether extrapolation guidance can steer sampling toward a higher reward without a full backward pass. To answer this, we introduce Reward-Adversarial Attention Guidance (RadAG), which constructs the reference by perturbing the attention logits of a single block against their reward gradient and extrapolates away from it. We prove that this update increases the reward of the clean estimate to first order, while its backward pass stops at the perturbed block instead of traversing the entire generator. On FLUX.2-klein-4B and 9B with PickScore and aesthetic rewards, RadAG achieves the highest target reward in every setting with 30-65% less time than gradient-based and candidate-based baselines.

items.reasoning: A clever resolution of a real trade-off in inference-time alignment (reward-directedness vs. gradient cost) with practical efficiency benefits for large generators. However, it refines an active but crowded area of guidance research rather than opening a new direction.

items.title: Pixel Auto-Encoder: Reconstructing Language Model Activations Through Pixel Art
items.content: Interpreting the high-dimensional internal representations of large language models (LLMs) remains a challenging problem. Recent approaches have explored translating these representations into human-understandable forms, particularly natural language. In this work, we explore the use of images as an alternative target modality for interpreting LLM activations. As a first step toward this goal, we introduce Pixel Auto-Encoder, which converts intermediate LLM activations into $32 \times 32$, 32-color pixel art and reconstructs them for subsequent computation within the model. By encouraging the intermediate representations to resemble predefined concept images, we investigate whether LLM activations can be expressed visually while preserving the model's language capabilities. We find that the model can produce target-aligned images for some concepts, and that replacing pixel representations with concept images can influence next-token predictions. However, we also observe a trade-off between visual alignment and language-model performance, as well as sensitivity to pixel-level changes that are difficult to interpret visually. These findings demonstrate the feasibility and limitations of image-based representations of LLM activations.

items.reasoning: A creative and genuinely unconventional direction for interpretability, testing images rather than language as an interface to LLM activations. As a first step, the results are preliminary and the practical payoff unproven, but the exploratory framing is honest and the idea could open a new interpretability modality.

items.title: Bias Cascade: Understanding the Gap Between Knowledge Alignment and Effect Replication in LLM-based Social Simulation
items.content: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to simulate participants in social experiments. Existing research has primarily focused on aligning social knowledge and isolated responses, while overlooking whether simulations can reproduce the collective effects of social interventions. This distinction is critical due to a failure mechanism we call a $bias$ $cascade$: similar individual states can lead to different actions, while agreement on isolated actions can still produce divergent outcomes through dynamic interactions. As a result, models may produce accurate social judgments yet fail to reproduce the outcomes of classic human studies. To investigate this problem empirically, we introduce $REFLEX$ (Reproducing Effects of Foundational Literature EXperiments), a benchmark of 30 counterfactual social experiments grounded in classic human studies that compares knowledge judgment with effect simulation. Knowledge judgment directly predicts the direction of an intervention's effect, whereas effect simulation fixes the scenario and participants while varying one prespecified social factor, with agents generating actions from local observations that are aggregated into macro-level average treatment effects. Compared with human-study findings, the best-performing model achieves net directional scores of 0.847 for knowledge judgment and 0.453 for effect simulation. Moreover, longer causal chains are associated with poorer effect replication, consistent with the bias-cascade hypothesis. These findings reveal a substantial gap between knowledge alignment and effect replication, showing that current methods remain inadequate for reliably simulating collective human behavior.

The authors introduce REFLEX, a benchmark of 30 classic human-subject experiments with reproductions, to empirically test whether simulations replicate group-level effects rather than individual judgments. The findings caution against over-reliance on LLM social simulations for causal claims.

Methodological quality is good; significance hinges on the field's uptake, but the distinction between response alignment and effect replication is broadly important.

items.title: Eidetic Code World Model
items.content: Executable code can preserve a world's structural layout, yet video renderers frequently alter the appearance of previously visited places once they leave the camera view. We present Paintress, a code-conditioned world model that couples an executable geometric proxy with an independently parameterized 3D Gaussian appearance memory in a shared metric coordinate frame. While the proxy enforces structural and visibility constraints, 3D Gaussians capture the visual realization synthesized by emitted observations. To balance stable incremental fusion with consistent readout, Paintress separates writing from reading: newly emitted frames update a persistent raw Gaussian map under confidence-gated selection, whereas a cloned reader copy is globally refined against the observation archive and rendered with coverage masks to condition generation. We also introduce Expedition-33, a benchmark for generated-appearance retention across 11 static scenes, five route families, and 15, 30, and 60 s target absences (165 settings per system). Excluded from the opening image, targets are synthesized during a shared prefix and scored against each system's own first visit at matched return cameras. Across ten systems (1,650 videos), Paintress achieves 0.1220 ROI-LPIPS, 0.0613 MAE, and 52.12% detail retention (vs. 0.2731, 0.1401, and 10.91% for CWM), with lower discrepancy at 60 s (0.1630) than CWM, AgentGarten, and Lyra 2.0 achieve at 15 s.

items.title: A Design Space for Data Agents: Insights from KDD Cup 2026
items.content: Data agents interpret analytical requests, gather evidence from heterogeneous sources, and compute results within finite resource budgets. We analyze the final code submissions of the ten highest-ranked teams in the KDD Cup 2026 Data Agents for Complex Data Analysis competition. We organize the observed design choices into three interacting layers, covering workflow orchestration, analytical functions, and working state. The comparison reveals recurring patterns for allocating computation in response to task progress, structuring evidence for computation and assessment, and preserving reusable artifacts with their provenance. Candidates that rely on the same evidence can inherit the same error, so interpreting their agreement requires tracing those dependencies. The design space motivates controlled evaluations of how resource allocation, evidence sharing, and targeted recovery affect task completion and correctness.

items.title: Elicitation format changes zero-shot classification accuracy in a medical vision-language model: a two-center evaluation on colorectal histopathology
items.content: Background. Verbalized confidence from a hosted medical vision-language model is usually treated as packaging around an unchanged prediction. Methods. We held a nine-class colorectal histopathology prompt fixed except for the requested response format and evaluated MedGemma-27b-it on 10,004 validation and 7,180 external-center PathMNIST patches, with preregistered endpoints, randomized ties, and random floors recomputed for each patch set. Results. Requesting probabilities over all nine classes instead of a ranked top-3 reduced accuracy by 14.8 points on validation, -0.1475 [-0.1594, -0.1353], and 13.4 at the external center, -0.1341 [-0.1484, -0.1196], against chance accuracy of 0.1111. The nine-class prompt uniquely forbade commentary, reasoning, and a chosen answer; removing that prohibition at matched cardinality and token budget recovered +0.1878 [+0.1623, +0.2134] and +0.1911 [+0.1648, +0.2181], while changing cardinality with the prohibition absent moved accuracy by -0.0013 [-0.0300, +0.0280] and -0.0214 [-0.0494, +0.0071]. The nine-class format returned no parseable distribution on 7.6 and 7.7 percent of patches, mostly zero vectors in the two least-textured classes, and deferring these failures first explained its measurable selective-prediction gain. Across four vision-capable models, accuracy did not grade the cost: two models matched on accuracy differed five- to sevenfold. First-token logit entropy routed better than any elicited signal, +0.1820 [+0.1722, +0.1974] versus +0.0493 [+0.0377, +0.0649] relative to each signal's random floor. Conclusions. Response format changes a medical vision-language classifier, and the operative component here was the instruction suppressing an answer. Use logits when available; otherwise request a short ranked list without prohibiting reasoning or a chosen answer.

The study uses preregistered endpoints and randomized tie handling.

items.title: Hypothesis Generation and Semantic Attribution in Inverse Perturbation Modeling
items.content: Understanding gene regulatory relationships at scale can help identify intervention points and anticipate unintended effects, but connecting a black-box model's learned computation to biological knowledge remains difficult. We investigate whether a sparse, typed gene network can generate inspectable hypotheses for steering malignant transcriptional programs toward expression patterns associated with favorable prognosis. Using LINCS L1000 CRISPR/Cas9 profiles paired with matched plate controls, we train a graph neural network to recover the perturbed gene from baseline and endpoint expression. Nodes combine ProTrek-derived protein representations with expression features; edges encode signed regulatory relationships and other gene interactions. We use this inverse formulation to nominate interventions for a desired multigene expression change in a specified cancer-cell context, and use integrated gradients and conductance along a path from the cell baseline toward the requested endpoint to attribute each nomination to gene states, typed messages, and residual connections. In A549, the model nominates TTK although its expression is unchanged in the request; the account assigns supporting credit through the checkpoint-associated MAD1L1 relationship and opposing credit through the E2F4 transcriptional-regulatory channel. Across 333 screened nominations in nine held-out cell lines, request-path attribution shows positive line-averaged correspondence with finite message-deletion effects at every transition. Existing TTK knockout measurements show requested-direction agreement across other markers at the 98.2nd percentile (10 wells), and ten of seventeen measured cases in the illustrative screen meet the predefined support criterion. These analyses make competing biological accounts of a nomination examinable and open to experimental test.

items.title: Decoding Transformer Dynamics via Koopman Subspaces
items.content: We apply Koopman operator theory and Dynamic Mode Decomposition (DMD) to characterise how large language models (LLMs) process different input topics. Treating the layer-to-layer evolution of hidden states as a dynamical system, we fit a linear Koopman operator and take the subspace spanned by its dominant modes as a per-topic spectral fingerprint. Four findings emerge. First, the depth map is near-linear: a single linear operator predicts each next-layer state to within approx. 18% relative error (interior variance explained approx. 0.99). Second, over the 57 MMLU subjects the fingerprint is topic-discriminative, matching the MMLU taxonomy at 0.72 nearest-neighbour purity and each subject's semantic neighbourhood at 0.75 any-hit@3. Third, it is a reproducible signature (split-half self-retrieval approx. 0.97$). Finally, these findings are consistent across seven base models (Qwen2.5 0.5-7B, Llama-3 1-8B), with a suggestive trend of alignment rising with MMLU accuracy. The spectral fingerprint thus provides a probe of how transformers process different topics across depth. Code is available at https://github.com/DeepK/koopman-llm-eacl27.

items.title: Fixed or Deleted? External Feedback Lets Cheaper AI Coding Agents Repair Rule Violations
items.content: Many defects violate project rules that the code itself does not reveal, such as layering constraints or required tests. We study whether LLM coding agents repair such violations better when an external checker reports them, with their location and a repair goal. Three models, a small, medium and large model, driven by an AI agent, worked on 25 pull requests with 31 planted defects in ten open-source projects, plus 5 correct controls, five times alone and five times with findings from CodeAssure (CA), a commercial checker. We also compare with GitHub Copilot code review, and compare CodeAssure's detection with nine free static-analysis tools run out of the box, including Semgrep and SonarQube Community. Counting a run as repaired only when the repaired code also compiles and keeps its feature, CA findings raised the repair rate from 26% to 69% for the smallest model, from 46% to 90% for the medium model and from 45% to 93% for the largest model (pull-request-level p < 0.001), and from 39% to 84% over all runs. Every Java, TypeScript and Python repair compiled. We found that agents often cleared a defect by deleting a newly added file. Metrics based on whether the defect is gone count feature deletion as a success. The largest model alone did so in 44 of 125 runs. CA includes a check for deleted files that largely prevents this. In an ablation with the check turned off, removals rose from 9 to 65 out of 375 runs and the repair rate fell to 54% (small), 70% (medium) and 85% (large model). The CA workflow also outperformed Copilot code review (p < 0.001). Together, the free tools detected 8 of the 31 defects, and CA detected all 31. With CA, the medium model repaired 90% of runs, against 45% for the largest model alone, at about one fifth of the mean cost per run ($0.17 against $0.91).

items.title: PhyCoVE: Benchmarking Physical Counterfactual Video Editing across Diverse Material Dynamics
items.content: Physical counterfactual video editing turns a source video and a language-specified physical edit at a given execution frame into a counterfactual video that shows how the scene would evolve after the edit. Existing evaluations with counterfactual target videos mainly cover object removal or specific rigid-body motions, although real scenes also involve elastic deformation, fluid flow, and interactions among rigid bodies, elastic solids, and fluids. We introduce PhyCoVE, a benchmark of 533 cases on 110 source videos that covers rigid, elastic, and fluid dynamics in five interaction patterns, with edits that remove an object, change a physical quantity, or insert a new object. For the simulated cases, a language model proposes scene designs, coding agents build them with solvers suited to each material and physically based rendering and then simulate each edit from the source scene state, and humans check every stage. For the real cases, we record continuously from one camera position before and after each edit. We also propose counterfactual fidelity, a metric that applies across materials and their interactions and measures how much of the physical change from the source video to the target video a generated video reproduces. We evaluate seven open-source and commercial video editing models and find that counterfactual fidelity ranks them nearly as human preference does, but even the best model reproduces only about one seventh of the physical change. The models change how a scene looks but rarely how it evolves, whereas a physical edit requires understanding the dynamics that it changes. Physical counterfactual video editing thus remains far from solved, and PhyCoVE provides a foundation for developing and evaluating methods for it.

items.title: Edit-Induced Dependency Mismatch: Propagation Omissions, Recovery, and Evaluation Blind Spots in Coding Agents
items.content: During iterative code modification, coding agents may continue to rely in subsequent reasoning on outdated dependency judgments whose text remains fixed in the context, leading to errors in subsequent reasoning and leaving consumer defects undetected by the original task evaluations, thereby exposing blind spots in the tested benchmarks. We study actual agent execution trajectories collected on benchmark tasks: deepseek-v4-flash runs on DeepSWE and SWE-bench Verified, supplemented by Qwen3.8-Flash cases on FeatureBench. Focusing on edit-induced consumer obligations, a full-corpus blinded human audit of the DeepSWE runs identifies terminal mismatches, including diagnoses whose task scope remains disputed. Following supplementary execution checks, all retained DeepSWE terminal events have execution support. The audit also shows that recovery within a trajectory can coexist with terminal omissions in the same run. The process analysis links the presentation of relevant consumer code to explicit dependency judgments and subsequent synchronization actions recorded in the trajectories. An explicit dependency-review prompt reduces terminal omissions under the tested conditions, supporting re-derivation of consumer obligations after edits. Local replays of selected DeepSWE cases show that synchronizing the diagnosed consumers restores the target behavior while the listed controls continue to pass. Cross-benchmark execution counterexamples show that the original task evaluations do not fully detect edit-induced dependency mismatches: patches pass those evaluations, yet additional execution checks confirm unintended defects along existing consumer paths. These findings support measuring task scores, terminal propagation states, and recovery separately.

items.title: A2I-VLA: A Two-Stage Vision-Language-Action model with Semantic-Physical Alignment and Integration
items.content: Force and tactile feedback provide essential information about physical interactions in contact-rich manipulation that visual observations alone cannot reliably capture.However, integrating these signals into vision-language-action (VLA) models remains challenging owing to the representational gap between visual-language semantics and physical measurements.To address this challenge, we propose A2I-VLA, a two-stage VLA framework that first learns semantically Aligned force-tactile representations and then Integrates them into a VLA model.In Stage I, a cross-modal alignment loss is introduced to promote correspondence between semantic and physical representations. The tactile and force feature streams are then integrated through a hierarchical multimodal fusion network, and the resulting representations are jointly supervised by future wrench and action prediction losses. The former encourages the model to anticipate physical responses, while the latter associates force-tactile observations with task-relevant manipulation behaviors.In Stage II, a gated cross-attention bridge module adaptively integrates the hierarchical physical features learned in Stage I into the VLA model to guide action generation.Real-world experiments demonstrate that the proposed A2I-VLA significantly outperforms the baseline PI05 across three contact-rich manipulation tasks, improving the success rate from 70% to 95%.

It targets contact-rich manipulation where visual observations alone cannot capture physical interaction dynamics.
items.reasoning: Integrating tactile and force feedback into VLA models addresses a genuine representational gap and is important for contact-rich manipulation. The two-stage alignment-then-integration design is sensible, but similar multimodal VLA extensions are emerging rapidly across robotics labs, making this a competitive rather than pioneering contribution.

items.title: Polytropos: What Do Vision-Language Model Descriptions Make of a Cultural Object?
items.content: Vision-language models have become a new kind of describer, writing about almost anything people see, and their descriptions now shape how cultures are known by people and by other models. Descriptions of cultures tend to turn particular things into types, and what a description loses shows what its describer lacks. We introduce Polytropos, a benchmark that measures what model descriptions of cultural objects keep of the particular object by turning each description back into an image and comparing it with the original photograph. On 374 objects from the Metropolitan Museum of Art and the Getty, with 1,870 descriptions from five models and 230 written by curators, reconstructions are recognised as the recorded culture more often than the photographs, at 54.55% to 59.09% against 52.14%, yet 16% to 21% of objects change outcome and only 0.49% of reconstructions are identified as the specific object. On the same objects, models lose recorded cultures at a rate similar to curators but gain more. Model descriptions give each object many faces, each typical of its culture and almost none the object itself.

Strikingly, reconstructions are recognized as the recorded culture more often than the original photographs, yet lose object particulars, revealing how models typify rather than particularize culture. It offers a novel, humanities-grounded lens on multimodal model behavior.
items.reasoning: Original evaluation paradigm connecting VLM description fidelity to cultural representation, with a large curated dataset and curator involvement; niche audience but high conceptual novelty and interdisciplinary value.

items.title: Contact Harness: Enabling VLM Agents to Perform Contact-Rich Manipulation
items.content: Agents built on pretrained VLMs have demonstrated zero-shot control of real robots, but vision alone is often insufficient for reliable contact-state assessment in contact-rich manipulation. Force and tactile feedback provide complementary information, but their semantic ambiguity makes them difficult for agents to use directly. These signals must be interpreted according to their physical meaning, together with task phase and visual evidence. We propose Contact Harness, which uses reusable, optimized skills to guide a VLM agent in assessing contact states from multimodal feedback and selecting subsequent actions. A compliant execution mechanism regulates in-contact motions using real-time force feedback. The framework requires no model fine-tuning, task demonstrations, or simulation training. We conduct zero-shot real-robot evaluations using GPT-6 Astra on Rokae and Franka robots. With a single prompt skill, Contact Harness achieves a full-insertion rate of 90.7% across 15 connector types, with further evaluations on a real PC under variations in lighting, background, and position. Across four additional contact-rich tasks, including whiteboard wiping, writing, peeling, and pivoting, Contact Harness achieves an average success rate of 100%. On six simulated tasks, Contact Harness reaches 96.7% success, compared with at most 68.3% for pretrained VLA baselines fine-tuned on task demonstrations, showing the potential of agent-based manipulation for contact-rich real-world deployment.

It requires no fine-tuning, demonstrations, or simulation training.
items.reasoning: Practical and training-free integration of tactile/force semantics into VLM agents addresses a real gap in zero-shot robot control; strong systems contribution though built on existing pretrained models.

items.title: Direct Conditioning of Audio Diffusion Transformers on fMRI Reveals Cortical Contributions to Sound Reconstruction
items.content: Reconstructing audio from brain activity remains challenging. Existing brain-to-audio pipelines typically map neural responses to predefined stimulus representations before synthesis. While recent work in the visual domain has explored direct conditioning on brain activity, this approach has not yet been extended to audio diffusion models. We introduce MAAS (Multi-Area Auditory Synthesis), an end-to-end framework that conditions a pretrained audio diffusion transformer on ROI-wise fMRI responses without first supervising a decoder to predict an external stimulus representation. MAAS uses region-specific projections and learned brain tokens to condition Stable Audio through a dedicated cross-attention pathway. On a 7T fMRI dataset, we demonstrate consistent improvements over baselines, including two-stage fMRI-to-latent conditioning, across both acoustic and semantic evaluation metrics. In addition, we introduce a fidelity metric grounded in a computational model of auditory neural processing, which allows us to quantify the contribution of individual auditory cortical regions to reconstructed audio representations.

This bypasses the usual step of decoding neural activity into an intermediate stimulus representation. It shows consistent improvements in brain-to-audio reconstruction and offers insight into cortical sound encoding.

items.title: CompareDR: Benchmarking Deep Research Reports from Individual Quality to Comparative Merit
items.content: Deep research systems can produce reports with different evidence, analyses, and conclusions for the same query. A reader deciding which findings to rely on needs to know how well each report meets the task requirements and which differences matter to the answer. A score for a single report can summarize its quality, but it does not identify which contributions make one report more useful than another. We introduce CompareDR, a benchmark that combines task-specific pointwise audits with guideline-based pairwise comparisons. We use passage-linked report representations to locate relevant differences and selective evidence verification to check claims that could affect the judgment. The benchmark comprises 40 Chinese and English tasks from three existing benchmarks, 360 reports from nine systems, 1,099 human-reviewed evaluation criteria, and human preferences elicited through blinded comparisons of 80 report pairs. The hybrid evaluator matches 69 of these 80 preferences (86.25%, Cohen's $\kappa=0.746$). The benchmark supports both comparisons of research systems and examination of the evidence and analyses behind those judgments.

It uses passage-linked representations to locate relevant differences and selective evidence verification, spanning 40 Chinese and English tasks and 360 reports from nine systems.

items.title: One Checkpoint, Four Converters: Per Input Disagreement After On Device Conversion and a Probe Set That Catches It
items.content: A model converted for on device or accelerated inference ships once its top 1 accuracy matches the source model. Accuracy can match while individual decisions change, and the converter, its INT8 recipe and its calibration draw each move them. We convert 5 public checkpoints (four ImageNet classifiers and a sentiment model) with the documented FP32 and INT8 recipes of ExecuTorch, LiteRT, ONNX Runtime and TensorRT and compare every top 1 decision with the PyTorch source on 7,854 images and 1,938 sentences. All 34 strict FP32 conversions reproduce every decision, yet each of the 4 vision INT8 recipes that keeps accuracy equivalent flips more than 1% of decisions: ONNX Runtime static INT8 flips 4.07% (95% CI [3.65, 4.53]) of ResNet 50 decisions while accuracy moves by -0.15 points, and two builds of that recipe from different calibration draws disagree on 3.44% [3.06, 3.88]. Where accuracy is kept, the flipped inputs are the ones the source model barely decides (AUROC of the source margin 0.90 to 0.97 on ResNet 50, every 95% CI inside [0.89, 0.98]), but our preregistered claim that this holds for every recipe fails on the two mobile networks, where INT8 breaks accuracy outright. A probe set of the 200 training inputs with the smallest source margin, chosen before any conversion, flags all 40 vision stacks (recall 95% CI [0.91, 1.00]) and all 6 text stacks that flip at least 0.5% of decisions and none of the exact FP32 conversions, so conversion checks should compare decisions on such a probe set, not accuracy.

The authors release a probe set designed to catch such per-input disagreements.

items.title: Reasoning Beyond Imitation: Observation Conditioned Distillation for Video LLMs
items.content: Reasoning distillation offers a promising approach to transfer temporal reasoning capabilities of powerful Video-LLMs to open-source student models. However, teacher and student Video-LLMs may construct different temporal observations from the same video due to the adoption of distinct video sampling pipelines. A reasoning trajectory valid under the teacher's observations may rely on evidence inaccessible to the student and thus cannot be directly executed based on the student's observations. We formalize this as a conditional target mismatch, thereby revealing the Reasoning Acquisition-Execution Gap. To bridge this gap, we propose an acquisition-to-execution framework that first distills teacher trajectories into a student reasoning prior and then further optimizes the execution capability of this prior across multiple observations. We further introduce Execution-Aware Reference Regularization, which retains the existing prior when it is executable under current observations, while allowing a greater degree of adaptive adjustment when it is not. Experiments across multiple Video-LLM backbones and six video reasoning benchmarks show that explicitly optimizing observation-conditioned execution consistently outperforms supervised distillation and standard RL-based optimization, with gains extending to held-out out-of-domain benchmarks.

items.summary: This work identifies a Reasoning Acquisition-Execution Gap in video-LLM distillation: teacher and student sample videos differently, so teacher reasoning trajectories may rely on evidence the student cannot observe. However, teacher and student Video-LLMs may construct different temporal observations from the same video due to the adoption of distinct video sampling pipelines. A reasoning trajectory valid under the teacher's observations may rely on evidence inaccessible to the student and thus cannot be directly executed based on the student's observations. We further introduce Execution-Aware Reference Regularization, which retains the existing prior when it is executable under current observations, while allowing a greater degree of adaptive adjustment when it is not. Experiments across multiple Video-LLM backbones and six video reasoning benchmarks show that explicitly optimizing observation-conditioned execution consistently outperforms supervised distillation and standard RL-based optimization, with gains extending to held-out out-of-domain benchmarks.

items.title: When Simpler Beats Learned: Dual-Weighted Sampling vs. Machine Learning for the Pricing Subproblem in Graph Coloring
items.content: The graph coloring problem can be solved to optimality by branch-and-price (B&P), but its performance hinges on the column generation (CG) step, where each iteration requires solving a maximum weight independent set (MWIS) pricing problem. The state-of-the-art machine-learning (ML) pricing heuristic follows a prediction-sampling paradigm: a learned model scores each vertex of a graph, and independent sets are sampled from the induced distribution. We observe, however, that the scoring procedure does not need to be learned, and critically assess the role of ML by replacing the learned scores with the dual solution of the restricted master problem, resulting in Dual-Weighted Sampling, a proposed lightweight alternative that requires no feature engineering or training. Within a unified CG and B&P framework that varies only the pricing oracle, Dual-Weighted Sampling outperforms MLPH, hand-crafted heuristics, and exact solvers on the established graph coloring benchmark in both runtime and solution quality. In particular, it remains competitive on the DIMACS random family, where MLPH was shown strongest in the original evaluation, while achieving more than a two-fold speedup in CG runtime on recursive-sparse and real-world graph families.

items.title: Memphis: A Case Study in Seeding an Agent Task from a Model's Real-World Attempt
items.content: Agent benchmarks are usually made harder by scaling up the data their tasks are built from, yet models that do well on them still fail at real work. We propose building simulated tasks from a model's own attempt at an open-ended task in the real world, so that the model's failures in the simulation resemble its failures in reality. As a case study, we had GPT-6.1 Sol manage two human workers in Cairo over chat for five shifts, with a budget of 7,000 Egyptian pounds, to build as many USB desk lamps as it could. It built two. From the real-world attempt's transcript, we build Memphis, an evaluation in a model-simulated world. Memphis is hard: GPT-6.1 Sol delivers 1.0 lamp per trial on average and repeats its real-world mistakes, buying too few stands and giving up the search for them. With a one-page hint on where to buy parts and who can wire them, it delivers 9.2. Claude Opus 5.5 delivers 2.2 without the hint and 4.6 with it. We release the task, the trials, the audits, and a redacted record of the real-world evaluation.

items.title: Ego2Wrist: Bootstrapping Wrist-View Synthesis from Egocentric Video
items.content: Wrist cameras provide an action-centric view that is directly relevant to robot manipulation. However, collecting human wrist-camera videos at scale is challenging due to cumbersome setups that can interfere with natural hand movements. In contrast, head-mounted human egocentric videos are much easier to scale. We introduce Ego2Wrist, which synthesizes synchronized wrist-camera views from human egocentric videos and task descriptions. Trained on approximately 940 hours of paired head- and wrist-camera recordings, Ego2Wrist jointly generates three views. To evaluate generated wrist views without ground truth, we propose hand-centric cross-view consistency (HCC), which measures consistency between generated wrist views and corresponding hand regions in the input head view. HCC ranks model checkpoints comparably to ground-truth-based LPIPS, and human evaluators prefer HCC-selected generations in 77% of responses. Evaluated on four datasets, Ego2Wrist outperforms fine-tuned WorldWander, reducing LPIPS by 28% and receiving human preference in 76% of responses. More importantly, HCC facilitates recursive self-improvement on in-the-wild egocentric videos by selecting generated wrist views for further training. Generation quality progressively improves over three rounds. These results demonstrate a scalable approach to generating real-world wrist-view human manipulation videos for robot policy training.

items.title: Escriba-OCR: A 1B Vision-Language Model for Error-Preserving Transcription of Handwritten Portuguese Essays
items.content: Feedback tools and research on learner writing need transcriptions of handwritten essays that keep exactly what the student wrote: misspellings, line breaks, struck-through words and insertions. Vision-language models (VLMs) read handwriting well, but they also tend to rewrite it into correct language. We measure this on BRESSAY, 1,000 handwritten Brazilian Portuguese essays, with a benchmark that adds error preservation, invented errors, edit-markup precision and recall and line structure to the character error rate (CER) and uses paired bootstrap confidence intervals. We restrict the study to open-weight models that schools can run on their own hardware. Of 22 open baselines, the best, Qwen3-VL 235B-A22B, reaches 5.6% CER on the 199 test pages; none reproduces the edit markup reliably, and every VLM replaces 39-78% of the words absent from a Portuguese dictionary with dictionary words. We fine-tune LightOnOCR-3-1B on the 647 training pages in 85 minutes on one GPU. The resulting Escriba-OCR-1B reaches 2.06% CER, 3.5 points below the best baseline (95% CI [-4.2, -2.9]); under the ICDAR 2024 competition metric it reaches 2.1% CER, below the best published page-level results (2.2-2.4%). It recovers 67% of insertions and 77% of illegible deletions, and reproduces the line structure of 97% of the pages, but still normalises 60% of likely misspellings. Three seeds agree within 0.04 CER points, and quantised to 4 bits the model runs on an ordinary CPU at about one minute per page. On 40 letters of another corpus it matches its base model (without that model's appended comments) but misreads unseen words more often; weight interpolation recovers half the gap. A teacher's review finds that 45% of the judgeable apparent corrections are errors in the BRESSAY ground truth, so dictionary-based scores likely understate preservation. We release the model, the benchmark code and the review data.

items.title: Particle Belief Representations for Reinforcement Learning under Partial Observability
items.content: Particle filters flexibly represent complex, multimodal beliefs but expose them as weighted, unordered sets incompatible with conventional fixed-dimensional policies. We study particle-belief encodings as inputs to reinforcement-learning policies while holding belief estimation and policy optimization fixed. We compare statistical summaries, cumulant-generating-function (CGF) features, and permutation-invariant set encoders. Trainable encoders are learned end-to-end or pretrained through belief reconstruction or task-specific prediction. Across eight tasks, pooling-based set encoders and gradient CGF features are reliable end-to-end, while the Set Transformer achieves the highest performance with appropriate pretraining. Task-specific pretraining helps when its target captures decision-relevant belief structure, whereas reconstruction pretraining and latent alignment provide more selective benefits. For selecting and training particle-belief encoders in partially observable Markov decision processes, our results show that an encoding that reconstructs the belief well is not necessarily a good input for control.

items.title: Segment Anything In-Context via Visual Demonstrations
items.content: We present the Segment Anything Model via Visual Demonstrations (SAYD), a foundation model for in-context segmentation. Given visual demos comprising prompt images and their segmentation masks, SAYD segments coherent regions (e.g., objects or their parts) in a query image by establishing visual correspondences between the prompts and the query. SAYD generalizes to previously-unseen segmentation tasks, including those requiring tacit visual knowledge or involving concepts that are difficult to articulate unambiguously in language. We train SAYD on 12 public datasets originally curated for panoptic segmentation using our proposed techniques, including a lightweight mask decoder for prompt-agnostic mask generation and a learning mechanism for recognizing novel query classes absent in the prompts. These innovations enhance both computational efficiency and out-of-domain generalization. Consequently, SAYD significantly outperforms existing methods of in-context segmentation and open-vocabulary segmentation across 24 out-of-domain benchmarks, spanning natural, biological, ecological, cosmological, medical, pathological, and satellite imagery.

items.title: MORSE: Optimizing Streaming Memory Design via Open-World Auto-Research
items.content: A streaming video system must decide in a single pass what evidence to retain under bounded frame storage, before it knows which details a future question will require. Recent recursive self-improvement methods automate the design of the harness that stores and retrieves this evidence. They revise the harness in response to failures, but the editor must still devise each repair from its prior knowledge and a predefined set of tools. A failure that recurs across videos, however, may point to a problem that prior work has already addressed. We introduce MORSE (Memory Optimization with Recursive Self-Evolvement), an open-world auto-research framework that uses recurring failures to guide an online search for solutions. Its editor groups failures in training traces by cause, then searches papers, model cards, and code for methods it can adapt or pretrained perception models it can use. When the editor introduces a new perceptual capability, it can also revise how the harness stores and retrieves the resulting evidence for a frozen video-language model. On held-out validation streams, MORSE first selects revisions that improve answer quality, then seeks faster revisions that preserve those gains within a specified tolerance. Across three streaming video benchmarks, MORSE consistently achieves the highest answer accuracy within each frozen-backbone comparison. On OVO-Bench, our Qwen3-VL-8B harness answers queries in 0.30 seconds on average while achieving 75.1% accuracy, 3.1 percentage points ahead of the next-best evaluated harness using the same frozen backbone.

This extends recursive self-improvement beyond predefined toolsets, letting the system reuse knowledge from problems already solved elsewhere.
items.reasoning: An interesting step toward open-ended auto-research loops where systems draw on external literature to fix their own failures, addressing a clear gap in closed-tool self-improvement. The scope is bounded to streaming memory design, but the paradigm is broadly suggestive for agentic research automation.

items.title: A Polynomial-Time Best-of-Both-Worlds Algorithm for Matroid Semi-Bandit Problems
items.content: Follow-the-Perturbed-Leader (FTPL) offers a computationally attractive framework for online learning, with recent advances establishing Best-of-Both-Worlds (BOBW) guarantees for various bandit settings. For matroid semi-bandits, existing methods offering such guarantees primarily rely on Follow-the-Regularized-Leader (FTRL), which requires solving an optimization problem at each round. We establish BOBW guarantees for FTPL with Fr\'echet and Pareto distributions with a certain parameter with geometric resampling in the matroid semi-bandit problem, showing that FTPL can simultaneously achieve the minimax-optimal $O(\sqrt{mdT})$ regret in adversarial setting and a logarithmic regret in stochastic setting. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first polynomial-time algorithm for matroid semi-bandits that achieves BOBW guarantees.

This yields, to their knowledge, the first polynomial-time BOBW algorithm for this setting, avoiding per-round optimization required by FTRL-based approaches.

items.title: AutoSECO: Automated Skill Evolution for Cross-Problem Combinatorial Optimization with General-Purpose LLM Agents
items.content: General-purpose large language model (LLM) agents can develop complete solvers for combinatorial optimization problems. Their specialization, however, often relies on workflows engineered for individual problems, limiting the reuse of development expertise. We propose AutoSECO, an automated skill evolution method that learns reusable solver-development guidance from experience. The challenge is that external evaluation measures the completed solver, while the skill guides decisions during development. AutoSECO connects this feedback to guidance deficiencies by tracing performance shortfalls through solver code and recorded development decisions. Revisions are expressed as general instructions and retained only if a fresh solver developed under the revised skill achieves a lower mean evaluation gap. Evolved solely on the traveling salesperson problem (TSP), the skill guides fresh agents in developing solvers for capacitated vehicle routing, job-shop scheduling, and three-dimensional bin packing without further skill evolution. On TSP, the final mean benchmark gap is 0.52\%, compared with 0.98\% for the skill-evolution baseline SkillOpt. Across all four problems, the evolved skill achieves better aggregate results than no skill guidance, the initial skill, and SkillOpt. The same frozen skill also supports solver development under alternative model--harness configurations. These findings suggest that solver-development experience can be retained as reusable expertise for general-purpose LLM agents.

It traces solver performance shortfalls back to decisions made during development, revises skill instructions, and retains changes only when a freshly built solver improves. This turns one-off solver engineering experience into transferable knowledge.
items.reasoning: Novel angle on LLM agents: skill-level self-improvement across problem instances rather than per-problem workflow tuning. Relevant to autonomous agent research, though scoped to combinatorial optimization with limited apparent breadth of evaluation.

items.title: PathStream: Towards Streaming Diagnostic Copilots for Whole-Slide Pathology
items.content: Pathologists reach a diagnosis by integrating morphological evidence across regions and magnifications along viewing trajectories. Existing pathology AI rarely reflects this process: models predict from selected image regions, answer questions within fixed visual contexts, or navigate slides autonomously. We formalize pathologist-led streaming diagnosis, in which the pathologist controls navigation while a copilot selectively describes incoming views and synthesizes accumulated evidence into a final diagnosis. We record five pathologists' viewing trajectories on 1,791 TCGA whole-slide images (WSIs) spanning ten organs, with response labels, morphological descriptions, and session-level findings and diagnoses. We construct PathStreamBench to assess response timing, morphological description, and session-level diagnosis, alongside auxiliary video understanding. We introduce PathStream, which jointly learns streaming responses and diagnosis through two-stage training, with a diagnosis-attention loss guiding attention during diagnosis to relevant visual and textual evidence accumulated as the examination unfolds. PathStream outperforms 14 vision-language models and three domain-fine-tuned baselines on the core tasks, achieving a trajectory WSI Relevance score of 77.87, surpassing the strongest domain-fine-tuned baseline's 62.76. Without additional training, its diagnostic capabilities generalize to new educational pathology videos, three external centers, and an unseen organ.

items.title: PCC: Pivotal Channel Compensation for Layer Pruning of Large Language Models
items.content: Treating independent layers as the minimal pruning unit allows layer pruning to efficiently eliminate many redundant parameters and achieve high compression rates. Layer pruning has become a promising and prevalent structured pruning technique for large language models (LLMs). However, multi-layer removal can lead to significant performance degradation for LLMs. Although some works have explored various compensation methods for pruned layers, they are inefficient and costly. Observing that the expression of a large proportion of information is concentrated on a small number of pivotal channels, we propose a novel post-pruning compensation method for layer pruning, called pivotal channel compensation (PCC). PCC can achieve significant performance improvement by compensating for a small number of channels through learnable linear transformations at the pruning interface. Besides, we propose a new evaluation metric, called channel-wise average performance improvement (CAPI), which can measure the efficiency of channel-wise compensation. Our experimental results across various LLMs demonstrate that PCC can achieve significant and consistent improvements and high CAPI on language modeling and zero-shot question answering for the state-of-the-art cross-layer and consecutive-layer pruning methods. Compared with existing compensation methods, PCC can achieve competitive results with fewer additional parameters and less training cost.

items.summary: The paper observes that a large share of representational information concentrates in a few pivotal channels and proposes PCC, a post-pruning compensation method for layer pruning that adjusts only these channels. This yields significant performance recovery after multi-layer removal at far lower cost than prior compensation schemes.
items.reasoning: A practical efficiency contribution to structured pruning with an elegant, low-cost compensation idea; impact depends on generality across model sizes, and layer pruning is a comparatively narrow slice of the compression landscape.

items.title: Uncovering Separable and Composable Skill Mechanisms in Vision-Language Models
items.content: Recent work has sought to localize the internal mechanisms underlying visual reasoning skills in vision-language models. These methods largely overlook separability and composability in both mechanism identification and evaluation. We propose separability and composability as two important desiderata for skill localization. Separability requires identified mechanisms to contribute primarily to their target skills while having limited effects on other skills, enabling precise diagnosis and targeted intervention. Composability requires skill mechanisms to be combinable to support complex tasks, allowing a small set of mechanisms to account for broader capabilities. In this work, we propose a multi-skill interpretability framework DISCO, built around these two properties. For identification, we propose Separable Head Selection, which selects skill-specific attention heads based on their contributions across skills. For evaluation, we are the first to design metrics for measuring separability and composability of identified heads. Extensive experiments on three VLMs and four fundamental visual reasoning skills demonstrate the effectiveness of DISCO. It achieves the highest separability, outperforming the strongest baseline by 24.80, 18.38, and 13.75 points across the three models, respectively, while also achieving the highest composability on all three models.

items.reasoning: Mechanistic interpretability of VLM skills is an important emerging area; proposing formal desiderata plus a framework advances rigor, though results depend on the scale of models studied (abstract suggests academic-scale experiments).

items.title: Seeing Together, Acting Apart: Shared Environmental Understanding for Multi-Robot Navigation
items.content: Multi-robot embodied systems are typically designed to collaborate by coordinating actions, sharing trajectories, or learning joint policies. We ask a complementary question: can collaboration emerge before decision-making, by first building a shared understanding of the environment? We introduce Shared Environmental Understanding, a policy-agnostic representation that aggregates partial egocentric observations from multiple robots into a shared latent world model. This shifts collaboration from the policy space to the representation space, enabling decentralized decision-making with shared environmental context. To this end, we propose Shared Environment Encoding and Retrieval (SEER), a framework that organizes multi-robot observations into a shared memory, retrieves relevant context via spatio-temporal similarity, and encodes it using a predictive latent world model. The resulting representations are injected into downstream navigation agents as tokens. Experimental results demonstrate that SEER captures action-relevant environmental structure and consistently improves navigation performance across both specialized VLN agents and general vision-language model agents, while preserving single-agent capabilities.

Its SEER framework organizes multi-robot observations into shared memory and retrieves relevant context to support decentralized navigation decisions.
items.reasoning: An interesting conceptual inversion of multi-robot collaboration with a concrete memory-based implementation; strong authorship and a promising direction, but empirical validation scope is navigation-specific.

items.title: Learning Teacher Output Preferences from Final Responses for Reasoning Distillation
items.content: Many large language models (LLMs) use chain-of-thought (CoT) to solve complex problems, but hide their CoT traces to prevent reasoning capabilities from being distilled. While recent studies have shown that hidden CoTs can be reconstructed, existing methods typically require training a separate attacker for each target LLM. This paper studies model-agnostic CoT reconstruction, aiming to reconstruct hidden CoT traces from arbitrary target LLMs using only input prompts and visible final responses. We propose Final-Output Preference Learning (FOPL), which trains a single reconstruction model that generalizes to unseen LLMs without target-specific adaptation. To achieve this, the reconstruction model must learn which reasoning patterns match a given final response without knowing the target LLM's identity. We address this using preference optimization, training the reconstruction model to prefer native CoTs over synthetic alternatives for the same question and final response. By learning these preferences from LLMs with accessible CoTs, the reconstruction model learns to distinguish reasoning patterns based on visible responses. Experiments show that reconstructed CoTs capture distinct reasoning patterns across LLM families, including a family unseen during training. Moreover, students trained on reconstructed CoTs match or outperform those trained on native CoTs across several reasoning benchmarks.

items.title: Time Series Foundation Models on the Edge
items.content: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) forecast zero-shot with accuracy exceeding that of task-specific models, and the smaller ones fit on edge devices. Operational deployments must refresh their forecast as new observations arrive, and privacy and latency requirements often force this refresh onto resource-constrained edge devices. To serve as a forecasting system there, a TSFM must refresh quickly, keep latency and peak memory bounded as the stream grows, and retain its accuracy as the observed history accumulates. Refreshing incrementally without altering the forecast requires temporal causality: non-causal models recompute at every update, causal attention admits a KV cache that grows linearly, and causal recurrent models update a fixed-size state in constant time and memory. We make these states persist across refreshes for every causal architecture and verify equivalence to full recomputation. We evaluate nine TSFM configurations on univariate forecasting against all three requirements, measuring accuracy as a function of context length, single-refresh latency, and latency and memory on streams of up to one million time steps on a server-grade GPU and three edge devices. No model gains on average accuracy beyond its trained context and most lose it well before the full history is reached, while KV caches leave latency and memory growing linearly with the retained history. TiRex-2 is the only one of the nine configurations meeting all three requirements: it refreshes in 14 ms on the GPU and 120 ms on a Raspberry Pi 5, keeps latency, energy and peak memory constant over a million steps, and retains its accuracy on the untruncated history.

items.summary: This paper analyzes what time series foundation models require to serve as streaming forecasters on resource-constrained edge devices: bounded latency and memory as streams grow, plus accuracy retention under accumulating history. It establishes that temporal causality is key, distinguishing non-causal recomputation, linearly growing KV caches for causal attention, and constant-time fixed-state updates for causal recurrent models, with implications for model choice in deployment.

items.title: SCAN: Neural Additive Networks for Scalable High-Order Component Selection and Estimation
items.content: Functional ANOVA models express a prediction as a sum of main effects and interactions, but existing neural functional ANOVA models require the interactions to be specified in advance, which forces a trade-off between missing higher-order structure and the cost of enumerating many interactions. We propose SCAN (Scalable Component Additive Networks), which learns which features each basis function combines, so that components of different orders are selected and estimated jointly without enumerating candidates. The learned component index sets form a small candidate collection on which post-hoc identification is carried out efficiently. A global component-selection parameter shares information across basis functions, and truncating negligible component-selection weights gives a sparse model that is identified after training. We establish universal approximation, a minimax optimal rate up to a logarithmic factor, and component selection consistency, which together imply that the discovered components contain all identified true components with probability tending to one. In synthetic experiments, SCAN learns components whose maximum order is close to the true one, and recovers higher-order components more accurately than the baseline models, with post-hoc identification taking a few seconds for 100 inputs. SCAN also outperforms most neural functional ANOVA models in prediction on the benchmark datasets and trains at a much lower cost than exhaustive second-order models. We also apply SCAN to predict treatment response in breast cancer from 12,502 gene-expression variables.

A shared global component-selection parameter and truncation of negligible weights yield sparse, interpretable models.
items.reasoning: Solving the pre-specification bottleneck in neural functional ANOVA is a meaningful methodological advance for interpretable machine learning with interactions; the joint selection-and-estimation formulation is nontrivial, though the work targets a specialized modeling niche.

items.title: When Do Spatial Plans Help Text-to-Image Generation? Causal Control, System Utility, and Text Responsiveness
items.content: A generator can follow a spatial plan, but the benefit of supplying that plan depends on what the model can already do from text. In a controlled study with 18 paired training seeds, correcting predicted positions and sizes improves spatial intersection-over-union by 0.030, yet direct text is non-inferior at matched training compute. In a pretrained generator, a fixed rule layout improves two-object task success over the same text-only adapter by 12.50 percentage points, mostly by separating objects that already appear in the correct order. We then ask whether a more precise instruction can achieve the same separation across conditioning paths. On 288 new task families, adding a minimum-gap instruction improves success by 37.15 points with the text-only adapter, by at most 0.69 points with widely spaced regions, and by 6.94 points with tightly spaced regions. Under tight regions, 230 of 288 baseline images have the correct objects and direction yet miss the required gap, ruling out a high baseline success rate as the sole explanation for the weak text response.

items.summary: This controlled study examines when providing explicit spatial plans improves text-to-image generation, finding that plan corrections yield small gains and that direct text is non-inferior at matched training compute. However, a fixed rule layout helps pretrained generators on two-object tasks, and a minimum-gap instruction alone yields up to 37 points of improvement on text-only adapters. The results clarify that the value of spatial conditioning depends heavily on the model's existing text responsiveness.

items.title: Near-Far Attention: Region-Aware Sparse Retrieval for Long-Context LLM Decoding
items.content: Sparse attention reduces the cost of long-context decoding, but token selection introduces additional scoring and ranking overhead. Moreover, uniform page scoring overlooks differences in relevance between near and far context. We propose Near-Far Attention (NFA), which adapts retrieval to regional attention patterns while keeping candidate scoring lightweight. During prefill, the Lightweight Gate Estimator identifies regions that can be skipped during decoding, adding less than 1% to dense-prefill time. For the remaining regions, the Calibration-Free Subspace Extractor supplies compact features shared by page-level and token-level scoring without offline calibration. The Distance-Aware Two-Level Selector then scores near and far pages differently and jointly ranks candidate tokens under a shared budget. Evaluations across model families, parameter scales, and GQA/MLA architectures show aggregate task quality comparable to full attention. On Qwen3-8B at 512K context length, NFA achieves up to $5.49\times$ operator speedup and $2.97\times$ whole-model decoding speedup over FlashInfer, including selection overhead.

A Distance-Aware Two-Level Selector scores near and far context differently, reducing selection overhead relative to uniform page scoring.

items.title: RoboInF: A Benchmark for Instruction Fidelity in Robotic Manipulation
items.content: Precise language control requires embodied models to follow instructions governing both task outcomes and execution. Although recent methods train policies to follow increasingly detailed commands, existing benchmarks often assess instruction following alongside perception, planning, and generalization to unfamiliar scenes. Higher task success therefore offers limited evidence of closer adherence to instructions. We introduce RoboInF, a benchmark measuring how reliably manipulation policies adapt their behavior to changes in an instruction. For each of eight tasks, six to twelve expert-validated instruction branches vary the requested goal, procedure, or manipulation detail while holding the initial scene and robot state fixed. Task-specific checkers verify the terminal goal and use recorded trajectories, contacts, and event sequences to assess compliance throughout execution. The accompanying RoboInF-4K dataset pairs 4,242 expert demonstrations with simulator-derived annotations of motion and contact. We evaluate leading manipulation policies ($\pi_{0.5}$ and OpenWAM) and inference-only agents (GPT-6 Astra and Qwen3.8-Flash). All four models exhibit a gap between task completion and faithful execution, indicating substantial room for fine-grained instruction following.

items.summary: RoboInF measures how reliably manipulation policies adapt behavior to instruction changes, using eight tasks with six to twelve expert-validated instruction branches each that vary goal, procedure, or manipulation detail while holding scene and robot state fixed. Task-specific checkers verify terminal goals and recorded execution, separating instruction fidelity from perception, planning, and generalization confounds found in existing benchmarks. This provides cleaner evidence of true instruction following.
items.reasoning: Well-designed benchmark isolating a specific and important capability (instruction fidelity) with careful confound control; value depends on uptake and on what it reveals about current VLA models.

items.title: Reliable Recursive Memory for Causal Multi-scale Video Polyp Segmentation
items.content: Video polyp segmentation (VPS) is essential for computer-aided colonoscopy, as it localizes and tracks polyps frame by frame. However, VPS remains challenging because polyps resemble the mucosa and change quickly in scale, which calls for history beyond a short clip, and because blur, specular highlights, and occlusion often degrade only part of a frame. Existing methods keep history as whole frames, so their cost grows with the history length, and a partly degraded frame carries its degraded content to later predictions. To address these issues, we propose STREAM, a streaming framework for VPS that extends the causal multi-scale aggregation (CMA) of our conference work from a fixed clip to an online stream. STREAM introduces a Recursive Slot Memory (RSM) that summarizes multi-scale features and soft foreground and background cues into a constant number of slots, which the current features read and pass to CMA, supplying long-range history at a constant cost. Furthermore, we design Reliability-Aware Slot Writing (RASW), which estimates a pixel-level quality map from the current frame, supervised by its local error, and uses it to control which locations are written into RSM and how much each slot is updated. Experiments on SUN-SEG and CVC-ClinicDB demonstrate that STREAM achieves state-of-the-art performance, improving the Dice of the conference model from 81.3% to 85.7% on the hardest subset while running at 48 FPS with a constant state of 0.32 MB. Code will be released at https://github.com/wangtong627/STREAM.

items.title: GSDet: Gaussian Splatting for Oriented Object Detection
items.content: Oriented object detection has advanced with the development of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and transformers. However, modern detectors still rely on predefined object candidates, such as anchors in CNN-based methods or queries in transformer-based methods, which struggle to capture spatial information effectively. To address the limitations, we propose GSDet, a novel framework that formulates oriented object detection as Gaussian splatting. Specifically, our approach performs detection within a 3D feature space constructed from image features, where 3D Gaussians are employed to represent oriented objects. These 3D Gaussians are projected onto the image plane to form 2D Gaussians, which are then transformed into oriented boxes. Furthermore, we optimize the mean, anisotropic covariance, and confidence scores of these randomly initialized 3D Gaussians, using a decoder that incorporates 3D Gaussian sampling. Moreover, our method exhibits flexibility, enabling adaptive control and a dynamic number of Gaussians during inference. Experiments on 3 datasets indicate that GSDet achieves AP$_{50}$ gains of 0.7\% on DIOR-R, 0.3\% on DOTA-v1.0, and 0.55\% on DOTA-v1.5 when evaluated with adaptive control and outperforms mainstream detectors.

items.title: Omniprediction with the Minimum Number of Linear Scores
items.content: An $\varepsilon$-omnipredictor uses one forecast for an entire family of downstream losses. After postprocessing for each loss, its expected loss must be at most $\varepsilon$ above that of the best comparator for that loss. A binary single-index model (SIM) learns a norm-bounded weight vector $w$ and a nondecreasing link $\rho$. It reduces the features $x$ to one linear score $w^\top x$, then maps that score to a probability $p(x)=\rho(w^\top x)$. Hu, Tian, and Yang (STOC 2025) achieved $\varepsilon$-omniprediction for binary matching losses using $O(1/\varepsilon^2)$ SIMs and asked whether one SIM suffices. In the population model, we prove that one SIM suffices for exact omniprediction in their bounded-action setting. The result holds for any compact family of continuous nondecreasing target links.   With unrestricted actions and matching losses generated by $1/\beta$-strongly convex entropies, the SIM's link can also be $\beta$-Lipschitz. For $K$ classes and $d$-dimensional features with finite first moment, $\min\{d,K-1\}$ linear scores are necessary and sufficient in the worst case. A joint link maps these scores to class probabilities, and its Lipschitz bound $\beta$ is also sharp under the comparator's coefficient norm bound.   For bounded features and smooth entropies, we achieve $\varepsilon$-omniprediction for two or three classes using $\widetilde O(1/\varepsilon^2)$ samples at fixed confidence and regularity. This bound is independent of $d$ and tight up to logarithmic factors. For any fixed number of classes $K \ge 2$, the tight worst-case sample complexity for $\varepsilon$-omniprediction under the Dirichlet condition on the features is $\Theta_K(1/\varepsilon^2)$.

items.title: Hard to Translate, Harder to Detect: Human Analysis Remains Essential in AI Meme Translation
items.content: We present a dataset and evaluation setup for a problem in creative machine translation: translating culturally loaded passages that carry much of a text's meaning and humor that may depend on subtle or implicit discourse. We study Soviet comedy quotations that function as memes in Russian-language communication. Off-the-shelf difficulty estimators do not find these passages; current models searching the web find most but not all of them, but their own analyses of the difficulty do not help translation as well as a human-validated one. Given a brief human-validated analysis of why each passage is difficult, older models improve modestly; the strongest current translators (GPT-6 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5) improve more, and in human evaluation GPT-6 Sol comes close to the approved references on most films. Newer models have thus become much better at using such an analysis while still not reliably producing it themselves. We release (1) a dataset of five films' Russian subtitles with their audience-selected culturally salient passages, human-validated analyses, and reference translations (into English, Galician, and Spanish), together with every full-film LLM translation and evaluation produced in this study; and (2) an item-level MQM-style evaluation protocol that measures translator and evaluator noise to set the number of runs the evaluation needs, and whose automatic version tracks human judgment of these passages, which reference-free neural metrics do not, whether they score the whole text or the passages alone.
