items.title: Same Seed, Different Picture? Deciding Early at Low Resolution for Seed-Faithful Few-Step Flow Sampling
items.content: Few-step samplers make large text-to-image flow models fast, but from the same noise they no longer generate the image of the standard 50-step sampler. Subjects, attributes and layout change, not just fine detail. We trace this loss of seed fidelity to the start of sampling. The coarse part of the initial noise decides coarse structure first, while the noise level is still above 0.9. Few-step samplers cross this range in their first steps, which account for 25-52% of their distance to the 50-step reference. Because this decision is coarse, a half-resolution run from the same coarse noise can make nearly the same decision at a third of the cost. We therefore propose Decide-then-Render (DtR), a training-free sampler that decides the composition in a few low-resolution steps, rebuilds the full-resolution state with the seed's own noise and renders the details. On 4 large models, DtR runs 11-25$\times$ faster than the reference sampler. At each speed-up, it is closer to the reference and rated higher by ImageReward than every compared sampler, including few-step schedules calibrated per budget and published multi-resolution samplers. On FLUX.1-dev, it remains the most faithful sampler down to about $8\times$, ahead of caching accelerators. A user study on this model found DtR's samples closer to the reference in 86% of pairwise trials. DtR transfers to a held-out model and to video, and distilled models can serve as its renderers. Project link: https://duanhuiran.github.io/DtR

It proposes Decide-then-Render, a training-free sampler that resolves composition in cheap low-resolution steps before rendering at full resolution, preserving seed faithfulness at a third of the cost.

items.title: Object Count Generalization Is an Interface Problem: Warping a Frozen Skill Instead of Retraining It
items.content: Reinforcement learning policies for robot manipulation degrade when the number of objects N in the scene grows beyond the training range. This is a covariate shift that also changes the dimension of the state. We propose WAVE (Warping Actions and Views of an Expert), which extends a pretrained single-object skill to many objects without updating its weights. WAVE has three parts. First, a selection policy picks the one object the robot works on next. Second, a warping policy reads a local view of the scene around that object, whose size does not depend on N. It emits a multiplier and an offset for every quantity the skill reads and every action it outputs. Third, the skill acts under this affine warp. It is shown a scene that holds a single object, while the warp steers it around the objects it is not shown and edits the actions that are sent to the robot. Both the selection and warping policies are trained with PPO on the multi-object reward and use the skill as a black box, so WAVE is task-general and skill-agnostic. It requires only that the skill was trained on the same embodiment and that every object has a goal pose. We also bound the number of attempts needed to place all N objects, assuming positive expected net progress per attempt, and measure this progress for each object count. We evaluate WAVE on cube arrangement tasks with a gantry robot and with a Franka Panda arm. Trained with at most nine cubes, it generalizes zero-shot to several times its training count, on the gantry to scenes of up to thirty cubes. Published methods that learn multi-object manipulation show count generalization up to six objects. Fine-tuning the skill, learning from the same local view without it, and an entity transformer, even when distilled from the pretrained skill, all collapse within their training counts under the same training budget.

items.title: PVFormer: Proper Velocity Transformer for Stable and Scalable Hyperbolic Representation Learning
items.content: Hyperbolic representations have shown remarkable success on hierarchical and tree-like data, and Transformers have become a central architecture for representation learning. However, a principled construction of hyperbolic Transformers remains challenging because the self-attention layer decomposes into three coupled primitives, transformation, similarity, and aggregation, that should all respect the underlying geometry. Existing hyperbolic Transformer designs are typically built in the Poincar\'e or Lorentz models, where bounded domains, time-like constraints, tangent-space detours, or projection steps make it difficult to keep the full block intrinsic and scalable. To address this gap, we propose PVFormer, to the best of our knowledge, the first Transformer architecture that operates natively in proper velocity (PV) space. The proper velocity model provides an unconstrained representation of hyperbolic geometry, and PVFormer exploits this structure to redesign the Transformer block in PV space. On the transformation side, we use PV homomorphism transformations to update query and value representations. On the similarity side, we generalize Euclidean inner-product attention with a PV Busemann score inspired by Busemann-based hyperbolic learning and a PV point-to-hyperplane key transformation. On the aggregation side, we replace Euclidean averaging with PV midpoint aggregation and further derive a scalable PV linear attention variant for large graphs. Extensive experiments support the effectiveness of PVFormer across graph, text, and vision benchmarks.

The goal is stable and scalable hyperbolic representation learning for hierarchical data.

items.title: Replay Before You Reply: Second-Look Prompting for Unified Multimodal Encoding
items.content: Solving multimodal tasks requires Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to form a unified understanding of the image and the question text. However, under causal attention in current VLMs, a token can attend only to what precedes it. Whichever modality comes first is therefore encoded under partial observation of the input, uninformed by the rest of the multimodal context. We introduce Second-Look Prompting (SLP), a training-free method that repeats the image-question pair in the input. In the repeated copy, every visual and textual token can attend to the complete input, yielding a unified multimodal encoding of the pair. Moreover, the added visual tokens contribute computation beyond re-exposing the image: even a blank image in their place can improve reasoning. Across 12 benchmarks, SLP improves the overall average score of every evaluated model, spanning nine open-source models (3B-72B) and three proprietary frontier models, with gains reaching 5.6 points for Gemini 3 Flash on MATH-Vision. Our analysis reveals two complementary mechanisms: the question guides where the second image attends, and the added visual tokens act as a prefill scratchpad whose hidden states retain answer-relevant information from the image and question. These findings highlight input presentation as a simple yet effective way to improve VLM performance.

items.title: Personalization of a Commercial Powered Knee Prosthesis Under Clinically Realistic Conditions via Reinforcement Learning: A Feasibility Study
items.content: Personalization of powered prosthesis control to individual user needs remains a significant challenge. To address this challenge, policy iteration with constraint embedded (PICE), a reinforcement learning (RL) tuning approach, has been developed and validated. This feasibility study investigated whether the developed approach can personalize a commercial powered knee prosthesis under clinically realistic conditions. To reduce the time for personalization, tuning was initialized with a policy learned offline from one non-disabled participant walking on a treadmill and was then applied to three other non-disabled participants walking with the knee through a bypass adapter on a 5-meter walkway. All participants reached the goal within 8-18 tuning steps (1.7-4.2 minutes of walking), reducing the knee-kinematic feature error by 64-90% on average. These results support the feasibility of implementing the RL-based tuning approach in clinically realistic conditions with space and equipment constraints.
items.author: Xinyi Liu, Atli \"Orn Sverrisson, David Langlois, Ming Liu, Varun Nalam, and He Huang

Initialization from an offline-learned policy allowed each participant to reach personalization goals within 8-18 tuning steps, i.e., only 1.7-4.2 minutes of walking.

items.content_html: Personalization of powered prosthesis control to individual user needs remains a significant challenge. To address this challenge, policy iteration with constraint embedded (PICE), a reinforcement learning (RL) tuning approach, has been developed and validated. This feasibility study investigated whether the developed approach can personalize a commercial powered knee prosthesis under clinically realistic conditions. To reduce the time for personalization, tuning was initialized with a policy learned offline from one non-disabled participant walking on a treadmill and was then applied to three other non-disabled participants walking with the knee through a bypass adapter on a 5-meter walkway. All participants reached the goal within 8-18 tuning steps (1.7-4.2 minutes of walking), reducing the knee-kinematic feature error by 64-90% on average. These results support the feasibility of implementing the RL-based tuning approach in clinically realistic conditions with space and equipment constraints.

items.title: Generalizing Agentic Robotics via Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation
items.content: Building general-purpose robots is a central goal in robotics. Agentic robotics pursues this goal with planners that control robots through tool calls. However, existing methods either rely on proprietary models accessed through APIs, which incur high costs and latency, or post-train a planner with reinforcement learning (RL) in a single domain, requiring a separate specialist for each domain with incompatible tools. In large language model (LLM) post-training, multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) has been used to consolidate domain specialists into a single generalist. Yet whether MOPD can build a generalist planner for agentic robotics, how well it performs, and how it compares with other consolidation methods remain unexplored. In this paper, we systematically study these questions: we introduce Robo-MOPD, which trains a single student on closed-loop rollouts in simulation under token-level supervision from matching frozen specialists, and compare it with weight merging, off-policy specialist supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and multi-domain online RL. Experiments on LIBERO-PRO and RoboCasa365 show that a single 9B Robo-MOPD planner reaches 72.9% and 44.8% success (58.9% average), surpassing all consolidated baselines in average success and both 9B specialists on their respective benchmarks. Robo-MOPD excels on long-horizon tasks, outperforming multi-domain online RL by 13.0 percentage points on LIBERO-10.

items.title: WildAnySplat: Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting in the Wild
items.content: We present WildAnySplat, a feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting framework that enables robust novel-view synthesis from in-the-wild multi-view images. Unlike controlled captures, real-world images often contain multi-view inconsistencies caused by transient occluders, illumination changes, and camera ISP, which degrade the quality of existing feed-forward reconstruction methods.   To address this challenge, we introduce a student-teacher framework that learns transient-robust and appearance-consistent 3D representations. A teacher network operates on clean images, while a student processes the corresponding in-the-wild inputs. The teacher provides clean supervision to guide the student toward a consistent canonical representation. Since paired clean and in-the-wild data are scarce, we use a hybrid data strategy, combining real paired captures, synthetic augmentations, and pseudo-clean labels generated from optimization-based reconstructions, bridging the domain gap between synthetic and real-world data.   We adopt a transformer architecture with dedicated DPT heads for camera pose, depth, and Gaussian prediction. We additionally predict per-view transient masks to reweight photometric supervision and suppress unreliable Gaussians. To account for cross-view appearance variation, we incorporate a bilateral grid module that models per-image color transformations and enables recovery of a canonical radiance representation.   Experiments on challenging in-the-wild benchmarks show that WildAnySplat improves robustness to transient occlusions and appearance variation while retaining the fast inference of feed-forward Gaussian Splatting.

items.title: Habitats: A Framework for Open-Ended Evolution of Agent Objectives
items.content: Designing what an agent should optimize can be as difficult as optimizing the agent itself. Existing language-model-based reward-generation methods typically refine objectives for predefined tasks and couple the decision of what to explore with the synthesis of how to implement it, potentially narrowing the resulting behavioral repertoire. We introduce Habitats, a framework for open-ended evolution of executable agent objectives. Habitats maintains a population of reward-policy pairs and evaluates every policy under every population reward, producing a cross-fitness matrix that exposes self-mastery, transfer, and functional diversity. A population-level Planner uses this information to select parent rewards and issue targeted mutation directives, while a separate Mutator translates those directives into validated reward programs. We evaluate Habitats in a discrete Card Sandbox and three continuous-control environments (Cart-Pole, Hopper, and Cheetah) against Independent Generation and Direct Mutation baselines. Across four environments and three random seeds, Habitats achieves the highest macro-averaged final Specialist Quality and Behavioral Diversity, with final diversity reaching 1.8x that of Direct Mutation and 2.5x that of Independent Generation. Finally, across ten downstream objectives unseen during evolution, frozen Habitats policy libraries achieve higher paired win rates than size-matched Direct Mutation and Independent Generation libraries at 10,000 adaptation episodes, while also surpassing task-specific policies trained from scratch for 20,000 episodes. These results suggest that separating population-level planning from reward synthesis enables the discovery of diverse, learnable, and reusable behaviors.

items.title: CO-GRAFT: Attributing Reinforcement Learning Gains in Search Agents via Role-Level Policy Grafting
items.content: Reinforcement learning (RL) improves large language model search agents by up to 32 exact-match (EM) points over their pre-RL initializations, yet overall accuracy gains do not identify which underlying functional capabilities improve or interact during training. We introduce CO-GRAFT, a reward-agnostic interventional attribution framework in which an RL-trained agent and its pre-RL initialization jointly generate a single trajectory under closed-loop execution with live retrieval. Each policy controls a mutually exclusive subset of four functional roles: intermediate reasoning, search-or-answer decision, search query generation, and final answer extraction. Evaluating all 2^4=16 role assignments without modifying weights or retraining defines a cooperative game whose Shapley values decompose the total RL gain across roles, while M"obius interaction terms distinguish standalone role improvements from multi-role coupling. Applying CO-GRAFT to Search-R1 agents across Qwen2.5 and Llama-3.2 models (spanning two sizes, base and instruction-tuned initializations, GRPO and PPO optimizers, and NQ and HotpotQA datasets), we show that query generation never exceeds 15% of the total gain; instead, gains are governed by pre-RL answer validity, search retention, model scale, and fixed task-level search budgets, shifting credit from reasoning toward answer extraction in larger or well-formatted answer response checkpoints while smaller base models rely on reasoning--decision coupling.

Shapley values from this cooperative game reveal which capabilities actually improve or interact during training.

items.title: Efficient Memory-Constrained Video Object Segmentation via Subspace Optimization
items.content: Memory-based architectures for video object segmentation (VOS) have achieved remarkable performance by maintaining dense feature representations from past frames in a streaming Memory Bank. However, storing these features over time incurs substantial memory overhead and computational cost. In this work, we identify significant temporal redundancy in memory representations, where consecutive frames exhibit highly overlapping low-rank subspaces that remain stable over time. Building on this observation, we propose Memory Subspace Iteration (MSI), a training-free, model-agnostic plugin that exploits temporal subspace stability to efficiently compress streaming memory features. Extensive experiments on standard VOS benchmarks demonstrate that MSI preserves segmentation accuracy across multiple architectures while reducing the memory bank footprint by up to 25%. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/Hai-Anh-LE/MSI_WACV2027.

A clean efficiency contribution applicable to existing memory-based VOS models.

items.title: When Recognition Meets Discovery: Learning Need Not Be Entangled in One Representation Space
items.content: Generalized Category Discovery (GCD) aims to recognize known classes while discovering novel categories from unlabeled data containing both old and novel samples. Existing methods typically optimize recognition and discovery within a shared representation space, implicitly assuming that the same representation geometry can serve both objectives. Through controlled spectral analysis, we uncover a striking asymmetry: old-class discrimination is increasingly concentrated in the dominant singular directions, while novel-class structure is better preserved in the complementary residual space. More importantly, strengthening the former can even degrade the latter, revealing that recognition and discovery compete for representation capacity rather than merely for optimization weight. Motivated by this observation, we propose Dual-Space Spectral Routing, which dynamically decomposes the representation via online SVD and routes supervised recognition and unsupervised discovery to complementary discriminative and general subspaces. We further exploit their distinct responses to old and novel samples to construct a dual-space novelty signal, which guides Subspace Relation Aggregation (SRA) for organizing candidate novel categories. Extensive experiments across multiple GCD baselines, backbones, and benchmarks demonstrate a consistently improved recognition-discovery balance without introducing additional inference parameters. Code will be open source.

items.title: Variable Importance Recovery in Tabular Foundation Models: A Simulation Study
items.content: In machine learning, identifying which variables contribute predictive information can be as important as predictive accuracy. Tabular foundation models have matched or exceeded the predictive performance of tuned gradient boosting trees on many small- and medium-sized tabular datasets. Yet their ability to recover population-level variable importance has received little attention. We design and conduct a Monte Carlo simulation study to compare variable importance recovery across tabular foundation models and established machine learning baselines. Our framework distinguishes multiple population estimands, pairs each one with an aligned model-agnostic importance estimator, and evaluates recovery in terms of ranking, support, and relative magnitude. Our results show that tabular foundation models are generally competitive with established machine-learning baselines in recovering population variable importance, and often more accurate. We thus extend the evidence for their capabilities to a previously underexamined dimension, further strengthening their appeal.

items.title: Defending Vision-Language-Action Models against Transferable Attacks via Visual-Proprioceptive Consistency
items.content: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong capabilities in a wide range of robotic tasks. However, adversarial attacks in VLA models have shown strong transferability across robotic tasks, posing significant threats to robotic systems. Despite their different attack strategies, we observe that these transferable attacks share a common consequence: they disrupt the VLA model's perception towards the robot itself. Motivated by this observation, we propose a proprioception-grounded defense framework that leverages trusted proprioceptive information to detect and mitigate transferable adversarial attacks. Specifically, we utilize the robot's proprioceptive states to establish a trusted spatial reference, and compare it with the robot's perceived location inferred from visual features. Discrepancies between these two sources provide a reliable signal for detecting adversarial attacks. Extensive experiments demonstrate effective detection of transferable adversarial patches and improved closed-loop performance. Real-robot experiments further demonstrate the effectiveness of our defense on real-world robotic tasks.

The robot's proprioceptive state establishes a spatial reference compared against visually inferred position to detect and mitigate attacks. It offers a cheap, sensor-redundancy-based robustness mechanism for VLA systems.

items.title: SoK: Splitting the Trigger or Adding Attackers? Disentangling Distributed Backdoor Attacks in Federated Learning
items.content: Distributed backdoor attacks split a trigger among several federated learning clients, so that the backdoor appears only in the aggregated model. Since DBA, a line of work has reported that such attacks are stronger, more persistent, and stealthier than a single attacker with the full trigger. We systematize this literature and test this belief. We code nineteen primary studies and fifteen papers that evaluate against DBA. The reported advantage is rarely measured against a complete trigger delivered by the same attackers, and none of the fifteen evaluations tests whether individual pieces remain effective. We then run 875 paired federated runs that separate adding attackers from splitting the trigger. In our image experiments, adding attackers raised attack success in every seed of all 30 cells where we measured it, by 7.5 to 83.4 percentage points on average. Splitting the trigger among the same attackers had a smaller effect, and its sign depended on the piece layout, the allocation, and the attackers' local training. With DBA's compact layout, splitting lowered attack success on CIFAR-10. A larger penalty on small CNNs vanished once the attackers trained longer, and an FCBA-style allocation gained a few points. Widely separated pieces helped on CIFAR-10, its grayscale version, and GTSRB. No model required all pieces. Neural Cleanse suppressed single pieces together with the full trigger, but split backdoors with separated pieces survived it better than complete ones. We derive reporting requirements for attack and defense evaluations.

Findings indicate adding attackers, not trigger splitting, drives the reported success advantage, and prior evaluations never tested whether individual trigger pieces remain effective. A valuable myth-busting contribution to federated learning security.

items.title: From atomic events to material degradation across metre and year scales
items.content: Material degradation emerges from microscopic events whose consequences accumulate over years, yet mechanism-resolved simulations remain confined below engineering timescales. The challenge is not just the sheer number of events: atomistic evolution is dominated by recurrent local motion, with only a tiny fraction driving lasting structural change. This distinction is not encoded in an instantaneous atomic configuration. Locally indistinguishable states can exhibit different event competition, escape times, and long-horizon outcomes, revealing missing kinetic context as a critical information bottleneck. This context spans space and time: the future consequence of a local transition depends on its surrounding defect environment and the kinetic history leading to its current state. To solve this, AtomWorld reconstructs a predictive kinetic state from multiscale structural observations and trajectory history, distinguishing transient fluctuations from microscopic pathways that drive persistent structural evolution. Learning operates only over transitions admitted by the underlying kinetic Monte Carlo (KMC) process, preserving event legality, state evolution, and physical time. Across BCC Fe-Cu precipitation, FCC Ni-Cr-Al ordering, and HCP Zr-H interstitial transport, restoring kinetic context consistently advances persistent evolution while maintaining physical fidelity and transferring to unseen conditions. In irradiated reactor-pressure-vessel steel, this approach achieves up to 420-fold greater persistent evolution under matched event budgets. Combined with scalable execution, it successfully extends mechanism-resolved trajectories to service-year timescales across metre-scale heterogeneous domains.

items.title: CHORD: Closed-loop Human-Object Rectified-flow Decomposition
items.content: Text-driven 3D human-object interaction (HOI) generation requires synthesizing whole-body human and object motions that stay coupled through contact. Yet existing generators either entangle the core variables that govern an interaction (object pose, contacting regions, and limb posture) with dozens of subordinate joints, or plan only end-effectors or coarse trajectories. No stage of generation holds the interaction in a form that is both settled and observed, which leaves contact to external guidance, post-hoc refiners, or internal guidance without a surface measurement. We present CHORD, a two-stage rectified-flow framework that settles the interaction in a compact plan and observes that plan against the object surface while it is being generated. First, Draft uses twelve part tokens per temporal patch to jointly plan the 6-DoF object trajectory, contact states, and the end and middle joints of every kinematic chain. At each flow step, Draft decodes the expected interaction from the closed-form clean estimate, measures it against the object surface, and routes this feedback to the responsible part token with zero extra network evaluations. Second, Full keeps this plan unchanged and infills the remaining body and finger joints. On InterAct, CHORD reduces FID by 33% and lifts hand contact F1 from 0.730 to 0.834, while its feedback improves contact on unseen objects and transfers plug-and-play to existing HOI generators.

items.title: HighwayVerse: A Chain-of-Inspection Benchmark for Highway Infrastructure Anomaly Understanding
items.content: Practical highway infrastructure inspection entails progressive diagnostic reasoning from visual perception to maintenance decisions, yet existing benchmarks remain confined to isolated tasks, leaving Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) insufficiently evaluated across sequential inspection stages. Meanwhile, current datasets focus primarily on highway pavement defects, falling short of real-world inspection across diverse infrastructure components such as highway pavements, guardrails, glare screens, and drainage systems. To address these gaps, we formulate the Highway Infrastructure Inspection Progression Chain (HIIP-Chain), spanning Anomaly Detection, Anomaly Recognition, Condition Analysis, and Maintenance Resolution, and introduce HighwayVerse. HighwayVerse comprises 14,143 real-world Ground and Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) inspection records spanning 100 and 17 anomaly categories, respectively, with 84,858 expert-reviewed question-answer pairs. We evaluate 12 open-source and closed-source MLLMs using the chained metric Final, which credits a correct maintenance decision only when all preceding diagnostic stages are completed correctly. Results show that although models achieve relatively high accuracy when initially judging whether an anomaly is present, their markedly lower Final scores expose struggles across downstream recognition, analysis, and decision-making. This discrepancy indicates that current MLLMs do not fully comprehend specific highway anomaly patterns beyond superficial initial judgments. Furthermore, we propose LaneRAG, a training-free retrieval-augmented framework that provides hierarchical reference guidance achieving consistent performance improvements across diverse MLLMs. Our dataset, evaluation benchmark, and source code will be publicly released.

items.title: More Is Never Less: Affordable Robustness to Additive Attacks via Monotone Multiple-Instance Learning
items.content: Static malware detectors that represent each sample as a bag of extracted features, such as permissions, API calls, or imported functions, are cheap to deploy and remain state-of-the-art under temporal drift and in selective classification. Yet, attackers can evade them by adding benign-looking content that outweighs malicious evidence. Canonically, detectors encode the presence of a few thousand features, selected during training, as sparse multi-hot vectors over a fixed vocabulary. Features that emerge after training remain invisible. We show that linear models and multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) over this input are sum-pooled set models in disguise. Sum-pooling lets added benign features cancel malicious evidence. Instead, we cast malware detection with set-shaped static features as a multiple-instance learning (MIL) problem. To this end, we propose MalSets, which uses max-pooled Deep Sets models with a monotone head to ensure that any malicious evidence remains undiluted; thus, more is never less. Under MIL, a general text encoder maps any feature string to an embedding, thus eliminating the long-standing out-of-vocabulary problem at test time. Max-pooling retains the malicious evidence regardless of how many benign features an attacker adds. Since max-pooling can only grow when features are added, constraining the head alone makes the malware score monotone under additions, even against a white-box attacker adapted to this architecture. While monotone detectors are never evaded by state-of-the-art black-box or white-box attacks, they often significantly pay for this robustness in clean performance since benign features cannot count as evidence. However, by combining a non-monotone set encoder with max-pooling and a monotone head, MalSets maintains the robustness of prior monotone classifiers while achieving state-of-the-art performance.

items.title: From Dense to Sparse: Morton-Ordered Sparse Mapping for Efficient 3D Mesh Generation
items.content: Unified 3D understanding and generation require compact sequences preserving spatial structure. Dense grids yield long sequences, while serialization can separate spatial neighbors. We propose Sparse Proximity Aware Compression (SPAC), a shared sparse SDF vocabulary combining sparse encoding with reversible spatial merging. A Sparse SDF VQ-VAE quantizes near-surface features while retaining explicit coordinates, using reconstruction supervision for surface fidelity and detail. 3D Byte-Pair Encoding (3D-BPE) merges recurring face-adjacent patterns using relative offsets before serialization. Macro tokens expand exactly into leaf tokens and coordinates. After Morton serialization, a shared LLM reads geometry for captioning and predicts tokens that decode into meshes for text-conditioned generation. With fixed geometry, architecture, and band width in voxels, sparse encoder cost grows approximately quadratically with resolution. 3D-BPE reduces mean complete LLM sequence length by 45.4 percent, including coordinates, text, and control tokens. SPAC achieves strong results in both 3D captioning and text-conditioned mesh generation. Ablations show gains over leaf tokens and Morton 1D-BPE in both tasks. The project page at https://yangjj007.github.io/spac/ .

items.title: RAGA: Refreshable Animatable Gaussian Avatars from a Single Photo
items.content: Avatars created from a single photo are fixed once made: regions the photo never showed, such as the back of a garment, are hallucinated and remain that way. We present Refreshable Animatable Gaussian Avatars (RAGA), a full-body Gaussian avatar that is created from a single image in about one second and can be refreshed whenever new images of the same person become available, without retraining or gradient-based optimization. RAGA maps each new observation into canonical UV space, accumulates it as visibility- and angle-weighted running sums, and re-decodes the fused map with the same decoder used for the photo. Although this decoder is trained only on single images, it makes use of the fused evidence. On 163 clips from five datasets, RAGA created from one photo outperforms LHM, LHM++ and IDOL, including on three datasets never used in training. Refreshing from later frames adds 0.49 dB PSNR overall and 0.68 dB on views turned at least 135{\deg} from the photo, where SSIM and LPIPS also improve. Given the same 16 images on all clips, LHM++ gains 0.15 dB, against 0.48 dB for RAGA. Creating an avatar takes 1.08 s and animating it 48.1 ms per frame on a laptop RTX 3080 GPU, with body fitting and matting included in creation and pose estimation included in animation. Code will be released on GitHub.

items.title: SilentWAM: Planning in the Masked State of a Diffusion World Model
items.content: World-action models learn from future prediction, but accessing their future representations directly at test time can require costly frame generation. Methods that generate future frames before planning incur additional forward passes, while future co-training methods omit explicit future predictions at inference. We introduce \method, a planner that reads the hidden states of masked future tokens without decoding future frames. We pretrain MMaDA-Parallel-M on driving video using frame-level masked world modeling, which predicts a masked suffix of future frames and explicitly includes inputs with all future frames masked. Learned planning queries attend to these masked positions and the observed context, and a continuous head predicts the trajectory in the same forward pass. With a single front camera, \method reaches 92.0 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 and 89.3 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2, with an end-to-end latency of 60.3\,ms.

items.title: Can an Agent Trust Its Own Zoom? Cross-Magnification Provenance Verification for Whole-Slide Images
items.content: Visual agents navigate whole-slide images through magnified observations associated with claimed locations. However, a visually plausible observation does not necessarily originate from its claimed location, particularly across magnifications and in regions with similar tissue structures. We formulate cross-magnification provenance verification (CMPV) to evaluate whether visual evidence supports a claimed spatial association, recover the source when possible, and abstain when evidence is insufficient. We introduce PyraFault, a benchmark of 3.06 million coordinate-supervised examples from 2,200 cases across five TCGA cohorts, covering within-context substitutions, absent-source faults, and geometric perturbations. We further propose ZoomTrace, a claim-independent verifier that estimates the observation's source before evaluating its agreement with the claimed location. It combines physical-scale alignment, visual retrieval, geometric refinement, and reliability estimation using spatially disjoint competing matches. On 503,320 test examples, ZoomTrace achieves 0.969 AUPRC and 0.987 AUROC, compared with 0.789 and 0.903 for Efficient LoFTR. Further evaluations reveal trade-offs in reliability estimation and limitations in vision-language models, cross-dataset retrieval, and calibration. Integrating ZoomTrace into visual agent tool paths reduces exposure to corrupted observations and silent failures, while downstream accuracy improvements depend on the agent and verification threshold.

items.title: Tacinf: A Unified Tactile Infrastructure for Robot Manipulation
items.content: Force-aware manipulation requires robots to infer appropriate interaction forces from task context and tactile feedback. We present Tacinf, a low-cost, modular infrastructure that enables policies to predict robot actions and fingertip forces from task language, vision, and touch. Task instructions can optionally specify the desired force level. Tacinf integrates simulation data synthesis and tactile benchmarking (Tabero), vision-tactile-language-action (VTLA) policy learning, handheld data collection using the same gripper as robot deployment (Tacumi), and task-aligned sim-to-real evaluation (Taco). Together, these components form an integrated workflow connecting data collection from multiple sources, foundation-model training, and hardware deployment. We validate each component, including the simulation data, benchmark, controller, and Tacumi, and are releasing the full stack as open source. A foundation model fine-tuned solely on tactile simulation data transfers zero-shot to different real-robot tasks. Across eight policy variants, mean task success rates are strongly correlated between simulation and the real robot (Pearson r=0.998, mean maximum rank violation MMRV=0.010). For the four policies with reported force measurements, mean grip force is higher under firm instructions than under gentle instructions on all three tasks in both domains. When both object positions and instances are randomized, a mixture of teleoperation, simulation, and Tacumi data raises mean real-robot task success from 20% with teleoperation alone to 60%.

items.title: RadioWorld: Transferring World Models to Radio-Frequency Radiance Fields
items.content: Electromagnetic (EM) wave propagation in the physical world constitutes a Radio-Frequency (RF) radiance field, providing rich information for 6G communication and sensing. However, existing neural RF field methods suffer from three fundamental limitations: (1) they predominantly rely on per-scene optimization and cannot generalize to unseen scenes; (2) they require costly reference RF measurements in each target scene; and (3) they degrade severely when extrapolating beyond the vicinity of reference measurements. To overcome these limitations, we present RadioWorld, a general framework that adapts a world model to synthesize RF radiance fields directly from physical scene geometry and transceiver locations, without requiring any reference RF measurements at inference. Specifically, RadioWorld couples two specialized modules within a dual-stream Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) architecture: a Scene-Understanding Transformer that encodes 3D scene geometry and transceiver locations to extract environment-aware global EM propagation features, and a Field-Generation Transformer that attends to these features to synthesize the RF radiance field with the local query conditions. We also establish UrbanRF-Bench, a large-scale ray-traced benchmark spanning 657 urban scenes and 32,850 RF radiance fields across seven global cities. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RadioWorld significantly outperforms specialized baselines and accurately synthesizes RF fields at arbitrary locations in unseen cities. Code, datasets, and checkpoints will be released upon acceptance.

items.title: SWIFT: A Handcrafted, Arithmetic-Minimal FPGA Engine for Real-Time Audio Deepfake Detection
items.content: Generative voice cloning threatens voice-based authentication, yet current deepfake detectors rely on power-hungry, high-precision models unsuited to edge hardware. We present SWIFT (Streaming Whiten-Integer Forensic Trust-Engine), a handcrafted detector that works in the high-frequency noise domain where synthesis artifacts concentrate. A first-order integer high-pass residual drives nine families of fixed-point descriptors, among them integer lifting-wavelet cepstral quantiles, Mahalanobis anomaly distances, Poincar\'e phase-space geometry, and phase jitter, fused by calibrated gradient-boosted trees and a sparse L1-regularised meta-learner. Under leakage-controlled nested cross-validation, with one shared preprocessing chain for real and fake audio, this reference model reaches accuracy of up to 99.86% and an Equal Error Rate (EER) as low as 0.03% across eight benchmarks. Its integer front-end and a fixed-point linear classifier run on the programmable logic of a PYNQ-Z2 (Zynq-7020) board, with a 7.85 microseconds per-frame datapath latency (127.4k frames/s) at 1.734 W and 11.2% LUT utilisation. Integer-only audio deepfake feature extraction is thus feasible at the edge without pretrained neural models or floating-point units.

items.title: Can Speech LLMs Recognize When Audio Evidence Is Insufficient? A Diagnostic Study and a Pre-Generation Probing Mitigation
items.content: Speech large language models are usually evaluated on questions that have answers. We ask what they do when a recording establishes none, and whether the standard way of finding out is sound. Diagnosed on synthesized speech the answer looks clear: Qwen2-Audio fabricates an answer to 92.5% of unanswerable questions, while an ASR cascade reading the same recordings reaches 2.5% hallucination at 6.7% over-refusal, placing the failure in reasoning rather than in perception. The identical protocol on 376 native SQuAD 2.0 questions over human-read recordings removes that conclusion: the cascade hallucinates on 67.7% against the end-to-end model's 69.8%, at a higher over-refusal cost. A paired subset asking the same questions of a synthesized and a human recording of each passage localises the effect in the ASR stage -- the end-to-end model's abstention behaviour does not move with the speaker, the cascade's goes from 11.1% to 65.9%. Reliance on synthesized speech has been named as a limitation of audio benchmarks but not quantified; we quantify it, and show it large enough to reverse a finding. Since no prompt we tested repairs the residual failure, we transfer pre-generation attention probing to the multimodal setting. A probe over frozen prompt representations reaches 0.773 AUROC at predicting which unanswerable questions the model will answer anyway, where semantic entropy over ten sampled generations is at chance: the model fabricates the same answer every time, so sample disagreement cannot see a failure it is confident about.

The authors also propose a pre-generation probing mitigation.

items.title: Fill in the Blanks: Non-Autoregressive Schema-Parallel Key Information Extraction with CTC Decoding
items.content: Vision-language models (VLMs) extract structured data from documents by generating the requested JSON one token at a time, so their sequential steps grow with the length of the answer. Yet in key information extraction (KIE) the schema already fixes the answer's structure: keys, nesting and lists are known before decoding, and only the values are unknown. We exploit this with a non-autoregressive extractor that writes the structure from the schema, sizes every list with a count pass, and predicts all values in parallel, in a fixed number of passes that does not grow with the document. Each value is decoded with connectionist temporal classification (CTC) in its own block of slots, so its length never has to be predicted, and a value that is still open after its block gets a larger token budget. Zero-shot on VAREX, CORD and FUNSD, our 4B extractor is 3.5$\times$ faster than the diffusion-VLM competition on average (up to 5.6$\times$) and more accurate, with 4--6 forward passes per document where block diffusion needs 12--74. The same extractor also drafts for speculative decoding with its own autoregressive base: it runs 8.3$\times$ faster than autoregressive decoding (up to 10.4$\times$) within 0.4 points of its accuracy, and 3.3$\times$ faster than speculative diffusion decoding while 13.0 points more accurate. We release the model and code.

items.title: Breaking the Cascade: Compact Nonlinear Optical Computing with Single-Layer Encoder-Decoder Co-Localization
items.content: We demonstrate that nonlinear computing can be achieved with a single linear diffractive surface under coherent illumination. We introduce a compact encoder-decoder co-localization (E+D) architecture in which an input-dependent dynamic encoder and a static optimized decoder are integrated within the same phase-only diffractive plane. Following free-space propagation, coherent interference between the encoder and decoder fields, combined with intensity detection, generates programmable nonlinear input-output mappings without requiring nonlinear optical materials or multiple diffractive layers. We prove that the proposed E+D optical processor is a universal approximator for arbitrary real-valued band-limited nonlinear functions and identify the physical factors governing its approximation fidelity, including the decoder degrees-of-freedom, detector aperture, and axial propagation distance. Crucially, we demonstrate that introducing a trained, frozen phase bias to the encoder region systematically enhances functional expressivity, providing robustness against coarse phase quantization on spatial light modulators. Using this framework, we accurately synthesize diverse nonlinear functions, including commonly used neural network activation functions and complex-valued nonlinear functions. Finally, we experimentally validate the proposed approach using a visible-light optical set-up trained through in situ learning, demonstrating the parallel approximation of 9 nonlinear functions in a single optical forward pass. By collapsing nonlinear optical computation into a single diffractive surface, the E+D architecture substantially reduces hardware and alignment complexity while preserving powerful function-approximation capabilities, providing a compact and scalable framework for analog information processing.

items.title: How Multi-Timescale Memory Cools Optimization: Theory and Evidence from AdEMAMix
items.content: Augmenting AdamW with multiple momentum timescales improves large language model pretraining, yet the mechanism driving these gains remains poorly understood. We identify an interaction between multi-timescale optimizer memory and the geometry of normalized networks: memory changes parameter norms and thereby controls how fast parameters rotate. Starting from exact norm dynamics under decoupled weight decay, we show that the parameter norm depends on the temporal correlation of the updates, with weight decay controlling how long these correlations influence optimization. We show how an independently weighted slow momentum can substantially increase the norm of parameters, while contributing negligible power to the instantaneous update, therefore acting as an endogenous annealing schedule. We study this mechanism in AdEMAMix for language-model pretraining. Controlled interventions show that this scheduling mechanism has clear practical consequences and is an important factor behind AdEMAMix's advantage over AdamW.

The paper derives exact norm dynamics and shows weight decay controls how long update correlations influence optimization.

items.title: GravHMR: Coupling SLAM and Human Mesh Recovery in a Shared Gravity Frame
items.content: Recovering globally consistent 3D human motion from monocular videos remains challenging under dynamic camera motion. Although SLAM and human mesh recovery (HMR) provide complementary camera and body estimates, directly combining them often leads to inconsistent orientations and accumulated trajectory drift. We present GravHMR, a training-free, plug-and-play framework that couples SLAM and HMR through a shared gravity-aligned reference. By allowing gravity to be estimated independently of the HMR backbone, GravHMR accommodates world-grounded HMR models with or without explicit gravity-view representations. Specifically, Yaw-Aware Orientation Optimization (YAOO) resolves heading inconsistencies by correcting body and velocity orientations about the shared gravity axis. Conditioned on these corrected orientations, Gravity-Aware Trajectory Optimization (GATO) anchors root trajectories in the metric SLAM world by jointly leveraging 2D reprojection, the metric scale implicit in the human body, and the body's own motion. On EMDB-2, GravHMR achieves state-of-the-art performance with 154.0 mm W-MPJPE100 using ViPE and 189.8 mm using masked DROID-SLAM, outperforming TRAM (222.4 mm) under the same masked DROID-SLAM camera estimates. It further reduces W-MPJPE100 by 44.3% over GVHMR (276.5 mm) and by 20.0% over GVHMR + HTD-Refine (192.4 mm) with the same HMR backbone.

items.title: Why Units Die in the Layer After a Frozen Random Encoder, and What the Number of Live Units Measures
items.content: Reinforcement-learning agents can learn Atari games through a convolutional encoder whose random weights are never trained. They reach expert play in Pong and, without random action repeats, in Breakout, but training takes far longer and few ReLU units in the layer after the encoder stay alive. A dead unit outputs zero for every input and cannot learn. In earlier work we took the number of live units to measure the game's complexity. Here we ask why units die and correct that conclusion. We find that more units die as the layer's inputs lie farther from zero relative to how much they vary. We call this ratio the offset. Earlier work showed this in sparse autoencoders at the start of training. We saw it after training in agents, image classifiers, a reservoir computer and sparse autoencoders on GPT-2. A random encoder leaves the offset of its input roughly unchanged, and a formula predicted its median offset within 25 percent in all 44 cases. So a game with a bright, mostly unchanging screen gives the next layer a large offset. In Pong, subtracting the average screen raised the number of live units from between 3 and 6 of 64 to between 59 and 63, so the number alone cannot show a game's complexity. On unaltered screens none of the agents reached a training score of 18 in 50 million steps. With the subtraction all did within 5 million, about as fast as a trained encoder on unaltered screens. In Breakout the subtraction left more units alive, but average training scores did not clearly improve, and a large gap to a trained encoder remained. So we do not treat their number as something to raise for its own sake. The evidence is from small networks and three games, and in agents and image classifiers changing the offset also changed the size of the inputs. We suggest measuring the offset before training a layer on a fixed front end and, if it is large, trying to subtract the mean input.

items.title: Generating Safety-Critical Driving Scenarios from Role-Typed Signal Temporal Logic Specifications Drafted by Large Language Models
items.content: Safety-critical scenarios are rare in recorded driving and must be generated to test and train motion planners of automated vehicles. In guided diffusion models, each scenario type needs its own weighted objective, separate from the validity check. Optimized together with the attacker, the vehicle under test can cancel the attack or draw it toward itself. We state each scenario as a signal temporal logic specification with clauses typed by role. Every clause names the agent it may change and the agents it may read, and the vehicle under test reads the attacker only from the attack onset. A large language model drafts the specification from a description, and a type checker accepts it. A compiler derives the optimization: it edits a diffusion model's samples by the smallest change that satisfies the specification, each clause moves only its owner, the attacker is solved against the unreacted vehicle under test before its response, and the monitor of the same specification decides acceptance. On nuScenes and CommonRoad, judged independently of the specification, one parameter set produced valid scenarios at a rate 0.14 above a weighted objective tuned per scenario type, and descriptions yielded at least one valid scenario for 11 of the 16 pre-crash types expressible in the public data. Learned planners fail more often on the generated scenarios than on their seeds. Fine-tuning on them lowers a planner's failure rate on critical scenarios, and the time headway one clause of the label requires, not the generator, sets the size of the gain.

A compiler then derives an optimization that edits diffusion model samples to realize the adversarial scenarios, addressing the problem of the vehicle under test cancelling or absorbing attacks.

In guided diffusion models, each scenario type needs its own weighted objective, separate from the validity check. Optimized together with the attacker, the vehicle under test can cancel the attack or draw it toward itself. We state each scenario as a signal temporal logic specification with clauses typed by role. Every clause names the agent it may change and the agents it may read, and the vehicle under test reads the attacker only from the attack onset. A large language model drafts the specification from a description, and a type checker accepts it. A compiler derives the optimization: it edits a diffusion model's samples by the smallest change that satisfies the specification, each clause moves only its owner, the attacker is solved against the unreacted vehicle under test before its response, and the monitor of the same specification decides acceptance. On nuScenes and CommonRoad, judged independently of the specification, one parameter set produced valid scenarios at a rate 0.14 above a weighted objective tuned per scenario type, and descriptions yielded at least one valid scenario for 11 of the 16 pre-crash types expressible in the public data. Learned planners fail more often on the generated scenarios than on their seeds. Fine-tuning on them lowers a planner's failure rate on critical scenarios, and the time headway one clause of the label requires, not the generator, sets the size of the gain.

items.title: Arcadian: Open-Source Humanoid Ecosystem for Accessible and Customizable Research and Education
items.content: Reproducing and modifying a meter-scale humanoid remains challenging for research and teaching groups with limited fabrication resources and engineering support. This paper presents Arcadian, an open-source humanoid ecosystem that offers accessible and customizable humanoid hardware and software with community support. Arcadian aims to strike a balance among cost-effectiveness, structural durability, and full customizability, lowering the barrier to entry for research and education. Specifically, this meter-scale humanoid adopts metal-embedded 3D printing to achieve a high strength-to-cost ratio, eliminating the need for computer numerical control (CNC) machining while retaining design flexibility. Extensive simulation and hardware tests validate the design: a reinforcement-learning (RL) locomotion policy trained in simulation transfers to the hardware, and a virtual reality (VR) teleoperation interface drives both arms for simple manipulation tasks. The robot is around one meter tall and costs approximately $6,800 to build. All computer-aided design (CAD) models, the bill of materials, assembly documentation, and training and deployment code are publicly released, distributed through Tnkr.ai and MakerWorld and supported by a Discord server and a project forum through which community feedback informs design updates. The ecosystem resources are available at https://anonymous-humanoid.gitbook.io/docs.

items.title: MoMa-NMP: Scene-Scale Neural Motion Planning for Mobile Manipulators
items.content: Mobile manipulators operating in homes and other complex environments must coordinate their base and arm over long horizons, navigating around obstacles, through narrow passages, and between constrained workspaces. Neural motion planners can provide fast closed-loop planning from partial observations, but scaling them to room-sized environments is difficult because generating high-quality training trajectories is itself a challenging motion-planning problem. To address this, we introduce MoMa-DemoSmith, a demonstration-generation pipeline that separates the problem into global path discovery for large complex scenes and local motion refinement for collision avoidance. This key separation enables the generation of millions of challenging whole-body trajectories across our procedurally generated scenes. We train MoMa-NMP on these demonstrations through behavior cloning (BC) followed by privileged on-policy distillation, achieving 87.0% success on our simulation benchmark and 77.5% across 80 trials in unseen real-world scenes. See video results at https://adamhkan.com/moma-nmp/.

These demonstrations train neural motion planners (MoMa-NMP) for fast closed-loop, room-scale planning for mobile manipulators coordinating base and arm.
items.reasoning: The key insight of decomposing trajectory generation into global and local stages unlocks scalable training data for whole-body neural planning, a significant practical bottleneck. Deepak Pathak and Kenneth Shaw are credible authors in robot learning; abstract-level results on real-world transfer are not fully clear.

items.title: Fast 4-bit KV-Cache Decoding on Hopper GPUs: Why Existing Kernels Are Slow and How to Fix Them
items.content: A 4-bit KV cache reads about half the bytes of FP8, but Hopper GPUs have no FP4 hardware and little instruction-issue capacity per byte of memory bandwidth, so 4-bit values must be decoded in software. On H200, vLLM's NVFP4 KV path (FlashInfer's decode) reaches 10-20% of memory bandwidth and is up to 1.7x slower than FP8. NVBit instruction counts show two causes: the kernels behind vLLM's 4-bit paths (FlashInfer NVFP4, Triton UltraQuant) execute 2-6x Hopper's issue budget per byte and serialize loading, decoding and matrix multiplies. Our Hopper-native decode kernel overlaps a TMA producer warp with two compute warpgroups, lays the cache out at write time so decoded values feed the tensor cores from registers, and swaps the matrix operands so small query groups need no padding. On H200 it reaches 67-75% of peak bandwidth at batch 32-128 and at all 11 shapes is 1.12-1.49x faster than the faster of XQA and FlashAttention-4's proposed native FP8. Inside vLLM, with an accuracy recipe (K mean removal and rotation, 4 BF16 sink tokens, BF16 layer 0), it decodes 1.12-1.64x faster per step on Llama-3.1-8B than vLLM's FlashInfer FP8 path at batch 8 and above (1.04-1.24x over FlashAttention-4's FP8), is level at batch 1, and holds 1.63x as many tokens. On one H200 under a reasoning-like request stream, the highest rate at which 99% of requests meet the latency targets is 1.23-1.32x FP8's on Llama-3.1-8B and 1.67-2.20x on Qwen2.5-72B, as the cache becomes the limit; prefill-heavy streams are worse (7% slower prefill). On five 7B-32B models, repeated runs show no significant accuracy difference from BF16 KV. In Qwen2-family models, whose reasoning variants collapse under FP8 KV, layer 0's key mean is almost entirely the key-projection bias identified by prior work, seen through RoPE and computable from the weights alone; keeping that layer in BF16 restores FP8 KV and, with K mean removal, 4-bit KV.

On H200 it substantially outperforms existing FP4 paths.
items.reasoning: Highly practical contribution with direct impact on LLM inference cost, given that KV-cache bandwidth is a dominant bottleneck in long-context decoding. The root-cause analysis via NVBit instruction counts is rigorous, and the fix is concretely validated, though the scope is one GPU architecture.

items.title: Ultrasound Watermark: Real-time Acoustic Watermarking against Voice Scams on Smartphones
items.content: Recent advances in text-to-speech (TTS), voice conversion (VC), and AI-driven speech synthesis enable adversaries to convincingly impersonate trusted individuals during phone calls. Existing defenses often rely on offline analysis, degrade under telephony distortions, or remain vulnerable to adaptive attacks. To address these limitations, we present Ultrasound Watermark, a real-time, smartphone-native framework that protects live calls by binding speech to the caller's physical articulatory motion through acoustic watermarking. During a call, the smartphone emits ultrasonic signals and captures reflections from facial articulatory movements using only its built-in speaker and microphone. Ultrasound Watermark extracts motion features from these reflections and fuses them with outgoing speech to generate a dynamic watermark. Because the ultrasonic measurements are physically and temporally coupled with speech production, they are difficult to spoof without the underlying articulatory motion. A synchronized generator-detector architecture enforces cross-modal speech-motion consistency against replay, synthesized speech, and articulation-mimicking attacks. Ultrasound Watermark operates continuously with less than 200 ms latency overhead and requires no additional hardware. We implement Ultrasound Watermark on iOS and Android and evaluate it using over 2.5 hours of synchronized speech-ultrasound recordings from 22 speakers across eight smartphones and four real-world environments. Results demonstrate robustness to diverse attacks and telephony distortions while preserving perceptual audio quality.

This counters TTS and voice-conversion impersonation without offline analysis.

Robustness to adaptive attackers and telephony channels is the key open question, but the approach is original and practically deployable, giving it solid applied security value.

items.title: OmniSenMo: A Unified Multisensory Language Model for Generalizable Human Motion Estimation, Understanding, and Prediction
items.content: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) estimate, understand, and predict human motion, but mainly from RGB cameras. Depth, LiDAR, mmWave, and WiFi complement RGB under poor lighting, through occlusions, and in privacy-sensitive applications, but existing multisensory models cover only some of these sensing tasks. Covering all of them from any sensor subset is challenging, since the tokens of heterogeneous sensors are semantically inconsistent and spatially misaligned, paired multisensory data are scarce, and the tasks need different temporal granularities. We present OmniSenMo, a multisensory language model that takes the human skeleton as a common reference for all sensors. Its skeleton-grounded motion representation turns each sensor into joint tokens, one per body joint, so that any sensor subset is fused joint by joint and expressed in the motion vocabulary that the language model learned from motion capture and text. We pretrain it on all five sensors generated by our multisensory simulator, and Multi-Granularity Observation gives each task the frames it needs. On a cross-action split of MM-Fi, the same model with all five sensors outperforms the models compared on each task, including LEO-Fuse in pose estimation (84.1 vs. 89.0 mm MPJPE) and HoloLLM in unseen-action recognition (69.2% vs. 42.8%). Even without RGB, it outperforms both methods that use RGB, and in a cross-dataset validation on XRF55, it recognizes unseen actions far better than HoloLLM.

This skeleton-grounded tokenization addresses semantic inconsistency, spatial misalignment, and differing temporal granularities across sensors.

The skeleton-grounded tokenization is a neat generalizable idea, though empirical strength across tasks remains to be verified from the abstract.

items.title: AdvMTO: Multimodal and Temporal Adversarial Object Attacks via 2D Gaussian Splatting for BEV-Based 3D Object Detection
items.content: Adversarial object attacks pose a threat to BEV-based 3D object detectors in autonomous driving. Existing attacks typically target a single modality, coordinate camera and LiDAR observations at the current timestamp, or model temporal persistence mainly in camera streams. Without a unified construction of current and historical observations, attacks can leave part of the detector's accumulated evidence unsuppressed, limiting their effectiveness. In this paper, we propose AdvMTO, a 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS) framework for suppressing detection of persistent adversarial objects. Its oriented surfels encode appearance, geometry, and opacity in one object state, from which camera images and scanline LiDAR returns are generated. AdvMTO then constructs current and historical inputs through detector-native processing, regenerating LiDAR returns in each native source sweep for fusion detectors. We optimize bounded appearance perturbations for each detector, propagating gradients through historical BEV memory for temporal camera detectors. For fusion detectors, bounded geometry refinement along local normals further perturbs both sensing modalities. Experiments on nuScenes demonstrate effective suppression of traffic-cone detection across three BEV detectors. Temporal ablations further highlight the importance of detector-native history modeling for both attack construction and optimization.

Prior attacks were single-modality or temporally limited to camera streams.

items.title: Draft Forcing: Target-guided Speculative Drafting and Learned Verifier for Autoregressive Video Generation
items.content: Autoregressive video diffusion models enable streaming synthesis chunk by chunk, yet invoking the large model for every chunk remains costly. While chunk-level speculative decoding can offload chunks to a lightweight draft model, existing approaches suffer from two limitations: (1) an off-the-shelf draft diverges from the target's trajectory, compounding errors in history; and (2) they either omit verification or rely on costly post-decode aesthetic scores rather than verifying consistency against the target. We address both with Draft Forcing, a framework coupling target-guided drafting with an on-policy trained verifier. Specifically, to align the draft for high acceptance, we opt for feature-level drafting, conditioning it on multi-layer target hidden states persisted from committed chunks, whose outputs are pushed to match target trajectories with multi-aspect losses. For verification, we propose an on-policy trained feature-space verifier predicting CDF-calibrated frame-wise relative RMSE against the target. It is trained on speculative rollouts as contexts anneal from random to inference-aligned mixtures, and gates proposals without VAE decoding. On the 14B Self-Forcing target, Draft Forcing achieves $1.63\times$ DiT and $1.57\times$ end-to-end speedups on VBench with minimal quality loss, and up to $1.93\times$ DiT ($1.82\times$ end-to-end) when combined with orthogonal KV compression. It generalizes to accelerate a streaming variant of MiniMax-H3, generating over $50\%$ draft frames with competitive quality.

items.summary: Draft Forcing accelerates autoregressive video diffusion by offloading chunk generation to a lightweight draft model guided at the feature level by target hidden states, coupled with an on-policy trained verifier that checks consistency against the target. This addresses draft divergence and the lack of principled verification in prior speculative video decoding schemes.
items.reasoning: Applies speculative decoding ideas to expensive video generation with a sensible feature-level conditioning and learned verification design; practically valuable for inference efficiency in a commercially important domain.

items.title: Does coverage explain core-set active learning? Mean, max, and the choice of distance
items.content: Core-set selection casts batch active learning as a covering problem, in which the points to label minimise the covering radius of the pool. Its main argument is a generalization bound in which this radius controls the gap between the loss on the pool and on the labelled sample. We examine what this bound requires and what it says in practice. We first state it with the assumption that its proof uses at the labelled points, a zero conditional risk, and show that it then holds for any dissimilarity and any selection rule that uses no label outside the sample. The proof works point by point and involves two averages, the mean distance of the pool to the labelled sample and the purity of the cells attached to the labelled points. Keeping them gives, when labels are deterministic at the labelled points, a bound on the pool loss with no zero-loss assumption and without the factor C, the number of classes, of the original constant. We then compare scales, for deterministic labels and a regression function Lipschitz on the whole pool. With the original constant, the bound can be informative only if the radius is below the smallest distance between two classes divided by C. Without C, its radius form can be informative only once the nearest-neighbour rule built on the sample is exact on the pool. Finally, a misalignment criterion measures whether a quantity ranks selections as the gap or the test error do. Experiments on a Gaussian pool and on two image pools, digits and MNIST, the latter under eight distances, and with a network retrained at each cycle, show that the radius does not rank selections consistently with the gap and, on the image pools, that the bounds that do not use the labels of the pool are never informative and that covering in mean rather than in maximum, as greedy k-medoids does, gives a higher purity and accuracy than random sampling.

It clarifies what coverage arguments actually explain about active learning performance.
items.reasoning: A careful theoretical audit of widely cited active-learning justifications is valuable for the community, even if the paper is more corrective than constructive; rigor and conceptual clarity justify a solid score, though it concerns a somewhat narrow subfield.

items.title: GC-MoE K3: A Green-Context Role Graph for Latent Mixture-of-Experts Decode
items.content: Kimi K3 combines a latent routed mixture of experts with full-width shared experts. A complete feed-forward evaluation must score and select experts, project tokens into the latent space, exchange tokens across expert-parallel ranks, compute the routed and shared branches, and normalize and project the routed sum before joining the branches. We present GC-MoE K3, a datacenter Blackwell implementation that schedules this entire evaluation as a CUDA Graph across two Green Contexts. Five base roles split input projection, routing, dispatch, expert computation, and finalization. Dispatch can fill the routed input ring while the compute partition evaluates shared experts. Finalize waits for the expert owners needed by each token and overlaps routed reduction and RMSNorm with loading the output projection weights. Conditional roles reuse the communication partition for routed computation and reduce split-$K$ projection partials. On GB200 at EP8, EP16, and EP32, the operator is faster at all 24 measured configurations than the paired SGLang-style reference (mean speedup $1.1324\times$). A comparison with historical vLLM-style measurements gives $1.3651\times$ across the same 24 shapes. Both latency comparisons time single-layer graph replay on synthetic K3-shaped inputs with a residual prefix. The separate paired numerical suite passes all 142 cases and 2,936 rank checks.

This targets high-throughput decode for MoE architectures.

items.title: A Search Worth a Billion Pixels: Explaining Gigapixel Classifiers
items.content: Perturbation-based attribution methods explain model predictions without accessing their internal representations, but scaling them to high-resolution images requires balancing perturbation granularity and computational cost. Fine-grained perturbations require many model evaluations, whereas coarse masks may overlook small but relevant evidence. We introduce Wavelet Find-and-Refine (WaFR), a model-agnostic attribution method combining adaptive hierarchical search with sparse multiscale regression. By selectively refining regions that influence the prediction, WaFR maintains fine-grained localisation with a computational cost that depends on the spatial distribution of the evidence. As image resolution increases to 8,192 pixels per side, WaFR maintains a Pointing Game score of at least .995 in controlled localisation experiments, including at matched forward-pass budgets. On gigapixel whole-slide images, it requires a median of 176 forward passes and achieves the highest mean patch-level AUROC among the evaluated perturbation-based methods (.949).

items.reasoning: Practical and well-engineered solution to a real scalability problem in explainability, with strong quantitative results, but interpretability method papers of this type have moderate conceptual novelty.

items.title: WeMM-Ecom: Advancing Multimodal Content Understanding for WeChat E-Commerce
items.content: We present WeMM-Ecom, a family of multimodal large language models that deliver frontier e-commerce capabilities while achieving state-of-the-art general-purpose performance at their respective scales. The family spans five sizes, from a 0.8B dense model to a 35B mixture-of-experts model with 3B active parameters. Our training pipeline begins with two-stage continued pre-training that progressively raises the proportion of e-commerce data within a diverse multimodal data mixture, followed by hybrid-thinking post-training that combines on-policy distillation and reinforcement learning to support both non-thinking and thinking modes. For evaluation, we construct a comprehensive suite of 28 e-commerce benchmarks (23 in-house and five open-source) covering eight business scenarios and complement it with 64 public general-purpose benchmarks. On the e-commerce suite, WeMM-Ecom-35B-A3B surpasses substantially larger open-source flagship models, including Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, HY4, and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. On the general-purpose suite, every WeMM-Ecom model surpasses its similarly sized Qwen3.5 counterpart, with the lightweight variants (e.g., WeMM-Ecom-2B) showing clear advantages over leading lightweight models such as Qwen3.5-2B, MiniCPM-V-4.7-1B, and LFM3-VL-2B. Beyond benchmarks, WeMM-Ecom now powers hundreds of production use cases in WeChat, including catalog management, multimodal product search, and livestream commerce, serving billion-scale requests per day. We publicly release all model weights and detail our data curation, training recipe, and benchmark construction to facilitate future work on domain-specialized multimodal models. We have released the model weights and code to facilitate future research at https://github.com/Tencent/WeMM-Ecom.

items.title: CocoonBench: Can Multilingual Search Agents Escape Language Information Cocoons?
items.content: Multilingual search agents can access the global Web, yet may remain trapped in a language environment with insufficient evidence; we refer to this failure as a language information cocoon. However, existing search benchmarks largely operate within a single language, especially English, overlooking entity connections across multiple languages. We introduce CocoonBench, a benchmark that evaluates whether multilingual search agents can escape such language information cocoons. CocoonBench mines answer-centered relational paths from a frozen Wikidata-derived graph and selects clue sets that are individually necessary and jointly identify a unique answer. Using language-specific entity names, it records each task's minimum language cover, removes direct identifiers, and renders each task as matched prompts in three languages together with its construction certificate and provenance. Across 10 state-of-the-art models, mean accuracy on CocoonBench ranges from 33.8% (DeepSeek-V4-Flash) to 69.7% (Claude-Opus-4.8), leaving even the strongest system below 70%. The same construction certificates support path-aligned trajectory analysis, enabling diagnosis of model failures in language routing, evidence-path recovery, and answer use. The result shows that escaping a language cocoon requires more than switching languages: successful cross-lingual search depends on both covering the correct languages and connecting the evidence found across them.

items.title: AvatarAnyone: Agentic Reconstruction of Mesh-Based Layered Avatars from YouTube Video
items.content: We introduce AvatarAnyone, a method for reconstructing avatars from casual YouTube videos as layered meshes, with each garment and footwear as a separate mesh layered on top of the body mesh. In such videos, people differ in garment classes, clothing types, and layers, and each combination needs a different reconstruction. A single fixed layered reconstruction pipeline therefore fails. AvatarAnyone solves this problem with AI agents that plan a custom optimization for each person's reconstruction. The agents predict the garment classes, the clothing type, and the layering. They use these predictions to choose an initialization and stage the optimization. Because the avatars are layered meshes, they support applications such as virtual try-on and cloth simulation. We change the clothing layers of an avatar and render it in different garments and poses. We can also simulate a clothing layer as cloth over the animated body with a standard cloth simulator. Most existing avatars are one fused surface or a set of Gaussians and cannot do this. We load the avatars directly into Blender, Unreal Engine, and robotics simulators such as MuJoCo. As the avatars are meshes, they support contact modeling with other objects. We show results from around 150 YouTube videos. On four datasets, AvatarAnyone outperforms existing mesh-based methods for animatable monocular reconstruction. Our project page is available at https://miraymen.github.io/avataranyone.

items.title: Precise Asymptotics of Non-Convex M-Estimators
items.content: Precise asymptotic theory for M-estimators in high-dimensional settings is largely limited to convex or mildly non-convex formulations, yet non-convex loss functions as well as regularizers are widely used in practice. We study M-estimation in generalized linear models (GLMs) where the loss function or the regularizer can be non-convex. Under rotationally invariant design matrices in the proportional asymptotic regime, we analyze the problem through Vector Approximate Message Passing (VAMP), whose iterates are described by a low-dimensional deterministic recursion called State Evolution (SE). Existing proofs of SE require the proximal operators of the loss function and the regularizer to be Lipschitz, but a non-convex loss or regularizer can have a discontinuous proximal operator, and the usual Onsager terms in VAMP then miss the contribution of the discontinuities. Assuming that the proximal operators are special functions of locally bounded variation, we derive a correction to the Onsager terms using a distributional Stein's lemma. We prove that SE holds for the corrected VAMP. We apply the theory to analyze group sparse regression with an $\ell_0$-type penalty and to robust regression with the Cauchy loss.
