The key technical hurdle is that non-convex losses can have discontinuous proximal operators, breaking standard Lipschitz-based proofs.
items.reasoning: Fills a real gap in high-dimensional statistical theory by handling genuinely non-convex formulations that are widely used in practice; strong theoretical contribution with credible methodological lineage, though purely theoretical.

items.title: Parsing Visual Latents for Multimodal Spatial Reasoning
items.content: Spatial reasoning across multiple views requires inferring the 3D relations between objects and the camera from 2D observations, which depends on cross-view correspondence and scene geometry that vision-language models (VLMs) do not reliably extract. Pretrained vision encoders already capture this information in their latent features, with CLIP linking objects to image regions, DINOv3 matching semantics across views, and VGGT encoding multi-view geometry. However, VLMs do not benefit from these features when we present them directly in context as grayscale feature images. We therefore propose LatentParse, a training-free framework that parses latent features into explicit spatial evidence for VLMs. In LatentParse, an analyst VLM probes the features of all three encoders with predefined tools that locate objects, track them across views, and measure motion between views. It then distills the results into a concise text report, which is provided together with the images to the VLM to answer the question. We evaluate LatentParse on MMSI-Bench, MV-RoboBench and SPAR-Bench, where it improves all five VLMs over the photo-only baseline by 0.7-2.4 percentage points on average. On MMSI-Bench, it raises Qwen3.8-27B from 34.4% to 39.5%, with the largest improvements of 19.2 percentage points on the camera-related questions. These results suggest that latent features become useful for spatial reasoning once they are parsed into relation evidence, without training. Code is available at https://github.com/Harvard-AI-and-Robotics-Lab/LatentParse.

items.title: SurgeCount: A Protocol-Guided Composition Harness for Bimanual Surgical Sponge Counting
items.content: We present SurgeCount, a system for auditable robotic surgical sponge counting that composes learned skills under a written procedural protocol. Retained sponges cause preventable harm, and surgical teams count every sponge before closure to reduce that risk. The robot repeatedly isolates one deformable sponge from a tangled pile and places it in the next numbered counting-tray slot, requiring handling of occluded grasp threads while preserving step order. We train one subtask-conditioned policy on eleven short skills and learn when each skill ends. At each learned boundary, a stateful vision-language model selects the next skill from an operator-authored specification of step order, visual verification, and recovery. This creates temporal commitment to each subtask and enables failures to be recovered by recomposing existing skills rather than using a dedicated recovery policy. We evaluate five methods across 100 real-robot trials using 20 matched layouts. SurgeCount fills 47 of 60 ordered slots and completes 12 of 20 procedures, compared with 27 of 60 and 3 of 20 for the strongest of four end-to-end policies trained on the same data. Replacing the detailed protocol prompt with a minimal prompt reduces performance to 29 of 60 slots and 5 of 20 completed procedures. These results show that long-horizon performance depends not only on visuomotor capacity, but also on how learned skills are committed, verified, and composed. This tabletop proof of concept motivates further evaluation of protocol-guided robotic sponge counting in clinically representative settings.

items.title: Revisiting Learning to Delegate: LLM Discovered Heuristics for Large-Scale Vehicle Routing
items.content: Efficient vehicle routing is critical to logistics and transportation, yet solving large-scale capacitated vehicle routing problems (CVRP) remains computationally challenging due to their combinatorial complexity. One approach to solve large-scale vehicle routing optimization is to identify promising subproblems and then optimize them using solvers. In this paper, we propose a framework of automatic heuristic design (AHD) in which a large language model (LLM) autonomously refines heuristics for selecting subproblems, enabling effective optimization of large-scale CVRP instances. Compared to prior approaches that train task-specific neural networks to select among heuristically constructed subproblems, our method discovers generalizable, interpretable LLM-generated heuristics to directly construct subproblems. Experiments show that our approach achieves comparable in-distribution performance while outperforming neural network-based policies on out-of-distribution instances with large-scale problems.

Unlike learned neural delegators, the discovered heuristics are generalizable and interpretable.

items.title: Tokens as Locality-Preserving Anchors: Scalable Novel View Synthesis with Target-Adaptive Token Routing
items.content: Transformer-based view synthesis models render each target viewpoint from the source images, without an explicit 3D representation, which lets them reproduce fine detail and view-dependent effects. However, their decoder attends to every source token for every frame, so rendering slows with each source image. Rasterization avoids this by culling primitives that the viewpoint does not see, but source tokens cannot be culled this way, as they have no explicit position or extent. Our key insight is that source tokens are nonetheless spatial anchors: each encodes a local region of the scene, so the decoder's attention for any viewpoint concentrates on a few of them. A lightweight router predicts these tokens from the source tokens and the viewpoint, and the decoder attends only to a fixed budget of top-ranked tokens, so its cost no longer depends on the number of source tokens. We supervise the router with the decoder's attention, using non-maximum suppression to demote redundant tokens. With 24 source images and two views' worth of tokens, our model renders 6.4 times faster than LagerNVS, at a PSNR only 0.68 dB lower. One ranking serves every budget, so the budget can change at render time.

items.title: Know When to Abstain: Conformal Confidence Estimation for Text-to-SQL
items.content: Text-to-SQL systems often return queries that execute successfully but answer the wrong question. Detecting these errors at deployment is hard because execution correctness is defined against a gold query, which exists only in labeled data. We formulate confidence estimation for Text-to-SQL as probabilistic query validation under a latent correctness variable that is observable at calibration time through gold-SQL execution and latent at deployment. Our estimator separates generation from validation. A generator LLM writes and executes the query, and a different critic LLM judges the query and its execution result. The critic's validation and execution-grounded alignment scores are fused with the generator's verbalized confidence, token-level uncertainty, and SQL-structural features in a Random Forest, using two sequential LLM calls. Two calibration steps give finite-sample guarantees. A Learn-then-Test threshold ensures, with probability $1-\delta$, that the error rate among accepted queries stays below a user-chosen budget. A conformal p-value bounds the false abstention rate. On Spider we use GPT-OSS-120B as generator and Gemma-4-31B as critic. The estimator obtains an AUARC of 0.899. Without abstention, 22.6% of queries are wrong. With a 15% risk budget ($\delta=0.1$), a threshold is certified on all 10 resampled splits, and the system accepts 52.4% of queries on average with 9.1% observed error. Five different critic models give similar results. In a controlled comparison on Spider with Olmo-3-32B as generator, the estimator obtains an AUARC of 89.5, compared with 81.2 for the strongest logit-based baseline. Applied to BIRD without retraining, the confidence scores remain informative (AUROC 0.72, against 0.79 on Spider), but the risk guarantee does not transfer, as expected without exchangeability.

items.title: BehaviorICL: Task-Conditioned Decoder States for Visual In-Context Learning
items.content: The usefulness of an in-context demonstration for a vision-language model (VLM) depends on both the query image and the task posed about it. We study whether the frozen target VLM's own decoder states, read before answer generation, can select such demonstrations. BehaviorICL represents each image and task by a task-conditioned processing signature, the hidden states at the final input position across all decoder layers. Its training-free variant, BehaviorICL-Raw, averages cosine similarities between corresponding layer states and passes the retrieved examples with their reference answers to the same VLM. When the same NICO++ images are asked about their object or their context, Raw retrieves largely different demonstrations for the two questions and outperforms an image retriever given task-matched demonstrations on both VLMs. Across two VLMs and eight classification and visual question answering datasets, Raw gives the highest average accuracy among training-free retrievers on both VLMs and exceeds RICES with a CLIP ViT-L/14 encoder by 3.83 points on Qwen and 1.85 on InternVL. A lightweight shared projection, BehaviorICL-Proj, brings further gains on classification. Analyses of extraction text, decoder depth and bank answers help explain these gains, and attention analysis describes how the task text shifts attention at the extraction position toward the classified object. These results support the target VLM's internal states as a practical basis for visual in-context learning.

items.title: STEGOGUARD-LM: Evaluating End-to-End Protection Against LLM Covert Channels
items.content: A defense that disrupts hidden messages may still provide little protection if its detector rarely triggers an intervention. We present StegoGuard-LM, a controlled framework for evaluating defenses against covert messages in large language model outputs. We examine token-rank and synonym channels, with Unicode concealment as a structural control, and track messages through detection, intervention, and recovery. Deterministic rewriting prevented full recovery of 103 of 104 synonym-encoded messages when applied unconditionally, but only one when intervention depended on a detector set to limit false alarms. In a four-round replay on a 48-response subset, an attacker selecting from a fixed catalog recovered more bits by switching channels, although paired gains were not statistically significant after correction for multiple comparisons. Randomized rewriting showed no sustained advantage in this pilot. A more sensitive detector improved protection but modified about one-third of clean responses. These findings show how uneven detection can undermine effective rewriting and why protection must be evaluated alongside attacker adaptation and intervention on legitimate text.

items.summary: Presents StegoGuard-LM, a controlled framework for evaluating defenses against steganographic covert channels in LLM outputs, tracking messages through detection, intervention, and recovery across token-rank, synonym, and Unicode channels. A striking finding is that deterministic rewriting stops nearly all synonym-encoded messages unconditionally but almost none when intervention depends on a false-alarm-limited detector.

items.title: FastD4RT: Training-Free Acceleration of Dynamic 4D Reconstruction and Tracking
items.content: Query-based 4D reconstruction models such as D4RT encode a video once into a global scene representation and obtain outputs by decoding independent point queries. However, inference is often influenced by dense outputs and long videos. Although D4RT separates encoding from decoding, a dense output still requires one decoder query for every pixel of every frame, and a long video is still encoded as many overlapping segments. In this work, we analyze the inference cost of D4RT and show that a large part of it is redundant. In particular, we find that the later decoder blocks attend to a small set of tokens shared by all queries. Based on these findings, we propose FastD4RT, a training-free framework that accelerates D4RT. By exploiting the smoothness of the outputs over time and across pixels, FastD4RT encodes and decodes only at sparse anchors and recovers the remaining outputs via interpolation. It decodes the remaining queries against a shared token set selected once per segment. We further characterize the errors introduced by both components. Experimental results show that FastD4RT accelerates D4RT by about 5 times on average across all its tasks with competitive accuracy, and further improves accuracy on long videos. Our code is available at https://github.com/Lycheemeng/fastd4rt.
items.author: Meng Bi, Yili Jin, Kaiyuan Hu, Xize Duan, Jiaxin Huang, Hong Huang, Xue Liu
items.summary: FastD4RT accelerates query-based 4D reconstruction model D4RT without retraining by exploiting the finding that later decoder blocks attend to a small shared token set and that outputs are smooth over time and pixels. It reduces the dense per-pixel, per-frame query cost and redundant segment encoding of long videos while preserving output quality.
items.reasoning: Training-free acceleration grounded in a concrete architectural observation (shared token attention in late decoder blocks) is practically valuable for a strong 4D reconstruction model, and the redundancy analysis is informative. The contribution is incremental in that it optimizes one specific model family rather than generalizing broadly.

items.title: Coupling-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Co-Evolving Graph Games
items.content: Building hydrogen station networks, electric vehicle charging grids, or vaccine distribution systems requires coordinating two separately operated graphs, demand-side facilities and the supply-side networks they depend on, where each operator's payoff depends on the other's choices. We formalize this as the Co-Evolving Graph Game (CEGG), a setting that sits between facility location, interdependent-network analysis, and graph-based multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) but is not jointly addressed by any of them. We propose Cross-Graph Attention with Policy Mirror Descent (CGA-PMD), pairing cross-graph attention, which lets each agent read only the partner-graph nodes structurally coupled to its own, with a policy mirror descent update for stable training. Across three reward domains and a range of practical network scales, we find that the structure of the coupling selects which method wins: at small scale most methods are competitive, but as scale grows or coupling becomes irregular, CGA-PMD is the one method that stays reliable: it attains the highest success count on each of five real city networks, while own-only, unmasked-attention, and Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO)-based variants degrade in distinct ways. Our theoretical analysis addresses the optimizer side: the Kullback-Leibler (KL)-regularized update admits an iteration-uniform cumulative drift bound, whereas the clip update admits no such bound on the iterations where the clip does not bind. The implementation is available at https://github.com/Mina-Kim-Github/cegg-cga-pmd.

It fills a gap between facility location, interdependent-network analysis, and graph-based MARL.

items.title: WorldWeave: Rethinking Embodied Navigation through Cross-Task World Modeling
items.content: Mobile embodied agents continuously alter their observations through their own motion, while external dynamics further shape future interactions. Different mobile embodied tasks therefore capture complementary patterns of state evolution, yet jointly learning world dynamics across such interactions remains less explored. We investigate this problem through Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) and Embodied Visual Tracking (EVT), which respectively involve navigation toward a stationary goal and interaction with a moving target. We propose WorldWeave, a cross-task world model that couples shared predictive dynamics with task-specific adaptation. Instead of conditioning state transitions on heterogeneous physical actions, WorldWeave learns latent actions from observed state changes via inverse-forward dynamics, establishing a shared transition representation across tasks. The resulting future-state predictions are adaptively integrated into task-specific representations for downstream decision making. Experiments across multiple VLN and EVT benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over specialized baselines.

It learns latent actions from observed state changes via inverse dynamics rather than conditioning on heterogeneous physical actions, enabling transfer between navigation toward stationary goals and tracking moving targets. This explores an underexplored joint-learning direction in embodied AI.

items.title: When Fog Becomes a Weapon: Atmospheric Attacks on Visible-Infrared Vision-Language Models
items.content: Existing adversarial attacks on vision-language models (VLMs) and cross-spectral perception primarily rely on conspicuous, unnatural artifacts, such as vivid adversarial patches or active light beams, that lack physical stealthiness, whereas prior weather attacks largely overlook how one atmosphere simultaneously affects heterogeneous sensors. This raises a key scientific question: can a purely natural, shared fog environment simultaneously disrupt complementary visible and thermal infrared cues without artificial surface modifications? We introduce Fog Manipulation Attack (FMA), a zero-gradient attack that optimizes a common 3D fog state to induce simultaneous semantic failures in visible-infrared VLMs. FMA links shared, depth- and layer-aware atmospheric propagation along scene paths with band-specific imaging physics---visible airlight scattering and thermal path radiance---allowing one realistic fog state to erode both modalities' distinct cues. Experiments show that FMA more than doubles simultaneous failure rates over fidelity-matched random fog, transfers to captioning and VQA, and removes cross-modal compensation, where restoring a clean companion view recovers 64%--74% of lost dual-input VQA answers.

This reveals a physically realizable, stealthy threat to multisensor perception.

items.title: OrthoLatentCAD: Orthographic Spatial Latents for Hand-Drawn CAD Program Generation
items.content: Freehand orthographic drawings capture early design intent, yet recovering executable sketch--extrude CAD programs from raster front, right, and top views remains challenging: noisy, dimension-free 2D layouts must be reconciled into an ordered construction history. We introduce Hand2CAD, a benchmark of 215K ABC-derived synthetic orthographic-drawing--CAD program pairs and 1,000 real three-view sets drawn by CAD-trained participants. Recovering CAD programs from orthographic drawings requires both cross-view geometric reasoning and alignment between visual features and program representations. We propose OrthoLatentCAD to address these two challenges. It fuses local geometry with global context on canonical planes, exchanges evidence between paired plane lines indexed by the same shared-axis coordinate, and maps the spatial representation to ordered program latents through queries inherited from a frozen CAD autoencoder. Across the evaluated one- to three-view configurations, OrthoLatentCAD outperforms protocol-matched baselines in procedural accuracy, compiled geometry, and CAD-kernel validity while benefiting from additional views. Without real-data fine-tuning, it also outperforms the baselines on held-out real drawings. We will release the dataset, code, and evaluation scripts.

This targets converting early design intent into structured CAD programs, a task relevant to engineering design automation.

items.title: Wavelet-CFM for the extragalactic millimeter-wave sky
items.content: We develop a Wavelet-factorized Conditional Flow Matching (Wavelet-CFM) framework to generate fast, accurate simulations of correlated astrophysical fields including gravitational lensing convergence ($\kappa$), the kinetic and thermal Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (kSZ and tSZ) effects, and cosmic infrared background (CIB) emission. Together these make up every bright extragalactic component of the millimeter-wave (mm-wave) sky apart from radio sources. Our approach combines multi-scale wavelet decomposition with conditional flow matching models, trained on $\sim$9$\times$9 deg$^2$ patches at 1-arcminute resolution. The four fields are generated jointly, including their cross couplings, and the model has a tractable likelihood, which to our knowledge has not previously been achieved for this set of components. The power spectra, one-point distributions and Minkowski functionals of the generated maps match a validation set to a few percent. These results show promise for enabling field-level cosmological analyses of mm-wave data.

This enables better forward models for cosmology analyses of the millimeter-wave sky. It is a strong domain application of modern generative modeling to scientific simulation.

items.title: LIBERO-MOR: A Multimodal Robustness Benchmark Across the Vision-Language-Action Pipeline
items.content: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have achieved strong performance on robot manipulation benchmarks. Translating this progress into reliable deployment calls for systematic evaluation of how policies respond to variations throughout the robot interaction loop. We introduce LIBERO-MOR, a multimodal robustness benchmark across the vision-language-action pipeline. Built on standard LIBERO, it covers five deployment-facing domains: vision, language, proprioception, action execution, and environment. The benchmark comprises 22 deployment-inspired perturbations, each evaluated at three severity levels across 40 tasks under a paired clean-perturbed protocol, enabling controlled and reproducible comparisons. We evaluate seven representative VLA models spanning diverse action-generation mechanisms. Our experiments reveal substantial robustness gaps behind high clean-task success, together with shared vulnerabilities and distinct model-specific failure patterns across domains. Severity analysis further distinguishes progressive degradation, collapse at stronger interventions, and failures triggered at the mildest tested level. By connecting aggregate performance to pipeline domains, individual perturbations, and intervention strength, LIBERO-MOR provides a systematic framework for diagnosing VLA robustness and guiding the development of more reliable robot policies.

items.title: CANDOR: A Multilingual Provenance-Documented Corpus for Dysarthric Speech Research
items.content: CANDOR assembles 61 corpora across 17 languages and five aetiological classes plus a mixed/other group. Its register counts 2,057 speakers classified as dysarthric and 19,538 healthy controls. The collection contains 4,469.7 hours of audio, including 1,178.8 hours in the dysarthric subset. Counts use speech-impairment labels where available and diagnosis labels otherwise. The collection includes 732 dysarthric speakers across 14 non-English languages; 194 speakers use six languages unsupported by Qwen3-ASR, the model underlying its non-English baselines. We document composition, chain of custody, licences and transfer terms, while distinguishing corpus-level provenance from participant-level consent records, which we hold for few constituents. Among 31 dysarthric-bearing corpora, open licences cover 29.0% of corpora, 10.5% of speakers and 8.2% of hours. Excluding the English Speech Accessibility Project raises the open hour share to 31.2%, showing its dependence on this collection's composition. CANDOR cannot be redistributed as a single audio resource; we specify public, restricted and conditional artefacts. Severity labels available in 15 corpora do not provide a validated cross-corpus mapping. Within the non-English ASR baselines, only Mandarin yields a real-speech estimate meeting our evaluation criteria. It differs sharply from the synthesis result and remains imprecise; an English challenge result uses a different model and protocol. CANDOR provides a documented basis for research on under-represented languages while making constraints on evaluation, comparability and sharing explicit.

items.title: When Wrong Answers Remain Unsettled: Failure Dynamics in Recurrent Reasoners
items.content: When a recurrent reasoner returns a wrong answer, is its computation finished or merely stopped? We test this on a trained Hierarchical Reasoning Model (HRM; 27M parameters, Sudoku-Extreme) by running the recurrence for one more inference budget and comparing with an unperturbed control. Solved answers persist (0.95 of 512 endpoints). Wrong answers mostly do not: 0.42 of near-miss answers (n=170) and 0.18 of all 512 wrong endpoints keep their answer. Perturbations from 0.05x to 20x the terminal-update scale barely change these rates, so the measurement reflects continued recurrence, not noise sensitivity. The solved-above-wrong ordering also holds in five further settings (a second seed, TRM, Maze, GRAM-guided TRM, N-Queens), but a fixed 1/2 persistence threshold does not, and neither do HRM's endpoint-spectrum and fast-versus-slow predictability patterns, which are not universal diagnostics. Perturb-and-reselect (known from prior work) is consistent with this: frozen noise gains 4.8 accuracy points (197 gained, 2 lost), but compute-matched extended depth gains 5.6 and Sudoku symmetry augmentation 34.6, so noise is not the best use of the budget. Conclusions are limited to finite horizons and one primary HRM checkpoint; they do not exclude asymptotic attractors.

items.summary: Testing a small trained Hierarchical Reasoning Model on Sudoku-Extreme, the authors extend recurrence beyond the normal stopping budget and find solved answers persist (0.95) while many wrong answers are unsettled and revise with more compute. The solved-over-wrong persistence ordering replicates across five further settings, though specific thresholds and dynamics do not generalize.

items.title: TesseraFlow: Scalable Video Diffusion for Dynamic Medical Imaging Inverse Problems
items.content: Generative priors are state-of-the-art for modeling medical images in image reconstruction tasks, but reconstruction with video priors takes tens of seconds to minutes per frame. Latent priors inherit the errors of their autoencoder, the memory of pixel-space whole-frame priors grows with the frame size, and pixel-space patch priors are slow for two reasons. First, their deep networks process every frame at full resolution at every sampling step, even though early steps resolve only low frequencies. Second, their samplers spend many network evaluations per sampling step on overlapping windows, multiple re-noising rounds, or backpropagation through the prior. We introduce TesseraFlow, a complex-valued pixel-space flow prior that reduces the first cost. A global encoder reads a low-resolution view of every frame once per sampling step. A single shallow decoder operates on this view during early steps and on full-resolution space-time tiles during later steps, so no network processes a whole frame at full resolution. Our sampler, ReTile, addresses the second reason. We use randomized grid shifting at every sampling step along with re-noising, which acts as a stochastic gradient instead of computing overlapping tiles, so a single network pass per sampling step suffices. On its own, ReTile speeds up an existing global-context patch prior by 6-9x, and our prior adds a further 3-5x speedup. TesseraFlow reconstructs about one 256x256 frame per second, 20-367x faster than patch and latent video priors, and can match or exceed the best generative baseline on cardiac, brain, and abdominal MRI and lung CT, at a fraction of its GPU time.

It targets making state-of-the-art video generative priors practical for dynamic imaging inverse problems.

items.title: What Makes Recurrence Generalize Across Lengths?
items.content: Multi-step reasoning requires models to preserve and update intermediate information as computation unfolds. State tracking captures this fundamental requirement, but models that succeed within a fixed range of state transitions may not generalize when substantially more updates are required. Recurrent Transformers offer a natural mechanism for addressing this challenge by repeatedly applying shared Transformer blocks, allowing computation to scale with problem length. We study when such recurrent computation generalizes beyond the training range in a controlled state-tracking task, varying operation representation, positional encoding, and recurrent capacity. We find that recurrence alone is insufficient: multi-token template representations and absolute positional encoding can severely limit extrapolation, whereas atomic operation representations enable substantially stronger length generalization. The effect of positional structure also varies with recurrent depth, with periodic positional encoding achieving the strongest mean performance at greater recurrent depth. Most importantly, scaling the recurrent operator extends the extrapolation horizon, reaching 35.1% exact-match accuracy on sequences of 20-40 operations after training only on 2-10, while substantially larger fixed-depth Transformers remain at 0%. Additional recurrent computation at test time can extend the range over which the model generalizes, but does not eliminate failure on much longer sequences. These results suggest that recurrent computation can support length-generalizable state tracking, but that its effectiveness depends critically on whether the learned computation remains reusable across sequence lengths.

items.title: QASparse: Query-Adaptive Sparse Attention with Tailored Budgets and Tokens
items.content: Long-sequence inference in large language models is constrained by the high cost of prefilling, where dense attention scales quadratically with context length. Exploiting similarity across attention heads offers a way to reduce redundant computation. Prior approaches in this direction have relied on localized query observations to determine head-level computation reuse or budget allocation. However, inter-head similarity does not imply uniform query requirements, leaving adaptation to varying budget needs and selection preferences across query regions a key challenge. We introduce QASparse, a Query-Adaptive Sparse attention mechanism with hardware-efficient execution. QASparse preserves the efficiency of shared cross-head importance estimation while adapting computational budgets and token selections to query requirements, and it executes these dynamic sparse decisions through dedicated kernels. Its query adaptivity stems from two complementary innovations: Local Budget Regression models local variations in computational demand along query positions to estimate budgets for different query regions and attention heads; Boundary Voting lets queries within each head vote over candidates near the selection cutoff using actual query/key scores, refining the retained set while preserving the initial selection size. To reduce the execution overhead of dynamic budgets, we further design length-specialized selection kernels that efficiently support query-adaptive sparse patterns across context lengths. Together, these designs efficiently combine shared estimation with local decisions while adapting both how much attention is computed and which interactions are retained. Experimental results demonstrate improved benchmark scores and faster prefill attention computation compared with existing sparse attention baselines.

The direction is well-trodden with many competing sparse attention methods, so impact hinges on demonstrated speedup-quality tradeoffs against strong baselines.

items.title: Probe Before You Learn: Allocating Prompts from Initial Gradients under Label Noise
items.content: Prompt learning provides a parameter-efficient way to adapt pretrained vision--language models through text and visual prompts, but noisy labels prevalent in real-world data inevitably bias prompt updates and thereby undermine adaptation effectiveness. Prior work on robust prompt learning focuses on suppressing unreliable updates under noisy supervision. We uncover a pivotal yet overlooked aspect--prompt allocation: shifting the parameter budget between text and visual prompts can substantially enhance robustness while keeping the training objective and total budget fixed. However, suitable prompt allocations vary across tasks and are unknown a priori, rendering brute-force candidate training computationally prohibitive. We propose GPrompt, a training-free method that derives allocation between text and visual prompts using only loss gradients at initialization before prompt optimization. Using a small sample of images and generated pseudo-labels as shared supervision, GPrompt performs an initialization probe to extract paired text and visual loss gradients, and characterizes the geometry of their trace-normalized Gram matrices through both concentration within each modality and overlap between modalities. GPrompt then derives a closed-form allocation, and projects it onto feasible prompt counts under the exact parameter budget, enabling task-specific selection without training candidate configurations. Experiments across eleven datasets show that GPrompt outperforms the strongest baseline by up to 7.75% while selecting configurations close to the best allocation identified through exhaustive training. The average runtime of gradient probe across datasets is 99.9% lower than that of exhaustive candidate training.

It derives allocations training-free from initial gradient statistics, avoiding costly candidate training. This is a practical, principled improvement to parameter-efficient adaptation.

items.title: Optimal Labelling Designs for Sequential Decisions on Language Model Updates
items.content: When a large language model (LLM) is updated, its developer must decide whether accuracy improved, worsened or stayed within a tolerance. An LLM judge can assess every prompt cheaply but imperfectly, while human labels are costly. We propose Sequential Decisions with Optimal Labelling Designs (SOLD), which labels one prompt at a time, uses the judge to correct the estimate of the change in accuracy and to choose the prompts, and stops once the evidence is conclusive. A wrong decision has probability at most a prespecified level whenever labelling stops. The commonly used Neyman allocation minimises the variance of the estimate and therefore rarely labels prompts that the judge is confident about. It can need far more draws when the outcomes of these prompts could still fall far below the judge's prediction. We instead derive the design that gathers evidence fastest, which labels each prompt with probability at least proportional to how far its outcome could fall below the prediction. As the level tends to zero, no procedure based on the judge-corrected estimates needs fewer draws than SOLD. In simulations and on the EVOUNA and MMLU-Pro datasets, SOLD needed fewer labels than the other methods.

items.summary: SOLD formulates the problem of deciding whether an LLM update improved accuracy as a sequential labeling design, using a cheap imperfect LLM judge plus selectively purchased human labels, with guaranteed error control at stopping. The paper shows Neyman allocation, the common variance-minimizing choice, can be highly suboptimal here and proposes a better design.

items.title: Music Circuit: Trace and Control Style Dynamics in Large Music Generation Model
items.content: Musical style, a global attribute that functions throughout a whole piece, is a lever widely used by users in modern large music generation models. Yet how style is represented inside these models, and which components drive it, remains largely unexplored. In language models, circuit analysis traces a representation to a sparse sub-network of a few key components, namely attention heads and MLP neurons, and has been used successfully to explain and control global attributes such as emotion. In this work, we use circuit analysis to study the mechanisms behind musical style. Based on YuE2, we build a dataset that pairs the same lyrics with five styles and design a three-step framework. Third, we therefore merge the activation differences across positions into one direction per style, and trace the neurons and attention heads that drive this direction into a sparse circuit. Without any style text, steering this circuit successfully transfers one piece into the target style, matching and even exceeding the style prompt. To our knowledge, this is the first work to analyze and control musical style at the circuit level in a large music generation model. items.title: Align the Pair, Not the Sample: Representation Alignment for Faster and Better One-Step Generato
items.content: Representation alignment markedly accelerates diffusion training, but one-step generators raise a question that diffusion does not: \emph{which training path should receive the loss?} A one-step generator sees two kinds of inputs. Corrupted real images come with their clean counterpart, which provides an instance-paired target. Samples generated from pure noise have no corresponding real image, yet this is where the final model operates. We study this question on Priming, which trains one-step generators from scratch by reconstructing corrupted images and then matching feature distributions with optimal transport. Aligning the generative path, the natural choice, collapses recall ($0.45\!\to\!0.15$--$0.25$) in all 17 configurations we test, including five target constructions and loss weights down to $0.05$. Aligning the paired reconstruction path with a frozen DINOv2 encoder instead helps in every setting we test. A short analysis explains this asymmetry: when the target carries no instance information about the input, the optimal aligned feature is constant within each class, so the loss pulls samples toward class prototypes. A control confirms this: aligning the paired path to a random same-class image instead of the input's own image removes most of the gain. Inside the generator, paired-path alignment creates an interface block through which post-training routes noise, and the image semantics carried through it predict sample quality across 16 models. The resulting recipe, \method, accelerates \emph{both} training stages on ImageNet $256\!\times\!256$: it matches the 160-epoch baseline with $2\times$ fewer priming epochs, surpasses its final quality with $4\times$ fewer post-training updates, and lowers FID to 1.30 (B) and 1.155 (L) at the standard budget. A joint single-stage variant trains native one-step generators and reaches FID 1.22 with 115M parameters.

items.title: Reducing Authorship Attribution Risk in Student Texts Through Style-Conditioned Rewriting
items.content: Building NLP applications for education is constrained by data scarcity due to student privacy concerns and data regulations. To address this, we propose a style-aware approach to rewriting student forum posts that retains analytical value while reducing identifiability. Our method isolates content, structure, and style as separate conditioning channels and aggregates over student-disjoint exemplar partitions within style clusters, extending Differentially Private In-context Learning (DP-ICL) with cluster-restricted retrieval. Across three educational NLP datasets, our approach achieves high style fidelity, preserves downstream task performance, and reduces authorship attribution risk relative to the original student-written texts, including against a dedicated authorship-attribution model.

items.title: ComplexIF: A Challenging Multi-Turn, Multi-Constraint Instruction-Following Benchmark
items.content: As frontier LLMs saturate existing instruction-following benchmarks, measuring further progress requires harder tests that remain faithful to real use. In practice, users often combine several constraints, add them at different turns of a conversation, and expect all of them to hold in the assistant's response. We introduce ComplexIF, a challenging benchmark for this setting, together with the automatic pipeline that generates it. The pipeline expands seed requests into multi-turn conversations, weaves constraints into their turns, and keeps only tasks that a strong model can solve, so difficulty can be raised by adding constraints or turns while every task stays solvable. ComplexIF's two splits test complementary sides of instruction following: a verifiable split of format constraints, checked by programs, and a rubric split of semantic instructions, such as a tone or an audience, checked with an LLM judge. Across 14 proprietary and open-weight models, even the strongest satisfies every constraint on fewer than half of the verifiable tasks, and no model leads on both splits.

items.title: Motion Mamba 2.0: Autoregressive Diffusion Mamba for Long-Horizon Humanoid Control
items.content: Long-horizon, real-time controllable motion generation is essential for interactive animation and humanoid robotics, where an agent must respond to changing instructions and spatial goals while moving. Existing autoregressive diffusion methods generate motion incrementally, but bounded attention caches limit access to distant history, while repeated denoising introduces substantial inference overhead. We present Motion Mamba 2.0, a Mamba-based root-body diffusion architecture that integrates local attention, resumable recurrent states, and persistent content memory (PCM) for long-horizon controllable motion generation. PCM transforms compressed motion history from Mamba recurrent states, together with state changes and text-conditioned features, into dynamically updated content slots accessible to local attention. To enable efficient inference, we further develop an execution scheme tailored to this architecture, combining CUDA Graph replay, fused kernels, and execution-flow simplification while preserving the canonical history update. Evaluations on retargeted HiPHI demonstrate accurate terminal control over rollouts of up to 39.52 s, while short-horizon comparisons on BONES Seed and retargeted HumanML3D show that the model also retains strong spatial control and text-motion matching. On an RTX 4090, the optimized execution reduces median complete-window latency from 1685.35 to 276.14 ms, achieving a median paired speedup of 6.138$\times$ while preserving identical outputs and committed states in the tested rollouts. Moreover, we conduct extensive real-world evaluation on the Unitree G1, demonstrating sequential text-guided action composition, expressive motion, and interactive locomotion through keyboard and mouse control.

items.title: How Relations Impose Embedding-Space Structure
items.content: Language models are known to encode simple relations, such as synonymy, in the geometry of their representations. It is unclear whether they also encode complex patterns of relationships such as those that drive analogy. We present a simple method, with no learned parameters, based on comparing the internal structural arrangements between disparate domains, to test this. Using our method we find over multiple models that representations are arranged consistently to encode complex relationship similarities. Models align distant representation clouds so that facets of meaning are easily comparable under simple mappings. Our work extends mechanistic accounts of representation space to the relative arrangement of representations that may be only weakly related to one another, showing that representation geometry is far richer than previously thought. Code and data: https://github.com/lcowley7/embedded_relationships

items.title: One Latent World for Heterogeneous LiDARs: A Scan Pattern Agnostic 4D World Model via Direct Ray Decoding
items.content: LiDAR world models generate and predict metric 3D observations in the form of LiDAR scans. They typically synthesize scans following the scan pattern of their training sensor or render them from an intermediate 3D surface or field. However, following one scan pattern limits transfer to LiDARs with other patterns, and rendering from intermediate geometry can cause incorrect depths and false returns. In this paper, we propose a scan pattern agnostic 4D LiDAR world model that decouples the scene from sensor observation, so one spatial latent can be observed by heterogeneous LiDARs at the same mounting position without regeneration. Our decoder predicts the hit probability and depth of each ray directly from the latent, combining global scene context with local features retrieved at a preliminary depth. Without an intermediate surface or field, it reduces incorrect depths and false returns, and as each ray is decoded independently from one latent, LiDARs that share a ray receive the same return and observe one consistent scene. Finally, a diffusion transformer generates scenes in this latent and predicts 4D sequences from observed latents warped by the given ego and object motion. On KITTI-360 and nuScenes, our model generates realistic scenes and reduces the registration error between predicted frames by about 70% relative to the best compared world model. Its decoder yields 19 to 28% lower depth error than the rendering used by other world models, and generated scans benefit several downstream tasks. Our code will be open-sourced. More details are available at https://minwoo0611.github.io/OneLatentWorld.

items.title: Context-Grounded Skill Internalization for Vision-Language Agents
items.content: Skill internalization offers a way for agents to learn useful behaviors from skills and use them without explicit guidance in context at inference time. A common approach is to generate demonstration trajectories with the skill in context and then fine-tune the same model on its own trajectories with the skill removed. However, this leads to the problem that the model may learn to reference the removed skill, which we named as context misalignment (CoMi). In this work, we first analyze agent behaviors related to CoMi under this common pipeline. Across ALFWorld, WebShop, and ARC-AGI-1, skill-removed fine-tuning consistently results in CoMi: 12.2-46.0% of test trajectories reference the removed skill. To address this problem, we develop Context-Grounded Skill Internalization (CGSI). CGSI uses a sentence detector to identify unsupported references and then masks or rewrites the selected sentences before fine-tuning. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of CGSI and reveal two key findings. (i) Compared with directly fine-tuning with the skill removed, CGSI reduces CoMi at test time by 72.5-94.6% while preserving task success. (ii) Compared with existing reinforcement learning-based skill-internalization baselines, CGSI achieves comparable performance with substantially less training time. CGSI also significantly reduces processing costs compared with large-scale trajectory auditing and correction.

The proposed CGSI method grounds fine-tuning to eliminate these stale references and improve internalized agent behavior.

items.title: Character Information in Language Models: A Prompt-Independent Word Store and a Late, Question-Driven Signal That Grows With Scale
items.content: Linear probes recover character properties of a word from a language model's hidden states, but a probe at the answer position cannot say whether the property was stored with the word or produced because the prompt asked for it. We separate the two with a word-position baseline: the same held-out-word probe applied to the query word's own tokens in a sentence that asks nothing. Across 16 open-weight models from seven families (0.6B--14B) and eleven character tasks, the word tokens encode \texttt{first\_letter}, \texttt{last\_letter} and \texttt{most\_frequent\_letter} above a word-only nuisance floor in all 16 models, and about 70\% of that signal is already present in the token embedding. Asking the question adds a second signal at the answer position. Its size grows with model scale for all four prompt-sensitive tasks (Holm-corrected permutation $p \leq 0.018$, also within model families), and the growth is confined to the late layers: restricted to the first quarter of the network, the slope is indistinguishable from zero. Small models' answer positions hold less linearly decodable signal than their word-level store; large models' hold more. Four controls bound these claims. Measured against the nuisance floor, the question-free signal that a majority-baseline analysis counts as retained largely disappears (\texttt{last\_letter}: $-0.01$). Count tasks become measurable only after length, repetition and query-letter shortcuts are removed by design. A pre-registered test finds that a question placed before the word does not change the word's own encoding beyond what an arbitrary prefix change does. Representation--readout gaps show no robust scaling once probe saturation is accounted for. Pre-registered criteria, a fixed estimator (held-out layer selection, cold-start folds) and all analysis code accompany the paper.

items.title: Revisiting Continual Learning in Language Models: A Three-Interface Diagnosis of Stability and Plasticity
items.content: Continual learning in language models is commonly studied in the incremental learning (IL) setting, where a model learns a sequence of tasks and is evaluated through its final classifier or language-model (LM) head. This interface, however, does not indicate where forgetting occurs: a drop in accuracy may reflect representation degradation in the backbone, readout mismatch in the head, or both. We therefore argue that backward transfer (BWT) and forward transfer (FWT) should be interpreted as interface-dependent quantities rather than as single modellevel properties. We study three evaluation interfaces: the trained head, which is updated sequentially with the backbone; a probe newly trained on frozen backbone features; and a classifier-free backbone diagnostic. They measure deployed performance, recoverability under a new readout, and representation separability, respectively. items.title: Confidently Lost: Silent Failure and Edge Deployment of Dense Visual SLAM under Photon Starvation
items.content: Dense visual SLAM built on learned two-view geometry is evaluated in good light; in low light it fails silently. Two frames of 9-level quantized noise, no scene at all, give MASt3R-SLAM's network a cross-view geometric self-consistency of 0.936; a real dark frame pair gives 0.935. Starved of structure, the network invents the same geometry for both views and the system trusts the agreement: on a dark sequence it consumes 1,605 frames, emits 7 keyframes, rejects no factor-graph edges and reports full frame rate, while over 95% of the correspondences it accepts violate the ground-truth epipolar geometry. One inflated statistic is read by two subsystems against thresholds in opposite directions, so keyframing starves while relocalization accepts almost every candidate. The same statistic, read at keyframe-pair baselines, separates the confident collapse from working runs on the ETH3D dark sequences without ground truth or extra computation (in-sample). Low-light-adapted weights take tracked trajectories from 1/6 to 5/6, as does retuning two thresholds; neither yields accurate ones, because the adaptation withdraws confidence from wrong geometry rather than finding right geometry. Replayed on a Jetson AGX Orin carried by a legged robot, the mechanism's signature reproduces on the two darkest of four routes, and which of its faces appears varies with route geometry and sensor encoding. The network does not lose confidence in the dark; it manufactures it.

items.title: RoomTokens: Masked Diffusion over Structured Tokens for Indoor Scene Synthesis
items.content: Generating 3D indoor scenes requires a representation that captures object semantics, instance identity, height structure, and orientation while respecting room geometry. Methods that model scenes as sequences of object vectors learn spatial constraints implicitly, leaving collisions and boundary violations to losses or post-processing; semantic-map methods make occupancy explicit, but collapse instance and directional structure. We introduce RoomTokens, a sliced structured-token representation in which each token stores semantic class, instance-color identity, and facing field. This representation allows a scene to be generated as a discrete grid while preserving cues for instance grouping, orientation estimation, and 3D extent prediction. To learn the RoomToken distribution, we propose MDIRT (Masked Diffusion over RoomTokens), a masked discrete diffusion model that denoises semantic/instance-color/facing channels jointly with a shared cross-slice backbone. Architectural tokens are clamped as explicit floor- plan constraints, so the model samples furniture layouts that respect room geometry while retaining instance and object-attribute structure. Experiments on 3D-FRONT show that RoomTokens with MDIRT improve layout fidelity and physical consistency over sequence/vector- and map-based methods, suggesting structured spatial tokens as a practical choice for discrete 3D scene synthesis.

items.title: RepoClean: Evaluating Coding Agents on Repository-Level Obsolete Code Cleanup
items.content: Large language model (LLM) agents have demonstrated strong repository-level programming capabilities. However, as software evolves, repository code may become redundant or obsolete, increasing maintenance costs and potentially introducing functional issues. Agents must therefore identify and remove unnecessary code safely, yet autonomous repository-level code cleanup remains insufficiently evaluated in isolation. To evaluate this capability, we introduce RepoClean, a benchmark of 200 cleanup tasks from 34 popular open-source Python repositories. RepoClean is constructed by automatically reintroducing deleted code from real repository histories into newer versions, preserving current implementations and retaining instances where previously passing tests consequently fail. To restore existing functionality without new feature development, agents must use repository interfaces and cross-file dependencies to determine which historical code to remove and which implementations to preserve. Evaluation of seven models shows that even the best-performing model, GPT-6 Astra, resolves only 23% of tasks. Further analysis reveals that agents remove substantially less obsolete code when cleanup is not explicitly requested. RepoClean provides a foundation for systematically studying these cleanup challenges and advancing coding agents toward autonomous software maintenance.

items.title: Revisiting LLMs as Context Engineers
items.content: As large language models (LLMs) are used in more and more new tasks, context engineering becomes a fundamental method to efficiently steer LLMs by constructing instruction prompts or metadata without intensive training. A growing number of LLM context engineering (LCE) approaches automate the task by casting the LLM itself as the engineer that draws generalizable instructions or experiences from offline trials as context. Although these methods resemble how humans learn from experiences, it remains unclear \textbf{when and how} LLMs can engineer effective context from data. To answer the question, we first establish a benchmark composed of datasets with different reasoning patterns. We compared different LCE methods with different LLM families in 8B size, showing that there is no single winner for all tasks, even compared with simple baselines like chain-of-thought. Even when scaling model capabilities via more parameters or generation iterations, LCEs do not consistently boost existing performance. Across all datasets and models, the performance gains of LCEs are negatively correlated ($r=-0.5, p\le 0.05$) with the diversity of the failure modes of reasoning trajectories. Investigating how LCEs work, we find that (1) the improvement in instruction adherence can explain some success of LCEs; (2) one major bottleneck is whether LLMs can extract effective experiences out of natively diverse failures. Through this study, we uncover the limited capabilities of LCEs in abstracting principled contexts from diverse failure modes and understand how LCEs work, providing guidelines for future work.

items.title: De Novo Generation of Odorant Molecules with Targeted Olfactory Receptor Activation Patterns
items.content: Odor perception arises from a combinatorial code in which each molecule activates a specific subset of olfactory receptors (ORs), and the resulting activation pattern determines the perceived smell. We present a framework for de novo generation of molecules predicted to match target multi-receptor activation profiles. We first construct a panoramic binding matrix over 20 ORs, then cluster it to discover representative activation patterns, and finally formulate a structured selectivity loss, combining pairwise ranking, distribution matching, and complexity constraints, to steer a molecular generator via reinforcement learning. Across nine target profiles of varying complexity, our method achieves high predicted selectivity within 18000 oracle calls and provides the largest gains on profiles that are rare under the prior, especially broad-spectrum and sparse-activator targets.

items.title: Seeing Is Locating: Spatial Awareness and Geographic Bias in Decision Language Models
items.content: Decision models, which output probability distributions over candidate labels instead of generating text, are increasingly used as classifiers and evaluators for inputs associated with real-world locations. However, it remains unclear whether they can leverage spatial context and whether their predictions are geographically biased. We introduce GeoDecisions, a multimodal benchmark for evaluating the spatial awareness and geographic bias of decision models. GeoDecisions comprises two tasks: (1) geo-aware image classification, and (2) location rating on objective and subjective topics. Evaluating six decision models against supervised task-specific models, we find that spatial awareness requires vision: textual coordinates alone provide insufficient context for classifying everyday photos and satellite images. We also find substantial geographic bias. On everyday photos, despite achieving higher accuracy, open-weight decision models exhibit more spatially clustered errors than supervised models. Moreover, across all five subjective topics, every decision model gives lower ratings to locations with lower socioeconomic conditions. Finally, we propose a training-free method that combines decision models with a location prior to improve their spatial awareness without substantially increasing performance bias. Our code is available at https://github.com/cruiseresearchgroup/GeoDecisions.

items.title: Vasicek Diffusion Bridge for Graph Generation
items.content: Diffusion-based graph generation models progressively transform Gaussian noise into structured graphs through stochastic dynamics. We observe that the effectiveness of this transformation is fundamentally determined by the evolution of the diffusion trajectory. Existing graph diffusion models often suffer from excessive uncertainty during diffusion and delayed growth of the signal-to-noise ratio, causing useful structural information to emerge only in the later stages of generation. To address this issue, we propose the Vasicek Graph Diffusion (VGD), a graph diffusion process derived from the Vasicek dynamics. The key insight of VGD is data-anchored mean dynamics with a closed-form solution, which analytically establishes a continuous transition from Gaussian noise to the target graph distribution. Unlike conventional graph diffusion processes that rely predominantly on stochastic evolution, VGD introduces a data-anchored drift that continuously steers the latent state toward the target distribution throughout diffusion. As a consequence, VGD maintains a smoothly evolving uncertainty while rapidly increasing the signal-to-noise ratio throughout diffusion, allowing informative graph structures to emerge much earlier during generation. Extensive experiments on multiple graph generation benchmarks demonstrate that VGD outperforms existing diffusion-based graph generative models in terms of generation quality and structural fidelity.

This counters excessive uncertainty and delayed signal-to-noise growth seen in existing graph diffusion models, so structure emerges earlier in generation.

items.title: ABI: Actor-Free Behavior-Induced Representations for Zero-Shot Test-Time Guidance
items.content: Behavior-cloning policies show strong ability in sequential control by generating coherent multi-step action chunks, yet their purely imitative objective limits zero-shot generalization to unseen tasks. While offline reinforcement learning offers principled policy improvement, existing methods either require task-specific reward supervision or remain tied to a specific actor during critic training or policy deployment, inflating training cost and restricting cross-policy generalization. We observe that evaluating actions under the data-collecting behavior largely preserves their relative value ordering across target policies, offering a way around actor coupling. Combining this property with reward-free successor prediction, we propose Actor-Free Behavior-Induced Representations (ABI) to learn multi-horizon action-chunk representations from unlabeled trajectories without reward supervision or actor training. At test time, pairing the frozen representation with lightweight task readouts forms a chunk critic that guides target policies without parameter updates and transfers directly across distinct unseen policies. Our analysis establishes when the value ordering is preserved across policies and when selecting among proposed chunks improves closed-loop return. Across 65 locomotion, navigation, and manipulation tasks, ABI's chunk critic guides weak imitation policies to match or surpass zero-shot RL baselines with high sample efficiency, outperforms existing zero-shot critics on identical proposals, and improves externally trained RL actors without retraining. From raw pixels, ABI delivers substantial guidance gains and surpasses prior zero-shot RL baselines on visual manipulation, highlighting its potential for visuomotor control.

Combining this with reward-free successor prediction, ABI learns representations that provide zero-shot test-time guidance for behavior-cloning policies on unseen tasks without task-specific rewards or actor coupling.

items.title: Coordinating Perception and Planning for Test-Time Adaptation in End-to-End Driving under Distribution Shifts
items.content: End-to-end autonomous driving has achieved significant milestones, yet its reliance on the i.i.d. assumption renders it vulnerable to real-world distribution shifts. While Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) offers a promising paradigm for on-the-fly enhancement, its application to driving is hindered by two barriers: (i) multi-task adaptation dependency, where updates to upstream perception also affect downstream planning, while perception confidence alone does not directly assess these downstream effects; and (ii) continuous adaptation instability, where recursive online updates over long horizons cause compounding parameter drift. To address these challenges, we propose P2-TTA, a plug-and-play TTA framework for the continual adaptation of end-to-end driving models. P2-TTA coordinates adaptation through a joint objective combining perception entropy minimization with a retrospective temporal planning consistency objective derived from observed ego motion. To stabilize online updates, we use an EMA teacher as a moving parameter reference and reject candidate updates that increase historical planning loss. Extensive experiments across multiple models demonstrate that, by updating an average of 0.11 per mille of parameters with an average adaptation time of 19.9 ms on different backbones, P2-TTA achieves average recovery rates of 36.4%, 30.0%, and 9.3% for L2, collision rate, and PDMS, respectively, under severe distribution shifts. Under a shared perception-planning objective, P2-TTA achieves the highest L2 and collision recovery among the compared TTA baselines on UniAD.

It uses planning-aware signals rather than perception confidence alone to assess downstream effects of upstream updates.

Strong relevance to autonomous driving; impact moderated by reliance on simulation-style evaluation typical of the field.

To stabilize online updates, we use an EMA teacher as a moving parameter reference and reject candidate updates that increase historical planning loss. Extensive experiments across multiple models demonstrate that, by updating an average of 0.11 per mille of parameters with an average adaptation time of 19.9 ms on different backbones, P2-TTA achieves average recovery rates of 36.4%, 30.0%, and 9.3% for L2, collision rate, and PDMS, respectively, under severe distribution shifts. Under a shared perception-planning objective, P2-TTA achieves the highest L2 and collision recovery among the compared TTA baselines on UniAD.

items.title: Predicting Rare-Mode Collapse in Recursive Generative Training from Single-Generation Calibration
items.content: Recursive generative training can preserve sample counts in a rare region while silently eroding its characteristic core. Mapping this finite-horizon collapse across real-data quotas, rare prevalences, and feedback perturbations via exhaustive multi-generation chains is computationally prohibitive. We develop a decoupled framework that forecasts multi-generation collapse probabilities and locates operating risk boundaries from independent single-generation conditional fits alone. Pairing an exact three-source multinomial count law with single-generation response banks propagates count marginals in closed form, backed by explicit calibration-error and boundary-resolution bounds. For additive Gaussian perturbations, we further prove that equal-variance all-row and sparse policies reverse their boundary-crossing order at a unique hyperplane distance. Across a 2,178-setting count benchmark, exact propagation cuts risk mean absolute error (MAE) from 1.85 to 0.49 percentage points (pp). Across ten two-dimensional learners, calibration achieves 2.60--5.69~pp six-round core MAE on nine stationary learners (65--81\% below an unperturbed baseline), diagnoses non-stationary outlier drift in standard DDIM (16.38~pp) via a stability probe, and resolves the predicted six-round geometric reversal. On Fashion-MNIST latent flow-matching chains, calibration outperforms direct-chain Gaussian-process interpolation at lower fit budgets and tracks the 20\% latent-perturbation boundary shift (3.14 versus 10.78~pp MAE for proportion copying) driven by opposing inflow to the rare region and outflow from its core.

items.title: LimeTree: Linear-Memory Graph Neural Networks over Tree-Graphs for Resource-Efficient Language Modeling and Context Extrapolation
items.content: The search for computationally efficient alternatives to the Transformer has yielded numerous architectures in recent years; however, most exhibit severe weaknesses in associative recall-such as key-value (KV) retrieval-and length extrapolation, where even standard Transformers struggle. This paper introduces LimeTree, a linear-complexity architecture in both memory and compute for sequence modeling. By integrating synthetic KV retrieval tasks directly into standard language modeling training, LimeTree achieves strong perplexity alongside reliable recall. Two variants were evaluated on WikiText-103 and PG-19 under strict compute constraints. On WikiText-103, LimeTree reaches a token-level perplexity of 19 in just 6 hours on four Quadro RTX 8000 GPUs, while maintaining 100\% KV retrieval accuracy even when extrapolating from a training context length of 512 to an evaluation length of 16,384. On PG-19, the model achieves a token-level perplexity of 13 in 35 hours on a single RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU with minimal hyperparameter tuning. These results position LimeTree as a competitive linear-complexity alternative to Transformers, combining superior perplexity and training throughput with robust in-context retrieval and length extrapolation.

items.title: Black-Box Comparator-Adaptive Network Regret
items.content: We study comparator-adaptive decentralized online learning with network regret, which evaluates each node's prediction on the loss of every node in the network. We show that existing gossip-based algorithms are fundamentally limited for this task, and cannot achieve sublinear network regret with only one gossip step per decision round. To prove this, we construct a two-node counterexample, which shows that gossip-based algorithms can produce exponential regret despite bounded disagreement, resolving a previously open question in the literature. We then introduce a black-box reduction, which uses local learners with sublinear comparator-adaptive regret to obtain sublinear comparator-adaptive network regret. Each node exchanges predictions with its neighbors once per decision round, and a universal choice of edge weights works on every connected undirected graph without graph preprocessing. We also characterize admissible edge weights and show how weights adapted to the graph improve the regret bound. For example, for the complete graph, this improvement is quadratic in the number of nodes. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data illustrate the counterexamples we propose and compare the reduction with decentralized baselines.

items.title: Head Anything: Correspondence-Guided Joint Generation of 3D Heads from Few Images
items.content: Large image-to-3D generators recover detailed heads from a single photograph but treat every image as a new object. For several images of one person, they hallucinate unseen regions independently without using information from the other images. We present Head Anything, which generates detailed head meshes from a few images with changing expressions and viewpoints. Instead of training a multi-image prior, we turn a pretrained single-image generator with a native 3D latent space into a joint generator that denoises all images together. Since global attention between images is hard to learn from scarce 3D head data, lightweight correspondence-attention adapters let every 3D token attend only to its corresponding points in the other images. We obtain correspondences by fitting a neural parametric head model to the generator's own single-image outputs, requiring no ground truth at test time. Training on both ground-truth and fitted correspondences makes the adapters robust to fitting errors. Each mesh stays pixel-aligned with its own image and borrows the unseen regions from all others. On head scans, Head Anything lowers the head Chamfer distance of the best image-to-3D generator by 32% and its cross-frame inconsistency by 47%, and its meshes improve face tracking. Code and models will be released.

Correspondences come from fitting a neural parametric head model, avoiding training a costly multi-image prior. This addresses independent hallucination across views in few-shot 3D head reconstruction.

items.title: AI-driven technique could help engineers design analog chips faster and with less expense
items.content:
A new technique developed by MIT researchers could help engineers use artificial intelligence to streamline the design and innovation of analog integrated circuits, semiconductor chips that perform vital functions like communication and power management in electronic devices.

In the future, this method could allow engineers to prototype faster, explore a wider range of chip designs, and discover new design schemes that might improve the performance and energy efficiency of robots, medical monitors, or industrial sensors.

Designing analog integrated circuits that meet specific requirements is usually a cumbersome manual process due to the enormous number of possibilities. Frontier generative AI models have shown success in automating the process, but using these resource-intensive, cloud-hosted models could expose proprietary circuit design and semiconductor foundry data to malicious users.

The MIT method, called Small LM Iterating on Circuits, or SLIC (pronounced “slick”), enables engineers to train a small language model to perform analog circuit design as well as or better than a frontier large language model (LLM). 

This small model is inexpensive and efficient enough to run on a laptop. Because it’s trained and deployed locally, it can use a company’s circuit design data without raising privacy risks. 

When compared to complementary baselines and open-weight frontier LLMs, a small model trained by SLIC more effectively generated designs that achieved the circuit objectives. 

“We’ve provided an alternative option to automate analog circuit design. With our technique, engineers can train a small, locally deployable model, using their own confidential data, and then deploy it in their own environment to ensure their assets remain protected,” says Yan Xu, an electrical engineering and computer science (EECS) graduate student and lead author of a paper on this technique.

She is joined on the paper by senior author Ruonan Han, a professor of EECS and a member of the MIT Research Laboratory of Electronics; Zhengqi Gao PhD ’26; Wenjie Lu PhD ’18, a former MIT postdoc who is now a principal research scientist at Analog Devices, Inc.; Xin Zhang, a research manager at IBM Research; Duane S. Boning, the Clarence J. LeBel Professor in EECS and MIT vice provost for international activities; and others at IBM Research and Analog Devices. The research will be presented at the 2026 Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems. 

“Through some specialized training and area-specific research, we can use much smaller models that consume far fewer resources to achieve almost the same results as flagship models in analog circuit design,” says Han. “This opens many more possibilities in the design of complex chips, especially if we care about costs, data privacy, and customization.”

Mimicking human learning

Analog integrated circuits enable a device to interact with the physical world. For instance, these circuits boost incoming wireless signals in smartphones and process outputs from sensors that track a car’s engine temperature. 

Real-world signals tend to be unpredictable, so engineers must balance a wide and complex array of targets and tradeoffs to maximize analog circuit performance. This has made the design problem especially challenging for AI models.

“To design a circuit, engineers find a good starting point based on their intuition and then, drawing on their knowledge of circuit design, tune a few knobs toward the performance they want,” says Xu. “There is no universal way to solve every circuit design problem.”

Even if a powerful, cloud-based model could design a circuit as well as a human, most companies would be reluctant to send their foundry-specific data to external AI service providers.

With SLIC, the MIT researchers created a training method that teaches a smaller, less expensive, faster language model to design analog integrated circuits that meet user specifications. 

The SLIC model uses a few billion parameters, making it several thousand times smaller than frontier models that use trillions of parameters and require enormous amounts of computational resources. 

“We tried to mimic the behavior of how a human learns to design a circuit,” Xu says.

They used a technique called multi-turn reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, where a model works through a multi-step task while adapting to environmental feedback. 

When given an analog circuit optimization task, SLIC uses a large LLM to generate several demonstrations of the open source design process. Then SLIC then uses these demonstrations to guide the small model in mimicking this design process. 

After the small model gains some initial knowledge about circuit design, SLIC lets it practice by tackling a new design problem on its own.

The model makes an initial guess of the design parameters, performs simulations, evaluates the results, and iteratively refines the design using knowledge it gained about analog circuits.

Once a design achieves the user’s goals, SLIC prioritizes additional marginal gains. This means the model keeps learning to make improvements that boost performance even when several designs meet the user-defined targets. 

An interpretable process

Importantly, because SLIC employs models that describe their reasoning using natural language, the user can understand the decisions it makes along the way.

“Although the whole process is automated, the user can see what is going on inside the model. This could help the user gain some new ideas about circuit design, and it also adds a lot of confidence about the decision-making process,” Han says.

An engineer could utilize SLIC by adapting the researchers’ trained model to their data using a fine-tuning process. Or they could employ the SLIC training process to build their own model with company data, allowing for more customization.

“We are seeing an increasing demand for analog chips, but the speed of design has not kept up. This research is trying to bring new capabilities to AI to solve a problem that industry has been stuck on for decades,” Lu says.

When the researchers tested SLIC’s ability to design a circuit that met desired performance metrics, their small model came close to matching the performance of the latest GPT model (GPT-6-Astra). It did this while using a fraction of the computational resources. 

The researchers also found that the SLIC model maintained its performance when tackling previously unseen circuit structures and adapting to more advanced technology nodes (design and manufacturing rules) and real commercial processes.

Because SLIC teaches a model the general chip design process, the system is not tied to any company. This makes it a more scalable approach that could be used by many organizations for a range of circuit applications.

“The knowledge the model has gained about circuit design is universal in nature. That is the powerful aspect of this tool,” Han says.

In the future, the researchers want to explore self-improving models that can independently learn to handle more diverse topologies and design targets. They also want to use SLIC to build a multi-agent framework, in which many small language models work on different parts of a complex circuit design task.

“Yan’s work shows that a locally deployable model can learn transferable design behavior and iterate with a circuit simulator to improve a design, which could reduce repetitive manual tuning for engineers. This is the kind of work the MIT-IBM Computing Research Lab makes possible. We see it as opening the door to more sophisticated custom design, including RF and microwave circuits, in the settings where industry actually works,” says Zhang.

This research is funded, in part, by Analog Device, Inc., IBM, and the John L. Ocampo Endowment Fund of MACOM Technology Solutions.
