items.title: iFeST: An Iterative Motion Correction Framework for Fetal Brain Diffusion MRI via Frequency-Spatial-Temporal Modeling
items.content: Fetal brain diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (dMRI) is a pivotal non-invasive tool for assessing the development of brain connectivity and microstructure. However, the prolonged acquisition times and complex sampling requirements render dMRI highly susceptible to unpredictable fetal motion. Existing motion correction methods typically process each dMRI volume independently and focus on inter-slice motion. Such strategies fail to utilize the coherent information between dMRI volumes along different diffusion directions and lack the ability to restore the intra-slice corruption. To address these limitations, we proposed iFeST, an iterative framework that combines frequency (k-space), spatial, and temporal (inter-slice) modeling for fetal brain dMRI motion correction. At each iteration, iFeST integrates information across diffusion directions into fiber orientation distributions (FODs). These distributions encode local fiber orientations within each voxel and serve as microstructural priors for intra-slice restoration and inter-slice alignment in the next iteration. To train the framework, we developed a fetal brain dMRI motion simulator that synthesizes compound motion artifacts from FODs. Evaluation on simulated datasets demonstrated that iFeST outperformed four inter-slice networks in motion estimation and three intra-slice networks in image restoration. Further validation on a real-world dataset confirmed significantly better volume reconstruction and FOD estimation than conventional pipelines. Overall, iFeST provides a learning-based framework for fetal dMRI motion correction, restoring motion-corrupted data and improving microstructural reconstruction for downstream diagnostic applications.

items.title: LeadVLA: Learning Follower-Aware Route Execution for Robot Leading
items.content: Robot leading requires executing a route while continuously adapting to a designated follower. Existing robot-leading systems often mediate follower understanding and physical route execution through explicit states, planners, or modular interfaces; directly learning this coupling through end-to-end trajectory prediction can instead entangle route execution with follower response. We introduce LeadVLA, a structured multimodal policy that preserves the route as an explicit Path reference while learning a Pace for route progress and a Residual for local follower- and scene-conditioned adaptation. To make this problem trainable and measurable, we develop LeadInfra, a configurable Unreal Engine-based closed-loop data-generation infrastructure from which we instantiate an approximately 4M-sample training corpus, and LeadBench, a standardized benchmark with 108 fully held-out closed-loop episodes. LeadVLA achieves the highest task success (39.6%) among evaluated robot policies on LeadBench while maintaining strong route fidelity and follower responsiveness, and transfers to unseen real-world environments without real-world policy fine-tuning. Project Page: https://louiszengCN.github.io/LeadVLA_PAGE/

items.title: EditGRN: Inversion-Free Image Editing by Source-Target Generative Synchronization
items.content: Text-guided image editing faces a persistent trade-off between preserving source content and realizing coherent target semantics. We explore this challenge through training- and inversion-free image editing based on discrete generative models. Existing inversion-free discrete editors primarily rely on post-hoc probability correction, creating a disconnect between local token-level adjustments and globally coherent semantic generation. To bridge this gap, we introduce EditGRN, a training- and inversion-free framework with trajectory-wide source-target generative synchronization in discrete space. EditGRN adopts a dual-branch design---the source branch constructs source references and the target branch generates the target image-enabling trajectory-wide synchronization between the two. Exploiting GRN's ability to recover clean tokens from arbitrary binary corruptions, the source branch directly constructs corrupted source states at each refinement step to extract useful editing features, without recovering a specific source-generation trajectory. The target branch synchronizes with the source branch through the same corruption schedule, fusing the corresponding source context with editable representations intra-model. By synchronizing source context with target generation along the entire trajectory, our approach faithfully preserves the background while producing high-quality edits that blend seamlessly with the surrounding scene through intra-model fusion. PIE-Bench show state-of-the-art performance on background preservation and text alignment across diverse editing tasks against continuous and discrete baselines.

items.title: Skill-Adaptive Noise Scheduling for Diffusion Policies
items.content: Recent advances in diffusion policies have demonstrated strong effectiveness when integrated into hierarchical skill-based learning frameworks, leveraging offline data to capture multimodal and temporally abstracted behaviors. However, prior approaches have rarely considered the diffusion process as a learnable component, adopting fixed noise schedules applied uniformly across skills, regardless of their distinct behavioral contexts. Such a design fundamentally limits the achievable performance, particularly for contact-rich and dexterous manipulation tasks where different skills exhibit distinct couplings between action dimensions. In this paper, we present a skill-adaptive noise diffusion framework (SaND) which introduces a learnable, skill-conditioned noise schedule that modulates the diffusion process per action dimension, adapting the noising dynamics to each skill. To prevent the learned noise schedule from collapsing into trivial solutions, we employ an auxiliary inverse objective that reconstructs the skill embedding from the Legendre coefficients of the derivative of the noise schedule, encouraging the schedules to remain skill-discriminative. This formulation naturally enables adaptive control over the denoising steps for each skill, where noise schedules are clustered in the Legendre coefficient space, and the appropriate number of denoising steps is determined at the point where reconstruction error abruptly increases. At inference, we identify each skill embedding's cluster from its noise schedule and apply the corresponding number of denoising steps, dedicating more compute to skills requiring fine-grained control and less to simpler ones. In simulation and on real robot hardware, SaND outperforms existing skill learning and planning baselines on contact-rich and dexterous manipulation tasks, achieving higher success rates while requiring fewer denoising steps.

items.title: Face Is Not All You Need: MIME Benchmark for Incomplete Multimodal Emotion Recognition
items.content: Multimodal Emotion Recognition (MER) is a fundamental task in multimedia understanding, where state-of-the-art methods have achieved prominent success relying on the assumption of complete, well-aligned multimodal inputs. However, real-world unconstrained scenarios often suffer from unpredictable modality degradation and information loss, leading to catastrophic performance collapse of existing MER models that heavily depend on facial cues as the core inference anchor. However, few systematic works evaluate model robustness under diverse, fine-grained incomplete settings, as prior works are limited to coarse-grained full-modality removal and neglect interpretable analysis of emotional reasoning. To bridge this gap, we formally define the Incomplete Multimodal Emotion Recognition (IMER) task, which benchmarks model generalization and robustness under multi-grained modality and emotional information loss. We further construct MIME, a dedicated IMER benchmark with 2,000 video segments covering realistic fine-grained facial-detail degradation, severe facial degradation, and extreme full-modality loss, surpassing the limited coarse-grained settings of prior works. We also propose the Chain of Emotion (CoE) analysis paradigm with tailored metrics to dissect the fine-grained emotional cue perception and reasoning process of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). Extensive experiments on seven mainstream MLLMs reveal that body language and scene context act as critical compensatory mechanisms under facial degradation, while a pronounced gap exists between models' basic visual perception ability and high-level cognitive reasoning. Our work provides a focused evaluation platform and actionable insights for advancing robust multimodal emotion recognition. Our dataset and code are public at https://yuxinokk.github.io/MIME.

items.title: SceneCast: Learning Indoor Scene Synthesis from Curated Synthetic Videos with LLM Reward
items.content: 3D indoor scene synthesis requires generating objects to form a complete and coherent scene. Existing approaches rely heavily on manually annotated datasets, leading to high costs and limited generalization. We present SceneCast, an annotation-free framework that trains on large-scale, unlabeled videos, addressing two key challenges: (1) Videos provide only partial views of a scene, requiring the model to extrapolate unseen 3D regions, which is inherently error-prone; (2) Raw videos available online are uncurated, suffering from uncontrolled conditions and variable data quality. First, we design a Transformer-based model that predicts objects sequentially and is fine-tuned with reinforcement learning (RL), where an LLM acts as a spatial common-sense evaluator. The LLM provides reward signals through chain-of-thought reasoning and code-executable geometric checks to refine object configurations. Second, we introduce \trim, a data curation approach that generates training videos with controllable video generation models. Crucially, it retains only high-quality prefix clips via multi-criteria quality assessment with an entropy-based weighting strategy. Evaluated on curated synthetic video sets, our annotation-free approach outperforms state-of-the-art supervised methods in scene quality.

It addresses partial-view extrapolation and uncurated video quality challenges.

items.title: IP-GNO: An Inductive Physics-Informed Graph Neural Operator for Automated Distribution System State Estimation
items.content: Distribution System State Estimation (DSSE) is a crucial tool for real-time monitoring, operation, and control of the new-age distribution systems (DSs) due to intensified voltage fluctuations and operational uncertainties introduced by volatile power injection at the nodes. Existing GNN-based approaches generally exhibit limited generalization across networks with different sizes and topologies, making zero-shot cross-grid transfer to unseen DSs a significant challenge. To overcome the aforementioned challenges, this article proposes an Inductive Physics-Informed Graph Neural Operator (IP-GNO) for scalable and transferable DSSE. The proposed framework frames complex bus voltage estimation as an operator-learning problem inspired by the Neumann series expansion of the inverse bus admittance matrix. An admittance-parameterized kernel, incorporating a self-admittance gate in the zeroth-order term and a persistent source-injection skip connection across network layers, captures the underlying electrical dependencies. Additionally, a Physics-Embedded Tree Encoding (PETE) scheme introduces five grid-size-invariant positional features derived from path impedance and a DC-linearized phase-angle prior. A sine-cosine output formulation is further employed to address phase-angle periodicity and ensure stable training. The proposed IP-GNO module is evaluated on two small (IEEE 33- and 69-bus), two medium (IEEE 123- and 136-bus), and one large (2522-bus) sized DSs. Particularly, its zero-shot cross-grid generalization capability is investigated by training the model exclusively on the IEEE 33-bus system and directly evaluating it on four unseen distribution networks of different sizes without retraining or fine-tuning. A detailed comparative analysis with the existing state-of-the-art DSSE tools proves the superiority of IP-GNO, enabling scalable DSSE across heterogeneous DSs.

items.title: TAP: Policy Interfaces for Diffusion Language Models
items.content: Diffusion language models denoise a masked canvas, making them a natural setting for selective generation decisions such as answering, waiting, clarifying, or refusing. We introduce TAP-DiLM, which adds a typed policy variable to masked diffusion LMs, and study how this policy should be attached to the denoising process. Across BERT-base, MDLMOWT, LLaDA-8B, and Dream-7B, we compare shared-vocabulary slots, dedicated slot heads, and CLS-based external heads. The results reveal a clear interface-backbone interaction: dedicated heads provide robust policy learning across scales, while sharedvocabulary heads can be effective when the LM-head geometry is favorable. A simple LMhead sharpness probe predicts when sharedhead policy internalization is reliable, giving a practical diagnostic for interface selection. Causal clamp and slot-injection tests show that dedicated policy slots can influence body denoising through feedback, especially at 8B scale. Safety-refusal experiments further show that TAP-DiLM supports competitive typed refusal behavior when trained with diverse unsafe prompts.

It finds dedicated heads are robust across scales while shared-vocabulary heads depend on LM-head geometry, and offers an LM-head sharpness probe as a diagnostic.
items.reasoning: A forward-looking study on controllable selective generation in diffusion language models, an emerging model class; the interface-backbone interaction findings and practical diagnostic add value, though the area is still early and results may shift as architectures mature.

items.title: Struct2Det: Grounding Category Structure in Visual Evidence for Few-Shot Object Detection
items.content: Few-shot detectors struggle to distinguish categories that look alike but differ in local components, because a few examples rarely reveal which differences determine category identity. Category descriptions specify components and relations but do not establish their presence in an image. We propose Struct2Det, which uses category structure to guide detection and verify candidates in three stages. Relational Structure Encoding maps category graphs to component embeddings and a global condition. Component-Grounded Detection uses component queries to retrieve multi-scale image evidence that, with the global condition, modulates category text embeddings for initial detection. Verification-Guided Refinement matches candidate regions with components expected by their top-scoring categories; when class scores are close and matches are reliable, matched pairs correct region features before the shared detector predicts again. Category structure informs both classification inputs: text embeddings integrate image-wide component evidence, while region features incorporate candidate-specific matches. We also construct InduSym, with 88,912 symbol instances across 275 categories from 674 engineering drawings and a structural graph per category. Struct2Det improves few-shot-category AP over the strongest baseline by 6.02 points on InduSym and 9.68 on Digitize-PID, with the highest base-category AP on both. InduSym ablations show few-shot gains from correct category structure, image-level retrieval, and candidate verification. Further tests show gains in few-shot natural-object detection and zero-shot Chinese character recognition.

items.title: VeriOrigin: A Proactive Image Protection Framework for Provenance, Tamper Localization, and Lossless Recovery
items.content: Versatile watermarking, which seamlessly integrates provenance and tamper detection, has recently attracted widespread attention. In this paper, we propose \textbf{VeriOrigin}, a comprehensive and unified image protection framework that not only robustly achieves provenance and highly precise tamper localization under various complex distortions, but also guarantees perfect recovery of the original cover in lossless channels. To realize this framework, we depart from conventional flow based architectures. Instead, we design \textbf{XOnet}, a CNN based invertible encoder. XOnet comprises two standard CNN based watermarking sub networks, Xnet and Onet, which achieve reversibility through cross residual prediction. Based on XOnet, we train the proactive protection scheme via a two stage strategy: first optimizing the watermarking branch, followed by the tamper localization branch. During inference, the cover image undergoes sequential watermarking and tamper residual embedding. Extensive experimental results on four datasets demonstrate that VeriOrigin achieves precise tamper localization and strong robustness, while guaranteeing lossless cover recovery for integrity authentication. Project page is available at https://veriorigin.github.io/

Its XOnet component is a CNN-based invertible encoder achieving reversibility through cross residual prediction between two subnetworks, replacing conventional flow-based architectures. Training uses a two-stage strategy.
items.reasoning: Useful integration of multiple watermarking capabilities in one invertible architecture with relevance to provenance in the era of generated media, but the core novelty relative to prior versatile watermarking work appears moderate.

items.title: Physics-Constrained Neural ODEs for Learning Traffic Dynamics and Trajectories from Road Entry/Exit Times
items.content: We consider the problem of learning microscopic traffic dynamics and reconstructing vehicle trajectories from section entry/exit timestamps (EET) recorded by cameras and from the positions of a probe vehicle leading the platoon. The dynamics are difficult to recover as each vehicle's position is measured only at two points, and its trajectory between them is unknown. By combining Neural ODEs with a local density approximation, we learn a follow-the-leader model whose speed--density relation is a neural network. With such sparse data, an unconstrained network may learn physically unrealistic relations, such as negative speeds or non-zero speeds on a fully congested road. We therefore introduce a normalization that, applied to a monotone neural network with a learned regime change, enforces the endpoint conditions, guaranteeing an admissible speed--density relation while provably retaining the ability to approximate any admissible one. We validate the method on first- and second-order simulations, recovering the speed--density relation of the first-order model and reconstructing the trajectories of both models, with mean maximum position errors of 2.50~m and 2.51~m, respectively, on a 125~m road segment. On real-world ring-road data, the proposed model still yields an admissible relation, whereas both baselines violate the constraints; the large spread in the data, however, highlights the limitations of a first-order model with homogeneous driver behaviors.

items.reasoning: Careful physics-informed ML work on a genuinely hard inverse problem with sparse data, but the application domain and method scope limit broader impact.

items.title: Motion on Demand: Adaptive Optical Excitation for Event Cameras
items.content: Event cameras respond only to brightness changes, so whether an edge is visible depends on image motion perpendicular to it---a motion that constantly shifts with camera and scene dynamics. Rotating a wedge prism in front of the lens introduces controlled image motion to reveal static or slow edges. However, a fixed rotation speed cannot adapt to changing motion conditions: when natural motion is already sufficient, additional optical excitation generates redundant events and introduces unnecessary alignment errors. Inspired by the division of labor between fast haltere feedforward and slower visual feedback in fly gaze control, we present EvGaze, an event camera system that adaptively regulates prism rotation speed. EvGaze employs a learned multimodal controller that integrates luminance, event, and inertial observations, with a fast inertial pathway that refines speed decisions between visual updates. To preserve geometric consistency during speed changes, we compensate for prism-induced image motion at individual event timestamps using measured encoder angles. On EvMotion, EvGaze recovers more edges than full-speed prism rotation with 39% fewer events. On DSEC with simulated optical modulation, it reaches 0.73 feature-tracking success (compared with 0.55 on native events and 0.67 at 180 RPM) while generating 26% fewer events than 360 RPM. Real-device experiments further demonstrate online closed-loop adaptation, reducing average event rates by 17% relative to full-speed rotation.

items.title: Trallie: from Free-Form Text to Structured Data with LLMs
items.content: Trallie is an open-source framework that leverages large language models (LLMs) to perform information extraction (IE) from natural language sources with or without user guidance. Unlike conventional approaches that rely on extensive labeled datasets or domain-specific training, Trallie enables the conversion of unstructured data into structured formats with minimal or no representative examples. The framework is designed with three key objectives: (i) reducing manual annotation by harnessing prompt-based zero-shot and few-shot capabilities of modern LLMs, (ii) flexibly parsing diverse document formats (i.e., HTML, PDF, TXT, and JSON), and (iii) improving accessibility for non-expert users by automatically inducing schemas from document collections, which can then be refined for extraction. We evaluate Trallie with open-weight LLMs on FDA 510(k) documents and on movie and university websites from SWDE. It outperforms previously reported systems when the target attributes are provided for text extraction and is competitive when it must discover attributes for the schema automatically. The project is available at https://github.com/PiSchool/trallie

items.reasoning: A practical, well-motivated open-source tool combining schema induction with zero/few-shot extraction; engineering-oriented rather than a novel algorithmic contribution, but high usefulness and accessibility.

items.title: Beyond Domain Randomization: Real-World Policy Adaptation in Learned Dynamics for Legged Robots
items.content: Reinforcement learning policies are often trained with static domain randomization for real-world deployment. However, real-world environments often exhibit unmodeled dynamic variations, such as payload changes or friction shifts, that lie outside the randomization distribution, leading to performance degradation upon deployment. We propose a framework that moves beyond static domain randomization by adapting a learned dynamics model to the deployed target conditions, with a concurrent teacher-student paradigm applied to both the policy and dynamics model. This framework integrates the dynamics model into an on-policy reinforcement learning pipeline, letting the performance of the policy align with the empirical target dynamics. Experimental validations on bipedal locomotion tasks demonstrate competitive adaptability under extreme physical variations, including a payload reaching 80% of self-weight and an oil-lubricated low-friction surface.

Experiments on bipedal locomotion demonstrate improved robustness to unmodeled dynamics such as payload and friction changes.
items.reasoning: Addresses a well-known sim-to-real gap with a sensible adaptive dynamics formulation and real legged-robot validation; the direction is increasingly explored but the integrated teacher-student design and empirical grounding are solid.

items.title: NeuroMotion: Aligning EEG to Discrete Motion Primitives for Continuous Motion Decoding
items.content: EEG-to-motion decoding remains challenging because noisy scalp EEG is difficult to map directly to continuous kinematics. We present NeuroMotion, a framework that aligns EEG representations to discrete motion primitives for continuous motion decoding across heterogeneous paradigms, including full-body free movement, lower-limb treadmill locomotion, and upper-limb freewill reaching and grasping. A VQ-based motion prior discretizes continuous motion into reusable primitives that serve as both alignment prototypes and intermediate prediction targets. Prototypical and supervised contrastive objectives align EEG embeddings to motion-derived prototypes and organize them according to primitive assignments. An E2M Transformer predicts motion-code sequences from the learned EEG representations, while a final geometric refinement stage improves continuous trajectory reconstruction through motion-level training. Under a last-session test protocol, NeuroMotion achieves the best mean reconstruction performance among the compared EEG decoding baselines across all three datasets, with the clearest gains on full-body motion in both reconstruction accuracy and distribution-level quality. Multi-subject ablations further support the contributions of EEG-to-primitive alignment, token prediction, and refinement. Code is available at https://github.com/Liuyi2351433/NeuroAction.

It works across heterogeneous paradigms including full-body free movement, treadmill locomotion, and upper-limb reaching and grasping.
items.reasoning: A creative use of discrete motion priors and contrastive alignment for a hard decoding problem, with unusually broad paradigm coverage; clinically promising but evaluation across truly wild EEG conditions remains a question.

items.title: Fast and Consistent Structure Learning in Graphical Models via Approximate Cross-Validation
items.content: Structure learning for sparse graphical models in high dimensions requires both computational scalability and selection consistency. Classical criteria such as (Extended) Bayesian Information Criterion can provide consistency, but rely on model-specific likelihoods and complexity calibration. In comparison, cross-validation avoids such analytic calibration and is therefore attractive for graph learning. However, cross-validation is computationally infeasible and theoretically inconsistent in structure learning. This creates a tension between consistency and flexibility in modeling. In this work, we resolve the tension by developing a scalable graph-recovery procedure built on approximate cross-validation. We demonstrate its effectiveness in learning large graphical models both theoretically and empirically, and establish selection consistency under mild signal strength assumptions.

They provide consistency guarantees and demonstrate effectiveness on large graphical models.
items.reasoning: A clean theoretical-plus-practical resolution of a known tradeoff in graphical model selection, with both consistency theory and scalability; strong for the statistics audience but not broadly visible to mainstream AI.

items.title: How Do Deep Networks Encode and Selectively Use Information? Shared Encoding and Conditional Signed Readout in Vision and Language Models
items.content: How can trained deep networks retain contextual information across internal representations while using it selectively in a decision? We study this question through controlled background-texture edits in vision classifiers and entity-binding edits in frozen language models. Across both modalities, factor perturbations preserve recognizable structure across pre-fixed, mutually disjoint blocks of hidden units: visual channel blocks match their complements more closely for the same image than for other images under the same texture edit, while language blocks transfer a relational direction fitted under one query role to rank relational states within held-out name pairs under the other role. We then decompose the local output change into signed channel and pathway contributions. In a convolutional classifier, net channel-level reinforcement ($R^{(512)}>1$) coexists on individual images with cancellation between positive- and negative-weight groups ($R^{(2)}<1$). Holding weights, the paired relation edit, and red/blue answer words fixed, switching prompt presentation reverses the mean finite selection effect in Qwen2.5. Two held-out tests validate this mechanism. Attenuating development-selected antagonistic units amplifies edit effects on unseen inputs; in a vision transformer, attenuating the same frozen units in one forward pass increases the mean magnitude of the background-edit effect on one class margin and reduces it on another, with the opposite pattern for a second group (four-cell paired interaction $+78.30\times 10^{-5}$ logit). Finally, combining conditional channel variance with fixed downstream readout weights predicts single-channel pruning recovery across ten cuts. These results show how shared encoding and conditional signed readout can coexist in vision and language models.

items.title: STEALTH: Steganographic Text Encoding Agnostic to Low-Level Tensor Hardware
items.content: Provably secure linguistic steganography hides a message inside text sampled from a language model, so that without the key, a stegotext is computationally indistinguishable from an honest model sample. Nearly every such scheme assumes the receiver can recompute the sender's token probabilities exactly bit for bit. We show this assumption is fragile: across three model families, bit-exact schemes decode almost none of our messages once the receiver's floating-point precision, quantization, or GPU architecture differs from the sender's, or even when the receiver merely scores a text in parallel versus one token at a time, with the same model, precision, and hardware held fixed. We present STEALTH, a scheme built for exactly this setting. The sender draws each token with an exponential race driven by keyed pseudorandom noise, so a receiver's probability mismatch flips a token only when the race is close; a rateless spinal code, decoded by beam search, absorbs the resulting flips without the sender and receiver ever agreeing on a single distribution. We prove stegotexts remain indistinguishable from honest samples under this construction. Empirically, STEALTH decodes every message we sent for every receiver in the sender's model family, at every precision and quantization level, on smaller models, and on a different GPU architecture. STEALTH is even robust across different model families with separate vocabularies and tokenizers, decoding every message we tested. Our approach carries far more payload per token than prior robust schemes, and trained steganalyzers and a targeted statistical test both fail to distinguish its stegotexts from honest model output.

items.summary: The paper demonstrates that provably secure linguistic steganography schemes break in practice when the receiver's floating-point precision, quantization, GPU architecture, or even batching differs from the sender's, since they assume bit-exact recomputation of token probabilities. STEALTH introduces an exponential-race token sampling scheme that remains robust to these hardware-level discrepancies.
items.reasoning: A technically sharp contribution exposing a fragile assumption underlying provably secure steganography and offering a hardware-agnostic fix; valuable for security and covert communication, but a relatively specialized corner of AI research.

Our approach carries far more payload per token than prior robust schemes, and trained steganalyzers and a targeted statistical test both fail to distinguish its stegotexts from honest model output.

items.title: Lorentz symmetry in self-supervised representation learning
items.content: Self-supervised learning (SSL) and explicit physical inductive biases have driven major advances in jet tagging, yet they are typically pursued along separate tracks. In this work, we unify both paradigms by integrating the Lorentz-equivariant Geometric Algebra Transformer slim (L-GATr-slim) architecture with the LeJEPA framework for representation learning. Pre-training on 100 million jets from the JetClass dataset, we optimize towards a latent space, which is invariant across physics-motivated jet augmentations. We demonstrate that enforcing Lorentz symmetry in the latent space is critical for representation quality and that this can be achieved either architecturally or learned via kinematic augmentations. With a standard non-invariant Transformer backbone, LeJEPA outperforms established autoregressive, masked particle modelling, and self-distillation baselines in linear- and MLP-probe accuracy, with L-GATr-slim providing further complementary gains. Across downstream benchmarks, our pre-trained models consistently outperform baselines trained from scratch or through different pre-training objectives.

items.title: NoveltyGate: Novelty, Not Error, Decides Which VLA Prefix Tokens to Compute Exactly
items.content: Flow-matching vision-language-action (VLA) models such as $\pi_{0.5}$ re-encode the camera images and the instruction with a 2B-parameter backbone at every control step, and the feed-forward layers of this prefix account for most of its compute. A natural way to save this compute is to send most tokens through a low-rank MLP and compute exactly only the tokens whose approximation error is large. We find that this intuition is wrong. Even a verifier that knows every token's exact error picks the wrong tokens, producing 1.3--1.7$\times$ larger action deviation than a simple test of whether a token's input is novel, that is, whether it falls outside the subspace seen during calibration. Large errors concentrate in tokens the policy relies on little, such as the third-person camera, while the novelty test favors the wrist camera, a view the action depends on heavily. We call this the error--reliance gap. Building on it, we propose NoveltyGate, a training-free method that routes each prefix token, once per layer and before any multiplication, to either a low-rank or the original MLP. Deciding once per layer instead of once per matrix product avoids moving wide intermediate tensors and keeps every shape static, so the whole prefix runs as a single CUDA graph. On LIBERO, NoveltyGate accelerates the $\pi_{0.5}$ prefix by up to 1.61$\times$, stays 2.7--2.9$\times$ closer to the original policy than channel pruning and low-rank compression at equal compute, and preserves closed-loop task success.

items.summary: This paper studies compute-efficient flow-matching vision-language-action models and shows that selecting which prefix tokens need exact computation based on approximation error is the wrong criterion: an oracle error verifier performs worse than a simple novelty test checking whether a token input lies outside the calibration subspace. The novelty-based gate yields 1.3-1.7x lower action deviation.
items.reasoning: A crisp, counterintuitive empirical insight for efficient VLA inference with clear practical implications, but it is a focused single-author contribution on one model family (pi-style flow-matching VLAs), so scope and generality are limited.

items.title: Data-Driven Identification of Uncertainty Sets with Conformance Guarantees
items.content: Formal verification and controller synthesis require accurate models. Conformance relations specify the required accuracy of a model such that properties established for the model carry over to the target system. Existing methods for establishing them from measured data are typically restricted to a single relation, a specific model class, or a downstream verification algorithm. We present ConfID, a unified framework that establishes reachset, trace, and simulation conformance with respect to measured traces by identifying uncertainty sets for a given, possibly nonlinear nominal model. Unmodeled effects are thus captured by nondeterminism rather than by refining the nominal dynamics. For all three conformance relations, the identification is a linear program that minimizes the size of the reachable sets; only its constraints depend on the relation. We further derive distribution-free bounds on the probability that the identified models are conformant for unseen behaviors. Experiments on simulated and real-world data evaluate the models identified for the three relations, confirm the guarantees, and show that these models cover unseen behaviors more reliably than baselines, with comparable or smaller sets.
items.author: Laura L\"utzow, Mykel J. Kochenderfer, and Matthias Althoff
items.summary: ConfID is a unified framework that establishes reachset, trace, and simulation conformance between a possibly nonlinear nominal model and measured traces by identifying uncertainty sets, treating unmodeled effects as nondeterminism. For all three conformance relations the identification reduces to a linear program minimizing set size. This enables formal verification and controller synthesis guarantees grounded in data.
items.reasoning: Theoretically clean unification with practical convexity properties, from a credible control-theory group (Althoff, Kochenderfer); relevance is strongest in formal methods and control rather than core machine learning.

items.title: EEG Decoding in Context: A Framework for Tuning-Free EEG Foundation Models
items.content: Electroencephalography (EEG) decoding is a central route toward brain-computer interfaces for communication, rehabilitation, cognitive assessment, and neurological monitoring. Recent EEG foundation models have substantially advanced reusable signal representations, but their downstream use still typically requires a task-specific decoder, gradient-based adaptation, and validation-driven model selection. We investigate a complementary foundation-model paradigm based on in-context learning: labeled EEG recordings define the decoding task as context, and new recordings are predicted without updating model parameters. We first pair raw EEG features with a pretrained general-purpose in-context predictor. This direct formulation provides a promising starting point, but its performance remains limited and unstable and does not generalize reliably across EEG paradigms. We find that suitable context construction can address these limitations by improving the effective signal-to-noise ratio and exposing temporal and spatial structure. Building on this insight, we introduce a general framework that combines EEG-specific context construction with a frozen in-context predictor and a metric-based context adaptation mechanism, which matches each downstream task to an appropriate context representation without relying on validation data. Across ten datasets spanning seven EEG decoding paradigms, our method achieves the highest mean BAcc among eleven specialized and fine-tuned EEG baselines, without task-specific parameter updates or validation-based model selection. This framework provides a practical path toward tuning-free EEG foundation models in which adaptation is expressed through context rather than parameter updates.

items.summary: The paper proposes an in-context learning paradigm for EEG foundation models in which labeled recordings define the decoding task as context and new recordings are decoded without parameter updates, eliminating task-specific decoders and gradient adaptation. Direct pairing of raw EEG features with a pretrained general-purpose in-context predictor is a promising but limited starting point that the framework then improves. Relevant to brain-computer interfaces and cross-domain transfer of in-context learning.
items.reasoning: Interesting transfer of the in-context learning paradigm to biosignals with clear practical value for BCI deployment; novelty lies mainly in the application domain, and EEG data scale constrains how far results will generalize.

items.title: Matching Under Metric Privacy
items.content: We study how to represent and randomize points in $d$-dimensional Euclidean space to obtain accurate bipartite matchings under metric privacy. Given $n$ private and $n$ public points, we analyze local mechanisms that randomize each private point or its distances to the public points. Using the public points' affine span, we construct a smaller representation that preserves all matching costs. When a trusted server receives the private points, we establish privacy and utility guarantees for Gumbel matching, which randomizes edge costs and releases only the assignment. Through upper bounds and worst-case constructions, we establish the tight rate $\Theta\!\left(n\min\{d,\log n\}/\varepsilon\right)$ for expected cost above the nonprivate optimum. Benchmark experiments support $d\approx\log n$ as a practical guide to the transition between directly randomizing point coordinates and using Gumbel matching. Extensions to squared Euclidean costs enable private nonparametric two-sample hypothesis testing. These results show how the application's trust model guides representation and dimension choices for better utility: under local privacy, low-dimensional point representations reduce excess cost, while under central privacy, distance representations achieve the optimal rate even in high dimension.
items.author: Hongyi B. Hu, Dung Nguyen, M. Amin Rahimian
items.summary: This theoretical work studies how to randomize private points in d-dimensional Euclidean space so accurate bipartite matchings can be computed, establishing the tight rate Theta(n min(d, log n)/eps) for expected cost above the nonprivate optimum. It analyzes Gumbel matching under a trusted server and constructs compact representations preserving matching costs using the affine span of public points.
items.reasoning: Rigorous theory with tight privacy-utility bounds for a well-defined problem at the intersection of differential privacy and algorithm design. Solid contribution, but the problem setting is specialized and immediate practical impact is limited.

items.title: Comparing AI R&D compute caps and deployment lags
items.content:
I’m publishing this a bit rougher than usual because it’s very pertinent to Evan Hubinger’s recent shortform, which advocates for blocking internal deployment as a pacing mechanism over compute reallocation (he mostly discusses it in the context of a risk-assessment-based regime, while this post discusses the policies standalone). (see my response to Evan which also summarizes this post.)

I compare 2 classes of policies:

- AI R&D compute cap: A cap on the percentage of compute used for capabilities R&D, as proposed at pacing-ai.com.
- Deployment lags/freezes: An X-month lag means that you have to use models X months old for AI R&D (or, AIs at most as capable as the AIs you trained X months ago). [1] A freeze means you pick a capability level above which you can’t use models to do AI R&D. I sometimes separate out internal-only lags/freezes from internal+external (“uniform”) ones. If I just say lag, I mean it as shorthand for lag/freeze.

Overall, I think compute caps are similarly good or slightly better than deployment lags/freezes (very possible I’ll change my mind in the future). Ignoring political feasibility, I think the best would be to combine both of them in order to get the immediate slowdown of the cap and the long-term + structural benefits of the lag/freeze.[2] I think it’s close enough that if one is significantly more feasible than the other, we should push for the more feasible one.

I prefer internal deployment lags to external deployment lags because I think the societal awareness benefits are larger than the verification costs.

Factor

Cap vs. lag/freeze

Reasoning

Capability curve shape

Compute cap (weak)

Let’s consider lag 6 months vs. cap 10% implemented in Mar 2027, which result in similar TED-AI dates.

Compute caps slow now->SAR more than lags, while lags slow SAR->TED-AI more. Here's a quick screenshot of an illustrative example comparing the 2 policies:

Aggregating uplift-years, varying point of no return (PONR): The higher the capability level of the PONR, the better lags look relative to caps; if it’s ~SAR then caps look slightly better, if it’s ~TED-AI lags look much better. With lags, you delay higher capability milestones more than you do with caps.

We’ll look at total uplift-years divided by a racing baseline, with a baseline of SAR in Jul 2027 and TED-AI in Nov. Uplift-years = ∫ (AI R&D uplift of the best model trained) dt from Jan 2027 until the PONR capability level is passed.[3]

- No China, SAR PONR: Cap ~2.2x, lag ~2x
- No China, TED-AI PONR: Cap ~1.8x, lag ~3x
- No China, uncertainty over PONR [4] (35% before SAR, 65% before halfway from SAR to TED-AI, 80% before TED-AI; same PONR for both policies): Cap ~2x, lag ~2.2x
- With China + TED-AI pause until China catches up, uncertainty over PONR: Both ~2.4x

Other considerations in favor of relatively stronger immediate pacing relative to later pacing:

- China might just not race in the first place, even if the US did.
- Pacing is more cooperative than racing.
- Stronger immediate pacing means more serial time to make a deal, or adjust the pacing regime to be better at higher capabilities.
- AI improvements harm the ability to do international deals even if they aren’t directly dangerous. See here.
- Going slower now is more robust against others failing to slow down further in the future.

Other considerations in favor of relatively weaker immediate pacing relative to later pacing:

- Going slower now leads to more overhang, meaning faster progress if the regime is lifted. The effect size of this appears to be fairly modest in our modeling; e.g., if both policies are ended right before the lag gets to SAR, the lag takes 2.1 months to go from SAR->TED-AI while the cap takes 1.9 months. [5]

Differences in point of no return capability level

Deployment lag

Not using your best AIs for AI R&D potentially pushes back the point of no return substantially because it makes it harder for AIs to adversarially prevent humans from aligning future AIs. This effect seems potentially quite large if you’re using e.g. current-level AIs or lower for your AI R&D.

Some quick modeling using my highly uncertain estimated PONR gap distribution says that this effect might be very important, e.g. changing lag 6 months vs. cap 10% from roughly equal geomean of uplift-years to lag 6 months being ~2.5x higher.

Verification ease / robustness

Uniform lag > compute cap ~= internal-only lag.

Uniform lag > compute cap ~= internal-only lag.

See below for more.

Societal awareness

Against external deployment lag

(Pushing in the opposite direction of verification ease/robustness)

Enabling safety research

Compute cap (weak)

In both proposals, there’s the question of handling safety research:

- In the AI R&D compute cap proposal, can you have a carve-out for using the non-AI-R&D compute for safety R&D?
- In the deployment lag proposal, can you have a carve-out for using the non-lagged model to conduct safety R&D?

Both seem like similarly difficult problems. Let’s consider each situation in turn:

- If both have a safety carve-out, then an AI R&D compute cap is better than a deployment lag. The situation is similar except that under the AI R&D compute cap, most compute is forced to be spent on either safety or external inference, leading to more compute being spent on safety than in the deployment lag world.
- If there isn’t a safety carve-out, then it’s unclear, but my best guess is that an AI R&D compute cap is worse than a deployment lag. There’s a tradeoff where there’s probably less compute used for safety in the compute cap world, but a better model. It’s unclear to me how that shakes out, but at least Evan Hubinger has the intuition that it’s better in the deployment lag case because models are differentially worse at safety.

Maximum slowdown amount

Compute cap

A well-enforced compute cap of 0% could result in very nearly a full pause, while banning use of AIs for AI R&D would not.[6] See an example trajectory:

Important for: emergencies, international coordination, strong safety-case-based regimes

Robustness to different timelines

Unsure

Caps are better on short timelines and worse on long ones.

## Verification

In terms of ease of verification: Uniform lag > compute cap ~= internal-only lag.

Our guess is that with a uniform lag, ~5% verification error can be achieved with significantly less effort / auditing access, though we’ve done less analysis than for the compute cap.[7] We discuss this attack surface here.

### Attacks against compute caps and internal deployment lags

Depending on their implementation, the verification problem for compute caps and internal deployment lags via auditors will need to deal with three overall classes of attacks:

- Attacks that free up compute. These are attacks that allow the company to use compute in a way that auditors don’t have visibility into. These attacks include getting off-books compute (hidden compute), using compute that is declared to be idle (fake idle) and having spare compute by actually running workloads more efficiently than what is declared or observed (hidden efficiency). Attacks 1-3 in our previous work.
- Attacks that turn external inference into capabilities benefits. These are attacks that allow external inference to be used as if it were internal inference by just directly having employees use the external API (launder internal inference), collaborating with third parties for R&D or data generation, or training directly on outputs generated via external inference. This only applies to internal-only lags (because uniform lags also restrict external inference). Attacks 4-6 in our previous work.
- Attacks that consist of exploiting the ‘non-capabilities’ exemption. This only applies to deployment lags that include an exemption for safety research. Attack 7 in our previous work.

Additionally, internal deployment lags have to deal with a fourth class of attack:

- Doing internal deployment via training runs. This would involve having AIs do AI R&D during training runs, e.g., as part of RL rollouts in post-training. Attack 8 in our previous work.

In our previous work, we analyzed how the first 3 classes of attacks are all applicable to a compute allocation cap, unless you did a version of the proposal that had no carve-out for ‘non-capabilities R&D’, in which case you could avoid attack 7, or if you didn’t allow serving customers as a category (in which case you could avoid attacks 4-6).

In this supplement on internal deployment lags, we identify three possible ways of implementing an internal deployment lag:

- Uniform Deployment Lag — covered models must be in cold storage, with no internal or external deployment.
- Internal Deployment Lag — covered models cannot be internally deployed.
- Internal Deployment Lag with safety carve-out — covered models cannot be internally deployed except for a carved-out application area (e.g., AI safety research).

#1 requires defending against attacks 1-3 and 8, #2 against attacks 1-6 and 8 (it avoids attack 7), and #3 against all eight.

### Verification measures

Quantitatively, we are most worried about attacks #5 and #7. This makes a uniform deployment lag highly attractive from a verification perspective. More here

In order to sufficiently defend against attacks in general, it seems necessary to adopt a significant fraction of the measures listed below. Read more

Measures 1-7 would be the most important as they address attacks 5-7 (assuming an internal deployment lag or a compute cap).[8] These will require an extensive auditing effort with privileged (not just entry-level employee) access and a lot of technical expertise on the auditing teams. Measure 6 in particular will require having multiple different entities submit to audits, so will greatly increase the auditing capacity necessary.

Measures 8-15 might become increasingly important to ramp up to as well, but appear less urgent initially. That being said, they generally have long lead times, so effort put into them early might be necessary in order for the verification to keep error sufficiently low for long enough.

- ^ Unless noted, lags apply at once: AI R&D switches to the older model on the start date, with no grandfathering of models already in use.
- ^ In the model the delays roughly add: from Mar 2027, cap 10% plus a 6-month lag delays TED-AI by 23 months, against 11 for each alone.
- ^ Under a lag this counts the frontier model even though AI R&D can't use it, so it assumes that model still does useful work elsewhere (outside users, wakeup, or a safety carve-out). Counting only the AIs allowed to do AI R&D, the lag scores ~0.7x / ~0.4x / ~0.6x of racing (SAR / TED-AI / uncertain PONR) and the cap is unchanged.
- ^ Another way to think about this is it’s weighting how much we care about each capability level. From this perspective, one reason to care about higher levels of capability less is that we have more time to intervene before then if the initial policy is suboptimal.
- ^ The effect is a bit larger if we instead assume they both get lifted at SAR; it takes the lag 2.2 months to get to TED-AI, vs. 1.5 months for the cap.
- ^ Note that it might be very hard to actually get to ~0%. pacing-ai.com estimates ~6% error even with robust auditing. It might similarly be hard to get to a ~zero error deployment lag/freeze.
- ^ By 5% verification error, we mean a capabilities gain equivalent to adding a marginal 5% capabilities compute (against the margin of a 20% compute cap).
- ^ For a uniform deployment lag, these attacks don’t apply, and so these measures aren’t necessary.

Discuss

  • No China, uncertainty over PONR [4] (35% before SAR, 65% before halfway from SAR to TED-AI, 80% before TED-AI; same PONR for both policies): Cap ~2x, lag ~2.2x
  • With China + TED-AI pause until China catches up, uncertainty over PONR: Both ~2.4x

Other considerations in favor of relatively stronger immediate pacing relative to later pacing:

  • China might just not race in the first place, even if the US did.
  • Pacing is more cooperative than racing.
  • Stronger immediate pacing means more serial time to make a deal, or adjust the pacing regime to be better at higher capabilities.
  • AI improvements harm the ability to do international deals even if they aren’t directly dangerous. See here.
  • Going slower now is more robust against others failing to slow down further in the future.

Other considerations in favor of relatively weaker immediate pacing relative to later pacing:

  • Going slower now leads to more overhang, meaning faster progress if the regime is lifted. The effect size of this appears to be fairly modest in our modeling; e.g., if both policies are ended right before the lag gets to SAR, the lag takes 2.1 months to go from SAR->TED-AI while the cap takes 1.9 months. [5]

Differences in point of no return capability level

Deployment lag

Not using your best AIs for AI R&D potentially pushes back the point of no return substantially because it makes it harder for AIs to adversarially prevent humans from aligning future AIs. This effect seems potentially quite large if you’re using e.g. current-level AIs or lower for your AI R&D.

Some quick modeling using my highly uncertain estimated PONR gap distribution says that this effect might be very important, e.g. changing lag 6 months vs. cap 10% from roughly equal geomean of uplift-years to lag 6 months being ~2.5x higher.

Verification ease / robustness

Uniform lag > compute cap ~= internal-only lag.

Uniform lag > compute cap ~= internal-only lag.

See below for more.

Societal awareness

Against external deployment lag

(Pushing in the opposite direction of verification ease/robustness)

Enabling safety research

Compute cap (weak)

In both proposals, there’s the question of handling safety research:

  • In the AI R&D compute cap proposal, can you have a carve-out for using the non-AI-R&D compute for safety R&D?
  • In the deployment lag proposal, can you have a carve-out for using the non-lagged model to conduct safety R&D?

Both seem like similarly difficult problems. Let’s consider each situation in turn:

  • If both have a safety carve-out, then an AI R&D compute cap is better than a deployment lag. The situation is similar except that under the AI R&D compute cap, most compute is forced to be spent on either safety or external inference, leading to more compute being spent on safety than in the deployment lag world.
  • If there isn’t a safety carve-out, then it’s unclear, but my best guess is that an AI R&D compute cap is worse than a deployment lag. There’s a tradeoff where there’s probably less compute used for safety in the compute cap world, but a better model. It’s unclear to me how that shakes out, but at least Evan Hubinger has the intuition that it’s better in the deployment lag case because models are differentially worse at safety.

Maximum slowdown amount

Compute cap

A well-enforced compute cap of 0% could result in very nearly a full pause, while banning use of AIs for AI R&D would not.[6] See an example trajectory:

Important for: emergencies, international coordination, strong safety-case-based regimes

Robustness to different timelines

Unsure

Caps are better on short timelines and worse on long ones.

Verification

In terms of ease of verification: Uniform lag > compute cap ~= internal-only lag.

Our guess is that with a uniform lag, ~5% verification error can be achieved with significantly less effort / auditing access, though we’ve done less analysis than for the compute cap.[7] We discuss this attack surface here.

Attacks against compute caps and internal deployment lags

Depending on their implementation, the verification problem for compute caps and internal deployment lags via auditors will need to deal with three overall classes of attacks:

  • Attacks that free up compute. These are attacks that allow the company to use compute in a way that auditors don’t have visibility into. These attacks include getting off-books compute (hidden compute), using compute that is declared to be idle (fake idle) and having spare compute by actually running workloads more efficiently than what is declared or observed (hidden efficiency). Attacks 1-3 in our previous work.
  • Attacks that turn external inference into capabilities benefits. These are attacks that allow external inference to be used as if it were internal inference by just directly having employees use the external API (launder internal inference), collaborating with third parties for R&D or data generation, or training directly on outputs generated via external inference. This only applies to internal-only lags (because uniform lags also restrict external inference). Attacks 4-6 in our previous work.
  • Attacks that consist of exploiting the ‘non-capabilities’ exemption. This only applies to deployment lags that include an exemption for safety research. Attack 7 in our previous work.

Additionally, internal deployment lags have to deal with a fourth class of attack:

  • Doing internal deployment via training runs. This would involve having AIs do AI R&D during training runs, e.g., as part of RL rollouts in post-training. Attack 8 in our previous work.

In our previous work, we analyzed how the first 3 classes of attacks are all applicable to a compute allocation cap, unless you did a version of the proposal that had no carve-out for ‘non-capabilities R&D’, in which case you could avoid attack 7, or if you didn’t allow serving customers as a category (in which case you could avoid attacks 4-6).

In this supplement on internal deployment lags, we identify three possible ways of implementing an internal deployment lag:

  • Uniform Deployment Lag — covered models must be in cold storage, with no internal or external deployment.
  • Internal Deployment Lag — covered models cannot be internally deployed.
  • Internal Deployment Lag with safety carve-out — covered models cannot be internally deployed except for a carved-out application area (e.g., AI safety research).

#1 requires defending against attacks 1-3 and 8, #2 against attacks 1-6 and 8 (it avoids attack 7), and #3 against all eight.

Verification measures

Quantitatively, we are most worried about attacks #5 and #7. This makes a uniform deployment lag highly attractive from a verification perspective. More here

In order to sufficiently defend against attacks in general, it seems necessary to adopt a significant fraction of the measures listed below. Read more

Measures 1-7 would be the most important as they address attacks 5-7 (assuming an internal deployment lag or a compute cap).[8] These will require an extensive auditing effort with privileged (not just entry-level employee) access and a lot of technical expertise on the auditing teams. Measure 6 in particular will require having multiple different entities submit to audits, so will greatly increase the auditing capacity necessary.

Measures 8-15 might become increasingly important to ramp up to as well, but appear less urgent initially. That being said, they generally have long lead times, so effort put into them early might be necessary in order for the verification to keep error sufficiently low for long enough.

  • ^ Unless noted, lags apply at once: AI R&D switches to the older model on the start date, with no grandfathering of models already in use.
  • ^ In the model the delays roughly add: from Mar 2027, cap 10% plus a 6-month lag delays TED-AI by 23 months, against 11 for each alone.
  • ^ Under a lag this counts the frontier model even though AI R&D can't use it, so it assumes that model still does useful work elsewhere (outside users, wakeup, or a safety carve-out). Counting only the AIs allowed to do AI R&D, the lag scores ~0.7x / ~0.4x / ~0.6x of racing (SAR / TED-AI / uncertain PONR) and the cap is unchanged.
  • ^ Another way to think about this is it’s weighting how much we care about each capability level. From this perspective, one reason to care about higher levels of capability less is that we have more time to intervene before then if the initial policy is suboptimal.
  • ^ The effect is a bit larger if we instead assume they both get lifted at SAR; it takes the lag 2.2 months to get to TED-AI, vs. 1.5 months for the cap.
  • ^ Note that it might be very hard to actually get to ~0%. pacing-ai.com estimates ~6% error even with robust auditing. It might similarly be hard to get to a ~zero error deployment lag/freeze.
  • ^ By 5% verification error, we mean a capabilities gain equivalent to adding a marginal 5% capabilities compute (against the margin of a 20% compute cap).
  • ^ For a uniform deployment lag, these attacks don’t apply, and so these measures aren’t necessary.

items.title: Vision-Language Truck Driving Advisories Grounded in Provincial Rules and Forecast Risks
items.content: Vision-language models (VLMs) can generate context-aware driving advisories, but their outputs may conflict with road conditions or traffic rules, and they typically address a hazard only once it is visible. This matters for long-haul trucking, where heavy trucks need long stopping distances and a single trip may cross several jurisdictions with different traffic regulations. This paper proposes a data generation and distillation framework that integrates structured scene understanding, risk forecasting, and traffic-rule retrieval to generate truck driving decisions and natural-language advisories, with a consistency check on every record. The records, written by an 8B teacher, are then used to distill a 3B-parameter student model for onboard deployment. We also introduce a dashcam dataset covering four Canadian provinces, comprising 11,142 annotated lane-marking frames and 9,494 driving segments. On held-out driving data across all four provinces, the student passes the consistency check in 94.6% of the segments, against 20.2% for the untuned 8B teacher, and announces 26.2% of the risks in the next 10 to 30 seconds before they appear. Of the generated advisories, 97.7% conform to the provincial traffic rules and guidance. These findings suggest that the framework can produce rule-conforming training data for compact driving advisory models.

An 8B teacher generates records with consistency checks, distilled into a 3B student model for onboard deployment, accompanied by a new dashcam dataset. It addresses the practically important problem of long-haul trucking across jurisdictions with varying traffic rules.

items.title: SceneTether: Activity-Gated Value Anchoring for Long-Horizon Autoregressive Image Animation
items.content: Long-horizon image animation must keep the scene fixed while natural material (e.g., water, smoke, or fire) continues to move. Autoregressive video generators read recent frames for temporal continuity, but this history also carries accumulated appearance errors, and sparsifying it disrupts motion. We introduce SceneTether, a training-free attention-read policy that keeps where attention reads recent memory but changes what appearance that memory returns. SceneTether keeps every key of the newest latent, blends its low-activity values toward co-located source-image values, and leaves high-activity values untouched so motion can evolve; an activity map estimated from the first generated latents and then frozen decides where to blend. It adds no denoising evaluations and leaves the cache-update rule unchanged. On a Causal Forcing++ generator, SceneTether raises source-support PSNR by 5.15 dB over its framewise Echo host across two seeds with 1.5x its late activity, and by 7.31 dB over spatial Echo-Forcing on a preselected four-minute subset. At equal recent-memory coverage, value anchoring alone adds 8.14 dB. A post-hoc pixel composite with the same map matches static fidelity but retains nearly twice the moving-region color drift, and viewers in a small blinded study preferred SceneTether for its natural scene and motion preservation. Project page: https://minar09.github.io/scenetether/

An activity map estimated from the first generated latents and frozen thereafter gates the blending.
items.reasoning: A clever, training-free intervention addressing a well-known failure mode (error accumulation in long video generation) with no added denoising cost; practical and well-motivated, though evaluated on a specific generator family.

items.title: LoKiTO: Local Kinodynamic Trajectory Optimization for UAVs based on Memory-Efficient Neural Distance Fields
items.content: This paper introduces LoKiTO, a 3D local kinodynamic trajectory optimizer that combines a Chebyshev polynomial parameterization with an online neural Euclidean Signed Distance Field (ESDF) representation for aerial robotics. While current gradient-based planners often struggle with the high memory requirements of explicit volumetric maps or fail to strictly enforce dynamic limits, LoKiTO embeds kinodynamic constraints directly into a modular cost function and exploits the numerical conditioning properties of the Chebyshev basis. Collision awareness is provided by a continuous, memory-efficient neural ESDF updated online from LiDAR measurements, which drastically reduces map memory consumption to approximately 1.0 MB. Benchmarking in highly cluttered simulated environments against state-of-the-art baselines (Fast-Planner and EGO-Planner) demonstrates the superiority of our approach. Experimental results show that LoKiTO achieves over 99.4% dynamic feasibility compliance, significantly outperforming the baselines, and maintaining higher median clearance from obstacles. By coupling a well-conditioned continuous parameterization with explicit kinodynamic reasoning, LoKiTO provides a practical and extensible basis for local replanning in aerial robotics.

items.title: Accelerating wave-scattering simulations with learned search directions
items.content: Wave-scattering simulation requires solving a dense boundary-element system for every frequency, incidence and design. Krylov solvers build each search space from scratch, and it grows with problem size. Here we present BEMFormer, a solver that learns to generate search directions across systems of one integral equation and supplies geometry-specific directions through a coarse-grid correction. BEMFormer generalizes to unseen geometries, meshes and excitations, and to acoustic scattering after fine-tuning on eight geometries. It reproduces the measured radar cross-sections of benchmark targets. On a quadcopter with 1.04 million unknowns, 38 times the largest training problem, BEMFormer solves each system 30 times faster than a preconditioned Krylov solver. Both reach a radar cross-section deviation of about 1 dB, comparable to the difference between independent measurements and acceptable for engineering applications. These results show that solving million-unknown scattering problems in minutes is possible when the search space is learned rather than built from scratch.

Strong scientific computing result combining learning with classical numerical methods.

items.title: BitShare: Sensitivity-Aware Binning and Bit Sharing for Compacting LLM Weight Storage
items.content: Decoding with large language models at small batch sizes is limited by memory bandwidth, so the bits stored per weight largely set its cost. Group-wise integer quantization stores every weight of a group at the same precision, although the input channels of a group differ in sensitivity. We present BITSHARE, a codebook-free weight format that keeps the integer grid and the dequantizer of group-wise quantization but varies precision within each group. Sensitivity-aware binning places the channels of each group into three bins at fixed positions, and static bit sharing with optimal bit-value allocation lets the less sensitive weights share their lower bits, each stored once per group or once per pair of weights. A sharing-aware version of GPTQ chooses every stored value, with no fine-tuning and no codebook. BITSHARE has two modes. BITSHARE-U gives every group the same layout, so its decoder routes bits by fixed wiring, while BITSHARE-N chooses a layout per group within the same bit budget. With calibration on the Pile and at the same storage, both modes have lower perplexity than GPTQ at 3 and 2 bits on WikiText-2 and C4. At 2 bits across Llama-2 and Llama-3 models, BITSHARE-N lowers WikiText-2 perplexity by up to 70% against SliM-LLM and up to 35% against GPTAQ. At the 2-bit perplexity of SliM-LLM, BITSHARE-U stores 13.6-19.4% fewer bits per weight, cutting DRAM weight traffic by the same fraction. A verified hardware decoder implementation synthesized in SkyWater 130 nm reconstructs BITSHARE weights at the throughput of INT-n and SliM-LLM decoders.

This targets memory-bandwidth-bound small-batch LLM decoding.
items.reasoning: Practical compression contribution with an elegant bit-sharing idea compatible with existing group-wise quantization; solid but incremental within the busy LLM quantization space.

items.title: Bridging Blind Spots With Words: Decentralized Multi-View Spatial Reasoning via Language-Constrained Communication
items.content: As multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) get increasingly used as collaborative partners across embodied robotics, AR/VR, and multi-user systems, spatial reasoning is now often distributed across agents with partial environment visibility, necessitating spatial reasoning integration. Prior work in language-mediated spatial integration is however strictly limited to simplified two-agent scenarios. To address this gap, we first formalize the general problem of decentralized multi-view spatial reasoning, where N agents observe distinct viewpoints, exchange budget-constrained natural language messages, and collaborate to enable a listener to answer spatial queries. We then introduce a novel multi-view spatial benchmark to isolate queries that demand non-trivial multi-view integration. Through an extensive empirical study, we discover that the penalty of restricting decentralized spatial reasoning to natural language with limited budget is far smaller than suggested by prior two-agent literature. Nevertheless, we observe that substantial headroom still remains for multi-agent spatial reasoning in this setting, as evidenced by a significant gap between current centralized performance and an oracle best-of-K ceiling. Moreover, we show that reinforcement learning with credit assignment substantially bolsters the decentralized model, effectively closing the gap with the centralized baseline.

It extends language-mediated spatial coordination beyond prior two-agent settings.
items.reasoning: A well-posed generalization of an increasingly relevant problem for embodied and multi-agent systems, with a new benchmark that could serve the community, though grounded in existing multimodal LLM capabilities rather than new model techniques.

items.title: Denoised but Not Improved: What EEG Denoising Does to a Downstream Task
items.content: Scalp electroencephalography (EEG) is routinely denoised before it reaches a downstream model, and the denoising literature scores a method by how closely its output matches a clean reference waveform. That reference does not exist for real scalp recordings: it is synthesized by adding artifact templates to signals merely presumed clean, and even an exact separation would return cortical activity blurred by volume conduction rather than the activity itself. Fidelity to it is therefore an unvalidatable objective, and whether it predicts any downstream benefit has gone largely unexamined. We report an audit that examines it. Holding a seizure-detection pipeline fixed and varying only the preprocessing stage, we find that five standard denoising methods, spanning analytic, cross-channel and supervised deep families, all fail to improve on the unprocessed signal, and most degrade it. To say what such a stage must instead do, we formalize a label-only, classifier-free probe that reads it by the separability geometry it induces on task-relevant features, decomposing any change into a between-class distance and a within-class scatter term. On a transform that does improve the task, the probe attributes the entire gain to a roughly one-quarter reduction of within-class scatter, with class separation statistically unchanged. What a downstream model benefits from is therefore variance suppression on task-relevant structure, which waveform-fidelity metrics neither measure nor reward.
items.author: Xianglong Bao, Zhe Wang, Kewen Wang, Ming Jin
items.summary: This audit paper shows that five standard EEG denoising methods, scored by fidelity to synthesized clean references, provide no downstream benefit when inserted into a fixed seizure-detection pipeline. It argues the standard denoising evaluation objective is unvalidatable since the clean reference is synthetic and even perfect separation returns volume-conduction-blurred cortical activity.
items.reasoning: A well-reasoned negative-result audit challenging an established evaluation practice has methodological value for the neural signal processing community. The finding is important but confined to a specific modality and one downstream task, limiting general impact.

On a transform that does improve the task, the probe attributes the entire gain to a roughly one-quarter reduction of within-class scatter, with class separation statistically unchanged. What a downstream model benefits from is therefore variance suppression on task-relevant structure, which waveform-fidelity metrics neither measure nor reward.

items.title: RSLaA: Self-Reconfiguring Roadside LiDARs as Agents for 3D Traffic Perception
items.content: Cooperative perception with roadside LiDARs (RSLs) extends the sensing range of autonomous vehicles and resolves onboard-sensor occlusions, particularly at curves and intersections. Because infrastructure deployment is costly, existing work optimizes RSL configurations once, against road geometry and aggregated traffic statistics, and treats them as fixed thereafter. Traffic flow, however, is inherently dynamic, and a placement optimal on average can be far from optimal at any given moment. We introduce RSLaA (Roadside LiDARs as Agents), a framework in which each RSL adaptively adjusts its pose to the evolving traffic scene over decision-time windows. Since ground truth is unavailable at decision time, the framework centers on surrogate metrics computed solely from a probabilistic occupancy grid of historical observations, which predicts the next-window perception performance of candidate poses. We construct a co-simulation benchmark pairing five candidate surrogates with detector-agnostic ground-truth perception labels at every decision window, identifying the multi-view coverage metric J_mv as the most reliable predictor. Upon this validated surrogate we build two adaptive configuration methods, a receding-horizon (MPC) optimizer and a lightweight MAPPO-based multi-agent reinforcement learning scheme with centralized training and decentralized execution. Across 10 sites and 89 six-hour traffic scenarios (890 evaluation runs), adaptive configuration consistently improves the composite perception score over static deployment. Our results indicate that RSLs could be benefitted from being treated as agents.

items.title: HKD-ACPA: Heterogeneous Knowledge Distillation Adversarial Cyber-Physical Attacks in Power Grids
items.content: Learning-based algorithms assist power-grid control centers in localizing transmission-line attacks, yet existing adversarial attacks typically require white-box access or repeated online queries. We study a practical zero-query setting in which an adversary coordinates physical, denial-of-service (DoS), and false data injection (FDI) attacks using only local measurements and historical detector outputs. To bridge the input-view asymmetry between local adversarial observations and DoS-masked control-center measurements, we propose Heterogeneous Knowledge Distillation Adversarial Cyber-Physical Attacks (HKD-ACPA). HKD-ACPA distills historical detector predictions into a heterogeneous graph surrogate ensemble and trains a residual calibration module to correct the view-induced logit discrepancy. Over this calibrated surrogate, we formulate sparse, magnitude-bounded FDI synthesis with a group-balanced objective that jointly induces missed detections and false alarms, and solve the resulting hybrid discrete--continuous problem via bi-level projected gradient-based proximal policy optimization (PGPPO). Experiments on the IEEE 30-bus and 118-bus systems show that HKD-ACPA outperforms all surrogate-based baselines across every sparsity budget and surpasses online-query attacks in eight of ten system--budget settings without querying the detector model.
