items.title: GameAnything: From Any Inspirations to Playable Game Worlds
items.content: AI-driven game development holds the potential to transform diverse human inspirations into interactive experiences. However, existing systems and benchmarks primarily focus on explicit development specifications, with limited support for adapting multimodal references and evaluating actual gameplay experiences. We introduce GameAnything, an open-source agentic platform that transforms multimodal inspirations into playable extensions of existing games through iterative development. GameAnything integrates coding agents with an independent playtesting critic, persistent development state, and reusable experience memory to support continuous refinement. We further present GameAnything-Bench, a benchmark spanning diverse reference modalities, game creation objectives, and gaming environments, with exploratory gameplay testing to assess both functional correctness and gameplay quality. Evaluations of nine coding agent configurations reveal that current agents can adapt reference content but still struggle with playable interactions and precise modifications. Moreover, multimodal references improve content fidelity, while iterative refinement yields substantial but varying improvements across agents. These findings highlight both the potential and remaining challenges of inspiration-driven game development.

items.title: ContinuLoc: Continuous Pose Inference over Neural Fields for UAV Geo-Localization
items.content: Cross-view UAV geo-localization involves three design choices: how to represent the UAV observation, how to represent the geo-referenced map, and how to infer pose from their interaction. The dominant paradigm organizes the map as a discretized 2DoF candidate library, coupling map representation to pose inference and thus bounding spatial localization precision by candidate sampling resolution. We decouple map representation from pose inference by encoding the geo-referenced map as a continuously queryable semantic neural field, enabling localization to be formulated as explicit optimization over a continuous 4DoF pose space parameterized by 2D ground position, in-plane heading, and viewing scale. Pose hypotheses are evaluated on demand using global descriptors in a shared semantic feature space, bypassing the sampling bottleneck of retrieval. We learn 4DoF pose-sensitive visual representations under full 4DoF supervision provided by ContinuScenes, a multi-city benchmark with dense near-nadir UAV imagery and complete pose annotations. Inference proceeds hierarchically, progressing from broad pose-space coverage to adaptive concentration on high-compatibility regions. Experiments demonstrate substantial gains over representative localization paradigms under progressively stricter 4DoF accuracy criteria.   Code is available at https://github.com/ZhouWeikun/ContinuLoc/

items.title: Dual-Side Uncertainty Estimation: Calibrating Data and Model Uncertainty into a Shared Probability Space
items.content: Multimodal user intention analysis infers latent goals from heterogeneous behavioral observations but faces cross-modal input mismatch and output semantic errors. Existing uncertainty estimators focus on input reliability or output confidence and often reduce token uncertainty to simple statistics, overlooking structured dependencies. We propose DUE (Dual-Side Uncertainty Estimation), which jointly estimates input-side aleatoric and sentence-level epistemic uncertainty. From a single generation, Dirichlet perturbations of cross-layer representations produce an ordered token uncertainty sequence. A sequence-aware Normal-Inverse-Gamma estimator uses this sequence to quantify epistemic uncertainty and confidence in its estimate. Evidential multimodal alignment captures aleatoric uncertainty from noisy, incomplete, or inconsistent inputs. DUE calibrates both heterogeneous scores into a shared error-probability space and sequentially fuses them to estimate overall generation risk. Experiments demonstrate strong performance in input-mismatch detection, output semantic-error detection, and overall reliability estimation without repeated generation.

items.reasoning: Joint aleatoric-epistemic estimation in a shared probability space is a principled contribution to uncertainty quantification, and the single-generation design is computationally attractive. However, the framing around multimodal user intention analysis is narrow, and single-forward-pass uncertainty methods carry known reliability caveats.

items.title: Where Does Personalization Reside in Photo Editing? Evidence from One Photographer's Lightroom History
items.content: Personalized photo-editing systems must infer both a photographer's recurring preferences and the intent of a particular shoot, yet these signals are rarely evaluated separately. We study interpretable Lightroom adjustments in a longitudinal, private dataset of 3,193 edited photographs from 41 catalogs by one professional photographer, with holdouts formed at the batch level. We compare absolute and prior-relative targets, image-conditioned predictors, and estimators that receive a small set of edits from the target batch. Residual prediction improves validation error, but its advantage on held-out batches is small and not significant under a batch-clustered bootstrap (0.592 vs 0.582 EV exposure MAE). In a batch-shared protocol, closed-form shrinkage using 4, 8, or 16 same-batch anchors reaches 0.466, 0.457, or 0.453 EV with the best estimator at each k, compared with 0.586-0.592 EV for the prior-only baseline; the paired reductions are significant under a batch-clustered bootstrap. Learned anchor-conditioned heads do not improve on this closed-form estimator, and a negative-trained prior already yields a low cold-image false-edit rate, leaving little benefit for an additional gate. The recommended estimator is closed-form and auditable, and it requires only a handful of same-batch edits. A render-space check against 383 native Lightroom exports reproduces the ranking: at k=8, online EB lowers Delta E00 against the prior by 0.41 (p=0.042), and the photographer's true parameters lower it by 0.78 (p=0.034). An appendix extends the action space from six to thirteen global controls: a same-batch median look lowers rendered chroma toward the export, while a per-photograph residual head again fails to transfer. The study is limited to one photographer and does not claim that slider accuracy measures aesthetic preference.

items.summary: This paper analyzes 3,193 Lightroom edits from a single professional photographer to disentangle recurring personal preferences from shoot-specific intent in personalized photo editing. The work matters because it provides careful, statistically grounded evidence that personalization signals in creative workflows are harder to exploit than commonly assumed.

items.title: A Multi-Criteria Evaluation of Color Normalization Methods in Histopathology: Nuclei Preservation, Artifact Sensitivity, Background Fidelity, and Downstream Performanc
items.content: Deep learning models for nuclei detection and classification may generalize poorly across medical centers because of variations in staining and scanning. Although color normalization aims to reduce these variations, its effects on nuclear structure, background preservation, artifact sensitivity, and nuclei detection and classification performance have not been systematically evaluated. We present a procedure to benchmark 11 classical and deep learning normalization methods using 7 public and private nuclei datasets. Additionally, we investigate the effect of 7 input color spaces. The normalization methods differed in their effects on nuclear structure, background, and sensitivity to artifacts. However, detection and classification performance varied more across datasets than across normalization methods, and the input color space had limited influence. No single method performed best on all criteria, and image-level metrics did not reliably predict downstream performance, highlighting the need for nuclei- and structure-aware normalization methods. To support this work, we introduce WSI Quality Control and Normalization (WSI-QCN), a publicly available pipeline for robust whole-slide image quality assessment and color normalization; the source code is available on GitHub.

items.title: Self-Refining VLA Sampling
items.content: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models typically use flow-based generative modeling to learn a rich, often multimodal, distribution of robot actions. Generating samples from flow-based methods involves iteratively updating random noise, and distinct noise samples from the same state can result in distinct trajectories and task outcomes. Existing test-time scaling methods improve action chunk generation via selection, aggregation, or correction, but commonly require the generation of large ensembles of candidates or the training of an external corrector. We adapt Predict-and-Perturb (P&P), a self-refinement procedure for flow-based models originally used for mode-seeking in video generation, to the robotics domain. We find that applying P&P to VLA models requires modifications to the refinement process used in video generation due to differences in the underlying structure of the data. Across 400 episodes of LIBERO evaluated using SmolVLA, P&P improves upon the stock baseline by 5.3 percentage points. Further, episode-level P\&P uncertainty correlates strongly with task failure (AUC 0.851).

Required modifications to the refinement procedure are identified for the robotics domain.
items.reasoning: Useful efficiency contribution to VLA test-time compute, transferring an established technique cross-domain with domain-specific adaptation; solid but incremental.

items.title: Who Plays What: Same-Instrument Music Separation from Video
items.content: When two musicians in an ensemble play the same instrument, they sound alike and their instruments look alike. Audio-only separators, and audio-visual separators that rely on appearance, cannot tell them apart. What still differs is how each player moves, and when. We study same-instrument per-player separation: a user clicks one musician in a video and receives that musician's sound alone, even when other players in the video play the same instrument. Our model follows the clicked player and describes them with high level video features and the velocities of body and hand keypoints. A pretrained music separator attends to these tokens through cross-attention. Earlier motion-based separators were scored only on synthetic mixtures of solo videos. We give the first per-player evaluation of same-instrument separation on real ensemble recordings. On 58 players in URMP, each sharing an instrument with at least one other player in the piece, our model reaches a median SDR of 5.3 dB, while four released separators, audio-only and audio-visual, stay at or below 0.3 dB. The gap is wider on same-instrument duets, and our model also beats the audio-visual baselines on their own MUSIC benchmark. Tests show that the gain comes from movement: replacing the video with a still frame removes it, and so does shifting the video by a fraction of a second against the audio.

It provides the first real per-player evaluation rather than synthetic solo-video mixtures.

items.title: Agentic Discovery of Simple Symbolic Inventory Policies
items.content: Designing simple inventory policies becomes increasingly difficult as operational features and system configurations expand. We develop an Agentic Inventory-Policy Discovery System based on explicitly defined simple operational formula (SOF) policy and template classes. Large language models (LLMs) revise symbolic structures, while a numerical engine fits parameters separately for each instance and evaluates the induced policies. Multicriteria parent selection, state-specific operational diagnostics, and reusable symbolic motifs guide structural evolution. A three-stage progression develops shared templates across instances and configurations with varying state dimensions. Experiments on 15,600 instances spanning 50 demand distributions cover lead times, perishability, their combination, and lead times with limited customer patience. The discovered templates improve aggregate empirical performance over evaluated SOF benchmarks and are competitive with policies requiring more elaborate online computations. For a lost-sales system with a three-period lead time, we develop an average-cost decomposition and prove that, under specified demand and cost conditions, a capped dual-shortfall specialization of a discovered policy strictly outperforms every policy in the considered capped base-stock benchmark class. This analysis links the performance advantage to the discovered replenishment mechanism. Together, these results highlight the potential of agentic discovery to generate simple inventory policies with strong empirical performance and identify operational mechanisms amenable to rigorous theoretical analysis.

It is validated at scale on 15,600 instances across 50 demand distributions covering lead times and perishability.

items.title: Label-Efficient LiDAR Semantic Segmentation with 2D-3D Vision Transformer Adapters
items.content: LiDAR semantic segmentation models are typically trained from random initialization as universal pre-training is hindered by the lack of large, diverse datasets. Moreover, most point cloud segmentation architectures incorporate custom network layers, limiting the transferability of advances from vision-based architectures. Inspired by recent advances in universal foundation models, we propose BALViT, a novel approach that leverages frozen vision models as amodal feature encoders for learning strong LiDAR encoders. Specifically, BALViT incorporates both range-view and bird's-eye-view LiDAR encoding mechanisms, which we combine through a novel 2D-3D adapter. While the range-view features are processed through a frozen image backbone, our bird's-eye-view branch enhances them through multiple cross-attention interactions. Thereby, we continuously improve the vision network with domain-dependent knowledge, resulting in a strong label-efficient LiDAR encoding mechanism. Extensive evaluations of BALViT on the SemanticKITTI and nuScenes benchmarks demonstrate that it outperforms state-of-the-art methods on small data regimes. We make the code and models publicly available at: http://balvit.cs.uni-freiburg.de.

items.title: LithoFormer: A Robust Framework for Stratigraphic Inference via Transformers
items.content: Accurate geological characterization of subsurface reservoirs from well log data is essential to support projects such as carbon capture and storage (CCS), geothermal development, and extraction of natural resources. Existing automated techniques for geological characterization primarily use sliding-window classification, which limits their ability to understand broader geological contexts, often leading to misaligned formation layers. To overcome these limitations, we introduce LithoFormer, a robust framework for stratigraphic inference using a Seq2Seq transformer model that ingests entire multivariate well logs in a single pass. The framework utilizes a channel-independent PatchTST backbone enhanced with rotary positional embeddings (RoPE) to capture long-range geological dependencies across entire multivariate well logs. A decoupled multi-task head is employed to jointly predict geological zonation and precise boundary probabilities, while a geology-informed loss function enforces physical constraints such as the Law of Superposition. Validated and deployed on three real-world datasets, LithoFormer demonstrates a 90% reduction in median boundary error and eliminates stratigraphic order violations compared to traditional sliding-window baselines. It also achieves a 80% reduction in manual expert labor and eliminates stratigraphic inconsistencies, providing a scalable and reliable solution for large-scale subsurface modeling.

It targets subsurface reservoir characterization relevant to carbon capture, geothermal, and resource extraction. The whole-sequence approach captures long-range geological context and improves formation-layer alignment.
items.reasoning: A solid applied-domain architecture contribution adapting modern sequence-modeling components (PatchTST, RoPE) to a scientifically meaningful geoscience task, though niche in impact and not from a major lab.

items.content_html: Accurate geological characterization of subsurface reservoirs from well log data is essential to support projects such as carbon capture and storage (CCS), geothermal development, and extraction of natural resources. Existing automated techniques for geological characterization primarily use sliding-window classification, which limits their ability to understand broader geological contexts, often leading to misaligned formation layers. To overcome these limitations, we introduce LithoFormer, a robust framework for stratigraphic inference using a Seq2Seq transformer model that ingests entire multivariate well logs in a single pass. The framework utilizes a channel-independent PatchTST backbone enhanced with rotary positional embeddings (RoPE) to capture long-range geological dependencies across entire multivariate well logs. A decoupled multi-task head is employed to jointly predict geological zonation and precise boundary probabilities, while a geology-informed loss function enforces physical constraints such as the Law of Superposition. Validated and deployed on three real-world datasets, LithoFormer demonstrates a 90% reduction in median boundary error and eliminates stratigraphic order violations compared to traditional sliding-window baselines. It also achieves a 80% reduction in manual expert labor and eliminates stratigraphic inconsistencies, providing a scalable and reliable solution for large-scale subsurface modeling.

items.title: Reset Dependence Is Embodied: Training Protocol Changes Which Morphologies Appear Optimal
items.content: Robot co-design benchmarks rank bodies after training their controllers under a fixed episode protocol, but that protocol can change the ranking itself. Consequently, two studies can select different bodies from the same corpus even when they use the same task and evaluator. We study one part of that protocol, the reset rule, which ends a training episode when the robot's torso falls below a height threshold. We train proximal policy optimization (PPO) controllers for 100 DERL-evolved UNIMAL bodies with this threshold at 20% of each body's starting torso height (Standard), at 50% (Strict), or with no threshold (Reset-free), and score every controller with the same evaluator. The threshold changes which bodies look best: the rankings after Strict and Reset-free training correlate at only 0.21, against about 0.89 if seed noise were the only difference. Removing fall resets costs some bodies far more than others. Bodies evolved on flat ground lose 45% of their per-step reward relative to Standard training, and those evolved on variable terrain only 16%. Permutation tests over bodies support this difference, and on 24 bodies, flat-ground bodies gain the most from Strict over Reset-free training under both PPO and soft actor-critic (SAC). Choosing bodies by their worst reward across the three protocols costs little: in sample, they keep at least 91% of the reward of each protocol's best bodies, and over 80% averaged across held-out seeds. Co-design benchmarks should state their reset rule, test whether their rankings depend on it, and report bodies that stay strong across protocols. Project page: https://reset-dependence.github.io.

items.title: Estimating Silenced Tokens in Quantized LLMs
items.content: Quantization is the standard way to shrink large language models, and it is usually judged by perplexity and task accuracy. We ask a different question: after quantization, which words can the model still say at all? A token is silenced when no hidden state can make it the top choice of the output layer, so a greedy decoder can never produce it. We give a simple, scalable way to estimate how many tokens a quantized output head silences, combining three checks: a direction that lets a token win (so it is safe), an upper bound on how close a token's row is to being trapped inside the others, and an exact match that proves a token can never win. Each count is therefore a certified range: exact matches give its lower end and flagged tokens can only raise its upper end. In nearly all settings we report down to 3 bits the two ends coincide, so the counts are exact. Across three open models we find that quantization silences tokens: on large-vocabulary models it already appears at 8-bit precision, up to a few hundred previously reachable tokens on a 1B-parameter model, and grows as precision drops, while a small-vocabulary model resists until 3 bits. The loss is far from uniform across languages: on a multilingual vocabulary the silenced tokens are overwhelmingly non-Latin (Korean, Chinese, Thai, Arabic and Hebrew), even though Latin tokens dominate the vocabulary. Silencing is thus a measurable, language-sensitive side effect that standard averages miss, and it should be reported alongside them.

items.title: Action Windows Are Inherently Temporal: A Benchmark for Time-Sensitive Robotic Manipulation
items.content: Vision-language model (VLM) agents have surpassed learned-policy baselines on existing robotic manipulation benchmarks. However, these agents still struggle with time-sensitive everyday tasks that existing benchmarks for VLM agents cover only partially. In these tasks, evolving physical processes create finite windows for successful intervention. These action windows are inherently temporal and impose a shared time budget on decision making and physical execution. Coordinating intervention within this budget requires agents to determine when the window opens. We introduce AWAIT, a simulation benchmark that evaluates task completion within action windows while accounting for decision and execution time. Our evaluation reveals difficulties in recognizing window onset and shows that successive decisions and movements can exhaust an action window even when each decision takes less than the window duration. Project page: https://eyja42.github.io/await-site/.

Evaluation shows agents struggle to recognize window onset, and existing benchmarks cover such temporal constraints only partially.
items.reasoning: Fills a genuine gap in embodied-agent evaluation by emphasizing time-sensitive interventions; as a simulation benchmark its impact hinges on community adoption.

items.title: Wactorz: Self-Writing LLM Agents That Discover, Repair, and Migrate at the Edge
items.content: Most LLM agent frameworks build a crew that runs a task and exits. Physical environments (e.g., homes, labs, factory floors) need agents that stay up for months, survive their own bugs, and run on whatever hardware is already next to the sensors. We present Wactorz, an open-source runtime in which LLM-generated agents are long-lived, supervised actors: a planner turns a chat request into Python, compiles it into a new actor at runtime, and a supervisor restarts that actor alone, with its state intact, when it crashes. All coordination rides on MQTT, so agents can be spawned on, and live-migrated between, edge nodes such as a Raspberry Pi, and every internal event is a topic external systems can subscribe to. The recorded demo builds a camera-to-lamp automation from one chat request, adds a second agent that is auto-wired to the first by topic and carries a deliberate division-by-zero, watches that agent repair its own code without losing its count, then deploys a fresh Raspberry Pi node and live-migrates the agent onto it, in under four minutes of wall-clock time and \$0.13 of model usage. This extended version adds what the two-page demonstration paper could not: the Wiring view of the topic graph, Wactorz as a library for hand-written agents, how trained models are stored, sent to nodes and replaced, the security model, and the system's limitations.

items.title: How Seasonal Reference Choice Changes the Apparent Gains of Chronos Models in Electricity Load Forecasting
items.content: When a forecasting model is said to beat a simple baseline, the size of that win depends on which baseline was used. We measure how much this matters for two zero-shot foundation models, Chronos-Bolt and Chronos-2, on hourly electricity load. The study uses 60 fixed cases drawn from eight series in four public collections, with forecasts 24 and 168 hours ahead and up to 2,048 hours of history. Each model is compared with daily persistence, weekly persistence, a weekday hybrid, a daily-weekly blend, and a reference chosen from these on a validation period. We keep every origin-level forecast and estimate uncertainty with paired circular block bootstrap intervals using 168- and 336-hour blocks. A week ahead, Bolt clearly beats weekly persistence in 21 of 30 cases but the validation-selected reference in only 14, and its median gain falls from 17.3% to 11.9%. For Chronos-2 the clear-win counts are 18 and 15. Chronos-2 has lower week-ahead MAE than Bolt in 24 cases, yet only 12 of those differences are clear. The selected reference is not always the harder baseline, since on some test windows it does worse than weekly persistence. The choice of baseline therefore changes both how large the reported gain is and how sure we can be of it. The results are exploratory: the series and windows are related, an earlier pilot was inspected, pretraining overlap cannot be ruled out, and the case-level intervals are not corrected for multiple comparisons.

items.summary: A single-author methodological study showing that apparent advantages of zero-shot foundation forecasting models (Chronos-Bolt, Chronos-2) over baselines on hourly electricity load depend heavily on which seasonal baseline is chosen, using 60 fixed cases, bootstrap uncertainty, and validation-selected references. A week ahead, Chronos-Bolt beats weekly persistence in 21 of 30 cases but gains shrink against better-selected references.
items.reasoning: A valuable caution about baseline selection inflating foundation-model claims in forecasting, with careful paired bootstrap statistics. Scope is narrow (one domain, two models, single author), limiting general impact, but the message generalizes to evaluation practice broadly.

items.title: Loop-Count Schedules in Looped Transformers: An Empirical Study
items.content: Looped transformers apply one block of layers several times with shared weights, trading parameters for repeated computation. We study how the schedule of the loop iteration count R during training determines whether each extra pass acts as a full layer or as a small correction, using a controlled ladder of 46M-110M-parameter models trained on 2B tokens with learned residual gates on every loop pass and three schedules: R fixed to 2, R sampled uniformly from {1,...,6}, and R sampled from {2,3,4}. We find that the lower bound of the sampling range is the decisive choice. If the sampled range includes R=1, so that some training steps run the block only once and compute the loss on that single pass, the gates collapse to 0.1-0.5 and each additional pass becomes a small correction to the first; if the range starts at R=2, so that every training step runs the block at least twice, the gates stay at 0.6-0.9 and each pass keeps the strength of a full layer, while the model can still be run at any R from 2 up to twice the largest trained value with validation loss within a few hundredths of a nat of its best. The {2, 3, 4} schedule gives the best looped model, 2.909 nats against 2.951 for the parameter-matched plain model, and degrades by only 0.038 nats when run at twice its trained depth. We further show that under a fixed R the direction of the residual stream converges geometrically beyond the trained depth while the loss diverges, which refines a recent finding that static-depth training does not converge, and that reusing the first pass's keys and values on later passes costs 0.01-0.03 nats in every regime while making the per-token iteration uniformly contractive and halving the inference cache. The loop recovers about a third of what real depth provides at equal parameters. The code, trained weights, and per-token traces are released.

The scope is narrow (small models, limited data) and the contribution is empirical rather than conceptual, limiting broader impact, but the finding is genuinely useful for weight-sharing research.

items.title: UniDR: Learning To Generate Anatomical Deformations From Images via Unified Diffusion Modeling and Registration
items.content: This paper presents a novel framework, Unified Diffusion modeling and Registration (UniDR), which learns to generate arbitrary anatomical deformations from images with preserved topology. Existing approaches often model the generative process separately from registration-based deformation estimation; hence making them prone to propagated errors from the registration stage. To address this limitation, we propose a unified paradigm based on a conditional diffusion model over deformation fields that are jointly optimized from the registration process. A principled registration-guided score-matching objective function is then introduced to align the diffusion process with the deformation distribution induced by registration. As a result, our UniDR establishes an explicit connection between generation and registration: the diffusion model enables exploration of the space of plausible anatomical deformations, whereas registration provides structured supervision for learning transformations consistent with observed images. Once trained, UniDR is able to sample diverse, anatomically plausible transformations conditioned on any single input image. We evaluate UniDR across multiple real-world applications and demonstrate its effectiveness in generating high-fidelity image samples compared to the state-of-the-art. Additionally, we demonstrate that these generated samples improve performance in downstream medical image analysis and vision tasks.

A registration-guided score-matching objective aligns the diffusion process with the deformation distribution, avoiding the error propagation that arises when generation and registration are treated as separate stages. This has direct relevance to medical imaging and image registration tasks.
items.reasoning: The unified generative-registration formulation is a principled and technically interesting contribution, connecting diffusion models with classical registration in a way that could reduce cascaded errors in medical image analysis. The authors include researchers with established expertise in medical imaging. That said, the scope is relatively niche, the work appears to be from an academic team rather than a major lab, and impact hinges on empirical validation across anatomical settings.

items.title: Seeing Beyond Names: Image-Grounded Concept Linking for Robust Vision-Language Recognition
items.content: A zero-shot vision-language classifier is highly sensitive to the class names it receives. Even when images remain unchanged, replacing familiar labels with synonyms, abbreviations, or ontology terms can significantly alter predictions. We investigate this \emph{vocabulary shift} using a leakage-free evaluation protocol across Tiny ImageNet, ImageNet-R, ImageNet-A, and ImageNetV2. With CLIP ViT-B/16, alternative class names reduce top-1 accuracy by $14.8$--$17.6$ percentage points. To address this issue, we propose \emph{image-grounded concept linking}, a training-free method that maps class names to visual concepts and uses a reliability gate to improve predictions. The method outperforms a template ensemble across all four datasets, achieving a pooled gain of $1.8$ points. We further evaluate five vision-language backbones across four datasets. Our method improves performance in $16$ of $20$ backbone--dataset combinations, with no significantly negative results. It also reduces pooled negative log-likelihood across all five backbones. Stronger text linking and transductive refinement provide no consistent improvements, suggesting that accurate visual class-name linking remains the main challenge. A second CLIP ViT-B/16 seed confirms the improvement on ImageNetV2, but not on ImageNet-A.

items.summary: This paper quantifies vocabulary shift in zero-shot CLIP classifiers — alternative class names (synonyms, abbreviations, ontology terms) reduce top-1 accuracy by 14.8-17.6 points — and proposes a training-free image-grounded concept linking method with a reliability gate, yielding a pooled 1.8-point gain over template ensembles across four benchmark datasets.

items.title: CarlHOI: Counterfactual Predictive Imagination for Generalizable Multi-Humanoid Object Interaction under Constrained Environments
items.content: Recent advances in physics-based humanoid control enable teams of varying sizes to coordinate their movements and cooperatively transport shared objects. However, adapting learned cooperative behaviors to unseen environmental constraints remains challenging, particularly when obstacles require coordinated detours and changes in team configuration. We propose CarlHOI, a counterfactual predictive imagination framework built upon a counterfactual-anchored relational latent world model (CarlWM) for human-object interaction (HOI), enabling multi-humanoid teams to adapt to unseen environmental constraints without retraining their underlying cooperative control policies. CarlHOI explicitly represents the shared object, individual humanoids, and environmental obstacles as interacting entities. Trained offline using counterfactual simulator rollouts, the model imagines alternative collective futures under different shared waypoint commands, predicting how the coupled humanoid team and object would respond. By evaluating these imagined outcomes through predicted progress, failure, and contact risks, and long-horizon value estimates, CarlHOI selects adaptive guidance commands while preserving the pretrained cooperative controller. We introduce a benchmark comprising three challenging obstacle-constrained transport tasks to evaluate adaptation and generalization. Despite being trained exclusively with four humanoids, our model generalizes without retraining to teams of two to ten humanoids, unseen obstacle geometries and placements, unseen objects, and novel combinations of environmental constraints. Extensive experiments demonstrate improved cooperative transport success over evaluated baselines across diverse configurations. Results highlight the potential of counterfactual predictive imagination to extend pretrained multi-humanoid cooperative skills beyond their original training conditions.

items.summary: CarlHOI proposes a counterfactual-anchored relational latent world model enabling multi-humanoid teams to adapt cooperative object-transport behaviors to unseen obstacles without retraining the underlying control policies. It explicitly models the shared object, individual humanoids, and obstacles as interacting entities for planning under environmental constraints.
items.reasoning: Novel combination of counterfactual world modeling with multi-humanoid cooperation, addressing a real generalization gap; however, evaluation scope and comparison baselines are unclear from the abstract, and multi-humanoid simulation remains far from deployment.

items.content_html: Recent advances in physics-based humanoid control enable teams of varying sizes to coordinate their movements and cooperatively transport shared objects. However, adapting learned cooperative behaviors to unseen environmental constraints remains challenging, particularly when obstacles require coordinated detours and changes in team configuration. We propose CarlHOI, a counterfactual predictive imagination framework built upon a counterfactual-anchored relational latent world model (CarlWM) for human-object interaction (HOI), enabling multi-humanoid teams to adapt to unseen environmental constraints without retraining their underlying cooperative control policies. CarlHOI explicitly represents the shared object, individual humanoids, and environmental obstacles as interacting entities. Trained offline using counterfactual simulator rollouts, the model imagines alternative collective futures under different shared waypoint commands, predicting how the coupled humanoid team and object would respond. By evaluating these imagined outcomes through predicted progress, failure, and contact risks, and long-horizon value estimates, CarlHOI selects adaptive guidance commands while preserving the pretrained cooperative controller. We introduce a benchmark comprising three challenging obstacle-constrained transport tasks to evaluate adaptation and generalization. Despite being trained exclusively with four humanoids, our model generalizes without retraining to teams of two to ten humanoids, unseen obstacle geometries and placements, unseen objects, and novel combinations of environmental constraints. Extensive experiments demonstrate improved cooperative transport success over evaluated baselines across diverse configurations. Results highlight the potential of counterfactual predictive imagination to extend pretrained multi-humanoid cooperative skills beyond their original training conditions.

items.title: DictaRashi: A State-of-the-Art OCR Model For Rashi Script
items.content: We release DictaRashi, a Tesseract OCR model for scanned Hebrew books printed in the so-called "Rashi" font. We trained DictaRashi on over one million manually corrected lines of text from over 100 different books of Rabbinic and post-Rabbinic literature. On a held-out set of 1,120 manually transcribed lines from scanned Rashi-script pages, DictaRashi reaches a character error rate (CER) of 0.86% and a word error rate (WER) of 3.38%, setting a new state-of-the-art for publicly-available Tesseract models. We provide a full comparison of our results to those of the 31 other publicly available Hebrew Tesseract models; the best of those models achieves a 2.98% CER and 11.86% WER. We further demonstrate that DictaRashi outperforms the current frontier LLMs on this OCR task. We release the test set of Rashi-script documents so that it may be used as a benchmark for future work in this area. We are pleased to release the model and test set to the community under a CC BY NC 4.0 license.

items.title: Revisiting RadioGalaxyNET: modern detectors for radio galaxy detection and host identification
items.content: RadioGalaxyNET is the public benchmark for finding extended radio galaxies in EMU pilot-survey images, classifying them and locating their infrared hosts. Its best published results date from 2023: 54.5 box AP (Gal-YOLOv8) and 48.1 host keypoint AP (Gal-DINO). We train three current detectors, D-FINE-seg, YOLO26-pose and RF-DETR, on the same data and score them with the benchmark's own evaluation code, which reproduces the published Gal-DINO numbers exactly. All exceed the published results. D-FINE-seg M reaches 67.1 box AP and 72.4 host AP, 12.6 and 24.3 points above the best published results, and the highest host AP of the detectors we tested; on boxes it is level with YOLO26. Its host lead over YOLO26 comes from host-centered images, which make up most of the benchmark. End to end, D-FINE-seg S is the fastest model at 1.9 ms per image; engine against engine, YOLO26 is faster at the same size. We also report what matters for anyone using the benchmark: its scoring protocol adds 5 to 10 AP, its host labels sit at the image center, its box labels are offset from the image by 1.5 pixels, and its images can be rebuilt from the public survey data, which recovers sky positions and doubles as extra training data. We suggest that future work report host identification F1, as a measure closer to catalog use: D-FINE-seg M 71.8, YOLO26-pose M 70.5, RF-DETR 63.8, Gal-DINO 59.2.

items.title: LexiDet-OVD: Benchmarking Lexical Sensitivity in Open-Vocabulary Object Detection
items.content: Open-vocabulary object detectors localize objects from free-form text prompts, but their reliability depends on how users describe the target. Standard evaluations usually test a fixed class name, leaving prompt-induced failure modes underexplored. We introduce LexiDet-OVD, a benchmark and metric suite for studying lexical sensitivity in open-vocabulary object detection. We organize prompt sets into equivalent, conditional, and broad semantic scopes, and evaluate four detector families on fixed COCO and LVIS samples, each covering 30 classes (800 held-out COCO images and 1,000 LVIS images). Beyond mean and worst-prompt AP50, we report P10, CVaR at 20%, leave-one-prompt-out influence, detection agreement, box consistency, and confidence variance using one-to-one multi-instance matching. Equivalent-prompt best-to-worst gaps range from 5.3 to 23.4 points on COCO1000 and from 5.1 to 29.9 points on LVIS1000-30c, showing that strong average accuracy and lexical stability are distinct properties. We compare maximum-score selection, weighted-box fusion, Prompt Consensus, and an exploratory fusion rule. Aggregation recovers performance in several settings, but no method dominates all model-dataset pairs. A controlled Detic/SHiNe comparison further shows that semantic hierarchy enrichment does not by itself eliminate lexical sensitivity. These results support reporting prompt-distribution robustness alongside conventional open-vocabulary detection accuracy.

items.title: World Models Are the Right Foundation for Simulating Mars Terraforming
items.content: Terraforming Mars is a long-horizon, action-conditioned control problem that requires predicting atmospheric responses to interventions over centuries to identify effective policies. This position paper argues that physics-regularized recurrent state-space world models are the most promising foundation for this setting. Data-driven climate emulators lack action-conditioning, and physics-based general circulation models (GCMs) are too expensive for policy search. Among learned world models, recurrent state-space architectures with physics constraints are better suited than transformer-based alternatives: they provide native uncertainty quantification through their stochastic-deterministic decomposition, remain stable under sparse non-terrestrial training data, and enforce physical consistency at each rollout step. To make this position concrete, we describe a potential architecture combining JEPA-inspired latent encoding, universal differential equation constraints, and a Dreamer-lineage planning head. We also introduce MarsWorld, an open benchmark proposal for intervention-conditioned planetary world models, and discuss broader implications and objections.

items.title: Safe Quantum Stochastic Linear Bandits
items.content: We initiate the study of safe quantum stochastic linear bandits, in which a learner maximizes an unknown linear reward while satisfying unknown linear mean constraints at every interaction. Under coherent unitary access to the joint reward-and-constraint distribution, we develop QRS-COLTS, a staged quantum resampled-scaling analog of constrained linear Thompson sampling (COLTS). With high probability, QRS-COLTS plays only feasible actions and achieves regret that is polylogarithmic in the query horizon and scales only with the square root of the number of constraints. We also study a model in which the learner queries superpositions of actions while an unsafe-action flag, a "bomb" that terminates the interaction upon violation, is measured after every query. In this setting, the bomb provides exact membership access to the safe set, and query regret is evaluated over the action superposition. For this model, we propose BCO-QLinTS, which selects feasible actions via bomb-certified quantum convex optimization without estimating the constraint matrix. Its query-weighted regret remains polylogarithmic in the horizon, with the constraints entering the bound only through the geometry of the safe set.

It also analyzes a superposition-query model with an unsafe-action flag measured per query.

items.title: Beyond PINNs: Boundary-Enriched Holomorphic Networks for Laplace Problems
items.content: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) solve partial differential equations by penalizing their residual, but this formulation can be difficult to optimize for solutions with singular behaviour. We focus specifically on the two-dimensional Laplace equation, whose strong analytical structure allows the governing equation to be enforced directly in the neural representation. We compare a hybrid harmonic-neural model with a holomorphic neural network whose output is harmonic by construction and therefore requires only boundary training. We further enrich the holomorphic model with singular functions chosen according to the interior angle and boundary conditions at each junction of boundary segments. On six singular benchmarks, the enriched model is the most accurate of the neural models we compare. On the four with a closed-form solution, however, that solution lies in the span of the enrichment terms, and a least-squares fit of these terms alone is exact to rounding error. On Motz's problem and the cracked beam, the neural core reduces the relative error of the recovered leading singular coefficient from about $10^{-2}$, for a least-squares fit with the same four terms, to about $10^{-6}$, and on four variants whose solution has a smooth part outside the span, the network is $4\times10^{4}$ to $2\times10^{7}$ times more accurate than a fit of its singular terms alone; classical least-squares fits with more singular terms, or with harmonic polynomials and rational poles, are more accurate still. Our results demonstrate how exploiting problem-specific analytical structure can provide an alternative to base and residual PINNs for challenging scientific computing problems.

items.title: SAGE-Drive: Benefit-Aware Adaptive Reasoning for Autonomous Driving Planning
items.content: Explicit reasoning enables autonomous vehicles (AVs) to interpret complex traffic interactions and support trajectory planning, but introduces additional computational demands. Determining when explicit reasoning can improve planning accuracy remains a key challenge, as its benefits vary across driving scenarios. To address this challenge, this study proposes Scene-Adaptive Gating of Explicit Reasoning for Driving (SAGE-Drive), a benefit-aware adaptive reasoning framework for autonomous driving planning. First, paired planning outcomes with and without explicit reasoning are analyzed to measure the reasoning benefit, i.e., the reduction in planning error achieved by explicit reasoning, which serves as the supervision label. SAGE-Drive then learns to predict these benefits using geometric features of the initial trajectory planned without reasoning and multimodal scene information, and invokes explicit reasoning only for the scenarios with the highest predicted benefits under a predefined reasoning budget. Experiments on 1,497 paired driving scenarios reveal that explicit reasoning improves planning accuracy in 53.5% of cases while degrading it in 46.5%, yielding a near-zero average benefit. On the test set, with a 20% reasoning budget, SAGE-Drive achieves an average displacement error (ADE) of 1.5191 m, compared with 1.5252 m for random selection. At a 35% budget, it achieves an ADE of 1.5148 m, close to the 1.5141 m obtained when reasoning is applied to every scenario. These findings establish the predicted reasoning benefit as an effective criterion for reasoning selection, allowing explicit reasoning to be invoked where it improves planning accuracy at a fraction of its computational cost.

This reduces computational cost while preserving accuracy in scenarios where reasoning helps. The adaptive gating idea addresses a real efficiency concern for reasoning-augmented AV planners.

items.title: When 1+1 $\neq$ 2: Benchmarking Civil-Time Reasoning in Large Language Models
items.content: Calendar arithmetic is non-linear. When 1:59 AM + 1 minute occurs during daylight saving spring-forward, the result is 3:00 AM, not 2:00 AM, as the hour is skipped. We introduce CivilTime-Bench, a benchmark for civil-time reasoning covering daylight saving transitions, non-hour offsets, date-line crossings, and ISO week boundaries. With 60,011 training and 10,500 evaluation examples under strict output-contract evaluation, we benchmark seven LLMs (six instruction-tuned models and Llama-3.1-8B base) and find: zero-shot exact match varies substantially across models, contract-aware prompting often improves format compliance but yields inconsistent accuracy gains, few-shot in-context learning provides model-dependent improvements, and fine-tuning achieves 74.6--86.6% EM on synthetic evaluation but only 36.6--45.2% on HumanTime-500 for models with valid results on both splits, highlighting substantial limitations in generalization. We release the benchmark and code.

It exposes a concrete class of arithmetic-adjacent reasoning failures in LLMs.

items.title: Wavelet determinantal samplers: Optimal approximation rates adapting to regularity
items.content: We construct wavelet-based determinantal samplers on manifolds and geometric graphs whose approximation rates adapt to the regularity of the observable. On a Riemannian manifold of dimension $m$, our wavelet DPPs satisfy variance reduction of order $n^{1-2s/m}$ for linear statistics of both $s$-H\"older and $H^s$ observables, where $0<s\le1$. Using these samplers, we further construct unbiased quadrature rules with root mean square error $O(n^{-1/2-s/m})$ using at most $3n/2$ function evaluations, matching the classical optimal randomized integration exponent. For point clouds sampled from an $m$-dimensional manifold, we develop corresponding determinantal samplers on two standard classes of geometric random graphs: $\varepsilon$-graphs and symmetric $k$-nearest-neighbour graphs. These samplers satisfy the same variance reduction for linear statistics of $s$-H\"older observables and yield conditionally unbiased estimators of empirical averages with root mean square error $O(n^{-1/2-s/m})$, using at most $2n$ function evaluations. In both settings, the rates are governed by the intrinsic dimension $m$ and the regularity $s$ of the observable.

items.summary: The authors construct wavelet-based determinantal point process samplers on Riemannian manifolds and geometric graphs whose variance reduction adapts to the regularity of the observed function. They derive optimal unbiased quadrature rules matching classical randomized integration rates with modest function evaluations, extending to epsilon-graphs and k-nearest-neighbor graph settings.

items.title: Spiking World-Action Models for Robotic Manipulation
items.content: World action models (WAMs) predict how the world responds to actions and offer a promising path toward general embodied intelligence, but they are large and run the network many times per plan, so they are hard to deploy on robots. Spiking neural networks (SNNs) compute with sparse binary spikes and use additions instead of multiplications, which saves power. However, existing WAMs use dense videos as the world state, so a spiking version would spend most of its computation on the background. We therefore introduce SpikingWAM, the first spiking WAM, which uses a sparse task skeleton as the world state. Inspired by biological motor control, which attends only to the key positions of a task, the Task Skeleton State (TSS) keeps the keypoints of the arm and the task objects, and a small spiking front end estimates the object keypoints from images. Body Frame Spike Coding (BFSC) and Grid Coincidence Attention (GCA) keep millimetre precision, and the Persistent Single Step Readout (PSR) runs the network once per plan. On the simulated benchmarks LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus and RoboTwin 2.0, SpikingWAM achieves competitive success rates with far less energy than ANN methods and surpasses all compared methods on LIBERO-Plus. Real robot experiments further confirm its effectiveness. These results show that a task skeleton lets spiking networks implement WAMs at very low energy, offering a new solution for low power embodied intelligence. Project page: https://wxqnl.github.io/spikingwam/

items.title: Diagnostic Accuracy Is Not Deployment Value: Decision-Aligned Reliability Evaluation for Foundation MLIPs in Materials Discovery
items.content: In AI-guided materials discovery, machine-learning models increasingly decide which candidate materials should receive expensive first-principles or experimental evaluation. Standard reliability metrics such as uncertainty, calibration, novelty, and ranking accuracy evaluate properties of the predictions, but success on these metrics does not necessarily imply a better downstream screening decision. We study this mismatch for foundation machine-learned interatomic potentials (MACE-MP, CHGNet, Orb V3) used to rank candidate crystal structures before DFT verification. We evaluate three representative reliability interventions (novelty detection, sparse DFT calibration, and chemistry-level ranking audits) using a deployment objective that measures how much DFT can be avoided while maintaining a required recall of near-hull candidates. Across all three, a reliability signal can succeed on its immediate target without improving the final screening decision: novelty detects distribution shift but weakly ranks failure severity; calibration can improve pooled ranking metrics while leaving screening unchanged or degrading it; and sparse audits identify MLIP-chemistry combinations with poor ranking reliability without yielding a robustly beneficial routing policy. A two-oracle analysis further shows that the source of failure depends on the screening decision itself: under formation-energy screening, even perfect knowledge of average ranking reliability can select the wrong model, whereas in the evaluated hull-aligned variant the oracle target becomes decision-aligned but finite-budget audits still fail to realize the value. Reliability should be evaluated relative to the decision it supports: the relevant question is not whether a model is uncertain or inaccurate, but whether acquiring and acting on additional information will improve the final discovery decision enough to justify its cost.

items.title: Correlated by Construction: Endpoint Choice and the Validation of Protein Screening
items.content: Machine learning for protein engineering depends on functional measurements collected at screening scale, but the designs those measurements rank are deployed in processes that run elsewhere. Whether a miniaturized assay remains informative under the conditions of use is usually assumed rather than demonstrated. We describe an automated production and screening platform and test the transfer of its solution-phase metal-affinity measurements to immobilized rare-earth separation. Primary pKd-derived separation factors tracked those measured on covalently immobilized protein across 82 protein-metal-pair measurements from 35 proteins, with pairwise Spearman correlations of 0.878 to 0.923 (pooled Pearson $r$ = 0.836; Spearman $\rho$ = 0.869). Separation factors at a fixed metal pair are insensitive to the ordering shared across the lanthanide series, so these coefficients report protein-specific correspondence directly; permutation of protein identity confirms it, giving a mean scrambled correlation of 0.003 and, for the 17 proteins measured on all three pairs, $r$ = 0.917 against 0.001 ($p \approx 0.001$). Profiles compared as profiles behave differently. An independent comparison against published LAMBS profiles for the same protein backbones (417 proteins, 5,212 paired measurements) reproduced normalized raw elution at $r$ = 0.870, but reassigning protein identity still reached 0.840. High profile-level agreement across assay formats is largely attributable to metal preferences shared across the series rather than to protein identity. Transfer can be demonstrated, but the endpoint decides whether a correlation shows it: a pairwise contrast removes the shared ordering; a normalized profile retains it, and needs a null that reassigns protein identity.

items.title: Optimal Private Gaussian Multi-sampling
items.content: We give polynomial-time algorithms for Gaussian multi-sampling under approximate $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-differential privacy, with optimal sample complexity up to logarithmic factors. Our main construction uses $\widetilde{O}(m+d\sqrt{m}/\varepsilon)$ independent input samples from a $d$-dimensional Gaussian $P$ with unknown mean and covariance to generate $m$ exactly independent outputs. Their joint distribution is $\alpha$-close in total variation to $P^{\otimes m}$. Our lower bounds hold even for dependent outputs under the same joint accuracy guarantee, showing that exact independence incurs no additional sample cost beyond logarithmic factors.   The single-sampler of Iverson, Kamath, and Mouzakis [COLT 2025] uses $\widetilde{O}(d/\varepsilon)$ input samples. Running it on a separate input dataset for each of $m$ outputs therefore costs $\widetilde{O}(md/\varepsilon)$ in total. Our construction reduces this dimension-dependent sample cost from linear to square-root dependence on the number of outputs.   Our approach builds on the stable weighted statistics of Brown, Hopkins, and Smith [COLT 2023], also used for Gaussian single-sampling by Iverson, Kamath, and Mouzakis. To control privacy loss when the entire batch shares these statistics, we compare the joint output densities and obtain a privacy bound that scales with the square root of the batch size. The stability step downweights influential records and can reject the entire batch. Both actions can make the outputs dependent. Our correction restores exact independence while preserving differential privacy and joint accuracy.

items.title: FiRE: Fine-grained Ranking Evaluation for Machine Translation
items.content: Developing reliable machine translation (MT) systems hinges on our ability to distinguish superior translations from inferior ones. However, existing evaluation paradigms, whether limited to coarse overall rankings or misaligned with human preferences, fail to deliver interpretable, fine-grained feedback in reference-free settings. We present a Fine-Grained Ranking Evaluation method (FiRE) that leverages off-the-shelf large language models to perform criterion-driven pairwise comparison across three complementary dimensions: faithfulness, fluency, and consistency of style, instead of producing a single holistic judgment. To enable rigorous meta-evaluation of evaluation paradigms in the absence of any suitable testbed, we construct the first human-annotated, reference-free benchmark for fine-grained ranking evaluation, achieving substantial inter-annotator agreement. Through meta-evaluation on this benchmark and existing MQM datasets, FiRE demonstrably outperforms regression-based and error-analysis metrics in aligning with human comparative judgments, while providing more informative insights into translation quality. Finally, our examination of LLM evaluator biases (position and self-enhancement) and their handling of tied cases offers guidance for more nuanced MT evaluation. Code and benchmark resources are available at https://github.com/wygao8/FiRE-MT.

items.title: ToWo-VTON: Take-Off Wear-On Virtual Try-On via Topology-aware Decoupling
items.content: Virtual Try-On (VTON) aims to synthesize garment transfer without physical trials. Although recent methods perform well on upper-body garments, they still struggle in lower-body and full-body scenarios with complex occlusions and large silhouette changes. To address this limitation, we introduce ToWo (Take-Off Wear-On), a two-stage paradigm that decouples body structure estimation from garment synthesis. Take-Off first generates a tight-fitting body proxy that provides estimated structural guidance, and Wear-On then synthesizes the target garment conditioned on this prior. This decoupling reduces source-garment interference, supporting garment placement under substantial silhouette variations. Built on this paradigm, we propose ToWo-VTON, a unified topology-aware framework with structure-aware supervision. We construct the Body-Fitting DressCode (BFDC) dataset via body-aware diffusion and VLM-based filtering to provide body-proxy supervision across upper-, lower-, and full-body cases. We instantiate ToWo-VTON on both diffusion-based and MLLM-guided backbones. For diffusion-based models, we fine-tune on BFDC using the body proxy as the person input. For the MLLM-guided model, we use native backbone conditioning for the body proxy and target garment, and add Garment Boosting Attention (GBA) to preserve garment details. Experiments on VITON-HD and DressCode demonstrate improvements over the evaluated baselines, with KID reductions of 26.1% and 58.6% for diffusion-based and MLLM-guided implementations, respectively. The combined BFDC-training and Take-Off/Wear-On strategy also produces more coherent limb layouts and garment boundaries across the evaluated garment categories.

items.title: TriSegAgent: Context-Efficient 3D Annotation with MLLMs via Tri-Planes
items.content: Interactive segmentation models turn a few clicks into a segmentation prediction across domains, so annotators only decide where the prediction still needs correction. Annotation thus becomes a loop of inspecting the prediction and clicking again. Each step of this loop is a visual judgment, which suits general-purpose multimodal large language model (MLLM) agents. In this work, we focus on letting these agents run this loop on 3D volumes. However, the MLLM in such an agent takes only 2D images as input, so the agent must observe the 3D volume in 2D. Since the loop calls the MLLM many times, this observation must be token-compact enough to keep every call cheap, yet informative enough to show error regions in the 3D prediction. We meet both needs with tri-planes, the three orthogonal planes that cross at one point in the volume. We show, both theoretically and empirically, that tri-planes are context-efficient yet keep sufficient detail to show error regions in the 3D prediction. Building on tri-planes, we introduce TriSegAgent, an MLLM agent that refines the 3D prediction iteratively. Within the agent, the MLLM only judges the prediction on tri-planes, while a visual harness turns each judgment into a 3D action in code. To make the loop reliable, the harness places each click at an exact voxel in the volume and checks whether to accept the 3D prediction. To evaluate the agent, we build a diverse benchmark of 690 regions of interest (ROIs) from 35 public medical datasets across three imaging modalities. With frontier MLLMs, TriSegAgent reaches an overall Dice about 10 points above the strongest baseline, and its lead is even larger on targets below 3 cm. With flash-level MLLMs, it outperforms a recent 3D segmentation agent built on a frontier MLLM.

items.title: RigidAnchor: Cross-View Geo-Localization for UAV via Iterative Planar Rigid Alignment
items.content: A UAV that flies without GNSS has to estimate its absolute position and heading without any external signal. Most existing methods for UAV-to-satellite cross-view geo-localization (U-S CVGL) treat the task as image retrieval: they compress the UAV image and each satellite tile into separate descriptors, rank the tiles by their similarity, and return the center of the best tile. The output can therefore only lie on a pre-defined grid, its accuracy is limited by the tile size, and no heading is produced. Regressing the pose in a single pass removes the grid, but it leaves no chance to correct the estimate afterwards. We observe that satellite tiles are not independent samples. They are laid on the map at a fixed spacing, scale and orientation, so neighboring tiles join into one continuous satellite block with a consistent metric, and a nadir UAV view of that block differs from it by a planar rigid transform only, i.e. a 2D translation plus an in-plane rotation. We therefore reformulate U-S CVGL as solving for this transform between two images of different sizes. Position and heading then become parts of one geometric quantity, and the accuracy is no longer limited by the tile grid. We propose RigidAnchor, which solves the transform iteratively. The network encodes the two images and builds a multi-level correlation pyramid between them. At each iteration, it indexes the pyramid with every aerial cell carried through the current estimate, pools the descriptors of all cells into one hidden state, and lets two decoupled heads predict a translation increment and a rotation increment, the latter being composed rather than added. On Bearing-UAV-90K, the cross-view mean errors are 78.6% lower in position and 69.7% lower in heading than Bearing-UAV, and HSR@15 increases by 19.06 points. Code is available at https://github.com/wwsource/RigidAnchor.

It exploits the known fixed spacing, scale, and orientation of satellite tiles.

At each iteration, it indexes the pyramid with every aerial cell carried through the current estimate, pools the descriptors of all cells into one hidden state, and lets two decoupled heads predict a translation increment and a rotation increment, the latter being composed rather than added. On Bearing-UAV-90K, the cross-view mean errors are 78.6% lower in position and 69.7% lower in heading than Bearing-UAV, and HSR@15 increases by 19.06 points. Code is available at https://github.com/wwsource/RigidAnchor.

items.title: When Does Reasoning Help Entity Disambiguation? Small LLMs In-Domain and Under Shift
items.content: Entity disambiguation (mapping ambiguous mentions in text to entities in a knowledge base) is a foundational step in tasks such as knowledge graph construction, question answering, and information extraction. Recent work has applied LLMs to this problem, achieving stateof-the-art performance. Notably, reasoning LLMs have been shown to perform entity disambiguation in a true zero-shot fashion, generalizing across knowledge bases and domains. However, it is unclear whether this capability survives, or remains competitive, with smaller LLMs, where entity disambiguation has typically relied on reranking rather than reasoning. We ask when reasoning is worth its cost at small scale. We compare pointwise, listwise, and reasoning-based candidate-selection components within a classical coarse-to-fine entity disambiguation pipeline, across the classical, few-shot and true zero-shot settings. The reasoning paradigm is trained with distillation and reinforcement learning recipes. The benefit of reasoning grows with domain shift: negligible in-domain, decisive in the true zero-shot setting. We show that two distinct factors are at work: the reranker's uncertainty over the candidates locates where the paradigms disagree, while shift governs which is right when they do.

items.title: AirVT-15k: A Query-Diverse UAV Video-Text Dataset and Query-Adaptive Evidence Alignment Network for Retrieval
items.content: Unmanned aerial vehicle video-text retrieval (UAV-TVR) requires matching language to both scene context and subtle object changes. A harbor-layout query relies on global scene context, whereas a departing-vessel query requires local functional cues and motion states. Existing benchmarks provide diverse aerial descriptions but give limited attention to distinct evidence needs within the same video. We introduce AirVT-15k, a benchmark of 15,504 UAV videos and 155,040 captions, with ten complementary bilingual captions per video describing scenes, object states, and temporal changes. We also propose AirFocus-CST, which selects query-relevant frames and patches, encodes temporal feature differences, and combines coarse-to-fine interaction (CFI) with optimal-transport alignment (OTA). Average mean recall reaches 63.67% on AirVT-15k and 24.41% on CapERA, improving over the strongest baselines by 2.96 and 1.91 percentage points, respectively. The dataset and code are available at https://chenxi000233.github.io/AirVT-15k-site/.

It emphasizes that different queries need different evidence within the same video.
items.reasoning: A substantial dataset contribution filling a gap in UAV video-text retrieval, paired with a competent matching architecture; valuable to a specific subcommunity but not broadly transformative.

items.title: Cost-Sensitive Reversibility of Non-Deterministic Actions
items.content: Determining action reversibility requires checking whether the effects of an action can be undone. Recent work has extended reversibility to fully observable non-deterministic (FOND) planning. It distinguishes weak reversibility, where reversal may succeed, from strong-cyclic reversibility, where reversal is guaranteed under fairness. These notions are qualitative: they say whether reversal is possible, but not how costly it is.   We introduce cost-sensitive reversibility for non-deterministic actions. Given positive action costs, we define weak and strong reversal budgets, $k$-bounded reversibility, and a distinction between finite strong reversal and strong-cyclic reversal with unbounded worst-case cost. We relate the resulting notions in a reversibility lattice, prove cost-aware policy-merging results, and show how to compute restricted weak and strong universal uniform reversal budgets using cost-optimal classical planning and worst-case-optimal FOND search, respectively. We also give an admissible lower-bound test for rejecting $k$-bounded reversibility. These notions support finer-grained safety decisions: a small finite strong budget bounds recovery cost, whereas a small weak budget certifies only a cheap possible recovery path. Actions without an acceptable strong bound may therefore warrant human approval, as in tool-using agent systems.
items.author: Giuseppe Canonaco, Alberto Pozanco, Daniel Borrajo
items.summary: The paper extends qualitative reversibility notions in FOND planning to cost-sensitive settings, defining weak and strong reversal budgets, k-bounded reversibility, and a reversibility lattice relating these concepts, with proven cost-aware policy results. This lets planners reason not just whether actions can be undone but at what cost.
items.reasoning: A rigorous theoretical contribution to classical planning that refines an existing line of work on reversibility; the lattice structure and cost-bounded notions are meaningful for plan repair and recovery, though of interest mainly to the planning theory community.

items.title: LiveMirror: Real-Time Diffusion Virtual Try-On on a Consumer GPU and Its Self-Supervised Adaptation to Indian Ethnic Wear
items.content: Diffusion virtual try-on (VTO) models produce convincing garment transfers from a single product photograph, but at hundreds of milliseconds to seconds per image every deployment today is offline or falls back to AR mirrors that need a rigged 3D asset per product. We present LiveMirror, a live-camera try-on mirror that renders a flat garment photograph onto a moving person with a diffusion model on one 16 GB consumer GPU. Its core is asynchronous keyframe try-on: generation never blocks the display, every displayed frame is an optical-flow warp of the latest generated keyframe, and keyframes are replaced only through a cross-fade. The display runs at camera rate (25 FPS at 720p) while a new try-on arrives every 370-490 ms; we measure the residual flicker, give a stage-by-stage latency budget, and report which accelerations (step count, consistency LoRA, tiny decoder, compilation) keep garment prints intact. We then show that the same GPU fixes the model's biggest cultural blind spot: try-on models trained on VITON-HD and DressCode render a knee-length kurta or sherwani as a torso-length top or a dress over bare legs. A thigh-covering mask, self-supervised pairs built automatically from 24.9k on-model e-commerce photographs, and 3.2 GPU-hours of attention-only fine-tuning of CatVTON halve the perceptual error on ethnic wear (LPIPS 0.137 to 0.077 on IndoFashion, 0.135 to 0.073 on Atlas; 200 held-out pairs per source) with no regression on Western tops. A two-pass hem-aware mask then removes the remaining failure, recoloured trousers below the hem, on all but 3-4% of pairs at no training cost; in the mirror the hem comes from the previous keyframe for free. The adapted model beats FASHN VTON 1.5 on every aggregate ethnic-wear metric at about $20\times$ lower inference cost, and its weights drop straight into the mirror.

items.title: AXE: AlpaSim E2E Closed Loop Challenge Technical Report
items.content: This report presents a comprehensive pipeline for developing an end-to-end (E2E) autonomous driving model for the Physical AI AV Track. The framework consists of data curation, HD map auto-labelling, data-driven imitation learning, and simulator-based reinforcement learning. To ensure safety in the closed-loop setting, we introduce a selection-based E2E planning approach that leverages object detection and BEV segmentation to filter out trajectory candidates likely to cause collisions or off-road driving. Trained on NVIDIA NuRec and the NVIDIA PAI-AV dataset, our method scores a fixed vocabulary of trajectory candidates for collision, drivable-area compliance, and progress learned from simulated rollouts, and selects the best candidate that passes the filter. This design highlights the effectiveness of combining E2E planning with perception-based trajectory filtering for safe and reliable closed-loop autonomous driving.

items.title: GeoRead3D: Grounding Part Descriptions for 3D Pointing and Reorientation
items.content: Language often refers to an object by its parts, as in asking to point to a part or to turn an arbitrarily posed object so that two named parts lie in given directions. Both tasks need the direction from the object's center to the part's center, not the part's own orientation. A natural approach segments the part and takes the centroid of its mask. However, high mask overlap predicts the pointing direction poorly when a part is spread out relative to its distance from the object center. Language-guided part segmentation is trained and evaluated by mask overlap, which leaves a gap between the masks it produces and the part geometry that these tasks use. We close this gap by learning point evidence, weights over the observed points whose weighted centroid gives the part's location. Geometric Readout Supervision (GRS) trains these weights through the centroid's position and adds direction supervision on the parts used in reorientation commands. GRS improves both tasks even with a single frozen encoder and a single input pose. We implement this supervision in GeoRead3D, a system for pointing and reorientation from part descriptions. A language model maps each description to a known part name. Dual-Route Part Evidence combines refined segmentation evidence with directly predicted point evidence to locate each part. On PartNeXt and Artiverse, GeoRead3D points within $22.5^\circ$ for 74.1% and 60.0% of queries, 5.8 and 7.3 percentage points above the strongest baselines. Its reorientation success exceeds the strongest baselines by 10.4 and 7.8 points.

It learns point evidence, weights over observed points whose weighted centroid gives part location, closing this gap. This enables grounding part descriptions for pointing and object reorientation.

items.title: Towards an Armenian Epigraphic Corpus
items.content: The Divan hay vimagrut'yan (1960-2017), the printed corpus of Armenian inscriptions, comprises nearly 7,600 records; a growing number of the inscriptions they describe, damaged or destroyed in recent decades, survive only in its pages. Armenian epigraphy nevertheless lacks a digital resource of the kind available for Greek, Latin or Georgian. This paper presents the Corpus Inscriptionum Armenicarum Electronicum, which turns the ten volumes of the Divan into an open digital corpus. Layout detection, OCR and a vision-language model produce a first structured reading of each record, which specialists then check on a proofreading platform. First corrections show that letters are read reliably and that residual errors concentrate in the editorial signs. The corpus is designed as a lasting platform for documenting Armenian inscriptions and as a source of silver data in Classical and Middle Armenian for language models and computational linguistics.

items.title: Tri-DNO: Trilateral Diffusion Noise Optimization for 3D Human Object Interaction
items.content: Generating realistic 3D human object interactions (HOI) is essential for applications, such as augmented or virtual reality (AR/VR) or character animation of interactive entertainment. A particular challenge lies in the faithful generation of hand grasps in human object interaction scenes, where even minor geometric inconsistencies, such as insufficient contact or interpenetration, can significantly compromise realism. While diffusion-based generative models have shown promising results in HOI synthesis, ensuring physically plausible hand-object interactions remains challenging.   We present Tri-DNO, a diffusion noise optimization strategy to sample from a pretrained multimodal HOI diffusion model, improving hand-object contact. Rather than modifying or retraining the generative model, our approach iteratively optimizes the initial noise of the diffusion generator, thereby generating firm hand object contact, while mitigating penetration and keeping the hand position realistic. Experiments on the GRAB dataset demonstrate improvements over the baseline in grasp quality without additional model training or increased computational cost compared to existing methods. We further demonstrate the applicability of our approach to practical media production scenarios.

It avoids retraining the generative model and targets AR/VR and character animation use cases where contact errors like interpenetration break realism.
items.reasoning: A sensible inference-time technique for a well-defined quality problem in HOI generation, but the contribution is an optimization wrapper around existing models with moderate scope.
