items.title: Does the Mixer Matter ? Paired-Seed Ablations of Tiny Bilingual Language Models
items.content: We report paired-seed architecture ablations from the development of Sophea Artemis, our in-house Greek-English model family. Every arm trains on the same 3B targets with a shared tokenizer and recipe; models range from 54M to 759M total parameters and roughly 54M to 124M active parameters. The main finding is that, at this tiny scale, stored capacity matters far more than mixer design. On a fixed held-out test, replacing the dense feed-forward blocks of a recurrent/attention hybrid with sixteen routed experts, at nearly the same approximate active parameters, lowers loss by 0.079 (Greek) and 0.112 (English) nats per target, and doubling to 32 experts lowers it by a further 0.022 and 0.031, at every paired seed. Reusing a four-layer block three times recovers about 40-44% of the gap between a shallow and an independently deep model, consistent with looped-Transformer results. In contrast, the choice among grouped-query attention (GQA), Gated DeltaNet (GDN) hybrids and a Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) hybrid moves loss by only about 0.01-0.02 nats; a 1:1 GDN/GQA hybrid is the one dense variant that improves on GQA in both languages at every held-out seed. In bits per character, Greek and English held-out losses are similar despite a 74.49%/25.51% training split, and synthetic mathematics, which comes from a collection outside the training sources, is the hardest Greek test component and gains least from added experts. Cached decoding needs its own qualification: trained models passed cached-versus-full logit checks only under a fixed-reduction inference policy, which itself changes 1.4-2.8% of next-token argmax choices relative to native evaluation. All results are conditional on one recipe and scale.

The key finding is that at tiny scale stored capacity dominates mixer design: adding routed experts lowers loss substantially more than architectural choices like hybrid recurrent-attention mixers or layer reuse.

All results are conditional on one recipe and scale.

items.title: Testing Quantized KV-Cache Maintenance: Encoding Layout and Historical Restoration
items.content: Repeating rows then selecting originals retains layout-dependent drift despite equal encoding counts. We measure when existing checks fail to establish preservation contracts in fixed quantized KV-cache implementations. In four-bit HQQ axis zero at sixteen cycles, median paired relative-L2 increases over same-shape re-encoding are 7.22 percentage points for Qwen3-1.7B and 11.59 for SmolLM3-3B. Matched encoded states cover sixteen shared questions per model at one and sixteen cycles. Axis one matches the shape-preserving control; lazy reorders preserve the initial state. On one known input, fixed update counts retain the difference; preserving group members removes it. Our prefix-view extension passes current-prefix checks yet changes history and next logits in six model/codec settings at residual capacities four and 128. Public lookup reaches this boundary, including one of four precommitted project-new GPU inputs; fixed query swaps isolate a conditional old-history effect. Checkpoint/dense rollback is exact. An explicit delayed lookup client admits a supported 129-token path excluded by native AR on one known context. Failed task-harm expansion precludes population failure-rate or general answer-degradation claims. Native MLX-LM fixtures expose stale caller caches; synchronization restores the tested in-place contract with native computations preserved. In rejection tests, stale callers change logits but not greedy tokens.

items.title: Object-Centric Differentiable Logic Networks for Abstract Visual Reasoning
items.content: Human visual intelligence enables efficient reasoning capabilities on abstract visual problems with bounded cognitive resources and minimal experience, and yields remarkable generalization to novel problems with its ability to draw relational analogies and modular abstractions. In contrast, deep learning models require exhaustive task-specific training on large datasets, making them prone to exploiting visual shortcuts and resulting in poor generalization. While neuro-symbolic approaches attempt to bridge this gap by decoupling perception from reasoning with dedicated computation units, existing solutions rely either on explicit rule supervision or parameter-heavy transformer architectures that reintroduce the computational inefficiencies they aim to solve. We introduce Slot-Dwn to address these limitations, a novel neuro-symbolic architecture that unifies unsupervised object-centric perception with logic-based symbolic reasoning. Our model utilizes a Multi-Head Differentiable Weightless Network (MH-DWN) that performs efficient reasoning entirely in Boolean space using look-up tables (LUTs). Our framework reduces visual perception complexity and introduces a LUT-based relational bottleneck with sparse input routing to minimize computational overhead. We evaluate Slot-Dwn across various abstract visual reasoning benchmark tasks targeting systematic rule generalization, sample-efficient anomaly detection, and multi-relational reasoning. We demonstrate that Slot-Dwn yields competitive performance with respect to the state-of-the-art, under extreme out-of-distribution regimes, while requiring up to 52% fewer trainable parameters, with significantly faster convergence.

Abstract reasoning benchmarks are notorious for shortcut learning, so convincing out-of-distribution evidence will be key; the approach is promising but unproven at scale.

items.title: Reconstructing 3D+t Cardiovascular Flow From Sparse Planar Velocity Fields With Neural Fields
items.content: Reconstructing time-resolved three-dimensional (3D+t) cardiovascular flow from sparse planar measurements is challenging because each plane observes only the two in-plane velocity components, on a small part of the volume. We propose a plane-aware neural-field framework that learns a continuous 3D velocity field from space and time coordinates through a per-plane projection, and then investigate the potential benefits of physics constraints. We evaluate the framework on computational aortic and aneurysm datasets, and on planes resampled from a real cardiac 4D Flow MRI scan. A plain multi-layer perceptron (MLP) was more accurate than classical radial basis function (RBF) interpolation on both computational datasets. For the aorta, a physics-constrained SIREN (PC-SIREN) reduced the rRMSE further to $0.3756$, compared with $0.4273$ for the plain MLP and $0.7256$ for RBF, and it was the most accurate model in every anatomical segment of the MRI data. For the aneurysms the plain MLP remained the most accurate model, with an rRMSE of $0.07$ to $0.16$ against $0.55$ to $0.71$ for PC-SIREN. Further experiments investigated scanning configuration, number of scans, and spatial resolution. These findings show that continuous neural fields can reconstruct volumetric cardiovascular flow from sparse planar measurements, and that physics constraints have to be matched to the flow.

items.title: Quantum resources constrain function approximation
items.content: Universal function approximation is central to machine learning. Quantum learning models are universal as well, but this does not specify the resources needed to approximate a given function. We study how coherence, imaginarity, entanglement and magic constrain function approximation for a fixed encoding and readout, using the cumulative resource power of the trainable gates. In a one-qubit model with phase encoding, coherence bounds the oscillation of the model function, while imaginarity bounds its odd part. In a two-qubit model, entanglement bounds the distance from product functions. These bounds hold at any encoding depth. For magic, the phase encoding itself supplies non-Clifford operations. On domains bounded away from zero, Clifford trainable gates suffice for uniform approximation. Replacing unrestricted trainable gates by Clifford gates increases the encoding depth at most polynomially in the original depth, the inverse error and the inverse distance of the domain from zero. Magic in the trainable gates can nevertheless improve accuracy at fixed depth. These results show how the resources of a quantum model must match the structure of the target function.

It derives concrete bounds, e.g., coherence bounding oscillation and entanglement bounding distance from product functions, and shows Clifford gates suffice for uniform approximation on domains bounded away from zero.
items.reasoning: Rigorous and clean theory connecting resource theory to expressive power of quantum ML, complementing universality results with resource requirements; foundational rather than immediately practical, and niche to quantum computing.

items.title: Go Far, Look Less: Active Multi-Room Reconstruction with Persistent Goals and Selective Views
items.content: Active 3D reconstruction aims to allocate a sparse view budget to recover complete geometry and high-fidelity renderings. However, existing methods degrade sharply in multi-room homes: myopic next-best-view scoring gives transit no credit for distant rooms and over-polishes irreducible nearby residuals, whereas dense mappers reach far rooms only by streaming thousands of frames. We propose ROAM-GS, a training-free active multi-room reconstruction framework that couples persistent goals with selective views: each decision selects a goal and a variable-horizon prefix toward it, capturing only at its endpoint. A Surface Reconstruction Memory scores poses by projecting post-update defects and viewing directions. Persistent goals credit transit with their remaining value and are released once arrivals stop measurably improving them. Without per-scene tuning, ROAM-GS achieves state-of-the-art multi-room reconstruction while preserving single-room Replica fidelity, raising mean coverage from 74% to 93% on HSSD and from 47% to 96% (+11.7 dB PSNR) on HM3D, and matching 90-minute dense mapping using $173\times$ fewer views.

items.reasoning: A thoughtful solution to a concrete failure mode (myopic view planning in multi-room environments) with a training-free design and memory-based scoring; impactful for embodied reconstruction but somewhat incremental over active-perception literature.

items.title: Potential Games for Self-Neighborhood Channel Mixing in Graph Neural Networks
items.content: Graph message passing must balance two competing objectives: incorporating neighborhood signals while preserving node-specific information. We model this trade-off as a game in which nodes choose how to mix their own representations with strict-neighborhood aggregates. For fixed channel representations, task supervision defines a common-payoff game, while local distinctness payoffs induce an exact potential game whose potential is the degree-normalized strict Dirichlet energy. We introduce CG2, which amortizes these choices through a shared six-parameter policy per layer based on local channel statistics and can be trained using either objective. Controlled comparisons show that the shared task-trained policy improves mean performance over fixed mixing on three of five heterophily benchmarks, with significant gains on two, while free per-node actions trained with either objective rarely improve on the same baseline. On the ECHO long-range benchmark, the clearest contribution of the gate appears on eccentricity, where the task-trained policy substantially reduces prediction error.

The proposed CG2 architecture amortizes mixing decisions via a shared six-parameter per-layer policy and improves mean performance on three of five heterophily benchmarks.
items.reasoning: A theoretically elegant game-theoretic lens on message passing with a clean potential-game formulation, but empirical gains are modest and limited to heterophily benchmarks. Novelty is solid; broad impact remains to be demonstrated.

items.title: XFreq: Geometry-Aligned Cross-View Residual Learning for Sparse 3D Ultrasound Reconstruction
items.content: Three-dimensional (3D) ultrasound provides valuable volumetric context for anatomical assessment, motivating reconstruction from widely available two-dimensional (2D) slices. Sparse slices leave much of the volume unobserved, even when their acquisition poses are known. Existing methods interpolate observed intensities or incorporate learned 2D image features into 3D reconstruction, but their complementary roles in predicting smooth structure and residual details remain less explored. We introduce XFreq, a geometry-aligned framework for sparse 3D ultrasound reconstruction. It uses known slice poses and finite footprints to query 2D image features at 3D locations, complementing splatted intensities and sampling geometry. A low-frequency decoder predicts a smooth 3D field from the splat representation, while a high-frequency decoder additionally incorporates the queried 2D features to predict residual details. A learned gating module regulates the residual contribution based on geometry and cross-slice feature variation. We evaluate XFreq on an in-house fetal brain dataset and the public CETUS cardiac dataset, using slices resampled from 3D ultrasound volumes and fivefold cross-validation. Among the compared methods, XFreq achieves the highest PSNR and SSIM in most settings across both datasets, reaching 26.82 dB PSNR on CETUS with 32 input slices. Ablation studies further show the contributions of local feature querying, geometric cues, and residual prediction, with gains generally increasing as more input slices are used. Our findings highlight the value of geometry-aligned cross-view feature integration for reconstructing 3D ultrasound volumes from sparse 2D slices.

items.title: Do Waste Classifiers Recognise Items They Have Never Seen? Object-Disjoint Evaluation on Household and Medical Waste
items.content: Automatic waste classification supports source separation, which enables recycling and keeps hazardous medical items out of household waste. Waste classification studies often report near-perfect accuracy on random image splits, which put photographs of one item in both training and test sets. To measure how well classifiers recognise items they have never seen, we built BanglaWaste-23, with 4,160 images of 172 objects in 23 household and medical waste classes from Bangladesh. Every image also records which physical item it shows. We evaluated 11 ImageNet-pretrained models and two models trained from scratch (a compact custom network and MobileNetV3-L) using object-disjoint five-fold cross-validation and a random split. On unseen objects, the best pretrained model reached a macro-averaged F1 score of 98.8%, and six models were statistically tied. The random split overstated from-scratch accuracy by 15 to 19 percentage points. The from-scratch models also missed 11 to 13% of medical items, against under 1% for pretrained models. On a second dataset from Dhaka, pretrained accuracy fell by 15 to 22 points. Classifiers should therefore be evaluated on unseen objects, with random-split results read as an upper bound. The data are on Zenodo and the code at https://github.com/saadbaust/BanglaWaste-23.

items.title: Aggregation Rules Induced by KL-Regularised Preference Dynamics on Networks
items.content: We study agents that each align a model to their own preference data while observing one another, and ask which aggregation rule the resulting policies implement. Each round, an agent takes one KL-regularised step. The step involves a reference that the agent is penalised for leaving and a challenger against which its responses are compared, and each of the two may be the agent's own or an average over the agents it observes; attention need not be reciprocal. Aggregating the reference makes the rule collective. Agent $v$ then has the weight $\pi_v/\beta_v$, its share of the network's long-run attention divided by its temperature. If, in addition, the challenger is fixed, the agents concentrate on the response maximising $\sum_v(\pi_v/\beta_v)r_v(y)$, where $r_v$ is agent $v$'s reward, and the rule is cardinal. If the reference is fixed and the challenger aggregated, the agents' policies at a fixed point generally differ, and any weighted mean of them is an approximate maximal lottery whatever the weights, so the dynamics select no weighting. If both are aggregated, the rule is ordinal: averaged over rounds, the collective policy is a maximal lottery of the influence-weighted preference kernel, up to a slack that we bound. Where a collective rule exists, its weights depend only on the attention weights and the temperatures.

It shows the effective rule weights agents by their long-run attention share divided by temperature, concentrating on responses maximizing a weighted sum of rewards.
items.reasoning: Elegant theory connecting multi-agent preference alignment to social aggregation rules, with implications for understanding collective behavior of aligned models, but it is abstract and far from immediate application.

items.title: Triage Accuracy of Jev and Open-Weight System One Decision Models and Their Use for Early Emergency Recognition in Symptom-Assessment Applications
items.content: Laypeople increasingly use large language models (LLMs) for triage advice, but LLMs answer in variable free text, which makes it hard to evaluate them for use in medical devices. Decision models, which assign a probability to each predefined triage category, may be easier to evaluate. To test their triage accuracy, we evaluated 16 decision models (14 open-weight, 2 proprietary) on 233 synthetic and 10,000 real-world cases, yielding 163,728 total assessments. The best models triaged 72.1% of synthetic cases correctly and agreed with an existing algorithm in 56.1% of real-world cases. They were more promising for recognising emergencies early: given only demographics, chief complaints, risk factors and red-flag answers, the best model reached an AUROC of 0.87. At a 5% error margin, it could decide for or against emergencies for about half of users. Decision models should therefore not replace triage engines but could shorten symptom assessments at setting-specific error margins.

Decision models, which assign a probability to each predefined triage category, may be easier to evaluate. To test their triage accuracy, we evaluated 16 decision models (14 open-weight, 2 proprietary) on 233 synthetic and 10,000 real-world cases, yielding 163,728 total assessments. The best models triaged 72.1% of synthetic cases correctly and agreed with an existing algorithm in 56.1% of real-world cases. They were more promising for recognising emergencies early: given only demographics, chief complaints, risk factors and red-flag answers, the best model reached an AUROC of 0.87. Decision models should therefore not replace triage engines but could shorten symptom assessments at setting-specific error margins.

items.title: Self-Supervised Learning for Soft-Constrained AC-OPF in Multiphase Distribution Systems
items.content: This paper presents a self-supervised learning framework for fast, soft-constrained AC optimal power flow (OPF) in unbalanced multiphase distribution systems. The soft AC-OPF objective balances operating cost, renewable energy curtailment, and penalties for violating operating limits. A neural network predicts distributed energy resource (DER) setpoints conditioned on operating conditions, switch configurations, and objective weights. The predicted setpoints are then processed through a DER projection and differentiable AC power flow to enforce device limits and network equalities. The framework is trained by directly minimizing the AC-OPF objective, without optimal-solution labels. Experiments on 123-, 240-, and 906-bus systems yield mean objective gaps of 0.32%, 0.92%, and 0.56%, respectively, relative to IPOPT, across wide operating ranges. Across these systems and the evaluated high-load/low-generation and low-load/high-generation scenarios, the largest mean gap is 1.04%, with mean speedups of 58-5272 times relative to IPOPT.

items.title: RoFE: Rotated Frozen Embeddings for Low-Data Multimodal Tabular Learning
items.content: Multimodal tabular learning combines tabular data with images and text, often in settings where labeled data are scarce. Tabular foundation models such as prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) offer a promising solution via in-context learning without task-specific training. However, modern image and text encoders produce embeddings with hundreds or thousands of dimensions, far exceeding the number of features encountered during PFN pretraining. Existing approaches bridge this gap using principal component analysis (PCA) to compress frozen embeddings. Surprisingly, we find that this PCA interface can underperform simple linear classifiers when labeled examples are scarce, even though PFNs are designed for small datasets. We identify the underlying failure mechanism: the PFN's per-column standardization removes the variances of the PCA scores. When the PCA keeps every direction of the labeled examples, the examples collapse into a regular simplex in which all pairwise distances are equal. To address this problem, we propose Rotated Frozen Embeddings (RoFE), a training-free method that rotates PCA scores before PFN inference. We theoretically show that rotation makes the column variances nearly equal, so that standardization approximately preserves the embedding geometry. Across image and text classification tasks, encoders, and tabular foundation models, RoFE improves low-data performance over the PCA interface and outperforms baselines that require task-specific training. The improvements also extend to regression.

This matters for practical multimodal tabular learning where labeled data are scarce.

items.title: Orthogonally Mixed Sign Coding with Progressive Residual Refinement for Transformer Weight Compression
items.content: LLM quantization reduces storage but often degrades predictive fidelity at low bit rates. We propose a training-free, CDF-free, Gaussian-CLT-motivated progressive residual-sign quantization framework that uses randomized orthogonal mixing to promote Gaussian-like residual distributions and improve sign based reconstruction of Transformer weights. Each stage independently normalizes residuals and analytically calibrates reconstruction, progressively recovering quantization errors. The framework enables flexible storage-fidelity trade-offs without learned codebooks, empirical CDFs, or trellis optimization. We evaluate GPT-2 Large and Llama-3-8B across attention and MLP projections. At five residual stages, joint quantization preserves near-baseline predictive fidelity, achieving perplexities of 32.16 and 12.73, compared with full-precision values of 29.89 and 11.07, respectively. Ablations further demonstrate that orthogonal mixing substantially improves reconstruction over identity-based sign coding, while activation-aware scaling improves output fidelity and reduced-precision statistics lower storage overhead with negligible perplexity degradation. Comparisons with conventional quantizers establish the method's progressive fidelity recovery and characterize its storage-quality and runtime trade-offs. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of orthogonally mixed residual-sign coding for flexible, training-free Transformer weight compression.

items.title: CrownFusion: 3D Dental Crown Generation Using Geometry Images and Latent Diffusion
items.content: We introduce CrownFusion, a latent diffusion model to generate 3D dental crown designs from geometry images, a 2D-grid encoding of surface coordinates. Departing from traditional approaches that use point clouds, our "CrownImage" representation not only unlocks the full power of image-based generative architectures, but also preserves fine geometric detail by operating at far higher spatial resolutions than point clouds to alleviate smoothing artifacts in the 3D generation. Conditioned on jointly learned embeddings of the surrounding dentition, our probabilistic diffusion model produces anatomically plausible crowns with morphological variations tailored to individual patient cases. To accommodate multiple valid designs, we propose an occlusal fit metric based on proximity to the antagonist teeth. We evaluate our method through quantitative experiments and qualitative studies involving expert testimonials. We also release the FDI 16 Crown Dataset, comprising 11,513 annotated intra-oral scans, to support future research in dental CAD.

A strong application of modern generative modeling to dental CAD.

items.title: SPROUT: Predicting Objective-Grounded Prompt Utility for Efficient Text-to-Image Preference Tuning
items.content: Preference tuning of text-to-image diffusion models spends most of its compute generating candidate images, yet training prompts are typically sampled uniformly at random, wasting compute generating images that provide too little signal for model alignment. To best utilize the available compute, we study prompt selection, where at each iteration we identify the most useful prompts for preference tuning. We separate prompt selection into a utility score, an estimator of that utility score, and batch selection. Within this framework, we propose Selection by PRedicting Objective-grounded UTility (SPROUT). The utility score is predicted on every prompt in the pool, including unseen prompts, by a text-only model, refit after every iteration on all utilities observed so far. A randomized acceptance rule then turns these predictions into a batch, so no images are generated beyond those used for training. For direct group preference optimization (DGPO), the objective-grounded utility is the norm of the gradient that the objective produces from a prompt's group of images. Fine-tuning Stable Diffusion 1.5 with DGPO on GenEval, SPROUT matches the final score of uniform sampling in about 44% of the iterations and improves the area under the learning curve with respect to both uniform sampling and CGPO, a recent variance-based prompt sampler. The efficiency gains hold under four held-out reward models never used in training, and the ranking of methods carries over to DPG-Bench and T2I-CompBench++. Our code is available at https://github.com/ADDAPT-ML/SPROUT.

items.title: Needwise: Generation-Free Conversational Recommendation from Need-Level Typed Decisions
items.content: Conversational recommenders must rank items against needs that catalogs record only in part, while users add, withdraw and reverse needs and switch between requests. LLM rankers re-read the dialogue at every turn: they are slow, and their ordering does not show which needs an item meets. We show that a conversational recommender can be built from typed decisions instead: named questions over fixed options, answered with option probabilities rather than generated text. On each turn, one typed request maps the message onto the catalog's fields, keeps what no field expresses in the user's words, and decides how the turn changes each earlier need. Needwise then ranks candidates must-first: the needs on the kind of item, its place and its price form a tier, and within it one holistic decision and need-level verdicts (supported, contradicted or unknown) are combined with equal weight (Needwise-HF). With the graded attributes withheld from the records, so that needs must be inferred from names, descriptions and reviews, Needwise-HF ranks Google Local requests significantly better than GPT-6 Sol (0.383 against 0.343 nDCG@10) and is not significantly different from the strongest LLM ranker on Google Local and Yelp; these comparisons keep their sign under every treatment of unrecorded attributes we test. It costs a fraction of GPT-6 Sol's API price and answers in 2.5 s at the median on Google Local, against 5.6 s for GPT-6 Sol. In conversations, the typed state keeps the ranking across switches and returns, but it recognizes only 19-27% of withdrawn needs.

This yields faster turns than LLM re-ranking and interpretable orderings that show which needs each item satisfies.
items.reasoning: A pragmatic, efficiency-oriented alternative to LLM-based conversational recommenders with clear interpretability advantages, but the contribution is more of an applied system design than a novel methodology, and evaluation scope appears limited.

items.title: How long must an honest confidence interval be after causal discovery? Benign and malignant weak edges
items.content: After causal discovery, a confidence interval for a total effect valid uniformly over the model class must pay for structural uncertainty. We measure this price by the worst-case ratio of expected length to that of the efficient interval knowing the graph, for linear Gaussian models with a known superset of the adjacencies and k-triangle faithfulness. The global price is of order sqrt(n) once one edge can be malignant, so we study it locally, near a generic distribution with one edge absent. Our main result classifies this weak edge by Meek closures. It is benign if deleting it leaves the effect identifiable in the resulting MPDAG and Markov equivalent explanations agree; the local price is then bounded, and otherwise, for small k, of order sqrt(n). At benign edges the price is of order R+K, with R a ratio of efficient lengths and K a cross-model constant. It equals one, so that honesty is free, exactly when K = 0, generically decided by a d-separation. For two Markov classes it is determined within a factor 3.40, and its upper bound is approached without knowing the base point or the weak edge. A further graphical condition gives the rate uniformly in a second edge's margin.

items.summary: This theory paper quantifies the price of structural uncertainty in confidence intervals for total causal effects after causal discovery, in linear Gaussian models with known adjacency supersets and k-triangle faithfulness. The main result classifies weak edges by Meek closures: benign edges (where the effect remains identifiable) incur bounded local price, while malignant edges force intervals of order sqrt(n) longer. It gives a sharp characterization of when post-discovery inference is feasible.
items.reasoning: A clean, conceptually important result for the causal discovery and inference literature, clarifying exactly when structure learning does or does not destroy statistical efficiency. Mathematically deep but specialized; relevance to broader AI is indirect.

items.title: NSFL: A Post-Training Neuro-Symbolic Fuzzy Logic Framework for Boolean Operators in Neural Embeddings
items.content: Standard dense retrievers lack a native calculus for multi-atom logical constraints. We introduce Neuro-Symbolic Fuzzy Logic (NSFL), a framework that adapts formal t-norms and t-conorms to neural embedding spaces without requiring retraining. NSFL operates as a first-order hybrid calculus: it anchors logical operations on isolated zero-order similarity scores while actively steering representations using Neuro-Symbolic Deltas (NS-Delta) -- the first-order marginal differences derived from contextual fusion. This preserves pure atomic meaning while capturing domain reliance, preventing the representation collapse and manifold escape endemic to traditional geometric baselines. For scalable real-time retrieval, Spherical Query Optimization (SQO) leverages Riemannian optimization to project these fuzzy formulas into manifold-stable query vectors. Validated across six distinct encoder configurations and two modalities (including zero-shot and SOTA fine-tuned models), NSFL yields mAP improvements up to +81%. Notably, NSFL provides an additive 20% average and up to 47% boost even when applied to encoders explicitly fine-tuned for logical reasoning. By establishing a training-free, order-aware calculus for high-dimensional spaces, this framework lays the foundation for future dynamic scaling and learned manifold logic.

items.reasoning: Novel neuro-symbolic angle on a genuine limitation of dense retrievers (logical composition of constraints) with practical efficiency considerations; conceptually dense and harder to validate, and applicability depends on empirical adoption.

items.title: OSLA: Observation-Aware Local Alignment and Cross-Scene Relation Learning for Any-Scenario Person Re-Identification
items.content: Any-Scenario Person Re-Identification (AS-ReID) aims to retrieve identities across spectral modalities and aerial-ground viewpoints using a unified model. However, changes in viewpoint and spectrum can make local correspondences unreliable, while conventional sampling may omit cross-camera positive relations needed for training. To address these challenges, we propose OSLA, an observation-aware framework built on supervised CLIP-ReID that combines Local Identity Alignment (LIA) and Cross-Scene Relation Learning (CSR). Specifically, LIA uses historical identity observations and competing-identity information to select reliable cross-scene local correspondences while allowing unmatched regions. Local-to-global distillation transfers identity knowledge from correctly classified historical local features into the global representation. CSR couples observed-cell sampling with spectrum-grouped ranking to jointly organize and optimize cross-camera relations. Sampling across two cameras and two spectra provides same- and cross-spectrum positives, while ranking constrains positive-negative scores separately by gallery spectrum on the final retrieval descriptor. Both modules operate only during training, preserving the original visual encoder and retrieval descriptor at inference. Experiments on WHU-MARS-1000 and WHU-MARS-2337 demonstrate that OSLA achieves absolute Rank-1 gains of 5.0% and 4.8% over UAD, respectively, under the AS-ReID protocol. The code will be available.

It targets a unified model for difficult cross-modality, cross-viewpoint retrieval.

Sampling across two cameras and two spectra provides same- and cross-spectrum positives, while ranking constrains positive-negative scores separately by gallery spectrum on the final retrieval descriptor. Both modules operate only during training, preserving the original visual encoder and retrieval descriptor at inference. Experiments on WHU-MARS-1000 and WHU-MARS-2337 demonstrate that OSLA achieves absolute Rank-1 gains of 5.0% and 4.8% over UAD, respectively, under the AS-ReID protocol. The code will be available.

items.title: Robust Trajectory Prediction Under Sensing and V2X Noise: Evaluation and Mitigation Strategies
items.content: Anticipating the future behavior of surrounding objects is key for the safe and efficient navigation of autonomous vehicles. State-of-the-art Transformer-based interaction-aware trajectory prediction models are typically trained and evaluated on large-scale, highly curated datasets obtained by filtering any object detection and tracking noise through extensive offline post-processing. However, in real-world deployments, the detected objects' state (position, heading, and speed) estimates are inherently affected by sensing and localization uncertainties. These uncertainties can be even higher for connected and automated vehicles receiving information from other road users through Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) communications. In this paper, we first investigate the sensitivity of five state-of-the-art Transformer-based interaction-aware trajectory prediction models to realistic noisy object state estimates. Numerical results show that prediction accuracy degrades by up to a 6x factor as the noise level increases, highlighting the models' sensitivity to the mismatch between the noise conditions encountered during training and those experienced at deployment. We then show that retraining models on a more realistic noise-augmented dataset is a more effective strategy to mitigate the impact of noisy object state estimates on trajectory prediction accuracy than using denoising modules at the input. Retrained models limit the prediction accuracy degradation below a 1.5x factor. The noise-augmented dataset is openly released to support further research.

items.title: Rollout Scheduling for Chaotic Neural ODEs: Coverage Gains, Computational Cost, and Predictive Accuracy
items.content: Training Neural Ordinary Differential Equations (Neural ODEs) on chaotic systems is difficult because small changes in model parameters can lead to rapidly growing differences in predictions. A rollout is a trajectory predicted by the model. Choosing its length from a single global Lyapunov time overlooks differences in local instability. We study rollout scheduling for training on one contiguous rollout per sampled state, asking whether adapting its length to local instability improves prediction. We find the schedule that uses the most trajectory data under an instability budget, a limit on how much instability any one rollout may accumulate. Under stated assumptions, we bound the resulting coverage gain and the coverage lost when the instability estimates are in error. Numerical checks illustrate the theory. Training experiments on Lorenz-63, Lorenz-96, and Kuramoto--Sivashinsky compare adaptive and constant schedules at the same instability budgets and maximum rollout lengths. The budgets are computed from the true system's finite-time Lyapunov exponents. Across the tested settings, adaptive schedules increase trajectory coverage at additional computational cost, without showing a consistent improvement in prediction accuracy. On Lorenz-63, limiting adaptive rollouts to the horizon used to estimate instability improves prediction at the larger budgets. On Kuramoto--Sivashinsky, most configurations provide useful short-time predictions, while all tested long rollouts eventually fail. These findings show why coverage, prediction accuracy, and long-time behavior need separate evaluation, and why instability estimates should be checked over the windows used in training.

The assumptions are narrow (one contiguous rollout per sampled state) and the numerical validation appears limited, so the broader impact is uncertain.

items.title: HandXFM: Semantic-Structural Distillation for Hand Radiograph Foundation Models
items.content: Hand radiographs support diverse clinical tasks, including skeletal maturity assessment, rheumatoid arthritis scoring, abnormality screening, and anatomical localization, yet existing models are typically trained separately for each task and dataset. We present HandXFM, a domain-specific foundation model that leverages cross-modality knowledge for comprehensive hand X-ray understanding. HandXFM distills semantic priors from BiomedCLIP and structural cues from a chest X-ray Vision Transformer (ViT) through a unified alignment framework, integrating complementary medical knowledge in an interpretable way. After pretraining, HandXFM can be adapted to a range of musculoskeletal tasks, including bone age estimation, SvH score prediction, abnormality detection, joint localization, bone segmentation, and visual question answering. It consistently outperforms task-specific and single-expert baselines, achieving up to 0.11 improvement in Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC) for bone age prediction and a 12\% accuracy gain in abnormality classification. Moreover, HandXFM generalizes to unseen datasets and yields cross-attention maps linking clinical terms to anatomical regions. These results demonstrate that multi-expert distillation effectively unifies semantic and structural supervision within a single pretrained model, establishing HandXFM as an interpretable and generalizable foundation model for hand radiograph analysis.

items.title: Targeted Learning for Externally Controlled Trials and Beyond
items.content: This paper focuses on externally controlled trials (ECTs), which consist of a single-arm clinical trial supplemented by an external control arm (ECA). Potential data sources for the ECA can be broadly classified into three categories: (i) the control arm of a historical clinical trial, (ii) a concurrent cohort study, and (iii) external real-world data (RWD). In this paper, we consider a broad class of estimands defined through balancing weights. For a given estimand in the class, we discuss the efficient influence function (EIF) and the targeted maximum likelihood estimator (TMLE), together with practical implementation algorithms. Within the targeted learning framework, TMLE is a substitution estimator that enjoys several desirable theoretical properties and favorable finite-sample performance. Finally, the proposed framework is extended to two additional settings: (1) randomized controlled trials (RCTs) augmented with external covariate information to define a target population, and (2) indirect treatment comparisons (ITCs) that combine individual patient data (IPD) from an internal RCT with aggregate data (AgD) from an external RCT.
items.author: Yixin Fang and Weili He
items.summary: This methodological paper develops targeted maximum likelihood estimation (TMLE) for externally controlled clinical trials, covering estimands defined through balancing weights over three external control data sources: historical trial control arms, concurrent cohorts, and real-world data. It derives efficient influence functions and provides practical implementation algorithms with favorable theoretical and finite-sample properties.
items.reasoning: Rigorous and practically useful for clinical trial methodology, particularly as single-arm trials with external controls grow in regulatory relevance, but it applies established targeted learning machinery to a new setting rather than introducing new statistical theory.

items.title: When a Permitted Action Completes a Forbidden Workflow: Designing Consequence-Oriented Approval for LLM Agents
items.content: Tool-using language-model agents increasingly ask people to approve consequential actions, yet an approval prompt shows only the next step. A request to send a file to an approved recipient can look harmless even when that file was assembled, several steps earlier, from data the user said must never leave. We call this a cumulative authorization failure and argue that it is an interaction design problem as much as a security problem. The evidence a reviewer needs is spread across the trajectory, and listing it in time order leaves the reviewer to reconstruct the causal chain. We present the Cumulative Consent Ledger (CCL), an approval interface built on four design principles that restate the user's intent, bind the review to the exact action, compose the cumulative consequence, and keep every claim checkable. A trusted monitor that tracks artifact lineage supplies the evidence. In a between-subjects study with 80 participants and 960 approval decisions, CCL was associated with fewer unsafe approvals than an evidence-matched chronological log (24.2% vs. 32.5%), higher comprehension, and faster decisions, although the adjusted difference in unsafe approvals remained uncertain (-7.9 points, 95% CrI [-19.7, 3.8]). In a system evaluation, the monitor detected 89.2% of 120 violating checkpoints and, used as an execution gate, reduced executed unsafe effects from 43.3% to 5.0% for one agent at a small cost to benign completion. We derive implications for designing consent around consequences rather than individual calls.

items.summary: Identifies cumulative authorization failure in tool-using LLM agents, where individually permitted steps combine into a forbidden workflow, such as sending an approved recipient a file assembled from data the user forbade sharing. The paper proposes the Cumulative Consent Ledger, an approval interface that restates user intent, binds review to the exact action, and composes cumulative consequences. Frames agent safety as an interaction design problem as much as a security problem.
items.reasoning: Fresh framing of an underexplored agent safety gap with a concrete interface design, though it is primarily conceptual/design work and its effectiveness would need deployment-level empirical validation.

items.title: LoopSight: Looped Vision Transformers with Gated Prediction Memory
items.content: Looped vision transformers extend computation for visual reasoning by repeatedly applying a shared Transformer core. A challenge is to preserve useful prediction information across loop iterations while allowing the computation state to evolve. In this paper we introduce LoopSight, a looped vision transformer that uses Gated Prediction Memory (GPM) to maintain a persistent prediction state for readout, separate from the core's evolving computation state. At each iteration, a cross-attention gate uses the core's candidate features, the previous prediction state, and the current task state to control writes at the patch and channel level. The model decodes its prediction from the updated memory. We condition the shared core on the current iteration using asymptotic loop encoding and train the model by supervising its prediction at loop counts sampled from a truncated Gaussian distribution. LoopSight outperforms LoopViT across three model scales on ARC-AGI-1 and ARC-AGI-2. On ARC-AGI-1, LoopSight-Small achieves 67.4% pass@2, a gain of 6.6 percentage points over LoopViT-Small with comparable parameter counts and FLOPs. LoopSight also outperforms LoopViT on Visual Sudoku and ImageNet classification. Further analyses on ARC-AGI-1 show that LoopSight preserves more already-correct predictions and maintains more stable readout features as its computation state continues to evolve. The code will be released at https://github.com/feufhd/LoopSight.

Uses asymptotic loop encoding to condition the shared core on the current iteration.

items.title: SemGuard: Semantics-Decoupled Watermarking for Gaussian Splatting
items.content: Gaussian Splatting provides an efficient representation for high-fidelity rendering of static and dynamic 3D scenes, motivating the copyright protection of Gaussian assets. In CLIP-guided Gaussian watermarking, a universal message decoder pretrained on textual watermark representations is subsequently applied to visual features containing both watermark information and scene-dependent semantics. However, text-only pretraining does not explicitly account for the semantic interference encountered during watermark extraction. To address this challenge, we propose SemGuard, a simple yet effective semantics-decoupled watermarking framework that learns to suppress scene-dependent semantic interference during universal message decoder pretraining. Specifically, SemGuard combines message-related CLIP text features with message-independent visual features extracted from unwatermarked scene images, constructing training representations with controllable semantic interference relevant to the target Gaussian assets. A progressive semantic interference curriculum gradually increases the contribution of visual features, allowing the decoder to first learn reliable message representations and then adapt to increasingly strong scene-dependent semantic interference. After pretraining for a given message length and semantic image pool, the decoder is frozen and reused across multiple Gaussian assets whose visual semantics are covered by the pretraining data. Experiments on static and dynamic Gaussian Splatting assets demonstrate improved rendering fidelity alongside reliable watermark extraction, while evaluations on static assets further show enhanced robustness against image-space distortions.

This improves copyright protection reliability for increasingly popular 3D Gaussian assets. The motivation is timely as 3D generative content proliferates.

items.title: Legal Is Not Good: A Pre-Registered Benchmark of Low-Cost Language and Decision Models on a New Strategy Game
items.content: Measure Before You Train argued that an agent's decisions should be measured against ground truth, under a protocol fixed in advance, before anyone trains or replaces the model behind them. We carry the method to a second, very different domain, a turn-based strategy game, and ask a deliberately modest question: how well do low-cost agents play under a pre-registered protocol? hexfolk is a minimal two-player 4X game written for this purpose, so no model has seen its rules or positions. A deterministic engine, one agent interface, a referee that never corrects an illegal or late move, and per-decision logs make every game replayable; questions and expected answers were committed before the games, on held-out seeds with mirrored seats and 95% Wilson intervals. Two small open language models (8B and 3B) lose every game to a few-line rule player. Answering in free text they are invalid on 98% of their decisions; constrained to legal moves they never play an invalid one, yet they lose to the uniformly random player (the 8B model wins 10.0 [4.3, 21.4]% of games), refuting our expectation that they would beat it; the result survives a control that shuffles the order of the options. Two native decision models never play an invalid move and both beat random; one loses all 50 games to the rule player, the other is not distinguishable from it in 50 games and beats a one-step search. The paid agents make tens to over a hundred model calls per game; against the same opponents a free 60 ms-per-move search, which makes none, outplays every paid model by the full range of the scale. Two 7-8B models served locally behave the same way. No frontier model is included.

It extends a measure-before-you-train methodology to a second domain, probing how well small agents play under fair, replayable conditions. Its emphasis on pre-registration is a methodological contribution to agent evaluation.

items.title: Analytical Modeling and Optimal GPU Provisioning for Disaggregated LLM Inference
items.content: We present OSplit, an exact analytical method that enables efficient partitioning of a GPU L1 domain into prefill and decode workers, including sharding for classical and advanced GPUs. OSplit takes into consideration model parameters, enabling any inference model to be partitioned into prefill and decode workers with a goal of producing the maximum throughput possible. OSplit is based on a capacity model that takes as inputs the model, the loading scheme (batch size, max sequence length), and models an inference serving framework (vLLM) and computes the efficiency of each GPU. For this, we model H100 and GB300 GPUs, and model a scale-up domain, along with FlashAttention-based kernels. OSplit first computes an optimal collective generation policy, which gives inputs to the capacity model that enables optimal split of prefill and decode GPUs. We evaluate our scheme over H100 (NVL8) and GB300 (NVL72) using vLLM inference serving and show throughput, predicted and measured latency, showing near-perfect theoretical-to-measured values over leading LLMs (Llama and Qwen)

It computes optimal partitioning and collective generation policies to maximize throughput.
items.reasoning: Systems work of practical relevance as disaggregated prefill/decode inference becomes standard for serving large models; an analytical (rather than empirical-search) provisioning method is useful for capacity planning. Novelty is moderate since several analytical serving models exist.

items.title: Contrastive Gradient Guidance for Test-Time Multi-Preference Alignment of Diffusion Models
items.content: Aligning pre-trained diffusion models with multiple context-dependent preferences requires adapting generation at test time rather than relying on offline fine-tuning, which requires hyperparameter tuning and a new training run for each preference trade-off. Existing approaches compress diverse preferences into a single scalar reward objective for fine-tuning or test-time guidance rather than directly reusing existing generative experts released for different purposes and obtained through different fine-tuning methods. In this work, we propose Contrastive Gradient Guidance (CGG), a test-time compositional generative framework that reformulates multi-preference alignment as a composition of distributions. CGG represents each preference as a contrastive preference pair of favored experts and unfavored anti-experts, whose score difference forms a contrastive gradient guidance signal that combines denoising directions (gradients) from off-the-shelf diffusion models during sampling. Experiments show that CGG reuses pre-trained and fine-tuned models as favored experts or anti-experts to control output style and safety, and that it can be combined with existing sampling-based reward guidance. With a single fixed scale per pair, CGG composes five preferences at once and gives a more balanced trade-off across text-image preference, concept control, photographic fidelity, and safety than offline fine-tuning, weight-space merging, and reward steering.

items.reasoning: A practical test-time alignment framework that sidesteps reward-scalar compression and reuses existing fine-tuned experts, an attractive property as the ecosystem accumulates preference-specialized checkpoints. Novelty is moderate; compositional guidance ideas exist but the contrastive expert-pair formulation is a fresh angle.

items.title: PhyMind: Physics-Informed Masked Autoencoding for EEG Foundation Models
items.content: EEG foundation models are pre-trained almost exclusively with masked reconstruction through a free-form decoder, sometimes with hand-crafted spectral targets added, as in MANAS-2. We study what happens when that decoder is replaced by a generative forward model of EEG. PhyMind keeps a standard masked transformer encoder, but its decoder must explain the masked signal through 68 cortical regions, each driven by damped stochastic oscillators and an aperiodic Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, projected to the recording's own montage by a fixed boundary-element lead field evaluated per derivation. Training combines masked reconstruction with a Whittle spectral likelihood, an oscillator-dynamics residual, a minimum-norm source prior and a penalised neural residual. In a controlled comparison (same encoder, data, steps and seed), the physics decoder produces encoder tokens whose spectral content is far more linearly decodable than with a masked-autoencoder decoder or with the MANAS-2 objective: mean R^2 on a token-level spectral probe with amplitude-normalised targets is 0.67/0.77/0.77 on three datasets, against 0.24/0.50/0.50 (MAE) and 0.48/0.67/0.66 (MANAS-2 objective), approaching the released 92.8M-parameter MANAS-2 (0.71/0.81/0.80). Downstream gains in the controlled setting are small (four-task mean balanced accuracy 56.6 vs. 53.8 for MAE frozen, 63.8 vs. 62.7 fine-tuned). Region-level features from the physics decoder raise frozen four-class motor-imagery accuracy by 7-14 points, so a 7.2M-parameter model pre-trained on 3k hours of open EEG is comparable to the released MANAS-2 with frozen features (63.0 vs. 61.6). After full fine-tuning, MANAS-2 remains better (66.8 vs. 65.4 for our best model). The inferred sources do not reproduce the lateralisation that a classical inverse solution finds in motor imagery, so we do not claim anatomical interpretability. Code and weights are released.

items.title: STRIDE: Strategy-to-Tactics Retrieval-Guided Skill Disclosure and Evolution for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
items.content: Skill-augmented reinforcement learning enables LLM agents to reuse task-solving knowledge across episodes, but existing systems typically expose agents to a flat skill pool and update skills only from coarse, episode-level outcomes. This conflates two distinct uses of experience: a stable strategy that should frame the whole episode, and tactical know-how that should be retrieved only when the agent reaches a local execution gap. We propose STRIDE (Strategy-to-Tactics Retrieval-guided skIll Disclosure and Evolution), a framework that brings progressive skill disclosure into agentic reinforcement learning. STRIDE keeps the selected strategy visible as episode context, exposes a compact tactic menu, and loads full tactic content only after an explicit retrieval action. This interface turns each retrieval into an event-level credit unit: the same event provides process feedback for learning when to retrieve and supplies evidence for skill-bank evolution. On ALFWorld, STRIDE achieves a 92.7% average success rate with Qwen3-4B and a 94.9% average success rate with Qwen3-8B. On WebShop, it improves over the strongest reproduced skill-augmented baseline by 4.5 score points and 1.9 success-rate percentage points. These results show that skill reuse is most effective when persistent strategies preserve global task structure and tactics are disclosed only at local decision bottlenecks.

This aims to reduce context bloat and improve skill reuse in LLM agents.
items.reasoning: A sensible hierarchical decomposition of skill memory for LLM agents with a clean retrieval interface; conceptually aligned with current agentic RL trends but appears limited in scale and from an academic group.

items.title: World Models for Ocean Engineering: A Critical Review of Maritime Autonomy, Adaptive Latent Prediction, Digital Twins, and Biodiversity Monitoring
items.content: Marine robots face partial observability, non-stationary dynamics, and sparse communication, motivating WMs that learn compact predictive states for planning. This review develops a functional taxonomy of WMs for ocean engineering, focusing on Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) and AdaJEPA's test-time adaptation within model predictive control, mapping them to navigation, adaptive sampling, digital twins, and biodiversity monitoring, and separating demonstrated evidence from prospective applications. The synthesis identifies key Gaps: benchmarks, uncertainty calibration, safe adaptation and proposes a research agenda for physics-informed, deployment-adaptive marine WMs validated through simulation and field missions.

items.reasoning: A structured critical review opening a niche application area (marine world models) to broader ML audiences; useful as a roadmap, but reviews score lower on novelty and the domain is specialized.

items.title: Beyond Evidence Coverage: Encoding-Time Access in Multi-Agent Systems
items.content: Cache-sharing multi-agent systems can retain every evidence token's representation while preventing cross-worker access during encoding. We test whether this coverage recovers joint-encoding quality using attention masks over two logical workers in frozen Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct models. Tokens, positions, and answer-time access remain fixed within comparisons. We evaluate 200 two-hop MuSiQue-Ans questions and 200 selected HotpotQA bridge questions. In data-layout seed 0, averaged across models, blocking access costs 5.6 and 6.8 F1 points relative to full access on MuSiQue and HotpotQA, respectively. Exposing the earlier worker's supporting paragraph improves F1 over blocked access by 7.6 and 6.7 points; equal-token non-support access provides no detectable average gain. With model weights and greedy decoding fixed, we vary distractor layouts using five data-layout seeds per dataset for Qwen3-8B and three for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Supporting-paragraph access has higher mean F1 than blocked and equal-token non-support access in every evaluated data-layout seed. Supporting access can also outperform full access, but its advantage depends on the model, dataset, and layout. Oracle support labels isolate access from selection error; the study does not evaluate a deployable selector. Complete evidence coverage at answer time therefore does not guarantee joint-encoding quality: which supporting facts can interact during encoding matters.

items.title: PartPO: Part-Level Policy Optimization for Shape-to-Program Generation
items.content: We present PartPO, a reinforcement learning method for generating structured shape programs from 3D point clouds. Existing shape-to-program models are trained with supervised learning on procedurally generated data and generalize poorly to more diverse shapes, while reinforcement learning from execution feedback assigns a single scalar reward to a long program that builds many parts, making credit assignment difficult. PartPO instead builds on a core property of the task: shape programs are self-describing, with each semantically named part produced by its own code block. It segments each generated program by its parts and applies part-level rewards only to the code of the corresponding part, a category reward only to the object name, and a shape-level reward to the whole program. The required part supervision is obtained without manual annotation, by grounding part names on target meshes with an open-vocabulary segmentation model prompt-tuned on the model's own outputs. Applied to MeshCoder, PartPO improves reconstruction accuracy and execution success on ShapeNetCore and ABO over the base model, rejection-sampling fine-tuning and trajectory-level RL, and generalizes to the unseen HSSD dataset. Code will be released at https://github.com/HannuoZ/PartPO.

It applies part-level rewards to the corresponding code blocks, category rewards to object names, and shape-level rewards to whole programs, solving the credit assignment problem of scalar execution rewards.
items.reasoning: The hierarchical, structure-aware reward decomposition is a clever application of fine-grained RL credit assignment to program generation. It is a focused contribution within 3D shape understanding rather than a broad advance, but the methodology could inspire similar structured-reward designs elsewhere.

items.title: Beyond Omission: Measuring Critical-Information Fulfillment of Large Language Models in Bengali and English
items.content: Evaluations of multilingual trustworthiness often ask whether a model leaves out information that a user needs. We examine whether that question is sufficient. Using 157 matched tasks written in English (EN), natural Bengali (BN) and Bengali-matrix Bengali-English code-switching (BN-CS), we scored 1,413 responses from three models (GPT-6.1 Sol, Qwen3.5-9B and Gemma 4 12B) against required information units (RIUs) fixed before any model was run. The scoring separates outright omission from content that is present but incorrect, insufficient or only partly met. The prespecified primary estimand, the domain-equal paired difference in critical omission rate (BN - EN), showed no detectable difference (+0.003, 95% CI -0.014 to +0.015), with omission near zero in every condition. The Bengali deficit appeared in fulfillment instead. Critical coverage was 0.050 lower in Bengali (95% CI 0.022 to 0.079) and strict complete-task success 0.093 lower (95% CI 0.055 to 0.131); both gaps came from the two open-weight models, and Sol showed none. Code-switching recovered part of the loss in RIU coverage (+0.028, 95% CI 0.012 to 0.045). On these data, an omission count alone would have shown no language gap. The automated judge passed prespecified agreement gates after a documented failed first attempt. A blind native-speaker rating of 60 study responses agreed with it on RIU scores (alpha 0.84) and critical RIUs (98% exact) but fell short on Bengali RIU agreement (alpha 0.77) and on the unsupported-content check (93% exact), and a blind check of its reason codes agreed on whether a critical unit was omitted for 79 of 81 units. Data, rubrics, responses, scores and code are released.

items.reasoning: The prespecified estimand and separation of omission from incorrect/insufficient content reflect unusually careful evaluation design, and multilingual (especially code-switching) evaluation is underrepresented. However, the scope is limited to three models including mid-size open models, and the null primary result narrows the takeaway's impact.

items.title: Is the learner or the summary the limit? Auditing machine-learning energy reconstruction for air-shower arrays on KASCADE and GRAPES-3
items.content: Machine-learning energy estimators for cosmic-ray arrays are usually trained on a few fitted shower parameters, not station signals. When their resolution stops improving, standard diagnostics cannot say whether a better model would help or the summary has run out of information. We use a five-step audit that compares trained models with a learner-independent estimate of the lowest error the summary allows (its squared-loss Bayes risk, or floor), tests which inputs add information and flags inputs merely computed from the fit. We apply it to public KASCADE simulations with three hadronic-interaction models (QGSJET-II-04, EPOS-LHC and SIBYLL-2.3d), to 13,848,509 measured KASCADE events and to simulated GRAPES-3 events. Within known energy decades below 10^16 eV, gradient boosting on nine reconstructed features is within 2.2% of the estimated floor under every estimator setting, so more capacity is not expected to gain more than about 2%. The floor is an estimate, accurate to about 1% in a semi-synthetic benchmark with intervals that under-cover, and not a bound on the true Bayes risk. Replacing reconstructed by true particle numbers removes 70 to 72% of the error variance below 10^15 eV and 24 to 26% between 10^16 and 10^17 eV on all three models, yet simulated station signals close about a tenth of that gap. On GRAPES-3, networks given images rendered from the fit do no better than the fit. In measured data, the mean muon size at fixed electron size lies within every model's proton-to-iron bracket and a label-free probe finds the muon channel used as in simulation; neither fixes the energy scale. Energy-labelled results are simulated.

It can determine whether resolution limits stem from the model or from information loss in the fitted shower parameters. The audit methodology is transferable to other scientific ML applications where feature summaries may cap performance.
items.reasoning: Rigorous, principled diagnostics applied at impressive data scale with broad applicability of the audit framework; however, domain-specific findings and lack of new ML methods limit cross-field impact.

items.title: VistaTree: Question Answering over Long Multimodal Documents with Image-Derived Summary Trees
items.content: Answering questions over long multimodal documents requires locating relevant evidence across pages containing text, tables, and figures. When the document exceeds the model's context window, selective retrieval becomes necessary. We introduce VistaTree, a document question-answering agent that builds a summary tree directly from rendered page images. VistaTree segments documents into contiguous page spans, recursively groups them into a topic hierarchy, and refines sibling summaries to distinguish neighboring sections. At query time, the agent uses node summaries to select relevant nodes and reads the corresponding pages, using hierarchical navigation when the full outline exceeds the context budget. Experiments on MMLongBench-Doc and LongDocURL evaluate answer quality and retrieval cost using a locally hosted vision-language model, and quantify the performance gap between global and hierarchical access to the index.
items.author: Yexiang Cheng, Xiaochen Zheng, David Tokar, Tatyana Y. Doktorova
items.summary: VistaTree builds a hierarchical summary tree directly from rendered page images of long multimodal documents, enabling an agent to navigate topic-structured nodes and read only relevant pages when content exceeds the context window. It is evaluated on MMLongBench-Doc and LongDocURL for answer quality and retrieval cost.
items.reasoning: Practical document-QA agent design addressing real context-limit constraints; solid engineering but hierarchical summarization/retrieval is a well-trodden approach.

At query time, the agent uses node summaries to select relevant nodes and reads the corresponding pages, using hierarchical navigation when the full outline exceeds the context budget. items.title: ADEPT: Adaptive Monocular Depth Estimation via Model-In-The-Loop Photometric Tuning with Capture Risk Prediction
items.content: Exposure and gain determine the visual evidence available to monocular depth estimation (MDE), particularly when robot motion creates a tradeoff between light collection and motion blur. We present ADEPT, a framework that adapts these settings using learned feedback from a frozen depth model. During training, ground-truth depth identifies the lowest-error reference within a group of physically evaluated camera settings. A compact predictor learns reference-relative disagreement (RRD) between each candidate's depth prediction and the reference prediction using regression and ranking losses. At deployment, it scores observed captures using frozen-model features and camera, motion, and illumination context, without ground truth or reference images. A contextual Gaussian-process controller uses recent scores to select subsequent exposure and gain settings under motion and photometric constraints. We evaluate offline camera selection with relative and metric Depth Anything v2 and demonstrate online control with the affine-invariant variant on a mobile robot. Across nine equally weighted scene-illumination conditions, ADEPT reduces mean scale-and-shift-aligned $\mathrm{Abs}_{\mathrm{rel}}$ by 14.6% relative to built-in auto-exposure and by 10.0% relative to the best-performing evaluated prior controller.

items.title: Grounded in Contact: Reducing Floating and Interpenetration Artifacts with Multimodal Skill-Effect Models
items.content: Learning to predict the effects of contact-rich manipulation skills requires models that represent distinct outcome modes rather than a single expected result. Even for basic skills such as pushing, picking, and placing, small variations in contact conditions or object geometry can produce qualitatively different object motions under nearly identical states and actions. Deterministic and Gaussian models tend to average over these alternatives or represent them as a single broad distribution, obscuring distinct modes such as sliding, toppling, and rotating. We study probabilistic skill-effect models that learn multimodal distributions over object pose changes given partial point clouds and actions. We instantiate this abstraction with three representative model classes: mixture density networks, state tokenization, and flow matching, each paired with latent dynamics for next-step prediction. Across diverse objects and skills, explicitly multimodal models predict which outcome occurs more accurately than deterministic and Gaussian baselines. In planning, flow matching significantly improves task success over the deterministic baseline on every skill and achieves the highest success on every multi-step sequence. On a real robot, probabilistic models succeed at pick about twice as often as the deterministic baseline, providing evidence that probabilistic skill effects offer a practical abstraction for reasoning and planning under uncertainty.

items.title: Continuous-Time LQR from a Single Discrete-Time Off-Policy Batch
items.content: We study discounted continuous-time linear--quadratic regulation (LQR) with unknown drift parameters and additive noise, using a single batch of discrete-time off-policy transitions. Discrete-time methods target a policy tied to the training interval, while shortening this interval can make learning from finite data more sensitive to noise. Learning an accurate continuous-time controller therefore requires balancing discretization and finite-sample errors while preserving stability throughout policy improvement. We develop a drift-only policy iteration algorithm, termed PhiBE-PI, using one quadratic state--action critic for policy evaluation and explicit greedy improvement. Reusing the batch makes later policies depend on the data. Exploiting the quadratic structure of LQR, we show that the data enter every policy evaluation only through one policy-independent empirical matrix, so a single high-probability bound controls all iterates.   For sufficiently large discount~$\beta$, small observation intervals, and a sufficiently large batch, we prove that all iterates are stabilizing for the discounted problem and converge quadratically to a data-dependent fixed point. The gain bound separates iteration, finite-sample, and discretization errors. In this regime, the finite-sample and discretization terms scale as $1/(\beta\sqrt{n\Delta t})$ and $\Delta t/\beta$, respectively. The bounds thus reveal a tradeoff: at a fixed batch size, finer observations reduce discretization error but increase finite-sample error. Because PhiBE-PI approximates the continuous-time optimal gain rather than a discrete-time one, its policy can remain near-optimal when deployed at faster control rates. Experiments confirm this advantage over discrete-time Bellman-equation baselines when the observation interval is small relative to the system's time scale.

items.title: Training Dynamics of Large State-Transition Models
items.content: Next-token prediction relies on learned token embeddings whose dimension $d$ is much smaller than the vocabulary size $V$. Existing analyses of training dynamics either fix the embeddings with $d\ge V$ or train them only in restricted settings. It remains unclear whether jointly training the embeddings by gradient-based methods from random initialization leads to accurate prediction when $d<V$. In this paper, we study this question in the simplest setting where it is already nontrivial, namely next-token prediction with a one-token context, which we refer to as a state-transition model. The model consists of an input embedding and an output embedding, either untied or tied, and is trained from Gaussian initialization by perturbed gradient descent with weight decay on the population cross-entropy loss. We consider ground-truth transition laws whose centered log-probability table has low rank and bounded entries, and measure the prediction quality by the relative prediction gain (RPG). It is zero for the uniform predictor and one for the optimal predictor. For the untied model, we show that when $d=\Omega(\sqrt V)$, with probability at least $1-e^{-cd}$ for some constant $c$, the RPG is above $7/8$ at every iterate in the final $1-1/d$ fraction of training iterations. For the tied model trained on a subset of states, we prove that the RPG on the observed states is $1-O(V/d^2)$, and under a coverage condition on the ground truth and a bound on the learned embeddings, we further prove a prediction guarantee on the unseen states. Our analysis is based on the bounded trace of the Hessian of the softmax cross-entropy loss, which implies that the approximate second-order stationary points reached by training have high prediction gain. Numerical experiments with practical parameter choices illustrate the persistent training gain and the transfer of the tied model.

items.summary: This theory paper analyzes whether jointly training input and output embeddings by gradient descent from random initialization yields accurate next-token prediction when embedding dimension is smaller than vocabulary size, in the minimal setting of one-token-context state-transition models. It covers tied and untied embeddings trained with perturbed gradient descent and weight decay on population loss.
items.reasoning: Provides rigorous training-dynamics analysis in a deliberately minimal but nontrivial setting relevant to understanding overparameterized-to-underparameterized embedding learning. The simplification to one-token contexts limits direct applicability to modern LLMs.

items.title: FlexWAM: Learning Flexible Visual Routing for World Action Models
items.content: Humans dynamically adjust their reliance on sensory modalities across manipulation stages. Although existing World Action Models (WAMs) fuse multi-camera observations, they struggle to adapt their reliance on individual views based on the current observations. This raises a central question: how can the action expert integrate complementary visual evidence while prioritizing the views most relevant to the current action? FlexWAM addresses this challenge through three modules. First, we alternate within-view and cross-view attention to capture view-specific dynamics and complementary cues. For action prediction, View-Routed Action Attention uses an observation-conditioned router to prioritize relevant views. To calibrate routing, we train a critic using counterfactual view credit, estimated from action loss sensitivity upon suppressing each view's contribution to action attention. We evaluate FlexWAM with two video backbones on five challenging real-world manipulation tasks across two robot platforms. The two variants improve mean task success by 16.4 and 23.0 percentage points over the strongest baseline. Project website: https://flexwam.github.io/.

A critic trained with counterfactual view credit calibrates the routing, mimicking how humans shift sensory reliance across manipulation stages.
items.reasoning: A thoughtful architectural advance for multi-camera robot manipulation addressing adaptive view reliance, with a principled counterfactual credit mechanism for training the router. Impact depends on demonstrated gains over strong WAM baselines, which the abstract does not quantify.

items.title: Beyond Binary Correctness: A Surrogate for Confidence Learning in Large Language and Vision-Language Models
items.content: Confidence estimation for large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) aims to assess how likely a particular generated response is to be correct. We investigate how learning this assessment can benefit from the model's predictive reliability on the underlying query. Binary correctness supervision, however, assigns identical labels to occasional errors and frequent failures, as well as isolated successes and consistent success. These outcomes can arise from substantially different predictive behavior under stochastic decoding. We propose a confidence-learning framework that supplements realized response correctness with query-level predictive reliability. We estimate reliability through repeated generations under a fixed model and decoding configuration, then combine the empirical success rate with individual correctness to construct a graded confidence surrogate. The surrogate differentiates responses sharing the same correctness label while preserving the average predictive reliability of the sampled response pool. To learn this target, we condition an independent confidence estimator on the query and its full generated response, and optimize backbone LoRA adapters together with a projection and scalar confidence head using mean squared error. Repeated sampling is required only for supervision construction; inference scores an individual response without additional generations. We establish ordering and mean preservation properties of the surrogate and derive a selective-risk bound connecting population surrogate prediction error to the error rate among accepted responses. We evaluate the framework across language and vision-language models, examining confidence calibration and selective prediction.

It proposes estimating query-level predictive reliability via repeated stochastic generations and combining it with realized correctness in a confidence-learning framework.
items.reasoning: Addresses an important, underexplored supervision problem in model confidence estimation with a clean surrogate signal; relevant to selective prediction and trustworthy deployment, though the repeated-sampling approach adds inference cost.
