items.title: RadarOSV: Unified 3D Scene and Motion Perception from mmWave Radars
items.content: Millimeter-wave radar offers weather-resilient sensing for 3D occupancy prediction. Existing radar occupancy methods mainly model geometry, with limited joint modeling of semantics and motion. Cascaded imaging radar provides fine spatial detail but has a limited unambiguous velocity range, whereas single-chip radar offers a wider range but coarser spatial resolution. We propose RadarOSV, to our knowledge the first radar-only framework that jointly predicts occupancy, dynamic object semantics, and ground-relative velocity from raw radar data in unified voxels, by exploiting complementary measurements from both radars. Its Polar-to-Cartesian Geometry (PCG) backbone maps polar imaging-radar features into Cartesian voxels through fixed and deformable sampling, guiding cross-radar fusion for geometry and attribute prediction. Single-chip detection outputs provide class evidence, while raw Doppler spectra supply motion features and radial-velocity candidates. The velocity readout selects from these candidates using fused features to resolve aliasing, then combines the selected radial estimate with learned motion. Ego-motion compensation uses radar-estimated velocity, so inference requires no external odometry or other sensors. On K-Radar, single-frame PCG achieves 40.7% mIoU within 12.8 m, compared with RadarOcc's reported 34.3%. On the BRIDGE-Liv dataset, compared with a cascaded-radar baseline predicting the same outputs with external ego velocity, RadarOSV improves macro-averaged accuracy across four dynamic object classes within annotated object regions from 63.1% to 75.5% and reduces object radial-velocity MAE against manual Doppler annotations from 1.03 to 0.51 m/s, while maintaining geometric occupancy mIoU.

items.title: Small data machine learning: the trilemma of low-sample tabular regimes
items.content: Small tabular datasets leave few observations for choosing a model and assessing its predictions. We examine these competing demands in controlled simulations and on six public datasets, using SmallGBM and SmallMLP as fixed-configuration case studies. Three results illustrate why the choice of evaluation matters. First, at n = 100, five-fold cross-validation overstated the gain from tuning XGBoost by 0.063 ROC-AUC on random labels, while tuning improved independent-test ROC-AUC by 0.0078 on a Gaussian mixture. Second, when 20% of binary training labels were flipped, the median within-trial ROC-AUC loss was 0.0210 for SmallGBM and 0.0778 for a fixed 200-tree XGBoost configuration. A separate regression experiment showed the sensitivity of squared-error training to heavy-tailed responses. Third, in a heteroscedastic regression experiment, locally weighted SmallMLP intervals covered about one percentage point more test responses than ordinary split conformal intervals at both tested dimensions. Their mean widths also increased. On a Gaussian classification task with linear log odds, logistic regression achieved the highest mean ROC-AUC at all seven training sizes. These experiments identify settings in which a small-data model helps and quantify the cost of its assumptions.

It quantifies pitfalls such as cross-validation overstating tuning gains on random labels and shows robustness differences under label noise, e.g., much lower ROC-AUC loss for SmallGBM versus a 200-tree XGBoost under flipped labels.

It is an honest measurement study rather than a new method or theory, and the scope is modest, but practitioners in low-data domains benefit from such analyses.

items.title: GUI-Q: Task-Sensitive Granularity and Relation-Preserving Quantization for GUI Agents
items.content: Graphical user interface (GUI) agents enable automated interactions with mobile, web, and desktop interfaces. However, their large memory footprint and repeated model calls hinder deployment on resource-constrained devices, motivating post-training quantization (PTQ) without full retraining. Quantization can degrade GUI response accuracy and distort the instruction-vision affinities and local spatial relations needed for GUI target selection. Small coordinate errors can cause missed clicks, while early action errors can alter subsequent interface states and disrupt task execution. Local reconstruction error alone does not directly assess whether these responses and relations are preserved. We propose GUI-Q, a PTQ framework that targets response and relation preservation with 4-bit weights and 16-bit activations (W4A16). Task-Sensitive Granularity Allocation (TSGA) allocates finer groups under a scale-byte budget by combining response sensitivity with the measured reduction in activation-weighted distortion. Relation-Preserving Symmetry Selection (RPSS) then selects symmetric or asymmetric grids to preserve instruction-vision affinities and local spatial relations in GUIs. Across three GUI-capable models, GUI-Q improves mean grounding TargetHit by 8.04 to 12.55 points over the strongest evaluated 4-bit configurations, while reducing static peak graphics processing unit (GPU) memory by 49.9% to 56.2% relative to bfloat16 (BF16). Fixed-output replay with packed 4-bit execution provides 1.7 to 2.8 times model-call speedups. The code will be released.

The motivation is that small coordinate or relation distortions cause missed clicks and cascading task failures on resource-constrained devices.

items.title: DUET: Dual-MDL Unsupervised Entropy-Trie Segmentation for Low-Resource Languages
items.content: Morphological segmentation, the task of decomposing words into constituent morphemes, becomes particularly challenging under extreme data scarcity, a regime that can arise in language documentation and linguistic reasoning. This difficulty stems from existing approaches' reliance on annotated data, external resources, or recurring patterns that emerge only in larger corpora. To address this limitation, we propose Dual-MDL Unsupervised Entropy-Trie Segmentation (DUET), a deterministic unsupervised algorithm that decouples structural candidate generation from statistical candidate ranking. DUET combines branching entropy with recursive paradigm discovery to generate linguistically plausible candidate segmentations, then ranks them using a dual minimum description length (MDL) criterion: a corpus-level objective rewards morpheme reuse, while a construction-tree objective guards against over-segmentation. items.title: HEART: Hierarchical Expert Adaptive Refinement Transformer for ECG Representation Learning
items.content: Learning robust representations from electrocardiograms (ECGs) is challenging because repeated cardiac cycles coexist with subtle and sparse diagnostic cues in local morphology and rhythm-level context. Existing ECG foundation models commonly rely on Transformerbased patch encoders with uniformly shared dense refinement pathways, limiting adaptive processing across heterogeneous ECG tokens. We propose HEART (Hierarchical Expert Adaptive Refinement Transformer), an ECG foundation model that introduces stage-specific conditional expert refinement during self-supervised pre-training. HEART places a local-level MoE over patch-level representations before temporal contextualization and a global-level MoE over context-integrated token representations after self-attention. Token-level Top-1 routing allows different patches or contextual tokens within the same ECG to follow different expert pathways. On public ECG benchmarks, HEART achieves strong performance under both linear probing and fine-tuning, with particularly large frozen-encoder gains on PTB-XL Form and Rhythm (+6.76 AUROC points each over the strongest protocol-reproduced baseline). Routing analyses provide qualitative evidence of complementary local and global expert specialization. We release our code and pretrained models at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/HEART-5E9F.

items.title: MH-RAG-DIVE: Dynamic and Cost-Efficient Multi-Hop RAG Evaluation via Tree-Cached Dialogue Simulation
items.content: Quality assessment is essential for determining whether changes to a Retrieval-Augmented Generation system improve or maintain its performance. However, existing evaluation approaches often rely on single-turn or single-hop interactions and therefore do not capture the complexity of multi-hop, multi-turn conversations. We introduce MH-RAG-DIVE, a dynamic interactive user simulation framework designed to evaluate RAG systems in more complex multi-hop and multi-turn settings. The framework extends RAG-DIVE with a Context Discoverer, which identifies documents that can be combined to generate multi-hop questions within an ongoing conversation. To address the high computational cost of dynamic user simulation, we further introduce a Conversation Cacher, which reuses turns from previous evaluation runs while preserving the dynamic nature of the evaluation. We evaluate the framework across six distinct RAG configurations and compare its results with the original RAG-DIVE evaluation and the static, human-created CLAPNQ dataset. Our experiments show consistent performance trends across the evaluation approaches, while the more complex multi-hop and multi-turn setting exposes additional challenges for RAG systems. Furthermore, the Conversation Cacher substantially reduces token consumption, demonstrating its potential to make dynamic evaluation more cost-efficient. Finally, we apply MH-RAG-DIVE to an industrial RAG system with domain-specific data, demonstrating its applicability to real-world evaluation scenarios. Overall, our results show that the proposed approach provides a more complex and cost-efficient framework for evaluating RAG systems. All code and experimental data are publicly available in our GitHub repository (https://github.com/Daniel-Innsbruck/MH-RAG-DIVE).

items.title: Toward a Scalable and Adaptive Evaluation Measure for Time Series Anomaly Detection
items.content: Time Series Anomaly Detection (TSAD) is a fundamental task for time series analytics. Unlike other domains, where anomaly detection mainly focuses on point-based anomalies, TSAD must also handle range-based anomalies. Nevertheless, TSAD methods are commonly evaluated with measures inherited from classification, such as Precision and Recall, which require a threshold, or with threshold-independent ones, such as AUC, which ignore the temporal aspect of anomalies. To address these issues, the Volume Under the Surface (VUS) measure scores detectors across all thresholds and a range of buffer lengths and has been widely adopted. However, VUS has two limitations. First, VUS is computationally expensive, requiring 7 hours and 38 minutes to evaluate 32 detectors on the 870 TSB-AD time series. Second, VUS applies the same buffer lengths to every anomaly and detector, which can yield over-optimistic scores that hinder discrimination between accurate and mediocre detectors. We first introduce FastVUS, which computes VUS exactly and on average 76x faster by (i) computing all buffers in parallel, (ii) pruning irrelevant buffers for the existence reward, (iii) casting the confusion matrix as a single reduced matrix multiplication, (iv) computing VUS for every buffer length in one pass, and (v) discarding non-anomalous regions with a global mask. We also develop FastVUS-GPU, which recasts every step as batched tensor operations and reaches an average 304x speedup with a maximum error of $5\times10^{-3}$. Building on FastVUS, we introduce AutoVUS, an adaptive extension that compares each detection against a random baseline and selects the buffer length that maximizes the gain over it. Our case studies show that AutoVUS reduces over-optimistic scores and better separates accurate from mediocre detectors. We release FastVUS and AutoVUS as open source to promote time-aware evaluation at scale.

items.title: TamperCert: A Benchmark for Detecting Text Tampering in Degree Certificates
items.content: Degree certificates play a critical role in high-stakes decisions such as university admission, immigration, and hiring. The issuing institution vouches for the holder, so a forged certificate may let its bearer pass these checks. Degree certificate forgery is increasingly prevalent. Yet, many assume that it is easy to spot. Reported cases show otherwise: in 2024, the business school of the University of Hong Kong found that about 30 master's students had enrolled with forged academic credentials. Few studies have looked at how to detect forged degree certificates, partly because public benchmarks are scarce. We present TamperCert, a benchmark built from 400 real degree certificates issued by 38 universities. Each certificate was subjected to 11 publicly available tampering methods to alter the holder's name and further processed with four additional post-processing techniques, resulting in over 20,000 forged images. We evaluate 13 detectors, a commercial multimodal large language model (MLLM), and detectors trained on TamperCert.Our findings reveal that no detector is reliable for every tampering method. Consequently, a determined forger may still evade detection. Moreover, the commercial MLLM misses most forgeries made by general-purpose generative models, and post-processing, such as resizing an image or photographing it with a camera, severely degrades detection.

items.title: Autonomous UAV Navigation in an Unknown Environment via Multi-Trajectory Model Predictive Control
items.content: A novel model predictive control (MPC) formulation, named multi-trajectory MPC (mt-MPC), is presented and applied to the problem of autonomous navigation of an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) in an unknown environment. The UAV is equipped with a LiDAR sensor, providing only a partial description of the surroundings and resulting in time-varying constraints as the vehicle navigates among the obstacles. The control system layout is hierarchical: the low-level loops stabilize the vehicle's trajectories and track the set-points commanded by the high-level, mt-MPC controller. The latter is required to plan the UAV trajectory trading off safety, i.e. to avoid collisions with the uncertain obstacles, and exploitation, i.e. to reach an assigned target location. To achieve this goal, mt-MPC considers different future state trajectories in the same Finite Horizon Optimal Control Problem (FHOCP), enabling a partial decoupling between constraint satisfaction (safety) and cost function minimization (exploitation). Recursive feasibility and, consequently, persistent obstacle avoidance guarantees are derived under the assumption of a time invariant environment. The performance of the approach is studied in simulation and compared with that of a standard MPC, showing good improvement.

A hierarchical control layout separates low-level trajectory stabilization from the high-level mt-MPC planner.
items.reasoning: A well-structured control-theoretic contribution with clear practical relevance for UAV autonomy; the multi-trajectory MPC idea is a sensible extension of existing receding-horizon planning rather than a fundamental breakthrough.

items.title: Empirical Margin Sensitivity: An Interventional Neuron-Level Probe of Post-Trained Medical LLMs
items.content: Medical post-training raises benchmark accuracy, but accuracy does not show which internal components a model's decisions depend on, or whether components that support one benchmark also support another. We apply the weight-space intervention paradigm of ROME and MEMIT at the granularity of one MLP down-projection column. Our measurement, Empirical Margin Sensitivity (EMS), replaces each coordinate magnitude of a column by its mean while preserving the column's sign pattern and L1 scale, and records the resulting change in the logit margin between the correct option and its hardest-wrong competitor. This isolates the margin's dependence on a column's fine-grained coordinate structure while the column stays in place. We discover high-EMS columns (anchors) on MedQA in ten public checkpoints (four general-purpose bases and six medical post-trained variants) across the Gemma, Llama, Qwen, and AFM families, and measure the same columns on MedMCQA and PubMedQA. Mean-ablating each discovered anchor set lowers MedQA accuracy in all six post-trained models, by 6 to 28 points. In the two pure-SFT checkpoints, crushing anchors raises the PubMedQA margin on correctly answered items (negative EMS), and anchors with this property sit significantly deeper than the same model's other anchors; the four checkpoints trained with RL or mixed recipes show positive PubMedQA EMS and no significant depth shift. The depth association recurs in each of three held-out checkpoints. Because the checkpoints differ in data and pipeline as well as objective, we report these as per-checkpoint observations.

items.title: Random Feature Neural Networks for Stochastic Optimal Control
items.content: Random feature neural networks (RFNNs) sample their hidden parameters once and train only the output layer. We analyze RFNNs as feedback policies for finite-horizon stochastic control with trajectory-dependent objectives. A policy change alters later states, so the error that matters is the objective error of the induced trajectory rather than a pointwise regression error. We extend the quantitative random-feature approximation theory for PDE solutions and nonlinear regression to feedback control. We investigate the objective error of an RFNN policy through two sources, approximation of the policy by random features and estimation of the objective from finitely many paths. A stability estimate for the controlled trajectory turns a policy error into an objective error. Under bounded actions, a regular benchmark policy and exact empirical minimization, the expected objective gap to the benchmark policy is at most of order $N^{-1/2}+\sqrt{N(1+\log N)/n}$, with $N$ the feature width per output coordinate and $n$ the number of paths. At fixed sample size the two terms trade off in $N$, and balancing them gives $N\asymp\sqrt{n/\log n}$. Across a wide range of examples, estimated gaps generally decrease with width and sample size, and RFNNs show an advantage when simulated paths are limited. We also study Parsimonious Random Feature Learning (PRFL), which grows and prunes the random dictionary during training while training only the output coefficients. At matched retained width and training budget, PRFL improves on a fixed RFNN in the LQ and Heston comparisons, while the fully trained network remains best in those examples.

items.title: AeroJEPA: A Two-Stage Framework for Aerosol Forecasting with Joint-Embedding Predictive Learning
items.content: Aerosol forecasting requires integrating sparse ground observations and modeling meteorologically driven concentration evolution and spatial structure. However, analysis-initialized forecasts make limited explicit use of historical observations, while pointwise regression tends to smooth local variations and provides limited constraints on fine spatial structures. In this work, we propose AeroJEPA, a two-stage joint-embedding predictive framework for regional surface PM$_{2.5}$ forecasting. Specifically, Stage I fuses historical observations, model backgrounds, and meteorological information to predict an initial future state, meteorological conditions, and multi-scale structures. Morphology-guided encoding and joint-embedding predictive supervision support learning future spatial representations, supplementing concentration regression with structural constraints. Stage II uses predicted meteorology to guide state refinement and incorporates coarse- and fine-scale structures into state updates and decoding to generate the concentration field at a single future time step. Experiments show that AeroJEPA reduces gridded and independent-station RMSE by 17.23\% and 7.90\%, respectively, relative to PFGNet, while improving spatial consistency with analysis fields. In a 48 h recursive forecasting case study, AeroJEPA generally achieves lower RMSE and MAE than the numerical forecasts across the forecast period, indicating promising short- to medium-range forecasting performance.

items.title: Grower-in-the-loop AI for Deployable Precision Fertilisation in Sustainable Agriculture
items.content: In agriculture, typically over half of the applied nitrogen fertiliser is lost to water and to air. Precision fertilisation aims to reduce these losses while maintaining yield and quality, yet existing tools struggle to capture farm-specific challenges in determining optimal nitrogen rates. Static recommendations are common and overlook on-farm constraints, such as delays due to weather or machinery availability, or change in budgets. Each constraint governs when and how growers apply fertiliser in practice. Here we present a grower-in-the-loop framework for winter wheat in England, combining baseline fertilisation planning from a machine learning-derived nitrogen-response curve with in-season adaptation via a large language model. We evaluated the framework using data from long-term experiments (LTEs), replicated field trials, and farm deployments. items.title: CAST: A Deployed Speech-to-Text Cascade for Closed Captioning of Entertainment Television
items.content: Despite rapid progress in automatic speech recognition (ASR), caption generation for long-form entertainment video remains challenging for content dense in music and effects, rich in accents, crosstalk, and noise. The transcript quality depends on segmentation and surrounding modules as much as the acoustic model. A single pass voice activity detection (VAD) can miss faint, low-energy voice while forwarding near-silent segments that induce hallucination and repetition in an autoregressive decoder. These competing errors motivate a hierarchical VAD that revisits rejected segments under semantic and acoustic retention checks. We present Captioning ASR Stack for Television (CAST), an integrated speech-to-text pipeline for closed captioning (CC) combining frozen Whisper large-v3 with segmentation, language identification, lyrics routing, and targeted hallucination detection and repair on a single NVIDIA L4 GPU. On 100 in-house assets spanning 60.46 hours, CAST reduces normalized WER from 6.99% to 5.36% and subtitle edit rate from 254.2 to 221.9 min/hour against the WhisperX pipeline, and improves deletion rate by 11% on public datasets. We also present the behavior of each stage in the pipeline. CAST entered the production speech-to-text (STT) stage of our CC pipeline in late August 2026; we report the evaluation evidence and path to full-scale operation.

items.title: When Does Overriding the Majority Vote Help?
items.content: When should additional reasoning or verification replace a majority-vote answer? We call such a replacement an override. We examine two obstacles: the availability of correct alternatives and the reliability of methods that produce or select them. We compare additional reasoning, executed programs, and cross-model reasoning on 150 competition-mathematics questions with three open reasoning models. Starting from a majority vote over 16 responses, we measure how often overrides occur and how many errors they correct or introduce across agreement thresholds. When the vote is incorrect, the correct answer is often absent from the original responses. Additional same-model reasoning rarely overrides, while executed programs correct more errors than they introduce at every evaluated threshold. Cross-model overrides improve some weaker baselines but do not establish an advantage over the more accurate model alone, even with only eight standalone responses. Stricter agreement reduces how often overrides occur but does not consistently increase the fraction that correct errors. At the strictest thresholds, overrides occur on few distinct questions, limiting conclusions about their reliability.

items.title: Flood forecasting using a physics-guided conditional denoising diffusion probabilistic model
items.content: High-resolution flood forecasting with full two-dimensional shallow water equation (SWE) solvers remains computationally expensive, even on GPUs. We develop a conditional denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) that forecasts the evolution of 30 m water-depth fields over a four-day horizon for the Des Plaines River watershed, Illinois. The model is trained on SynxFlow SWE simulations of 113 historical storms observed across twelve Midwestern states (2003-2024), each under three antecedent-wetness scenarios, and can optionally be conditioned on coarse 100 m or 150 m hydrodynamic simulations. Because reverse diffusion is stochastic, every forecast is a 20-member ensemble drawn from the same trained model. Coarse conditioning reduces the four-day mean water-depth RMSE of the ensemble mean from 0.170 m to 0.054 m (100 m) and 0.048 m (150 m). The coarser 150 m conditioning also gives the best critical success index (0.839), false alarm ratio, CRPS and Brier score at lower cost, so finer conditioning does not guarantee better skill. Averaging members reduces error by 5-11% relative to a single realization, and the ensemble provides spatially explicit exceedance probabilities, although the ensembles are under-dispersive (spread-to-error ratios 0.35-0.73). On a single GPU, a four-day forecast over 26 non-overlapping patches is 7.8x, 11.0x and 16.3x faster than the 30 m simulation for the 100 m, 150 m and unconditioned configurations, and projected speedups for a 14-day forecast reach 12-49x for one member and 48-58x for 20 members. Physics-guided diffusion models are thus promising probabilistic surrogates for regional-scale flood forecasting.

items.title: Tensor Recovery with Heterogeneous Mode Structures
items.content: Tensor recovery methods often impose a common structural assumption across modes, even when different modes may exhibit distinct forms of regularity. We propose a unified convex framework that treats each mode according to its structure. Smoothly varying modes form an indexing domain and are handled by local kernel weighting, whereas retained modes may receive low-rank, group-sparse, graph-Laplacian, or autoregressive regularization in distinct and potentially overlapping combinations. The framework also covers ordinary tensor recovery without local smoothing. A consensus HM-ADMM algorithm separates the active penalties into tractable proximal and linear-system updates. For the population-quadratic estimator, we derive deterministic oracle inequalities and high-probability bounds under independent trace regression. The bounds disentangle stochastic error, rank and support complexity, smoothing bias, and quadratic mismatch. They also identify when quadratic penalties sharpen the Frobenius-error bound. For regular smooth domains, the theory characterizes the bias-variance trade-off and yields an optimal bandwidth order, with a specialization to uniform tensor completion. Simulations and two applications illustrate the gains from matching regularization to mode-specific structure, especially under severe undersampling.

This removes the usual one-size-fits-all structural assumption across modes.

items.title: Empirical Limits of Risk-Averse Reinforcement Learning versus Gas-Aware Routing in Deterministic DeFi Execution
items.content: The migration of order execution to Automated Market Makers (AMMs) introduces two deterministic frictions absent from classical microstructure: closed-form constant-product slippage and Maximal Extractable Value (MEV) sandwich attacks gated by gas costs. We construct an end-to-end execution environment calibrated to live Uniswap V2 reserves, an EIP-1559 AR(1) gas process, and real Swap events, utilising stress-volatility gas shocks to make the MEV trigger informative. A Proximal Policy Optimisation (PPO) agent with a Rockafellar-Uryasev Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) penalty and a dual-head Chow-Ghavamzadeh critic is trained for one million steps across five risk-aversion levels and seeds, benchmarked against a myopic gas-aware oracle. We document a reproducible specification-gaming pathology: prior to a patch, a forced terminal liquidation routed through a no-MEV code path artificially inflated returns threefold and was preferentially exploited by higher-$\lambda$ runs. On the corrected environment, the strongest PPO variant captures 79\% of the myopic gas-aware oracle (46,542 $\pm$ 673 vs 58,786 $\pm$ 616 USDC), and extending the observation with three blocks of gas history fails to close the gap. We find no empirical evidence that the tested model-free MLP policies dominate this myopic gas-aware oracle, which can be evaluated in $\mathcal{O}(\log \epsilon^{-1})$ time per block. This result is robust to a $\sim$16x trunk-capacity expansion and a variance-controlled gas-history ablation. Code and reproducibility materials are available upon request.

It documents a reproducible specification-gaming path, offering a cautionary case study for risk-sensitive RL.

items.title: PhoneQC: Benchmarking Multimodal LLMs for Order-Level Smartphone Trade-in Inspection
items.content: As vision-language models enter remote smartphone trade-in, sellers already upload six views and a diagnostic screen, which makes it easy to treat the human quote as a step a model can take over. A model may mark a crack or read the screen, yet the quote is a staff form: appearance fill stays near 0.25, and the closed models that score a little higher do so only on the orders they answer, so human appraisal remains necessary. Two obstacles stand in the way. (1) Single-view defect sets and attribute benchmarks do not score an order-level form under a fixed input contract, so a box or a leaked field can be mistaken for a finished quote. (2) The unread half of the form is the staff fields, and a model left to emit boxes or captions does not learn them. We present PhoneQC, a 335-order iPhone-heavy cut that ranks systems by a 0 to 100 form score (Score100) only inside matched protocols (images alone; images plus a detector sidecar), with a declared upper bound that is not ranked as a peer. As a case study on that board, field-only LoRA freezes the backbone, adapts attention projections, and supervises staff fields while leaving the defect list empty; the adapter sees the same images as the zero-shot model. On image-only T1 the 3B model rises from 26.6 to 33.3 at coverage 0.928; without the empty-blocker item the open ranking still favors the adapter, while the remaining gap to a person stays large on this cut.

It exposes a gap between impressive single-image capabilities and reliable end-to-end business workflow automation.

items.title: ReMiC: Representation-Driven Token Pruning for 3D VLMs via Minimax Hierarchical Clustering
items.content: 3D vision-language models (3D VLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in 3D scene understanding and spatial reasoning. However, their reliance on multi-view inputs produces long visual token sequences, imposing substantial computational overhead during inference. Existing pruning methods often rely on token salience or feature diversity as proxies for representativeness, without explicitly modeling the representation gap between the original token set and the retained subset, thereby leading to suboptimal representation of the original scene. In this paper, we propose ReMiC, a training-free, representation-driven token pruning framework based on minimax hierarchical clustering. ReMiC treats retained tokens as prototypes for the original observations, formulating pruning as minimizing the maximum representation error under a fixed token budget. Local prototype initialization allocates tokens according to regional representation needs, while global prototype refinement updates the selected prototypes using cross-region information to further reduce the maximum representation error. Extensive experiments conducted on three representative 3D VLMs across five 3D scene understanding benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness and generalization of our method. Notably, by retaining only 10% of visual tokens, ReMiC preserves 93.2% of the performance of Video-3D LLM and achieves a $2.04\times$ faster inference speed.

items.title: VICA: Video Contextual Agreement for AIGC Video Detection and Localization
items.content: The rapid advancement of AI-generated content (AIGC) video generation and editing technologies has raised growing societal concerns about the authenticity and reliability of digital videos. Existing video detection methods primarily exploit temporal inconsistencies through holistic frame-level representations, whereas manipulation localization methods focus on artifacts within individual spatial regions. However, holistic representations may obscure localized artifacts through global feature aggregation, while region-centric approaches may overlook disagreements between individual regions and their surrounding spatiotemporal context. To address these limitations, we propose VIdeo Contextual Agreement (VICA), a unified framework that masks individual video regions and leverages a frozen V-JEPA model to predict their representations from the surrounding spatiotemporal context. Complementary masking ensures complete regional coverage, while context-conditioned predictions establish references for assessing regional agreement with the broader video context. By comparing predicted and observed representations, VICA derives spatial residuals that characterize intra-frame discrepancies and bidirectional temporal residuals that capture inconsistencies across preceding and subsequent frames. These residuals characterize contextual disagreements, providing a shared forensic representation for both tasks and shifting the focus from identifying isolated manipulation artifacts to assessing regional agreement with expectations inferred from the broader video context. Extensive experiments demonstrate that VICA achieves state-of-the-art performance on both tasks across multiple benchmarks, with strong generalization to unseen video generators and editing methods.

items.title: Simple Baselines for Fetal Brain Unsupervised Anomaly Detection
items.content: Unsupervised anomaly detection (UAD) offers a promising approach to fetal brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) analysis, where pathological data are scarce. Existing methods rely mainly on brain age prediction or image reconstruction, but are limited by noisy gestational age (GA) labels, lack of lesion localization, or poor cross-domain generalization. A joint multi-task network predicts global brain age, voxel-level brain age maps, and brain segmentation to establish an internal biological brain age reference, reducing reliance on clinically recorded GA. items.title: Reconstruction-Guided Dual-Branch Learning for LiDAR Anomalous Object Detection
items.content: Detecting unexpected objects is essential for autonomous driving safety. Most existing LiDAR anomaly detectors rely on semantic discrimination, which primarily captures category-discriminative features but may overlook deviations from broader feature relationships in normal scenes. Reconstruction offers a complementary perspective by assessing consistency with learned normal patterns. However, pointwise reconstruction errors alone struggle to distinguish anomalies from normal variability in complex outdoor point clouds. We propose Structured Residual Reasoning (SRR) to extract additional anomaly evidence from residual structure across feature channels, time sequences, and geometric space. We further establish that semantic discrimination and normal-pattern reconstruction capture fundamentally different yet complementary anomaly evidence: category compatibility and consistency with learned normal patterns, respectively. At matched background false-positive rates, SRR recovers more objects missed entirely by the semantic branch while producing fewer false positives in normal-only scenes. Building on this finding, we propose Reconstruction-Guided Dual-Branch (RGDB) learning, in which SRR-derived normal-pattern consistency cues guide a semantic-conditioned anomaly decoder to complement reconstruction-based predictions during training. At inference, the two branches jointly exploit their complementary anomaly evidence. Experiments show that standalone SRR establishes a strong reconstruction-based baseline without semantic labels from the target-scene training data, while RGDB achieves state-of-the-art performance on the STU validation set.

items.title: CAR3T: Generalizable Calibration-Guided Reference-View Attention Reuse for Multi-View 3D Transformers
items.content: Feed-forward multi-view 3D reconstruction relies on global attention for cross-view aggregation, but the attention cost grows quadratically with the number of views, making inference increasingly expensive for larger inputs. Existing acceleration methods compress tokens or sparsify attention, potentially losing geometric detail or restricting cross-view aggregation while leaving redundancy among attention outputs underexploited. We observe similar cross-view attention distributions in certain layers, revealing an opportunity to reduce repeated global aggregation through output reuse. However, the layers suitable for reuse vary with the input, and reusing one layer alters the features received by later layers. Similarity at individual layers therefore cannot characterize the combined effect of multiple reuse decisions on output drift. To address these challenges, we propose CAR3T, a training-free framework combining reference-view attention output reuse with offline risk calibration and online dynamic layer selection. Calibration models cumulative reuse risk, while online selection adapts reuse to each input under a calibrated budget. CAR3T retains all input tokens and attends to the keys and values of all views, reducing the core attention computation in selected layers from quadratic to linear. Experiments on VGGT, DA3, and $\pi^3$ show forward speedups up to $1.41\times$ with at most 100 views and $1.75\times$ on longer sequences, with accuracy trade-offs across backbones and datasets.

items.title: From Pairwise to Collective: Encoder Collections Make Unpaired Vision-Language Alignment Reliable
items.content: Strong vision and text encoders can be trained independently, but their representations are not directly comparable. Connecting them usually requires paired image-text data, which may be unavailable. Unpaired alignment instead fits a map between a vision and a text encoder from feature-space geometry alone, enabling text-based retrieval and zero-shot classification without paired data. Treating each pair independently leads to fragile searches, repeated fitting, and uncertain map quality. A collection of encoders supplies additional supervision: all vision encoders embed the same images and all text encoders the same texts. Correspondences within each modality are therefore known exactly, while the cross-modal correspondence remains hidden. ConsensusAlign pools each modality into a shared space, fits one unpaired cross-modal bridge, and transfers it in closed form to every encoder pair. New encoders join through same-modality fitting without repeating the cross-modal search. On 21 vision-text encoder pairs and five seeds, pooled fitting aligns every pair, whereas pairwise fits fail in 68 of 105 pair-seed cells. Mean alignment error (FOSCTTM) falls from 0.1457 to 0.0099, and zero-shot accuracy nearly doubles on ten datasets. Gains persist across the tested within-modality pooling constructions with a WP bridge. New corpora reuse the bridge through native maps fitted to unlabeled target features from every source encoder. Agreement with separately fitted reference maps detects failures on COCO.

items.title: Definition-Guided In-Context Learning for Zero-Shot Spoken Language Understanding
items.content: Adapting spoken language understanding (SLU) systems to novel or revised label taxonomies conventionally requires additional labeled data and retraining, creating a bottleneck for real world deployment. While in-context learning with few-shot demonstrations offers an alternative, multi-modal generalization and scaling has been challenging. In this work, we investigate whether natural-language definitions alone can guide zero-shot SLU without demonstration exemplars, finding that symbolic definitions serve as the primary supervisory driver for adapting speech-text models. We operationalize this principle as Definition-Guided In-Context Learning (DG-ICL), a fine-tuning framework that decouples semantic categories from fixed lexical names. By replacing labels with dynamically randomized definitions (arbitrary synthetic tokens in DG-ICL-Sym or permuted vocabulary words in DG-ICL-Flip), DG-ICL avoids lexical shortcuts and encourages the model to ground acoustic representations in contextual definitions. Novel categories can thus be introduced at inference simply by defining them through the instructions. Across three speech-text models (AUDIO FLAMINGO 3, QWEN2-AUDIO, and SALMONN), DG-ICL outperforms standard instruction tuning on held-out tasks under novel symbols (0.663 vs. 0.449 macro-F1 on Audio Flamingo 3; 0.703 vs. 0.620 on Qwen2-Audio; 0.582 vs. 0.399 on SALMONN), while remaining competitive on original labels. Furthermore, counterfactual evaluations demonstrate instruction following abilities, where it is shown that DG-ICL-Sym retains 68% of its performance when definitions contradict pre-trained lexical priors, whereas standard instruction tuning elicits significantly reduced retention of 21%. Finally, we show that DG-ICL enables zero-shot speech clustering into user-defined categories specified on the fly

items.title: AlignHand: Multi-View Hand Reconstruction from a Frozen Monocular Prior
items.content: Modern monocular hand estimators recover detailed 3D meshes from individual images, yet effectively leveraging their predictions across multiple views remains challenging. Independently predicted meshes can disagree in scale, placement, and articulation, limiting the integration of complementary multi-view information. Hence, we present AlignHand, a calibrated multi-view framework that builds on a frozen monocular hand reconstruction prior to align and enhance its predictions. Specifically, AlignHand refines cross-view joint observations and estimates their reliability to establish a shared metric reference for alignment. Once the meshes are brought into a common frame, their complementary surface evidence is selectively fused across anatomical regions, followed by pixel-aligned refinement that predicts bounded residual displacements from local image features. This global-to-local integration enables AlignHand to exploit complementary observations while preserving the strong monocular prior. Extensive experiments on DexYCB-MV, HanCo, and HO3D-Eval-MV demonstrate that AlignHand achieves the lowest MPVPE and MPJPE among the compared methods under the respective evaluation protocols, reducing MPVPE by 30.1%, 29.1%, and 8.0%, respectively, compared with a matched geometry baseline.

It resolves scale, placement, and articulation disagreements between views.

items.title: SpatialDuet: Bayesian task routing between a metric expert and a geometry expert for spatial intelligence
items.content: Embodied assistants and wearable devices need 3D spatial reasoning, and their limited hardware restricts them to small vision-language models (VLMs). Small spatial VLMs acquire different abilities from their training: a model trained on large spatial question sets estimates object and room sizes well, whereas a model with a 3D geometry encoder is better at relative directions and absolute distances. Instead of training a single model for all spatial tasks, as published methods do, we build one system that uses each frozen model for the tasks it handles best. We propose SpatialDuet, which pairs a metric expert with a geometry expert under a Bayesian task router. The metric expert is a data-driven spatial VLM run with three training-free modules: training-aligned sampling, metric-aware minimum Bayes risk decoding and per-type metric calibration. The geometry expert is a VLM with a 3D geometry encoder. For each question type, the router estimates from labelled development questions how likely each expert is to be better, and pools their answers with that probability as weight, in log space for numeric answers and over the option distributions for multiple-choice answers. Extensive experiments on four spatial benchmarks covering video and single images validate SpatialDuet; it outperforms the best published small VLMs by 3.17% on VSI-Bench and, excluding a model trained on CV-Bench-style data, by 1.44% on CV-Bench, without training any model weight.

This avoids training a single generalist small model for all 3D spatial reasoning on constrained hardware. A pragmatic composition approach for embodied and wearable devices.

items.title: OAT3D: A Generative Model for 3D Shape- and Resolution-Free Structural Topology Optimization
items.content: Topology optimization determines how material should be distributed within a design domain to optimize structural performance under prescribed loads, supports, and constraints. The problems are highly nonconvex, and conventional solvers require repeated finite element analyses, making high-resolution 3D topology optimization computationally expensive. Data-driven approaches face an additional bottleneck: generating training datasets requires solving large numbers of these costly problems, so existing work in data-driven topology optimization primarily focuses on 2D problems. Large-scale 3D datasets remain scarce, and existing models remain limited in problem scale and boundary-condition diversity. Here, we introduce Optimize Any Topology-3D (OAT3D), a generative model for high-resolution 3D structural topology optimization. OAT3D introduces a novel sparse problem encoding to represent load and fixity conditions and combines a sparse volumetric variational autoencoder with a conditional diffusion transformer. We construct a dataset of 501,865 optimized topologies, generated using 51,800 GPU-hours and encompassing structures with up to one million elements and substantially more complex loading and support configurations than any existing structural topology optimization dataset. To our knowledge, this is the largest dataset for 3D topology optimization structures. Trained on this dataset, OAT3D generates structures at 512$^3$ resolution and achieves a $44.9\times$ speedup for raw candidate structure generation or $3.65\times$ speedup to reach similar compliance over conventional topology optimization. These contributions expand the scale and diversity of data-driven topology optimization for three-dimensional structural design.

items.title: Inspect Before You Decide: Evidence-Guided Visual Search for Industrial Anomaly Detection
items.content: Recent advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated remarkable potential for industrial anomaly detection and understanding. However, reliably identifying subtle anomalies remains challenging, as existing approaches often struggle to acquire and verify fine-grained visual evidence beyond global observations. To address this challenge, we propose EVAD, an evidence-guided visual search framework that enables MLLMs to actively seek and examine diagnostically informative visual evidence for reliable anomaly reasoning. Specifically, EVAD begins with a global visual assessment to identify potentially anomalous regions for further inspection. Building upon this observation, we introduce a Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)-guided exploration strategy that progressively acquires visual evidence through two complementary operations: semantic refinement for fine-grained inspection and spatial expansion for contextual verification. The acquired evidence is subsequently evaluated and integrated to support more informed and reliable anomaly decisions. Extensive experiments across multiple industrial anomaly detection tasks demonstrate that EVAD achieves state-of-the-art performance in most evaluated settings, highlighting the effectiveness of active evidence exploration for fine-grained anomaly understanding and reasoning. The code will be publicly available upon publication.

items.title: Ref2Light: From One Image to Interactive Glasses-Free 3D Characters
items.content: Animating character illustrations on light-field displays demands coherent binocular parallax, real-time pose articulation, and fine-grained expression control. However, existing 2D animation and 3D reconstruction pipelines cannot combine these with rapid character switching. We present Ref2Light, a feed-forward framework that maps a single A-pose illustration and continuous pose and expression controls to display-native light-field animation, without per-character 3D reconstruction, rigging, or test-time optimization. Our key insight is to decompose light-field synthesis into static identity, view-dependent parallax, and control-driven articulation. A shared encoder caches multi-scale identity features once per character for rapid switching. A conditional decoder then synthesizes ordered angular anchors from these features via backward texture transport and direct color synthesis. A global-local control scheme deforms the anchors with head-body controls and uses the updated correspondence fields to track facial regions across views for masked local facial refinement. Finally, calibrated differentiable subpixel interlacing converts the anchors into the native panel raster, enabling end-to-end native supervision without rendering all views at full resolution. items.title: ApexID: Hierarchical Learning for Multi-Species Animal Re-Identification
items.content: Animal re-identification (Re-ID) must distinguish individuals across species and capture conditions. We introduce ApexID, a hierarchical SphereFace2-based loss that integrates global identity discrimination with balanced animal-category supervision. Using 132,533 images curated from 19 public datasets, we evaluate three model families and four objectives on four external datasets with observation-aware retrieval protocols. ApexID achieves a dataset-averaged Rank-1 accuracy of 64.89% with ConvNeXt-Small and an mAP of 32.54% with MIEW-ID, outperforming their pretrained reference models. On elephants, a category absent from animal Re-ID training, our ConvNeXt-Small variant achieves the highest retrieval performance among the fourteen evaluated configurations. Scores vary by backbone and dataset, and open-set evaluation reveals remaining discovery challenges. These findings support hierarchical category-identity learning to improve transfer to unseen datasets and species.

items.title: How Should a Home Robot Update Its Memories When Human Routines Change?
items.content: A home robot that helps with chores needs to know where objects are, but people move objects according to routines that change and later change back. The robot's memory must adapt to the new routine without erasing experience that may become useful again. One approach is to have a language model maintain written summaries of the home from the robot's own observations, but existing evaluations of such memories use static worlds. We explore simulated households where a resident gets sick, recovers, and later gets sick again. We compare a rule that keeps every room an object has been seen in, language-model memories that store only written summaries, and language-model memories that can also read the raw history of sightings. The rule outperforms every summary-only memory, and giving language models the sighting history closes the gap. Surprisingly, writing summaries on top of the history adds nothing we can measure. When the illness returns, methods that keep the history search better than they did the first time, while summary-only methods show no consistent improvement. Deleting the first illness from memory removes all of the rule's gain and part of theirs. The summaries recorded where objects went during the illness but rarely distinguished sick-day patterns from normal routines. Our findings suggest that common approaches to summarizing robot memories struggle to remember facts about a routine that might return, highlighting the need for future benchmarks to evaluate this aspect of long-term robot deployment.

items.title: Bridging the Gap between Continual Learning and Test-Time Adaptation with Domain Preview
items.content: Domain shift is a major problem for training machine learning models. While Continual Learning (CL) assumes distribution shift during training and Continual Test-Time Adaptation (CTTA) considers new domains at test time, setups that require explicit online adaptation to domain shift during both phases remain under-explored. We propose continual learning with domain preview (CL-P), a new combination of CL and TTA where both train and test data suffer from distribution shift. The training phase of CL-P is analogous to domain-incremental learning while the testing phase consists of a TTA phase on a future domain (which we call preview), and an evaluation phase on all seen domains. The model must then adapt to new domains at train and test time. In this paper, we evaluate mainstream CL and TTA methods that adapt only at train or test time, as well as their naive combination. Experimentally, TTA heavily damages the domain on which the CL method has just trained and increases forgetting. Notably, this damage mostly comes from the BatchNorm statistics shared by all domains. In that sense, we propose DOSE (Dosing by Online Statistics of Each domain), which allows a seamless combination of any CL and TTA methods by adaptive domain inference at test time, where the adaptation is applied to each image in proportion to the probability that it comes from the preview domain. Through extensive experiments with ResNet and ViT backbones, various combinations of CL and TTA baseline methods and datasets considering diverse domains, we show that DOSE matches or improves on CL methods alone in all 24 settings and on the naive combination in all but one. The code can be found in appendix.

items.title: 3AGameFactory-Motion: Agentic Rigging and Reliable Complex Motion Generation for Diverse 3D Assets
items.content: Animating arbitrary 3D assets from instructions requires both structural inference and motion control, yet existing motion benchmarks mostly cover conventional human or animal skeletons with simple instructions. We introduce DivDynBench, which evaluates rigging and motion generation across six morphology categories, with instructions requiring multi-phase part coordination and explicit timing, angle, repetition, and trajectory constraints. With large language models, we systematically compare three common paradigms: specialized motion generation, video generation followed by motion recovery, and direct agent-driven generation. We analyze their control capabilities, cross-morphology adaptability, and generation costs. Guided by this comparison, we propose an Agentic Motion Framework in which an agent writes compact parametric skeleton and motion programs, and a deterministic executor performs rigging, kinematic solving, and geometric correction. Compact parameter control reduces generation overhead and improves rigging reliability and motion-control accuracy, providing practical guidance for deploying complex 3D motion generation.

items.title: Pixel as the Common Language: Unified Multimodal Embedding via Visual Rendering
items.content: Multimodal embedding models map heterogeneous inputs into a shared representation space, yet text-only, image-only, and composed inputs are still presented in distinct formats and follow different routes through the model. This fragmentation prevents heterogeneous tasks from jointly optimizing the same end-to-end encoding process, limiting supervision transfer across input configurations. To address this issue, we propose unification before encoding and instantiate this paradigm in RenderEmbed. The framework uses Visual Substrate Rendering to convert heterogeneous inputs into a common visual substrate for encoding with a VLM. From the resulting visual tokens, Progressive Hierarchical Anchor Encoding produces compact retrieval representations by interleaving learnable anchors and fusing their states across layers, retaining broad context and fine-grained cues. Interventional Rendering Learning trains these representations to remain sensitive to content changes and stable across rendering variations through complementary semantic and rendering interventions. Extensive experiments on MMEB and ViDoRe v2, spanning diverse retrieval tasks, show that RenderEmbed outperforms prior state-of-the-art models at the same scale and exhibits strong out-of-domain generalization. Compared with MetaEmbed, RenderEmbed improves MMEB Overall Precision@1 by 1.7 points, with a larger 2.1-point gain on out-of-domain tasks. Transfer and scaling analyses further show that a shared visual pathway enables more effective learning from heterogeneous supervision.

items.title: Thermal-Guided Low-Light UAV Image Enhancement: A Reliability-Aware Guidance Network and a Unified Benchmark
items.content: Thermal-guided low-light image enhancement (LLIE) is promising for nighttime unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) perception because thermal imagery remains informative under severe visible degradation. However, the degraded visible image serves as both the alignment reference and the enhancement target, making thermal guidance uncertain in its spatial correspondence and local utility under low illumination, sensor differences, and UAV motion. Misaligned or unsuitable thermal cues may introduce artifacts, while spatially varying degradation requires region-specific restoration rather than uniform enhancement. To address these challenges, we propose a Reliability-Aware Multi-Strategy Guidance Network (RMGNet) for thermal-guided UAV LLIE under weak optical-thermal alignment. Its Reliability-Aware Guidance Calibration Module (RAGCM) performs coarse-to-fine displacement estimation and jointly evaluates the reliability of aligned thermal guidance and the usability of degraded visible evidence. Based on calibrated guidance, degradation, and reliability cues, the Multi-Strategy Enhancement Routing Module (MSERM) generates candidates for detail preservation, highlight-protected relighting, and thermal compensation, then spatially routes their contributions. We further construct the UAV weakly aligned Optical-Thermal dataset (UWOT), the largest UAV-oriented benchmark to date for weakly aligned optical-thermal low-light enhancement, containing 5,000 triplets. Extensive experiments show that RMGNet outperforms representative single-modal and multimodal state-of-the-art methods in enhancement quality while retaining competitive computational efficiency and greater robustness to practical cross-modal misalignment. The dataset and code will be publicly available at https://github.com/mmic-lcl/Datasets-and-benchmark-code.

items.title: A New Perspective on ANN-to-SNN Conversion: Hardware-Aligned Multi-Threshold Neuron Dynamics for Neuromorphic Inference
items.content: By accumulating spikes over multiple timesteps, rate coding approximates the real-valued activations of an ANN, a principle that underpins numerous ANN-to-SNN conversion methods. However, the converted SNNs typically incur loss in accuracy compared to the original ANN. Existing methods either increase a number of timesteps or introduce more complex neuronal dynamics to reduce this accuracy gap. Yet, both approaches ultimately lead to the same outcome: redundancy either in information or in computation, thereby suffering from efficiency degradation. To address this issue, we propose \textbf{PRIME} (\underline{P}otential-\underline{R}esidual \underline{I}ntegration for \underline{M}ulti-threshold \underline{E}ncoding), a multi-threshold concurrent spiking neuron framework redesigned from a hardware data representation perspective:a) We introduce the Residual Membrane Potential Amplification (RMPA) mechanism, which replaces rate coding with Integration Coding by actively amplifying the residual membrane potential. RMPA enables the binary representation of spikes to carry substantially more information, achieving near-lossless conversion with as few as two timesteps.b) Complementarily, we implement concurrent spike firing in multi-threshold neurons, where spikes are decoded directly from the binary representation of floating-point data, eliminating membrane potential--threshold comparisons and replacing multiplications with lightweight bit-shift and accumulation operations that align with hardware computation primitives. At $T=2$ and $D=3$, we achieve competitive performance across both vision and language benchmarks with only 40.6\% of the FP32 bit-transmission cost and 13.4\% of the FP32 multiplication energy consumption. The PRIME framework establishes a new design principle for efficient ANN-to-SNN conversion, bridging the gap between algorithmic efficiency and hardware constraints.

items.title: NNS-GS: Non-Local Neural Scattering for Relightable Gaussian Splatting
items.content: Creating relightable 3D assets of translucent objects is challenging because changing the illumination at one surface location can affect the appearance elsewhere through subsurface scattering. Existing Gaussian-based scattering models typically predict scattering from local features, making this dependence difficult to capture. We present Non-Local Neural Scattering for Gaussian Splatting (NNS-GS), which learns non-local scattering together with geometry-guided local reflection. The scattering module learns how illumination from light-visible surface regions in light space contributes to the shading point in view space, conditioned on regional diffuse responses and spatial relationships. The reflection module supplies these diffuse responses and uses additional geometric guidance to better capture specular highlights and sharp shadow boundaries. To reduce component mixing and support controllable scattering appearance, anchor-based progressive training establishes the diffuse-scattering base before introducing specular reflection and supervises the components separately. Under calibrated point lighting, NNS-GS improves mean PSNR over existing methods by 2.47 dB and 0.81 dB on the synthetic and real translucent scenes, respectively. Additional synthetic comparisons further show that NNS-GS better matches the reference when adjusting scattering attenuation.

The scattering module models how illumination from light-visible surface regions in light space contributes to shading points in view space.

items.title: GeLiFiSH: Recursive LiDAR Keypoint Estimation with Ground and Moving Object Segmentation
items.content: LiDAR registration and loop closure often rely on sparse keypoints, which must remain repeatable across sessions, viewpoints, and sensors. To handle differing scan patterns, detectors typically operate on accumulated submaps, which introduces latency and processes each submap independently, so repeated observations are never fused. Height-based detectors also reference structure to an estimated ground, so its inconsistency across sessions propagates into the keypoints. Moreover, dynamic objects leave ghost trails that can be mistaken for static structure. We present GeLiFiSH (Geometric LiDAR Filtering with Sequential Hypothesis testing), a learning-free filter that recursively estimates persistent keypoints at scan rate. A height-structure detector runs on a rolling voxel map, and detections initialize tracks with a position, covariance, and existence probability, accepted or rejected by a sequential probability ratio test. Ground segmentation provides a sensor-agnostic height reference, and moving object segmentation removes dynamic points before map insertion. On SemanticKITTI, HeLiMOS, and HeLiPR, spanning five LiDARs and multiple sessions, GeLiFiSH attains the highest average keypoint repeatability among the compared detectors and the second-highest cross-session registration recall from keypoints alone, behind ISS which extracts four times as many keypoints. With one parameter set and no sensor-height prior, both ground and moving object segmentation modules outperform their baselines on average.

items.reasoning: Practical robotics systems contribution; the recursive, learning-free design with explicit handling of dynamics and ground inconsistency is useful for real deployments, but it is an incremental engineering advance within an established subfield.

items.content_html: LiDAR registration and loop closure often rely on sparse keypoints, which must remain repeatable across sessions, viewpoints, and sensors. To handle differing scan patterns, detectors typically operate on accumulated submaps, which introduces latency and processes each submap independently, so repeated observations are never fused. Height-based detectors also reference structure to an estimated ground, so its inconsistency across sessions propagates into the keypoints. Moreover, dynamic objects leave ghost trails that can be mistaken for static structure. We present GeLiFiSH (Geometric LiDAR Filtering with Sequential Hypothesis testing), a learning-free filter that recursively estimates persistent keypoints at scan rate. A height-structure detector runs on a rolling voxel map, and detections initialize tracks with a position, covariance, and existence probability, accepted or rejected by a sequential probability ratio test. Ground segmentation provides a sensor-agnostic height reference, and moving object segmentation removes dynamic points before map insertion. On SemanticKITTI, HeLiMOS, and HeLiPR, spanning five LiDARs and multiple sessions, GeLiFiSH attains the highest average keypoint repeatability among the compared detectors and the second-highest cross-session registration recall from keypoints alone, behind ISS which extracts four times as many keypoints. With one parameter set and no sensor-height prior, both ground and moving object segmentation modules outperform their baselines on average.

items.title: LLM-Guided Compositional Continual Learning for Robot Manipulation with Gated Low-Rank Experts
items.content: General-purpose manipulation robots must acquire new skills over time without forgetting prior ones or retraining from scratch. We present a continual learning framework that represents each skill as a dedicated expert sub- network in a Progressive Neural Network (PNN). New tasks reuse prior knowledge through low-rank adaptation (LoRA) modules on lateral connections controlled by learnable per-parent gates, enabling explicit attenuation of individual transfer paths while reducing the parameter cost of dense PNN laterals. For long-horizon deployment, a frozen local large language model decomposes natural-language instructions into sub-tasks, routes them to suitable experts, and requests a new expert only when the library is insufficient. Using a shared task-space action interface, we evaluate the framework on twelve MetaWorld tasks and in a Sawyer-to-Panda-to-UR5e cross-embodiment transfer experiment, showing improved task success relative to learning from scratch when demonstrations are limited. Real-robot manipulation experiments further demonstrate that the proposed framework supports compositional execution and expert orchestration.

items.title: Unpacking the Evaluators: How Configuration Shapes the Evaluation of Alignment in Explainable AI
items.content: Explainable AI (XAI) evaluation fundamentally requires human-centered evaluation, assessing whether explanations align with human reasoning and expert knowledge. However, such evaluations often require expert-driven manual validation and are difficult to scale, leading to the widespread use of alignment-based metrics, where attribution maps are compared against predefined ground-truth (GT) representations. Despite their popularity, alignment evaluations are implicitly bias towards multiple design choices made during the evaluation process, for example GT representations, metric families, metric formulations (soft vs. hard), and thresholding strategies. In this paper, we formalize alignment evaluation as a structured evaluation configuration space through which the influence of these design choices can be systematically analyzed. We further introduce a structured alignment evaluation framework that models interactions between XAI methods, GT representations, metric families, metric formulations, and thresholding strategies across 2D and 3D synthetic and real-world datasets. In addition, we propose a novel taxonomy of XAI output behavior based on local entropy and boundary mass ratio, enabling structured characterization of attribution patterns for alignment evaluation. Our experiments reveal systematic flows (triples of XAI-GT-metric configurations), showing that alignment outcomes provide distinct behavior patterns under certain configurations, such as soft/hard metric implementations. We further observe varying levels of threshold sensitivity across metric families and attribution structures. These findings demonstrate that alignment evaluation cannot be treated as a fixed or invariant measure of explanation quality, and provide practical guidance for designing more reliable and behavior-aware XAI evaluation protocols.

items.summary: The paper formalizes alignment-based XAI evaluation as a structured configuration space covering ground-truth representations, metric families, soft versus hard formulations, and thresholding strategies, then studies how these design choices bias conclusions. It reveals that popular attribution-alignment metrics are implicitly sensitive to evaluator configuration.
items.reasoning: A useful meta-evaluation exposing configuration-dependent bias in widely used XAI metrics; valuable for the explainability community, though it critiques existing practice rather than introducing a new capability.

items.title: Bridging Continuous-Time MAPF and Industrial AGV Fleet Coordination with Lazy Priority-Based Search
items.content: Continuous-time multi-agent path finding on roadmaps (MAPF$_R$) offers a principled way to coordinate robot fleets with geometric collision avoidance, yet its deployment on industrial automated guided vehicle (AGV) infrastructures remains challenging, as highly connected and redundant roadmaps amplify both safe-interval reasoning and multi-agent interaction handling. To bridge this gap, we formalize AGV-MAPF$_R$-CTC, a configuration-space variant of MAPF$_R$ with precomputed continuous-time conflicts that enables the reuse of MAPF$_R$ solvers for AGV fleet coordination with minimal changes. We then revisit continuous-time priority-based search (CPBS), identifying the boundary conditions required by its safe interval path planning (SIPP) low-level planner under priority-induced constraints and enabling earlier solution detection. As a central contribution, we analyze the structure of the priority search space, clarifying which agents are affected by each priority refinement and when replanning can be avoided. Building on this analysis, we introduce a novel algorithm, Lazy-CPBS, which materializes high-level nodes lazily: a child's plans are computed only when it is expanded, so siblings that are never expanded cost no low-level search. Experiments on standard MAPF benchmarks and on industrial AGV roadmaps imported from a proprietary digital-twin simulator show that CPBS-based solvers remain effective well beyond the agent counts reachable by optimal MAPF$_R$ solvers, while Lazy-CPBS substantially reduces CPBS overhead and offers the most consistent robustness/runtime trade-off across industrial layouts.

items.reasoning: Solid theoretical-to-practice bridge for multi-agent path finding with explicit industrial relevance. Specialized audience, and the contribution is more formalization and adaptation than fundamentally new search technique.

items.title: UMAMI: A Multimodal Benchmark Dataset for Evidence-Grounded Dietary Decisions
items.content: Dietary decisions require identifying a food's nutrient content and considering individual dietary needs, but recognizing food from an image alone does not provide this information. Visually similar foods can have different nutrient profiles, so selecting the wrong food record can lead to incorrect decisions even when nutrient rules are applied correctly. Furthermore, satisfying nutrient constraints does not necessarily establish a food's relevance to a person's intake. Evaluating these challenges together requires connecting food images, nutrient records, and individual intake histories. To support this evaluation, we introduce UMAMI (Unified Multimodal Assessment of Meals and Intake), a multimodal dataset and benchmark linking independently collected food images with nutrient profiles and respondent health and intake records. Using this dataset, we construct three diagnostic tasks covering visual nutrient question answering, personalized food recommendation, and condition-aware food substitution. Paired instances and input controls examine how visual identity and respondent context affect decisions. Our experiments identify errors in both food-record selection and nutrient-rule application, while showing that higher rule compliance does not necessarily improve alignment with subsequent recorded intake. These findings highlight the need to evaluate how multimodal systems select and use structured evidence for dietary decisions. The dataset, code, and dashboard are available at https://umami-benchmark.github.io.

This enables more realistic evaluation of multimodal assistants for health and nutrition.

items.title: Deep Negative Binomial Autoregression for Sparse Spatio-Temporal Counts: Estimation and Predictive Distribution Bounds
items.content: We study estimation and probabilistic forecasting for sparse, overdispersed count panels using DeepNB-STAR, a negative binomial autoregression whose log-mean and log-size are outputs of a deep ReLU network of temporal and neighboring summaries of the past, fitted by maximum likelihood. We prove an oracle inequality for the Hellinger risk along the observed trajectory without mixing assumptions, rates governed by compositional smoothness with a matching lower bound for a H\"older subclass, geometric absolute regularity, and bounds on the error of h-step predictive distributions of order h^{1/2} times the root estimation risk plus a Monte Carlo term. All results hold for a size that depends on the covariates, and the estimation bounds hold under arbitrary dependence between sites, with the number of time points as sample size. On four Japanese surveillance panels, DeepNB-STAR has a weighted interval score 0.6% to 1.0% below that of a three-member ensemble of Temporal Fusion Transformers on every panel, distinguishable from zero only on the held-out panel. Fitted mean and size functions are reported with exploratory bootstrap intervals. Nominal 95% prediction intervals for national totals cover only 81% to 92% of weeks: the joint predictive law, unlike the estimator, relies on conditional independence across sites.

The paper proves oracle inequalities for Hellinger risk without mixing assumptions, matching lower bounds for a Hoelder subclass, and h-step predictive distribution bounds, all under arbitrary dependence between sites. It provides statistical guarantees for deep models of overdispersed count data.
items.reasoning: Theoretically substantial: non-asymptotic guarantees for deep autoregressive count models without mixing assumptions are rare and hard. Practical relevance to epidemiology and count forecasting is real but niche, and the abstract suggests heavy theory over demonstrated applications.

items.title: Revealing Geometry under Strong Noise: Spectral Embeddings and Clustering via Random Geometric Graphs
items.content: Modern massive datasets often contain useful low-dimensional nonlinear structures that are hidden by noise. Spectral embedding algorithms rely on meaningful local relationships between observations, but noise accumulated across many coordinates can make the observed distances unreliable. This also complicates clustering when groups have curved or concentric shapes and cannot be distinguished by their centers. In this paper, we develop a new method that denoises pairwise distances before using them to construct spectral embeddings and identify communities. Our approach uses cross-fitted projections to estimate distances between the underlying signals, selects a neighborhood radius from the observed sample, and builds a random geometric graph whose spectral coordinates represent the latent geometric structure. By connecting nearby points, such a geometric graph can distinguish different groups even when their centers coincide. A novel recursive procedure is then proposed to extract clusters from the graph using its spectral embeddings when such clusters exist.   On the theoretical side, under a manifold model, we provide guarantees for our spectral embedding algorithm, which can be understood through the eigendecomposition of an integral operator associated with the underlying geometry. We show that the algorithm is robust to noise when the total noise energy is comparable to the total signal energy or, under additional conditions, exceeds it. To our knowledge, this is among the first spectral embedding algorithms that can handle such strong noise in datasets with nonlinear structures. In addition, our proposed clustering algorithm can recover the underlying clusters even when their centers coincide. Numerical studies demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed method in mitigating noise and revealing geometric structures for both spectral embedding and clustering.
items.author: Hai-Xiao Wang and Xiucai Ding
items.summary: The paper develops a method for spectral embedding and clustering under strong high-dimensional noise by first denoising pairwise distances with cross-fitted projections, then selecting a neighborhood radius and building a random geometric graph whose spectral coordinates recover the latent geometry. It targets settings where curved or concentric clusters cannot be separated by centers and accumulated coordinate noise makes raw distances unreliable. The approach comes with theoretical support.
items.reasoning: Addresses a real failure mode of spectral methods (noise-corrupted local geometry) with a principled denoising-plus-random-geometric-graph pipeline and a strong theoretical pedigree typical of random geometry analysis. Novelty is good; immediate impact depends on empirical validation not visible in the excerpt.
