items.title: Import AI 482: Huawei kernel benchmarks; airborne drone detection; and a national lab's AI science benchmark
items.content:
Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers.

Subscribe now

Chinese researchers optimize Huawei chips with a kernel improvement benchmark:

…AscendGYM will help China do its own form of RSI…

Researchers with the Shenzhen Loop Area Institute, a Chinese research organization, have built and released AscendGYM, “a kernel optimization benchmark for Ascend NPUs”. The purpose of AscendGYM is to make it easier to use AI to develop custom kernels for Ascend chips from Huawei - especially important given the export controls that prevent Chinese organizations from acquiring frontier Western semiconductors and forcing them onto Huawei.

What AscendGYM does and contains: The goal is for AscendGYM to be the best way to evaluate the efficacy of AI-designed kernels as well as design new ones. The software is meant to help researchers answer this question: “Given a correct kernel implementation, can the specific agent further improve its performance for a target workload within an acceptable budget while preserving correctness?,” they write.

   “AscendGYM evaluates performance across multiple deployment cases, the best achievable performance for specific shapes and scenarios, and the optimization cost required to obtain these gains. Together, these dimensions characterize cross-case applicability, shape specialization, and optimization efficiency.”

    The software includes the AscendForge evaluation environment, which provides unified interfaces for “compilation, correctness checking, performance measurement, and feedback”.

How well can AI models optimize Ascend chips? In tests, the single best model is Opus 5, followed by GPT-5.6, followed by GLM-5.3. They test out models in Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode; Claude Code yields the best absolute scores, and GLM does well in it, while GPT does well in Codex. Opus 5 is more token hungry and GPT-5.6 more token efficient.

Why this matters - ingredients for Chinese RSI: For AI systems to be able to build themselves, they need to be able to develop and improve the software that is used for their own training and inference. Software like AscendGYM will be an essential ingredient for allowing China to rapidly improve the efficiency of its own compute substrates. The software will also have a bearing on export controls, where it provides a route to improve the performance of Chinese chips and close the gap with Western alternatives.

   Read more: AscendGYM: A Cost-Aware Kernel Optimization Benchmark for Real-World Workloads on Ascend NPUs (arXiv).

 Get AscendGYM here: AscendGYM (GitHub).

***

Lawrence Livermore scientists test out if AI scientists can communicate uncertainty about experimental results:

…Can AI systems be appropriately conservative?...

“An agent that reports a confident wrong number is worse than one that reports honest uncertainty, because nobody downstream can tell the difference,” write researchers from Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in a new paper that tests out how reliably AI systems can give accurate score ranges even when dealing with uncertainty.

Testing for uncertainty: The paper introduces SciResearch-Eval, “an interactive benchmark of scientific judgment built on a standard laboratory problem: measuring a material’s thermal properties by heating it and fitting a heat-conduction simulator”. The novel part of this eval is that “an agent designs its own experiments, uses a supplied simulator that may be under-resolved or physically wrong, and reports each property with a 95% interval. To our knowledge it is the first benchmark to combine agent-designed experiments, a deliberately flawed simulator, and proper scoring of calibrated intervals against exact ground truth”.

What they studied: They give AI agents a common materials science task - measuring a material’s thermal properties by heating a sample and fitting a heat-conduction model to its temperature response.

  “An agent receives a sample of unknown material, a simulator of heat conduction through it, one heating experiment, and budgets: four more experiments it designs, compute for simulations and fits, and a cap on actions. It must report the sample’s conductivity, heat capacity and rear heat-transfer coefficient with 95% intervals, and predict a measurement it may not run,” they write. “Hidden from the agent, the simulator may be under-resolved, physically wrong (the real sample has temperature-dependent conductivity, a glued joint, front-face radiation, or heat loss through its sides), or adequate but fed uninformative data”.

Results - only the most powerful frontier models can do this: “When the simulator is missing real physics, only GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.2 are reliable at default settings; the Claude 5.5 models recover only at their highest reasoning setting, and older and open-weight models not at all.”

   These models are able to do well by automatically trying to measure where the simulator is accurate and where it is less accurate then bases their estimates on that, making them more resilient to the different ways the simulator gets broken in experiments.

Why this matters - real scientists are careful, and so are powerful models: Papers like this are further indications that we’re entering an era of AI-driven science. Though many of today’s models can assist in scientific experiments, as this paper shows only a couple of the powerful models at the frontier are able to operate with such appropriate autonomous skepticism and inherent attendance to the scientific method that they can deal with unanticipated breaks in their equipment. This is both an indication of the science advancement to come and a sign of how the most powerful models are exhibiting more and more of an ability to generalize and make themselves robust to perturbations in their environment.

   Read more: SciResearch-Eval: Evaluating Scientific Judgment in Autonomous Experimental Agents (arXiv).

   Check out the leaderboard here (official site).

***

Stanford professors launch AI startup that wants to create a world where thousands of models define the frontier:

…Noeri sees two well-regarded AI researchers enter the neolab game…

Stanford profs Yejin Choi and Carlos Guestrin have launched Noeri, “a neolab to push the frontier of plural intelligence”. They have raised $110m and are relatively light on technical details, but their main vision is that they want to create a world where the frontier is defined by powerful models which rely on the proprietary data of distinct organizations. “Rather than one monolithic source of truth, we can nurture many small, specialized intelligences, each tuned to a place, a people or a problem,” they write.

Further details: “At Noeri, we are building intelligence that learns proactively and continually. Most AI today is trained once and then frozen, while the world it serves keeps moving,” they write. “We close that gap with living systems that grow out of our own research. Our work on test-time training showed that learning on the job after deployment can unlock new capabilities and lead to new discoveries. Our work on self-distillation found that a model can become its own teacher, learning from each mistake and solving hard problems in far fewer attempts. And our work on agentic orchestration demonstrated that a small model conducting a team of other models and tools can outperform frontier models at a fraction of the cost.”

Why this matters - the political economy of the singularity: Currently, the dominant AI models are massive pre-trained ones from companies like Anthropic and OpenAI and a tiny handful of other companies. What would it mean for the frontier to be instead defined by a broader set of actors? This is a core question inherent to the political economy of AI and startups like this show how some people are going to try and utilize technical approaches to make that different vision a reality.

   Read more in the announcement tweet from Yejin (Yejin Choi, X).

 Check out the official site here (Noeri).

***

Chinese researchers build an air-to-air drone identification set:

…A2A-UAV will help people add more visual intelligence to drones…

Researchers with Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics and Hong Kong University of Science and Technology have developed and released A2A-UAV, “a multimodal dataset for air-to-air UAV detection and identification”. This kind of dataset has obvious civil and military applications and will be used to create better AI systems for autonomous onboard sensing on drones.

What A2A-UAV consists of: 105,263 samples, split roughly equally across three different locations - a playground, a park, and a garden - and also split equally across day and night. “Each sample provides one RGB image and one panoramic image for annotation”, as well as thermal images, RF time-frequency images, a radar point cloud, and metadata. Bounding boxes are provided for the RGB and panoramic images, but not the other ones.

   One use case of this dataset could be to try and extend annotations to the other modalities: “Specifically, the bounding boxes can be transferred to the thermal images to support thermal UAV detection, and the radar points can be associated with the visual targets to support radar-based UAV localization,” the researchers write.

    The full dataset comprises 271 independently extractable.tar.gz archives with a total size of approximately 2.5 TB.

How the data was collected: “The data were acquired by a UAV-mounted platform equipped with an RGB-thermal gimbal camera, a panoramic camera, an RF spectrum analyzer, and a millimeter-wave radar,” they write. The data includes 15 target drones from 13 commercial models, including three separately labeled DJI Mini 4 Pro units.

Why this matters - fuel for the physical world: Datasets like this are the ingredients for making it easier for AI systems to operate robots and drones in the physical world. They also have potential dual use impacts, though my suspicion is that datasets like this are pretty irrelevant to militaries relative to the kinds of datasets that - and I’m speculating wildly here - might be being gathered in Ukraine right now given the extremely sophisticated drone-to-drone conflict there.

   Read more: A2A-UAV: A Multimodal Air-to-Air Dataset for UAV Detection and Identification (arXiv).

   Get a sample of the data from Google Drive here (Google Drive).

Tech Tales:

Machine architecture and the objectivity crisis of Machine Hermeneutics

[Memoir from a primary Machine Hermeneutics investigator, 2033]

“We shape our buildings; thereafter they shape us” - Winston Churchill, human politician, 1943.

The building was a vast representation of the proposed Upgrade Device and we walked around it, our footsteps echoing as the sound bounced off its curving walls, eventually dimming in the face of the baroque crenellations that covered the edges of every surface. We humans, a small group of us, the best of our kind, needed to make sense of this building and explain the science it represented, and only then could it be used.

As per the terms of the Sentience Accords, any novel machine-designed insight or equipment needed to be fully explainable by humans before the machines would be allowed to use it. In the early years, this so-called “conceptual verification” had mostly been a matter of time: machines performed science and delivered new insights to the world, then humans studied these insights and made sense of them, eventually generating human-readable explanations of the machine logic. Once this was complete, whatever insights or tools that had been created could be used.

But as the machines grew more advanced and their science went further, the work became more arduous: machines would invent ideas, then use these ideas to inform the design of new experimental equipment, and then use this equipment as the basis of some new discovery. To keep up, the humans had to understand each link in the chain as well as the chain itself.

This flood of scientific progress had caused the field of machine hermeneutics to come into existence in the mid-2020s. By the 2030s, the pinnacle of human achievement in the sciences was considered to be neither making breakthroughs nor wielding AI systems to advance science, but rather to be able to generate elegant, pedagogically useful explanations of the frontiers of machine science, so that other humans could build a mental map of this new territory.

But exposure to the buildings had verifiably sped up human understanding, with clear TTHUE (Time-to-human-understandable-explanation) improvements visible in cohorts of machine hermeneutics experts that experienced the buildings and those that didn’t. This led to its own arms race, with some of us specializing in the construction of the buildings as our primary work. We raced with one another, building ever more complicated spaces that could impart knowledge of ever more alien concepts.

We had all been electrons, appearing and disappearing in 3D transistors. We had been qubits, placed into spheres that rolled around vomit-inducingly when our position was indeterminate, then resolving us up or down at the moment of delivering an answer. We had laid our hands on surfaces suggestive of the textures and arrangements of novel forms of heat shield and solar panel.

Once I had walked for six miles through corridors meant to suggest the path a plasma might take through a fusion reactor, and instead of magnets I was buffeted on all sides by wind that forced me into the center of the paths.

The building meant to educate us about the Upgrade Device was larger than anything we’d seen before and was replete with ideas from many earlier machine inventions. All around us were indicators of complexity packed up into familiar architectural tropes that many of us had studied to understand past inventions. We dispersed throughout the building, walking its many levels and exploring its passages. At night we gathered in the entrance hall for a spartan dinner served at a low table, finding ourselves whispering to one another even though no one forced us to.

It had begun to feel to us as though the building was doing something more than teaching us - that in its various chambers there was something else being taught to us. Something about understanding the minds behind the concepts that it sought to explain to us. That in spending all of our effort on understanding the products of the machines perhaps we were being taught to think like them and behave as them.

Things that inspired this story: The singularity which has already begun; the rise of AI science; how when you look at things like the machine math papers that have proliferated this year you realize we may spend tens or hundreds of times more time on understanding them as people than the machines did in generating them; architecture; multi-modal representations.

Thanks for reading!

items.content_html:
Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers.

Subscribe now

Chinese researchers optimize Huawei chips with a kernel improvement benchmark:

…AscendGYM will help China do its own form of RSI…

Researchers with the Shenzhen Loop Area Institute, a Chinese research organization, have built and released AscendGYM, “a kernel optimization benchmark for Ascend NPUs”. The purpose of AscendGYM is to make it easier to use AI to develop custom kernels for Ascend chips from Huawei - especially important given the export controls that prevent Chinese organizations from acquiring frontier Western semiconductors and forcing them onto Huawei.

What AscendGYM does and contains: The goal is for AscendGYM to be the best way to evaluate the efficacy of AI-designed kernels as well as design new ones. The software is meant to help researchers answer this question: “Given a correct kernel implementation, can the specific agent further improve its performance for a target workload within an acceptable budget while preserving correctness?,” they write.

“AscendGYM evaluates performance across multiple deployment cases, the best achievable performance for specific shapes and scenarios, and the optimization cost required to obtain these gains. Together, these dimensions characterize cross-case applicability, shape specialization, and optimization efficiency.”

The software includes the AscendForge evaluation environment, which provides unified interfaces for “compilation, correctness checking, performance measurement, and feedback”.

How well can AI models optimize Ascend chips? In tests, the single best model is Opus 5, followed by GPT-5.6, followed by GLM-5.3. They test out models in Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode; Claude Code yields the best absolute scores, and GLM does well in it, while GPT does well in Codex. Opus 5 is more token hungry and GPT-5.6 more token efficient.

Why this matters - ingredients for Chinese RSI: For AI systems to be able to build themselves, they need to be able to develop and improve the software that is used for their own training and inference. Software like AscendGYM will be an essential ingredient for allowing China to rapidly improve the efficiency of its own compute substrates. The software will also have a bearing on export controls, where it provides a route to improve the performance of Chinese chips and close the gap with Western alternatives.

Read more: AscendGYM: A Cost-Aware Kernel Optimization Benchmark for Real-World Workloads on Ascend NPUs (arXiv).

Get AscendGYM here: AscendGYM (GitHub).

***

Lawrence Livermore scientists test out if AI scientists can communicate uncertainty about experimental results:

…Can AI systems be appropriately conservative?...

“An agent that reports a confident wrong number is worse than one that reports honest uncertainty, because nobody downstream can tell the difference,” write researchers from Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in a new paper that tests out how reliably AI systems can give accurate score ranges even when dealing with uncertainty.

Testing for uncertainty: The paper introduces SciResearch-Eval, “an interactive benchmark of scientific judgment built on a standard laboratory problem: measuring a material’s thermal properties by heating it and fitting a heat-conduction simulator”. The novel part of this eval is that “an agent designs its own experiments, uses a supplied simulator that may be under-resolved or physically wrong, and reports each property with a 95% interval. To our knowledge it is the first benchmark to combine agent-designed experiments, a deliberately flawed simulator, and proper scoring of calibrated intervals against exact ground truth”.

What they studied: They give AI agents a common materials science task - measuring a material’s thermal properties by heating a sample and fitting a heat-conduction model to its temperature response.

“An agent receives a sample of unknown material, a simulator of heat conduction through it, one heating experiment, and budgets: four more experiments it designs, compute for simulations and fits, and a cap on actions. It must report the sample’s conductivity, heat capacity and rear heat-transfer coefficient with 95% intervals, and predict a measurement it may not run,” they write. “Hidden from the agent, the simulator may be under-resolved, physically wrong (the real sample has temperature-dependent conductivity, a glued joint, front-face radiation, or heat loss through its sides), or adequate but fed uninformative data”.

Results - only the most powerful frontier models can do this: “When the simulator is missing real physics, only GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.2 are reliable at default settings; the Claude 5.5 models recover only at their highest reasoning setting, and older and open-weight models not at all.”

These models are able to do well by automatically trying to measure where the simulator is accurate and where it is less accurate then bases their estimates on that, making them more resilient to the different ways the simulator gets broken in experiments.

Why this matters - real scientists are careful, and so are powerful models: Papers like this are further indications that we’re entering an era of AI-driven science. Though many of today’s models can assist in scientific experiments, as this paper shows only a couple of the powerful models at the frontier are able to operate with such appropriate autonomous skepticism and inherent attendance to the scientific method that they can deal with unanticipated breaks in their equipment. This is both an indication of the science advancement to come and a sign of how the most powerful models are exhibiting more and more of an ability to generalize and make themselves robust to perturbations in their environment.

Read more: SciResearch-Eval: Evaluating Scientific Judgment in Autonomous Experimental Agents (arXiv).

Check out the leaderboard here (official site).

***

Stanford professors launch AI startup that wants to create a world where thousands of models define the frontier:

…Noeri sees two well-regarded AI researchers enter the neolab game…

Stanford profs Yejin Choi and Carlos Guestrin have launched Noeri, “a neolab to push the frontier of plural intelligence”. They have raised $110m and are relatively light on technical details, but their main vision is that they want to create a world where the frontier is defined by powerful models which rely on the proprietary data of distinct organizations. “Rather than one monolithic source of truth, we can nurture many small, specialized intelligences, each tuned to a place, a people or a problem,” they write.

Further details: “At Noeri, we are building intelligence that learns proactively and continually. Most AI today is trained once and then frozen, while the world it serves keeps moving,” they write. “We close that gap with living systems that grow out of our own research. Our work on test-time training showed that learning on the job after deployment can unlock new capabilities and lead to new discoveries. Our work on self-distillation found that a model can become its own teacher, learning from each mistake and solving hard problems in far fewer attempts. And our work on agentic orchestration demonstrated that a small model conducting a team of other models and tools can outperform frontier models at a fraction of the cost.”

Why this matters - the political economy of the singularity: Currently, the dominant AI models are massive pre-trained ones from companies like Anthropic and OpenAI and a tiny handful of other companies. What would it mean for the frontier to be instead defined by a broader set of actors? This is a core question inherent to the political economy of AI and startups like this show how some people are going to try and utilize technical approaches to make that different vision a reality.

Read more in the announcement tweet from Yejin (Yejin Choi, X).

Check out the official site here (Noeri).

Chinese researchers build an air-to-air drone identification set:

…A2A-UAV will help people add more visual intelligence to drones…

Researchers with Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics and Hong Kong University of Science and Technology have developed and released A2A-UAV, “a multimodal dataset for air-to-air UAV detection and identification”. This kind of dataset has obvious civil and military applications and will be used to create better AI systems for autonomous onboard sensing on drones.

What A2A-UAV consists of: 105,263 samples, split roughly equally across three different locations - a playground, a park, and a garden - and also split equally across day and night. “Each sample provides one RGB image and one panoramic image for annotation”, as well as thermal images, RF time-frequency images, a radar point cloud, and metadata. Bounding boxes are provided for the RGB and panoramic images, but not the other ones.

One use case of this dataset could be to try and extend annotations to the other modalities: “Specifically, the bounding boxes can be transferred to the thermal images to support thermal UAV detection, and the radar points can be associated with the visual targets to support radar-based UAV localization,” the researchers write.

The full dataset comprises 271 independently extractable.tar.gz archives with a total size of approximately 2.5 TB.

How the data was collected: “The data were acquired by a UAV-mounted platform equipped with an RGB-thermal gimbal camera, a panoramic camera, an RF spectrum analyzer, and a millimeter-wave radar,” they write. The data includes 15 target drones from 13 commercial models, including three separately labeled DJI Mini 4 Pro units.

Why this matters - fuel for the physical world: Datasets like this are the ingredients for making it easier for AI systems to operate robots and drones in the physical world. They also have potential dual use impacts, though my suspicion is that datasets like this are pretty irrelevant to militaries relative to the kinds of datasets that - and I’m speculating wildly here - might be being gathered in Ukraine right now given the extremely sophisticated drone-to-drone conflict there.

Read more: A2A-UAV: A Multimodal Air-to-Air Dataset for UAV Detection and Identification (arXiv).

Get a sample of the data from Google Drive here (Google Drive).

The full dataset will ultimately be available via Baidu Netdisk with the extraction code A2AD (direct link, Baidu Netdisk).

items.title: Bayesian Network Fusion of Large Language Models for Sentiment Analysis
items.content: Large language models (LLMs) continue to advance, with an increasing number of domain-specific variants tailored for specialised tasks. However, these models often lack transparency and explainability, can be costly to fine-tune, require substantial prompt engineering, yield inconsistent results across domains, and impose significant adverse environmental impact due to their high computational demands. To address these challenges, we propose the Bayesian network LLM fusion (BNLF) framework, which integrates predictions from three LLMs, including FinBERT, RoBERTa, and BERTweet, through a probabilistic mechanism for sentiment analysis. BNLF performs late fusion by modelling the sentiment predictions from multiple LLMs as probabilistic nodes within a Bayesian network. Evaluated across three human-annotated financial corpora with distinct linguistic and contextual characteristics, BNLF demonstrates consistent gains of about six percent in accuracy over the baseline LLMs, underscoring its robustness to dataset variability and the effectiveness of probabilistic fusion for interpretable sentiment classification.
items.author: Rasoul Amirzadeh, Dhananjay Thiruvady, Fatemeh Shiri
items.summary: BNLF is a late-fusion framework that combines predictions from FinBERT, RoBERTa, and BERTweet via probabilistic nodes in a Bayesian network for sentiment analysis, improving transparency and consistency relative to single models. Evaluation across multiple domains shows gains while avoiding costly fine-tuning.
items.reasoning: Solid, sensible ensemble methodology with explainability benefits, but it relies on older encoder models and standard techniques; incremental rather than frontier research with limited generalization beyond sentiment tasks.

items.title: Beyond Code and Pixels: Co-Generating Editable and Visually Rich Presentations
items.content: Generating PPTX presentations is a structured task that requires semantic planning, visual composition, precise layout, and editability, motivating collaboration among specialized agents. However, programmatic methods offer editability but often produce rigid designs, while image-based methods provide visual richness but flatten content into difficult-to-edit pixels. A hybrid system can combine these strengths, but must coordinate interdependent decisions across content, layout, and appearance. To address this challenge, we propose SlidesWeaver, a hybrid multi-agent system that coordinates language and vision agents through shared deck- and slide-level states. Specifically, it uses staged multimodal commitment, diffusion-based composition planning, and two generation schedules for different priorities between composition freedom and accurate text preservation, while preserving native text and geometry. Across 1,728 generations spanning 24 system-model configurations, SlidesWeaver achieves consistently superior overall quality across all evaluated dimensions while maintaining structural control, editability, and practical generation efficiency.

items.summary: SlidesWeaver is a hybrid multi-agent system combining programmatic (editable) and image-based (visually rich) presentation generation, coordinating language and vision agents via shared deck- and slide-level states with staged multimodal commitment and diffusion-based composition planning. It addresses the editability-versus-richness tradeoff in slide generation.
items.reasoning: Well-motivated multi-agent design tackling a practical generative AI task with a genuine tradeoff; strong engineering contribution, but presentation generation is an applied niche with rapidly moving competition.

items.title: REMORA: A Voice-First Memory Assistant for Grounded Personal Recall and Independent Living
items.content: Most of what matters in a day is spoken and written down nowhere: a dosing interval named at a clinic, a deadline moved in passing, the place a document was set down. Such information is consequential because it is operational, and fragile because it arrives during divided attention -- the moment its importance becomes clear is rarely the moment it was said. For people living with mild cognitive impairment, Alzheimer's disease or age-related episodic memory decline, that gap bounds independent living. Conventional aids close it poorly: notes, reminders and calendars require the user to notice, interrupt and transcribe, adding extraneous cognitive load exactly where attention is already committed. We present REMORA, a voice-first memory assistant that converts consented speech into structured, auditable memory records. REMORA transcribes and diarizes captured audio, extracts memory candidates -- tasks, appointments, names, instructions, object locations -- each retaining provenance into the conversation it came from, and holds records, embeddings and relationships in a single relational system of record. Recall combines lexical, semantic, relational and recency signals, since no one signal covers the ways people interrogate their own past, and reaches the user either through an explicit query or through a confidence-gated cue that stays silent unless it is likely to help. Generation is bound by a grounding contract: only retrieved evidence may be used, and absent a supporting memory REMORA abstains rather than confabulates, because a fluent invention about one's own past will be acted upon as fact. A requirements survey and a pilot study with memory-loss users indicate that conversational forgetting extends well beyond clinical populations, that grounded and concise recall is feasible in controlled settings, and that privacy, rather than accuracy, is the binding constraint on adoption.

It targets the gap where consequential spoken information (dosage intervals, moved deadlines) is never written down and conventional aids add cognitive load. The work is a socially meaningful applied system addressing assistive healthcare needs.
items.reasoning: Addresses a genuine unmet need with a thoughtful design rationale around attention and consent, but it appears to be a system/application paper; novelty relative to prior memory-assistant work and clinical validation strength are unclear from the abstract.

items.title: 5G NR Sensing of Robotic Arm Motion in Indoor Factory Environments
items.content: This paper investigates the performance of monostatic Integrated Sensing and Communication (ISAC) systems for tracking robotic arm kinematics in industrial factory (InF) environments. Building on a part-specific quasi-deterministic channel model previously derived from high-resolution robotic-arm measurements using our context-aware channel sounder and digital twin, we develop a framework for generating arbitrary articulated motion profiles through hierarchical kinematic transformations. By integrating this high-fidelity target model with the standardized 3GPP InF channel model, we employ 5G New Radio (NR) Positioning Reference Signals (PRS) as the sensing waveform to enable comprehensive system-level evaluation. Simulations are conducted for both sparse clutters (InF-SH) and dense clutters (InF-DH) scenarios using 3GPP-compliant antenna radiation patterns and analog beamforming, allowing us to assess the impact of industrial clutter on sensing performance. The results show that while high estimation accuracy is achievable under Line-of-Sight (LOS) conditions, dense clutter in InF-DH environments introduces severe blockage that significantly limits sensing reliability. In particular, the effective sensing coverage in InF-DH is drastically reduced, with detection probability dropping to approximately \(P_d \approx 10\,\%\) even when the robotic arm is located directly beneath the Transmission Reception Point (TRP). Furthermore, in InF-SH, achieving a high detection probability (e.g., \(P_d \geq 90\,\%\)) requires the target to remain in close proximity to the TRP, with an effective coverage radius of approximately 13 m.
items.author: Neeraj Varshney, Anuraag Bodi, Steve Blandino, Jian Wang, Camillo Gentile, and Nada Golmie
items.summary: This paper develops a framework for monostatic integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) tracking of robotic arm kinematics in factories, combining a quasi-deterministic channel model from high-resolution measurements with hierarchical kinematic transformations and the standardized 3GPP indoor-factory channel model. Using 5G NR positioning reference signals as sensing waveforms, it evaluates performance in sparse and dense clutter. It is a solid systems/communications engineering contribution toward industrial ISAC.
items.reasoning: Technically substantive work grounded in standardized models with realistic simulation, relevant to 6G/ISAC and industrial robotics; niche audience and simulation-only validation temper the score.

items.title: Scale-Aware Reference Attention for Mannequin-to-Model Gown Generation
items.content: Formal gowns are sold online with photos of models wearing them, and buyers zoom in to inspect sequins, lace and beading. Image editors can turn a photo of a gown on a mannequin into a convincing photo of a person wearing it, but they receive every reference photo without any notion of its magnification, and the fine detail of the gown is lost when the output is viewed up close. We propose scale-aware reference attention (SARA), which tells an open diffusion transformer the zoom level of the output and of every reference photo, biases the attention of the output toward references of a similar zoom level, uses macro photos of the fabric as references, and is trained on a mix of whole-garment and zoomed targets. To train and evaluate it, we introduce Kiss3000, a dataset of 915 high-resolution mannequin photos and 2274 on-model photos of formal gowns with cross-domain pairs and splits by style, and zoom-crop evaluation, which compares garment crops at full, half and local scale without pixel alignment and judges local fidelity with two vision-language models gated on control crops. With this protocol, Nano Banana Pro at 4K, the highest-resolution commercial editor we test, loses or redraws local detail on 14 of 20 test gowns. At 1536x2048 pixels, both judges prefer SARA over a LoRA fine-tuning baseline on 18 test items and the baseline on 6 (p=0.023), and over the base model on 26 against 4 (p=5.9e-5), while SARA keeps the gown design as often as the baseline.
items.author: Guang Yang, Fengchen Liu
items.summary: SARA makes diffusion-transformer image editing aware of the zoom level of reference photos, biasing output attention toward references at similar magnification and leveraging macro fabric photos to preserve fine details like sequins and lace. It is trained and evaluated on Kiss3000, a new dataset of high-resolution gown images. This addresses a concrete failure of reference-based editing: loss of close-up detail.
items.reasoning: Practical and well-targeted improvement for a commercial use case with a useful new dataset, but the core idea (scale-aware attention biasing) is incremental relative to broader image editing research.

items.title: ROSE-SAM3: Response-Oriented Prompt Selection for Open-Vocabulary Remote Sensing Segmentation
items.content: In open-vocabulary semantic segmentation (OVSS) of remote-sensing imagery, class-name prompts can miss objects with varied appearances, while richer descriptions can activate competing classes. We propose Response-Oriented Prompt Selection for SAM 3 (ROSE-SAM3), a training-free framework that selects descriptions using frozen SAM 3 responses on unlabeled target-domain images. We screen candidate descriptions for coverage beyond the native prompts while protecting reliable native class responses, retaining candidates that pass these checks on at least four of five image folds. An offline directed acyclic graph (DAG) search then evaluates candidate combinations and builds a compact PromptBank for each class. Each bank retains the native prompts and adds selected descriptions, which we call residual prompts. At inference, the bank is fixed, and Semantic-Instance Cooperative Head (SICH) uses instance evidence to refine semantic responses before assigning pixel labels. We also introduce RS-OVSS-C to evaluate robustness under six image corruption families across eight remote-sensing datasets, preserving their class vocabularies and reference labels. ROSE-SAM3 achieves 57.3% mean mIoU across eight clean benchmarks and 54.7% on RS-OVSS-C, achieving state-of-the-art performance among training-free methods. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/YanghuiSong/ROSE-SAM3.

It addresses prompt sensitivity in a domain where class-name prompts miss varied object appearances. Practical, well-motivated, and requires no retraining.

items.title: Seeing Beyond Pixels: Radar Feature Generation from Images and Sparse Returns
items.content: Camera-radar fusion benefits from complementary visual and geometric information but often relies on complete radar representations, leading to substantial computing overhead. However, the extent to which visual information can compensate for limited radar measurements remains insufficiently explored. Therefore, we propose Vision-informed Radar Token Generation (VRTG), which exploits cross-modal information to generate task-relevant radar features from camera images and sparse radar measurements. Specifically, VRTG first leverages image-derived object cues to select a limited number of informative radar points. It then establishes calibrated one-to-one associations between visual objects and radar returns, using matched measurements to refine object ranges while retaining visual estimates for unmatched objects. Finally, the associated object features and visual context are transformed into radar tokens compatible with existing camera-radar fusion networks. Experiments on RADIal demonstrate that VRTG achieves 90.76\% vehicle-detection F1 and 86.68\% free-space mIoU using only four radar points per frame, approaching the performance of the full-radar model.

items.reasoning: Addresses a practical efficiency problem in autonomous-driving perception with a sensible cross-modal generation idea, but the excerpt shows limited evidence of SOTA results and the approach is incremental within an active subfield.

items.title: The Value of Labels in Data Selection for Least Squares
items.content: Suppose a selector sees a finite labelled dataset and chooses $n$ of its rows, with repetition. Ordinary least squares is then fitted to the rows that were chosen, without weights, and the excess loss of the fit on the full dataset is measured in units of the optimal loss. Without further assumptions this ratio does not decay with $n$. We examine the problem for $d$ features and rows of normalized leverage at most $\kappa$, and determine or bound the leading constants. A selector that must establish its rule before seeing the labels has an optimal worst-case ratio of $d\kappa/n$ to leading order, whatever use it makes of the features. With scalar labels, a selector that sees the labels achieves a value between $d\kappa/(2n)$ and $d\kappa\Lambda_d/n$, where $\Lambda_d<1$ is the rounding constant of mean selection. For $d\le4$, the constant is then $d\kappa/2$, so that labels are worth exactly a factor of two there, and for one feature and $m$ outputs it is $\kappa\Lambda_m$. With two or more features the selector can change the proportions of the frequent rows and therefore reshape its own design matrix. We design a simplified optimization problem, which we call a game, that bounds the constant for datasets with exactly fitted frequent rows, then show that its value is at most one half of the gradient energy in several regimes, and that one half is exact along directions in which the frequent rows are rigid, such as an intercept. For grouped designs, in which reshaping amounts to the allocation of a common budget, the constant is $27d/128$ up to an additive constant, compared with $d$ without labels. Nevertheless, one half is not the constant in every dimension: we construct datasets of extremely high dimension and large leverage on which every selection has an excess ratio of at least $(e^{-1/2}-o(1))\,d\kappa/n$, so that labels are worth at most a factor close to $\sqrt e$ there.
items.author: Evan Borodow
items.summary: A theoretical analysis of core-set style data selection for ordinary least squares, determining optimal worst-case excess-loss ratios for selectors that may or may not see labels before choosing rows. With normalized leverage bounded by kappa, a label-blind selector achieves d*kappa/n while a label-aware selector achieves between d*kappa/(2n) and d*kappa*Lambda_d/n, characterizing the value of label access.
items.reasoning: Clean theoretical contribution quantifying exactly when label access helps data selection, with tight worst-case bounds; rigor is clear and results are of interest to the data-centric ML and statistics community, though confined to the least-squares setting.

items.title: torchtsetlin: Fast, Interpretable Tsetlin Machines for PyTorch
items.content: The Tsetlin machine learns propositional rules with teams of Tsetlin automata that are driven by reward and penalty rather than gradients, so its models are interpretable by construction and cheap to evaluate. Its software, however, consists of C and CUDA kernels behind scikit-learn-style wrappers that sit outside the deep learning ecosystem. torchtsetlin implements the Tsetlin machine family as ordinary PyTorch modules: vanilla and weighted, coalesced, regression, convolutional over sequences, images and volumes, and dense per-pixel segmentation. The automata are a tensor buffer, so a model moves with .to(device), is saved with state_dict() and learns from a mini-batch with one update(x,y) call. Its core technique is a batched formulation of Type I and Type II feedback, in which automaton transitions become event counts realised as binomial draws, with one commit per mini-batch. On ten benchmarks taken from the existing libraries, it matches their accuracy, and on all but the two smallest it trains 2.4-10.9X faster than PyTsetlinMachineCUDA and 10.3-81.2X faster than tmu on the same GPU. The package is pure Python, MIT-licensed and on PyPI; every number in this paper is reproduced by one script. Code: https://github.com/vlbthambawita/torchtsetlin; package: https://pypi.org/project/torchtsetlin/.

items.summary: torchtsetlin reimplements the Tsetlin machine family (vanilla, weighted, coalesced, regression, convolutional, segmentation) as native PyTorch modules, making automata a tensor buffer compatible with standard device movement, state saving, and mini-batch updates. Its core technique is a batched formulation of Type I and Type II feedback, integrating gradient-free rule-learning machines into the deep learning ecosystem.
items.reasoning: This is a solid engineering contribution that lowers adoption friction for interpretable Tsetlin machines and could increase their use, but it is primarily an infrastructure/library paper rather than a methodological advance. The batched feedback formulation is the main technical novelty.

items.title: Failure Modes and Data-Efficient Remedies for Transformer-Based Prediction of Viscoplastic Flows
items.content: Fast and accurate prediction of viscoplastic flows remains a challenge in computational rheology due to yield surfaces, discontinuous gradients, and strongly nonlinear transitions between yielded and unyielded regions. Transformer-based neural operators such as RheOFormer have recently shown strong potential for surrogate modeling of non-Newtonian flows. However, their applicability to viscoplastic systems and their efficacy in recovering realistic flows remain poorly understood. In this work, we present the first systematic investigation of RheOFormer applied to steady Bingham channel flow. By isolating the problem to a simple geometry and constitutive model, we examine how dataset structure, numerical value range, and input representation govern the model's ability to interpolate and extrapolate within the parameter space. The data regimes in which RheOFormer remains accurate and those in which errors emerge are identified, particularly for plug-dominated flows and for conditions outside the velocity scales or flow structures represented during training. Upon identifying these failure modes, targeted enhancements to the input representation and loss formulation are introduced to better predict low-gradient plug regions. Logarithmic velocity representations and gradient-aware loss formulations substantially improve accuracy in challenging regimes where the baseline formulation fails. In addition, extrapolation errors are reduced by augmenting the training set with only a few strategically selected cases spanning the missing physical regimes. Finally, a single partially developed snapshot suffices for an accurate steady-state prediction, and the model outperforms simply copying its input throughout flow development. These results highlight the importance of appropriate field representation and parameter-space coverage for data-efficient neural-operator prediction of viscoplastic flows.

The authors isolate how dataset structure, value range, and input representation govern interpolation and extrapolation, and propose data-efficient remedies. It matters for understanding when neural-operator surrogates fail on nonsmooth physics.

items.title: An LLM-Assisted Multi-Objective AutoML Framework for Efficient Network Intrusion Detection
items.content: Conventional Machine Learning (ML)-based Intrusion Detection Systems (IDSs) require manual design, optimize only detection performance, and neglect inference latency and model size, which are critical for resource-constrained Internet of Things (IoT) and Electric Vehicle Charging System (EVCS) deployments. Automated ML (AutoML) reduces manual effort but explores broad search spaces inefficiently. Meanwhile, Multi-Objective Optimization (MOO) methods lack guided search initialization, leading to long search times. This paper proposes a Large Language Model-Assisted Multi-Objective Automated ML (LLM-MOO-AutoML) framework for efficient intrusion detection. A local Llama 3.1 8B model analyzes a compact dataset profile and generates a bounded, validated policy for automated data balancing (AutoDP) and feature engineering (AutoFE). This policy narrows the search space for Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm III (NSGA-III), which jointly optimizes the LightGBM feature-selection threshold and key hyperparameters across three objectives: maximizing weighted F1-score, minimizing 99th-percentile (P99) inference latency ratio, and minimizing model size ratio. Experiments on CICIDS2017, IoTID20, and CICEVSE2024 demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves the highest weighted F1-scores on CICIDS2017 (99.788%), IoTID20 (99.778%), and CICEVSE2024 (99.989%), with feature sets reduced to as few as 10 features, P99 latency as low as 0.00038 ms, and model size as small as 0.1073 MB. The LLM-guided configuration reduced NSGA-III search time relative to unconstrained multi-objective search on all datasets at the largest trial budget and in most comparisons at smaller budgets, indicating that dataset-aware search-space reduction supports efficient, deployment-aware intrusion detection.

It targets the practical constraints of security ML on resource-limited edge devices.

The use of an older open-weight model (Llama 3.1) as a local component is sensible for privacy. Limited novelty beyond the framework composition.

items.title: Decision models for UAVBench and the viability of edge deployment
items.content: Small language models are often proposed for reasoning onboard a drone. However, a good benchmark score does not tell us whether a model will actually run, and run usefully, on an edge computer. In this paper we study three related questions using the UAV decision benchmark, UAVBench. First, are small structured decision models good candidates for these tasks? Second, can an ordinary local machine (a Mac) screen candidate models before we test them on physical devices? Third, what software and resource limits govern deployment? Our main Mac evaluation covers 24 model configurations on the same 2,000 validated multiple-choice questions from UAVBench. These include 20 size-and-precision configurations of 11 generative models, plus four open-weight structured decision models that received no additional UAVBench-specific training. A structured decision model, H2O Lightning 4B, achieved the highest accuracy we observed, scoring 77.65% on the Mac. This shows that these models are well suited to this kind of task. However, when we tried to deploy the decision models, we ran into conversion and runtime limits on the edge devices we tested, which we describe in detail. To test local screening, we ran matched evaluations of two generative models on both the Mac and a Qualcomm RB3 board. The accuracies did not match exactly, but the ranking did. LFM2 2.6B ranked above Qwen2.5 1.5B on both platforms. This supports using a local machine to shortlist candidates. That said, individual answers still differed between platforms, so testing on the actual hardware remained necessary.
items.author: Matthew Michelson, Goran Muric, Adrien Bibal, Steven Minton
items.summary: This study examines whether small language models benchmarked on UAVBench, a drone decision-making benchmark, can actually run usefully on edge hardware. It evaluates 24 configurations on a Mac to screen candidates before physical-device testing, covering generative models and structured decision models. The work connects benchmark performance to realistic deployment constraints for onboard drone reasoning.
items.reasoning: Practical, deployment-grounded evaluation filling a real gap between benchmark scores and edge viability, with a large validated question set. Academic-industry author team with sound methodology. Contribution is more empirical survey than novel technique.

items.title: A Hybrid Multi-Goal Path Planning Framework for Powered Wheelchairs in Dynamic Environments: From Simulation to Real-World Validation
items.content: Autonomous powered wheelchairs (PWs) operating in human-centered environments must combine efficient multi-destination path planning with continuous collision avoidance strategies in the presence of static and dynamic obstacles. This study presents a hybrid framework integrating Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP)-based global task ordering, Potential-Field (PF) guidance, and local Rapidly-exploring Random Tree (RRT) and A-star (A*) planners. PF guidance transfers global path information to local planners, helping the robot stay aligned with the global path during obstacle avoidance. Local planning is enhanced with direction-aware, extended-neighborhood A* or RRT using environment-aware sampling and two-step extension. The TSP-PF-RRT and TSP-PF-A* methods are evaluated in normal, crowded, and extra-crowded simulation environments using point-based and elliptical robot models. The elliptical model accounts for platform dimensions during collision avoidance phase. Hardware tests on the physical PW use motion capture (MoCap) for ground-truth measurements, while outside-MoCap experiments rely on onboard LiDAR and RGB-D sensing. Results show that incorporating the wheelchair geometry changes the observed collision behavior, yielding comparable collision avoidance performance between the two hybrid planners under the elliptical model.

items.title: When AI Should Not Decide: Evidence Sufficiency and Decision Stability in Automated Job Interviews
items.content: Artificial intelligence is increasingly used to assess employment candidates, yet consistent interview scoring does not establish whether automated recommendations are supported by sufficient evidence. This study introduces the Evidence Sufficiency and Decision Stability Assessment (ESDSA), which combines criterion-level evidence classification, deterministic quotation traceability and stability checks across linguistic variants assessed as substantively equivalent. We evaluated four approaches (scoring-only, evidence-aware, traceability-based and integrated ESDSA v2) using 540 synthetic interview responses from 60 evaluated scenario families across Software Engineering, Customer Support and Operations. In held-out testing (216 responses), integrated ESDSA achieved 85.19% actionable coverage and 3.80% disagreement among actionable recommendations against AI-assisted provisional references. Evidence-aware evaluation achieved 92.59% coverage and 4.50% disagreement; scoring-only evaluation achieved 71.30% coverage and 1.95% disagreement. The integrated stability gate deferred 11 additional previously actionable decisions, ten of which had agreed with provisional references. The findings demonstrate trade-offs between evidential constraints, decision consistency and abstention, rather than overall superiority of the integrated framework. ESDSA offers a reproducible methodology for examining when automated interview recommendations should be actionable or deferred. Synthetic responses and AI-assisted references do not establish real-world recruitment validity.

items.title: Decoding Frozen Vision Representations for Training-Free Few-Shot Pineapple Detection
items.content: Few-shot object detection in agricultural imagery is hampered by dense vegetation, repeated patterns, and scarce annotations. We present a training-free detector that turns dense features from frozen visual foundation models directly into detections, without fine-tuning, a learned head, or external proposals: a whitened foreground-background direction estimated from annotated support images scores every query patch, and the score field is decoded with an adaptive threshold and support-derived geometry. We also test whether predicted relative depth can be fed directly to RGB-pretrained frozen encoders. On aerial pineapple imagery, the detector outperforms PET-DINO and GeCo2 at every evaluated support size; at K=40, predicted depth alone reaches 92% of the RGB performance with DINOv2, and RGB-depth fusion lowers counting error for both encoders. We release the Pineapple Plantation dataset (4,908 aerial frames, 1,995 annotated with 17,609 boxes, predicted depth, leakage-aware splits) and analyse transfer to two further agricultural datasets.

items.title: CAMA: Calibrated Anti-Collapse Marginal Alignment for Test-Time Adaptation of Vision-Language Models
items.content: Test-time adaptation (TTA) updates a model using unlabeled test data to help it handle distribution shifts. However, prior work has found that image corruption causes a vision-language model (VLM) to produce more similar features for different images, a phenomenon known as feature compression. Under compression, entropy minimization, the most common TTA objective, can cause the model to favor a few classes and perform worse than before adaptation. Despite these observations, a detailed analysis of how these failures are connected and an effective strategy for preventing them are still lacking.   In this paper, we first analyze why entropy minimization fails for VLMs. We then propose CAMA, a new test-time adaptation objective that maximizes batch mutual information to encourage confident predictions for individual images while maintaining diverse predictions across the batch. CAMA also estimates a reference class distribution early in the test stream and aligns each batch's average prediction with this reference during adaptation. We prove that feature compression biases the predictions and that entropy minimization amplifies this bias into collapse, whereas CAMA is guaranteed to preserve every class. Across standard corruption benchmarks, we observe collapse on nearly every VLM backbone evaluated. CAMA prevents collapse in every observed case and, in turn, achieves the best accuracy on every backbone. Quantitative and qualitative analyses confirm that CAMA reverses the feature compression behind the collapse, and ablations show that each of its components contributes.

items.title: Walks2Maps: Learning Indoor Geometry from Crowdsourced Wi-Fi RTT and Motion Trajectories
items.content: Everyday smartphone walks offer a scalable source of indoor geometry, but their motion traces drift and their radio measurements are distorted by multipath. We present Walks2Maps, a physics-guided framework that reconstructs a shared metric map from Wi-Fi round-trip-time (RTT) and motion observations, without a floor plan, surveyed access-point (AP) coordinates, or position labels. Walks2Maps jointly estimates pedestrian trajectories, AP locations, and per-trajectory stride scales, then recovers the pathway layout from the reconstructed paths. Shared AP observations connect walks recorded in different local frames, while metric ranges constrain their relative geometry and scale. An asymmetric range loss accommodates multipath-induced excess delay. On 22 phone trajectories collected along 11 routes on an office floor with 30 APs, Walks2Maps achieves median AP and trajectory errors of 0.87 m and 0.89 m, respectively, and a walked-area F1 score of 0.985. Ablations show that radio similarity can recognize places while still producing a distorted map; retaining the metric information in RTT resolves this ambiguity. Asymmetric modeling further reduces AP error by 54% relative to a symmetric loss. These results demonstrate how radio and motion measurements can jointly reveal indoor geometry without a dedicated mapping survey. We will release the dataset and toolkit.

items.title: When and Where to Transfer: Learning Transferable Historical Contexts for Short-History Multivariate Time Series Forecasting
items.content: Related sources can improve multivariate time series forecasting when the target history is short, but their usefulness varies across source groups and historical periods. A key challenge is to identify informative historical contexts from the sources. This paper proposes Hierarchical Context Transfer (HiCT), a framework that adaptively weights source groups and their historical contexts to determine both \emph{where} and \emph{when} to transfer. A shared context encoder and cross-attention are used to learn weights over source groups and historical contexts. These weights guide regularized transfer estimation, followed by an optional target-specific correction. This paper establishes a target excess-risk bound for the context-weighted transfer estimator. Experiments demonstrate competitive predictive performance across four multivariate forecasting datasets and a favorable accuracy--runtime trade-off against the evaluated baselines. Source-corruption ablations illustrate the roles of group-level and within-group weighting in adapting to unreliable source histories.

items.title: Beyond Full-Context Accuracy: Context-Marginalized Evaluation of Test-Time Structure-Aware Inference in EEG-to-Image Retrieval
items.content: Test-time structure-aware inference can improve cross-subject EEG-to-image retrieval by exploiting relations among unlabeled test queries, but it also makes predictions depend on query-set composition. Existing evaluations typically report accuracy under a single full-query context, leaving unclear whether gains and comparative conclusions hold as context changes. We introduce Context-Marginalized Retrieval Evaluation (CMRE), which repeatedly evaluates each target query in sampled contexts using the corresponding rows of a fixed query-gallery similarity matrix. CMRE distinguishes structural exploitability, quantified by gains over independent retrieval, from context robustness, measured by same-query Top-1 context consistency. Under leave-one-subject-out evaluation on THINGS-EEG2 across six frozen representations and six structure-aware inference rules, structure-aware inference improves full-context Top-1 accuracy by up to 20.40 percentage points over independent retrieval. However, the rule selected under full-context evaluation is no longer optimal in 17 of 24 representation-context-size conditions (70.8%). Selecting the full-context winner incurs an average loss of 2.70 percentage points and a maximum loss of 8.29 percentage points under reduced contexts. Representation rankings are likewise inference- and context-dependent: the ordering under independent retrieval is not consistently preserved under structure-aware inference. Moreover, larger retrieval gains do not necessarily imply greater context robustness, showing that retrieval effectiveness and prediction stability provide complementary views of structure-aware inference. Full-context accuracy captures one operating point of context-dependent inference. CMRE complements it by characterizing how structural gains, context consistency, and comparisons of rules and representations change with query context.

items.title: DeCo: Decoupled Traffic State Modeling with Cross-Variable Coordination
items.content: Accurate forecasts of traffic flow, occupancy, and speed are essential for congestion management and travel planning. These variables exhibit distinct spatiotemporal patterns, and their coupled dynamics characterize the evolution of traffic conditions, such as the onset and dissipation of congestion. Existing methods often either neglect this coupling or struggle to capture the distinct dynamics of all three variables within a unified model. In this paper, we propose DeCo, a decoupled traffic state modeling framework with cross-variable coordination for forecasting flow, occupancy, and speed. Specifically, DeCo first trains a dedicated forecaster for each variable to specialize in its unique spatiotemporal dynamics. It then estimates a residual correction for each forecast by jointly leveraging the predicted trajectories and recent observations of all three variables, thereby exploiting cross-variable coupling and mitigating systematic prediction errors. We extend the flow-only PeMS03 and PeMS07 benchmarks to all three variables on their original sensors and release the aligned data. Experiments on PeMS03, PeMS04, PeMS07, and PeMS08 show that DeCo achieves the lowest mean absolute error for every variable on every dataset, up to 4.9% below RAGC, the strongest baseline. Code is available at https://github.com/lixus7/DeCo.

It addresses the limitation that unified models struggle to handle each variable's distinct spatiotemporal patterns. The work is relevant to smart-city and transportation applications.

items.title: When Local Semantics Disagree: Learning to Detect Fake News through Weakly Supervised Cross-Modal Reasoning
items.content: The rapid proliferation of multimodal social media content has made fake news detection a pressing challenge for the vision-language community. Most existing approaches rely on coarse global similarity between text and images, which overlooks subtle, uneven cross-modal inconsistencies -- such as sentiment-scene mismatches, object-level manipulations, or semantic dissonance between visual and textual cues. Moreover, these models treat all inconsistencies as equally informative, ignoring domain-specific variation in how such conflicts manifest, which limits both generalization and interpretability. To address these challenges, we propose DMIL, a dual-branch multiple instance learning framework that formulates multimodal fake news detection as a weakly supervised learning problem. Each news article is treated as a bag of visual and textual instances processed through two complementary branches: an embedding-space branch that aggregates global semantics via expert-guided modality fusion, and an instance-space branch that models cross-modal inconsistencies across local-to-global granularities. A retrieval-augmented, domain-adaptive router further contextualizes inconsistencies using retrieved domain exemplars and dynamically fuses multi-level cues. Extensive experiments on public misinformation benchmarks demonstrate that DMIL achieves competitive state-of-the-art performance and demonstrates strong discriminative capability against fake news across different domains.

This improves generalization and interpretability for vision-language misinformation detection. The topic is socially important though methodologically familiar.

items.title: ReCoRain: Reliability-Coupled Content and Noise Conditioning for Event-Guided Video Deraining
items.content: Event-guided video deraining depends on reliable cross-frame correspondences, yet events generated by scene motion, rain, and sensor noise can provide ambiguous matching evidence. In diffusion-based restoration, an incorrect match can transfer unrelated content and correlate initial noise between unrelated scene locations. We propose ReCoRain, an event-guided residual video diffusion framework that couples temporal content transfer and noise correlation through a common assessment of correspondence reliability. This assessment combines RGB appearance, interval-event evidence, and forward-backward motion consistency. The content path aggregates neighboring features according to alignment reliability, while the noise path uses composed backward motion fields and their associated reliability estimates to regulate initial-noise sharing across the latent sequence. We use the same conditional noise construction during residual flow-matching training and inference, incorporating temporal noise coordination into the learned restoration process. Temporal supervision matches motion-compensated inter-frame differences in restored and clean videos under the same teacher-estimated flow and visibility mask, accommodating legitimate appearance changes. ReCoRain achieves 32.09 dB PSNR on NTURain-Syn and 28.73 dB on RainSynLight25. Enabling reliability gates in both paths reduces warping error by 33.0% relative to disabling both gates.

items.title: Data-Driven Trajectory Prediction via Probabilistic Modes and Constrained Optimization
items.content: Predicting the future trajectories of surrounding agents is a fundamental requirement for safe autonomous driving. Since agent intent is inherently uncertain, multimodal prediction is essential to account for the full range of plausible future behaviors. We introduce Probabilistic Modes and Constrained Optimization trajectory prediction (ProMo-CoOp), a two-stage data-driven framework. At design time, trajectories are clustered into behavioral modes and a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) provides probabilistic mode assignments. At prediction time, a candidate trajectory is generated for each mode by solving a convex optimization problem that enforces consistency with the observed trajectory and uses the precomputed mode assignments to guide prediction toward the selected behavioral mode. The framework also supports Signal Temporal Logic (STL)-derived behavioral constraints, with predicate satisfaction probabilities estimated using Conditional Flow Matching (CFM). Experiments show that ProMo-CoOp outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, and that STL-based constraints can further improve performance when the predicted predicate satisfactions are reliable.

This combines probabilistic intent modeling with physically feasible, optimization-based prediction.

items.title: Dynamic Spectrum Re-parameterized Convolution for Cost-free Image Enhancement
items.content: Image enhancement spans degradations with distinct spectral characteristics. Standard convolutions use fixed kernels, whereas dynamic convolutions gain adaptability at additional inference cost. We propose Dynamic Spectrum Re-parameterized Convolution (DSRC), a plug-and-play module that learns task-adaptive spectral responses during training while retaining standard convolution at inference. DSRC decomposes convolution kernels into frequency bands, applies learnable high/low-pass modulation, and incorporates lightweight residual branches. Owing to the linearity of these operations, all training-time components are analytically fused into a single kernel for inference. Experiments on low-light enhancement, underwater enhancement, and image super-resolution show consistent PSNR gains and generally improved or preserved SSIM and LPIPS across twelve backbone-task configurations, with unchanged deployed parameter counts and theoretical FLOPs, and no additional inference operators.

items.title: Frozen by the Mean: Early Temporal Guidance Unfreezes Motion in Video Diffusion Models
items.content: Video diffusion models can render convincing frames while failing to produce the requested action. Increasing classifier-free guidance (CFG) can strengthen motion, but also saturates and shifts colors. Scalar CFG assigns the same coefficient to the averaged and frame-varying components of its prediction difference, limiting independent control of temporal variation. THAW, Temporal Harmonic Amplification during Warm-up, retains stock CFG and adds a separately weighted residual during an initial denoising window. Its dose specifies the added norm relative to the current CFG difference, giving the extra guidance a consistent relative budget across sampling steps. THAW is training-free and reuses CFG's two model predictions with an unchanged network evaluation count. It improves cost-matched motion over scalar and scheduled CFG on five video models, with positive point estimates against existing guidance methods on three of them. On VBench, THAW raises dynamic degree by about 14 to 15 points over stock CFG while increasing total scores on a different set of three models.

items.reasoning: A clean, training-free intervention with a clear diagnosis of why scalar CFG under-controls temporal variation, and zero added inference cost makes it adoption-friendly. Impact depends on how much motion quality matters relative to emerging specialized motion models.

items.title: ArrythML-II: An Optimized TinyML Framework for ECG Arrhythmia Detection and Multi-Class Beat Classification on Wearable Devices
items.content: This paper presents ArrythML-II, an optimized TinyML framework for on-device ECG arrhythmia detection and multi-class beat classification on wearable platforms. A systematic hyperparameter optimization framework is developed to identify compact autoencoder architectures for binary ECG arrhythmia detection. A custom scoring mechanism jointly considers detection performance, reconstruction-error thresholds, and model size to guide architecture selection. The framework is further extended to six-class ECG beat classification using a lightweight classifier derived from the optimized autoencoder architecture. Both models are INT8 quantized and deployed using TensorFlow Lite Micro on a custom-developed, battery-operated, single-lead ECG device based on the PSoC~6 microcontroller. The deployed autoencoder and classifier have model sizes of approximately 44~KB and 22~KB, respectively, with end-to-end processing times of 5.1~ms and 4.7~ms per ECG segment. Model inference accounts for 3.95~ms and 1.38~ms of these processing times, respectively. In the refined arrhythmia detection evaluation using the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database, the autoencoder achieved an accuracy of 84.76\%, precision of 82.68\%, and recall of 77.99\%. The multi-class classifier achieved 82.29\% accuracy, weighted precision of 90.18\%, and weighted recall of 82.29\%. Beyond offline model evaluation, the wearable platform is validated using preloaded ECG segments, live ECG signals, and an ESP32-S3-based ECG emulator that replays annotated MIT-BIH recordings as analog waveforms. The results demonstrate the feasibility of integrating optimized TinyML models into wearable platforms for real-time ECG analysis.

items.title: Beyond Raw IQ: Compact Semantic Representations for Task Oriented Automatic Modulation Classification
items.content: Automatic modulation classification (AMC) is an important component of modern wireless communication systems, but conventional signal representations can be expensive to store, process, and communicate, particularly under noisy channel conditions. This work investigates whether learned semantic representations can provide a compact alternative to high-dimensional in-phase and quadrature (IQ) representations while retaining robustness to noise. Starting from a 2048-dimensional IQ representation, we evaluate learned semantic representations with dimensions of 4, 8, 16, 32, and 64. Across the evaluated configurations, a 16-dimensional representation provides the strongest overall trade-off between classification performance, robustness, and representation size. The resulting representation achieves a 128x compression ratio and a 99.22% reduction in dimensionality. We further evaluate representation stability across signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs), compare semantic representations with a raw-IQ CNN, analyze per-class robustness, and perform five-seed validation. The five-seed evaluation produces an average accuracy of (49.22 +- 0.52)% and Macro-F1 of (49.27 +- 0.53)% across the evaluated SNR range. These results indicate that learned semantic compression can produce a substan- tially smaller representation while preserving useful classification information and improving geometric stability under noise.

items.reasoning: A reasonable empirical study relevant to semantic communication systems, with a clear practical takeaway about compact representations. The methodology is standard representation-size ablation and the scope is narrow, so novelty and broader impact are limited.

items.title: PointNeXt Adapter Improved Model for BIM Component Defect Association under Construction Images and Design Model Attributes
items.content: Construction site defect analysis increasingly requires linking field evidence to the correct BIM object, because a crack, spalling area, missing sleeve or misaligned support is useful for quality control only when it is connected with component identity, location, responsibility and design intent. This paper proposes a PointNeXt Adapter improved model for BIM component defect association under construction images and design model attributes. The method aligns site image crops, local point cloud patches, BIM component identifiers, geometry attributes, material categories, installation stage, inspection distance, viewpoint quality and source reliability tags into component level inspection windows. PointNeXt learns local geometry and deviation from as built point evidence, while the adapter injects BIM attributes so the same geometric irregularity can be interpreted differently for structural, envelope, MEP and embedded components. The fusion head outputs component link, defect class, defect probability, confidence, dominant evidence and recommended review action. A synthetic multisource BIM inspection dataset is used to evaluate repeated layouts, occlusion, sparse point clouds, registration errors and unseen component arrangements. Results show that attribute aware point learning improves association accuracy, defect recall and confidence calibration compared with image only, point only, simple fusion and adapter free baselines. The framework is positioned as traceable BIM issue review support, requiring manual confirmation and staged field validation before operational deployment.

items.reasoning: A useful application-focused contribution for construction quality control with a sensible multimodal fusion design, but it builds on established components (PointNeXt plus adapter) in a niche domain. items.title: Task-Conditioned Detail Allocation for Synthetic Segmentation Data
items.content: Synthetic images sharing a segmentation label can differ in their training value. We propose Task-Conditioned Detail Allocation (TCDA) to select useful candidates and locally edit some remaining images. We ask whether image details provide class-specific cues in the regions marked by the label. We train a small task reference on frozen image features from real training images. We compare its class responses before and after blurring each candidate, and score how well these response changes align with the labeled regions. This detail allocation score ranks candidates from the same source. Comparing their response--label alignment with that of the real source image also guides repair decisions and, in multiclass tasks, the choice of regions to edit. Selected candidates and accepted repairs are used for training with the original labels and the unchanged downstream segmenter. Experiments on camouflaged object detection, degraded salient object detection, and adverse-condition semantic segmentation show that our selection outperforms equally sized random and label-agreement subsets. Combining selection and repair improves over real-only training by up to 0.019 in $S_\alpha$ on COD10K and 2.86 mIoU points on ACDC.

The score ranks synthetic candidates and guides local edits or repairs, improving the training value of synthetic data for segmentation. It focuses on selective allocation of detail rather than uniform generation quality.
items.reasoning: A practical data-centric contribution with a clear, testable idea (task-conditioned detail scoring for synthetic data curation). The impact is moderate: useful for segmentation practitioners but incremental relative to broader synthetic-data research.
