items.title: Advancements in Diabetic Retinopathy Classification Using Novel Multi-Stacked U-Net Architectures
items.content: Diabetes leads to several health complications throughout the body, with the complication in the eyes being Diabetic Retinopathy. It leads to damaging or abnormal changes in the blood vessels' structure, causing vision loss. The need for massive screening of a large population of diabetic patients has created a necessity for computer-aided, fully automatic diagnosis of DR. CNNs have shown great promise in the classification of DR based on the Fundus images. Building a reliable model faces considerable challenges due to the limited availability of high-quality annotated datasets and issues with varying image quality and class imbalances. This paper aims to demonstrate the UNET, and its Stacked Architecture variant and their performance across several datasets. This paper has compared and studied the UNET architecture's performance across multiple stacks and has come to a soft conclusion that the architecture performs its best at three stacks, and any more leads to deterioration of its performance. The model aims at classifying the images into five categories, 0 to 4, where 0 is no DR, and 4 is proliferative DR.

items.summary: Evaluates U-Net and stacked U-Net architectures for diabetic retinopathy classification from fundus images across several datasets, addressing limited annotations, variable image quality, and class imbalance. The paper compares and studies performance across these settings for automated screening.
items.reasoning: Application-level study using established architectures with limited novelty; the described U-Net variants are not architecturally new and the evaluation scope appears modest.

items.title: Two Ideas for Promoting an AI Security Mindset
items.content:
Here are ideas that are designed to both jolt the AI companies into adopting a security mindset that’s appropriate for handling human-level AIs, and to modestly slow the race to superintelligence. These are not intended as full solutions to either goal.

It is becoming urgent for AI companies to improve the security of their computers, in order to reduce the risk that some arbitrary outsider can take control of the goals of a powerful AI.

### 1.

I want a bug bounty program loosely patterned after the Hack the Pentagon bug bounty program, with break-ins adjudicated by a government agency.

I propose that bounties be paid to people who can break into an AI company. Have the program plant a canary: a file in the training pipeline that only something with write access to critical systems could modify. Participating hackers get rewards for altering the canary.

The canary reduces the subjectivity of the adjudication, but the agency will still want to make some subjective judgments about the bug severity. I’m thinking of bounties in the $100K to $5M range depending on how hard it looks for the exploit to be used to alter AI weights undetected.

In order to ensure that the AI company faces strong incentives, it should be fined roughly 10 times the rewards that get paid to the hackers.

I want this program to continue indefinitely.

There’s some risk that the program will enable some theft of weights that wouldn’t otherwise be possible. I’m not too concerned about theft of today’s models, but I expect I will become a good deal more concerned about theft of weights in 6 to 12 months.

I suggest that this initially apply to Anthropic and OpenAI, and within a few months be extended to something like 6 or 8 other companies.

### 2.

My second proposal involves modest changes to liability laws, focused on what happens when a user gives an AI a prompt that causes the AI to do something illegal, or something that would be illegal if a human did it intentionally....

The core concern is that arbitrary outsiders could take control of a powerful AI's goals if lab security is weak. It is a concrete policy proposal post.

items.title: Moderately cursed questions of AI safety
items.content:
TL;DR

- AI safety has many moderately cursed questions (as opposed to the extremely cursed questions of s-risk, which we don’t discuss here).
- Taboo prevents open discussion of these cursed questions in AI safety spaces outside LessWrong.
- When cursed questions are left unasked, everyone stays confused or reaches private conclusions alone.
- Spreading decoupling norms, so that cursed questions can be discussed more openly, should be an explicit target of AI safety acculturation.

You’re having Thai food with your fiancée. The wedding is two months out, and you can’t slurp your green curry with the usual gusto. That cursed question keeps buzzing around your head like a hungry fly after your crispy tofu. You’ve been rehearsing ways to broach the subject:

“I was thinking, maybe we should get a prenup? I don’t think anything will happen, it’s just…”

Not that. Might as well say, “You’re cool, but my lawyer told me not to trust you.”

The prenup question is wrapped in taboo. Asking for one feels like pre-filing divorce papers. Yet even while the words stay unspoken, the thought can’t be undone. Unasked questions still exist, just internally.

AI safety has its own cursed questions. In this essay, I discuss four:

- Are we better off with a catastrophe big enough to summon the political will to pause AI, but small enough that we survive?
- Should AI safety proponents prepare to win a culture war via AI superpersuasion?
- Will there come a time when stopping the AI race is infeasible and we must pick a horse?
- When do we stop working on AI safety and make end-of-life arrangements?

items.title: Heroism in AI Safety
items.content:
What role do heroes have in AI safety?

MS Paint drawing by Opus 5.5.

This blog post was written in my personal capacity and free time. Gemini 4 Neon and Opus 5.5 assisted in ideating and writing up rebuttals for initial drafts.

In Gentleness and the Artificial Other, Joe Carlsmith brings up Timothy Treadwell—the subject of the documentary Grizzly Man.Timothy Treadwell was a man who loved bears: he was gentle with them, filming them up close, hanging out with them, even refusing to set up electric fences around his camp or to carry around bear mace. He did this for 13 years. Then he was eaten by a bear.

Looking into the eyes of one of Timothy Treadwell’s bears, Herzog famously observes “no kinship, no understanding, no mercy,” only nature, indifferent.

In AI safety, we have internalised this warning quite deeply. Looking at the prospect of misaligned artificial superintelligence, it can feel like only a mailed fist would suit these hands, the only responsible posture wariness, the only honest recourse violence. Indeed, Carlsmith’s essay is an argument for learning the “art of both”—holding, clinging onto wonder and openness toward the artificial Other without forgetting that we might still get eaten. It is important to both appreciate the stardust, comets, constellations in the inky maw, but also that we are indeed putting our head between its jaws....

The author argues for holding both openness toward the artificial other and clear-eyed recognition of danger, and reflects on what heroic conduct means for safety researchers.

items.title: A Novel Approach to Clustering Shape Data Using Iteratively Weighted Vectors with k-Means
items.content: Topological data analysis provides a collection of methods for analyzing data with shape structure, including point clouds, graphs, and images. Recent advances in topological vectorization have enabled the embedding of shape data into Euclidean spaces, facilitating comparisons and machine learning tasks. Vector summaries that effectively capture topological structures are particularly useful for shape classification and unsupervised learning tasks such as clustering. We investigate the use of vectorized topological data for clustering through k-means, which partitions observations into a fixed number of groups by minimizing a squared-error loss function. By incorporating an element-wise weight-update step into the iterative k-means algorithm, we improve clustering performance on both simulated and real-world shape datasets. We show that estimating these weights reduces to a least-squares problem, requiring minimal additional computation while allowing flexible coefficient constraints. Our approach also substantially strengthens the negative correlation between the loss and clustering accuracy, improving the effectiveness of selecting among multiple clustering solutions based on the lowest loss. These improvements remain robust to changes in vector length and the number of initializations. Furthermore, weighted topological vector summaries exhibit stability under small structural perturbations, particularly when weight constraints are imposed. The proposed method offers a flexible alternative for clustering topological data, accommodating different k-means variants, vectorization methods, and weight constraints.

items.title: From Vanishing Gradients to Recursive Self-Improvement: Evaluating the Most Influential Papers in Large Language Model Evolution (1997-2026)
items.content: The rapid proliferation of Large Language Model (LLM) research makes it increasingly difficult to distinguish incremental refinements from true paradigm shifts. This review evaluates 22 of the most influential publications spanning nearly three decades (1997-2026), organized through a causal, chronologically anchored taxonomy centered on the author's birth year (1999). Beginning "before 1999" with how recurrent neural networks (RNNs) forgot earlier context (much like forgetting Chapter 1 by the time a reader reaches Chapter 9), we trace how Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks introduced a "bouncer" mechanism of forget, input, and output gates to selectively preserve long-term memory. We then examine how Word2Vec turned language into vector mathematics (king - male + female ~ queen), why sequential RNNs hit a parallelization wall, and how the Transformer's all-to-all attention weights launched the modern LLM era alongside a quadratic bottleneck. Next, we analyze why scaling parameters alone leaves capacity under-trained unless data scales equally (Chinchilla), how Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) left alignment superficial, and how that gap compounded into adversarial jailbreaks and single-direction refusal subspaces (J-space), where instructing a model not to think of a restricted concept surfaces it much like the human "red ball" paradox. Finally, we synthesize the current state of AI (2024-2026), encompassing recursive model collapse, autonomous reasoning-model jailbreak agents, machine-speed agentic intrusions, and closed-loop recursive self-improvement (AIDE^2).
items.author: Saadh Jawwadh
items.summary: This review surveys 22 influential publications spanning nearly three decades of language model research, organized in a chronological taxonomy tracing the path from RNNs and LSTMs through Word2Vec to modern LLM topics including recursive self-improvement. It aims to distinguish paradigm shifts from incremental refinements using accessible analogies.
items.reasoning: Historical syntheses of LLM development can be pedagogically useful, but 22 papers is a very small selection for a 30-year survey, the taxonomy is idiosyncratic (centered on the author's birth year), and a single-author review adds limited original analysis. It reads as an educational overview rather than a research contribution.

items.title: Human military relevance is more important than economic relevance
items.content:
A very simple point that I've had to explain to many people, so I thought I'd make a post on it.

Some classes of people in the past were economically necessary for their labor, but militarily irrelevant and coercible: slaves, serfs. Others didn't do any economic work, but were militarily important: the aristocracy! Living fun lives, partying, traveling, making and enjoying art. Some of them felt a bit of ennui due to not working, but mostly it wasn't a big problem.

The reason aristocracy gave way to democracy wasn't because of rising productivity of the masses: a slave in a diamond mine can be very productive, but still remain a slave. Rather, it was because firearms lowered the cost of training a soldier, and thus made the masses valuable as potential soldiers. That gave the masses a bargaining chip which led to better economic and political standing.

If Alice wishes for a world where her labor (e.g. as a programmer) remains economically valuable, but all military jobs go to AI, then humans will lose the "potential soldier bonus" we've had for a couple centuries and revert to a powerless, exploited position. items.title: The Disappointment of a Satisfying Explanation
items.content:
## Argument from Various Disabilities

These arguments take the form, "I grant you that you can make machines do all the things you have mentioned but you will never be able to make one to do X." Numerous features X are suggested in this connexion. I offer a selection:

Be kind, resourceful, beautiful, friendly, have initiative, have a sense of humor, tell right from wrong, make mistakes, fall in love, enjoy strawberries and cream, make some one fall in love with it, learn from experience, use words properly, be the subject of its own thought, have as much diversity of behavior as a man, do something really new.

No support is usually offered for these statements.

[...]

The criticisms that we are considering here are often disguised forms of the argument from consciousness. Usually if one maintains that a machine can do one of these things, and describes the kind of method that the machine could use, one will not make much of an impression. It is thought that the method (whatever it may be, for it must be mechanical) is really rather base. (emphasis added)

Today, Scott Aaronson hosted an essay discussion at Inkhaven and selected Turing's classic 1950 paper that defines The Imitation Game. After reading it, I find all our present-day conversations about AI do not feel new, but instead feel old. Turing attempts to diagnose the causes of people's disagreement with his position that one day computers will be able to win the imitation game, and he does such a good job of it that most people talking about AI today are just showing the callowness of their youth. But the bolded line felt true and yet I didn't fully grok it, so now I want to understand it better.

What is going on here, with this "base" property? Why does it lead people to false conclusions, that computers cannot do things that humans can? If no longer in-principle, I feel this comes up at least as commonly in-practice in discussion of the limitations of LLMs....

items.title: Alignment from equivariance III - moraloids and tribal subgroups
items.content:
Reminder (since it's been two years!): we are hoping to build a definition of morality out of pictures like this:

... because such pictures have a very well-studied mathematical structure, enough that we have been able to use the pictures to impose a desirable consistency on computer vision models. In these posts we're hoping this can generalize to imposing moral consistency. This will have various potential advantages: if you can figure out how the pictures should work, there's established ways to build an AI that conforms to it, and it's easy enough to check that someone else's AI conforms to it. And because it's math, this checking may not even be that expensive - you can do loads of trolley problems with one question, so to speak (building the right bunch of diagrams in the first place, now that might be expensive).

## Background math: groups, subgroups, and monoids

I'm at risk of losing some of you by being overtly mathematical, but honestly, this bit shouldn't be that hard. If you don't get it, it's because I've explained it badly - over a drink I could have you get it in a minute or two.

Ok, so one of the main kinds of object that mathematicians and physicists have studied for the last 200 years has been "groups". I'll illustrate with two great examples of groups that you'll be familiar with: whole numbers and 3D rotations.

With whole numbers, you can add whole numbers (multiplication isn't necessary to see them as a group). And there's a special number, 0, such that X + 0 = X.

You know 3D rotations as well - you can turn your hand left and right 30° or 90°, turn it up and down and side to side, etc. For any two rotations you can do one, and then the other, and that gets you a third rotation. There's a special, very boring, rotation which is the rotation by zero degrees, call that rotation "I". If R is another rotation, we have that "R then I" = R. So the zero degree rotation does for rotations what the number 0 does for numbers....

The author hopes this structure can impose moral consistency on AI systems in a checkable, inexpensive way, discussing subgroup decomposition in moral domains. It is speculative alignment research conceptualization.

items.title: A Second-Rate Mind's Apology
items.content:
With the deluge of new proofs by AI, now including the Riemann hypothesis work, the place of mathematics as a human pursuit has been discussed with varied levels of hand wringing. Why would we, as individuals as well as societies, spend blood and treasure in the form of our most promising youths on the altar of abstruse proofs and mental contorsions when we have LLMs to do it for a fraction of the cost and effort?

I write this as a lover of mathematics. While much slower at it and lacking in the sort of brilliance that made some of my schoolmates insights in classe préparatoire seem downright promethean, I have enjoyed plodding my way on the well trodden paths of a Bourbaki algebra book or other; and I have recently started on a project of reading and understanding the complete (sadly inherited recently) library of my father in law, who was a celebrated applied mathematician for the french meteorology office. A capstone of this would have been a few books on Navier-Stokes. Why would I do that now? Why, if I was never to be a marginally useful contributor to the great human math project, did I even keep reading and learning as an adult outside of the useful tools of linear algebra that I use every day?...
items.author: shoubidouwah
items.summary: A personal essay reflecting on why humans should continue pursuing mathematics now that LLMs, including the recent Riemann Hypothesis work, can produce proofs at far lower cost. Drawing on the author's own experience plodding through Bourbaki and an inherited applied mathematics library, it argues for the intrinsic and personal value of doing mathematics regardless of marginal contribution to the collective project.

items.title: Green = Life - Rectangle
items.content:
Imagine a 2D plane with x- and y-axes labelled “tasty” and “American” respectively. Now, plot the whole space of possible foods, from linguine to Panda Express, along these axes.

This is what LLM representation spaces are like, except instead of projecting foods onto two dimensions, they fit every concept ever into 40,000.

The Linear Representation Hypothesis states that high-level concepts that emerge through training are represented as consistent directions inside the representation space of an LLM. The classic example is king−man+woman ≈ queen, suggesting the existence of a single direction vector that represents the concept of gender.

In the spirit of the Linear Representation Hypothesis, this essay proposes the following equation:

Green = Life - Rectangle

Let’s begin with the definition of Rectangle.

## Rectangle

This essay is inspired by the following meme:

By way of example, here are some rectangles:

Shown above: the Chicago skyline, tax forms, the Ka’ba, Manhattan, the Legend of Zelda NES world map, Fine Hall (the Princeton math building), office cubicles.

I was first exposed to rectangles by Book Review: Seeing Like A State. Scott A. (summarizing J. Scott) describes the evolution of scientific forestry practices in 18th-century Prussia:

Enlightenment rationalists noticed that peasants were just cutting down whatever trees happened to grow in the forests, like a chump. They came up with a better idea: clear all the forests and replace them by planting identical copies of Norway spruce (the highest-lumber-yield-per-unit-time tree) in an evenly-spaced rectangular grid. Then you could just walk in with an axe one day and chop down like a zillion trees an hour and have more timber than you could possibly ever want.

It turns out that replacing all the forests with a rectangular tiling of one tree is a terrible, horrible, no-good, very bad, disastrous idea, and the economy went up in flames....

items.title: Do Larger Fully Connected Neural Networks Generalize Better?
items.content: Greater neural-network capacity does not necessarily yield better performance on unseen data. This study investigates whether a deeper, fully connected neural-network architecture generalizes better than a shallower architecture on the Fashion-MNIST dataset. We compare two architectures under two learning rates and two L2-regularization settings, producing eight configurations. The architectures contain 95,410 and 561,470 trainable parameters, respectively, an approximately 5.9-fold difference. Checkpoints and the final configuration are selected by validation loss, and all configurations are evaluated on a held-out test set. The selected larger configuration achieves 89.82% validation accuracy and 88.77% test accuracy. Selecting the lowest-validation-loss configuration within each architecture yields test accuracies of 88.77% and 88.52%, respectively, a difference of 0.25 percentage points. Across matched training settings, the larger architecture achieves higher test accuracy in only one of four comparisons. Class-level errors are concentrated among visually similar garment categories, and qualitative pixel-removal analyses suggest sensitivity to shape and boundaries. Overall, the findings suggest that increasing architectural capacity alone does not guarantee better generalization, highlighting the importance of considering optimization and regularization when selecting neural-network architectures.

items.title: From epistemic innocence to sophisticated uncertainty
items.content:
When I was young I knew I didn't want to be a political ideologue like my parents.
But it seemed to me that that's just what adults were like, and I was protected only by my innocence.
Just as I was already beginning to make myself ridiculous acting on newly acquired sexual urges, perhaps becoming overconfident of grand narratives was just part of growing up?

Now I have acquired an ideology (transhumanist, for one thing).
And my ideology does come with convenient narratives.
Yet, if you'll let me flatter myself, I have not acquired an ideologue's overconfidence.

I did not protect my epistemic innocence.
I enjoy seeing the world from a new worldview, including an ideologically charged one.
But the result of such openness was that I became familiar with a variety of possibilities with different implications.

## Example: nuclear power

In my subculture of tech enthusiasts, you'll hear that the world was ready to transition to nuclear power in the '70s, in which case we would have avoided global warming.
However, this technological revolution was stopped by the anti-nuclear movement and burdensome safety regulation.

Probably at some point I was caught up in this narrative.
But because I was interested in energy, I read widely, and got caught up in other narratives.
That nuclear could not provide return on investment when electricity use was lower than forecasted, and natural gas plants could be built with cheap equipment and surprisingly abundant fuel....

items.title: Rats just wanna have fun!
items.content:
Eliezer Yudkowsy wears a gold glitter hat. He also opens posts like this:

Once upon a time in the medium-small town of Skewers, Washington, there lived a 52-year-old man by the name of Mr. Humman, who considered himself a top-tier chess-player. 

And

Growing up, as a kid, I was always told that every sapient life is precious, everything that thinks and knows itself -

And

(The year is 2010. eliezer-2010 is sitting in a nonexistent park in Redwood City, California, working on his laptop. A person walks up to him.)

person:  Pardon me, but are you Eliezer Yudkowsky?

My point is, LessWrong loves fun, personal posts! We also appreciate rigor and, especially in end-of-year reviews, technical depth. Sometimes, our authors seem to get stuck in droughts: long stretches of low-karma posts, typically un-fun, un-rigorous, and a bit technical. You might think these doldrums are the prelude to an impressive, well-received synthesis, but they're not. They just go on and on. When authors break through a drought with a great post, it's usually with a fun, personal, tangible, funny narrative or advice.

I hit on this framing after I spent the weekend using Claude Code to analyze the LessWrong corpus looking for patterns in what makes for a great post. Surface features of language and topic explain only a little of the variance in karma. The author's identity explains quite a bit more.

One of my main findings is that LessWrong shifted away from its early preference for dense technical topics, philosophy, statistics, and study advice, and has come to award higher karma in recent years to articles on health and disease, X-risk, and, of course, AI.

Using these surface attributes, I could only explain about half the reception any given post gets. It was a little discouraging to find that in general, authors mostly don't improve with experience, except perhaps the most prolific[1]....

items.title: The Clean Energy Transition as a Postformal Turn
items.content:
## 0. Scene-Setting

Two quotes and a joke to get started: 

“[People] have become the tools of their tools” 

– Henry David Thoreau 

“For books [theories] are not absolutely dead things, but do contain a potency of life in them to be as active as that soul was whose progeny they are; nay, they do preserve as in a vial the purest efficacy and extraction of that living intellect that bred them.”

– John Milton, in Areopagitica 

What does organized attention get for us? Infrastructure.

The following is an expansion of a quick answer I gave to @particlemania about what Autostructures research is trying to bring about. It began with a metaphor to the clean energy transition, and seemed to deserve a bit more attention on the properties that seemed relevant. I intend for this to be the first of a short series sketching related metaphors that have helped me make sense of some key pieces of Live Theory and how we should relate to highly adaptive technology, especially outside of the commonplace agentic frame. 

Thanks are due first and most directly to TJ’s instigation and the burst of complex ideas for me to juggle and work through. @Sahil’s work has (hopefully obviously) shaped most of the central ideas I’ve referenced, as well as my perspective on AI safety broadly. @magfrump  provided multiple helpful comments on an initial draft. The rest of our Autostructures AISC 11 team made for a wonderful base of support in developing these ideas in an up-close and hands-on fashion. 

I suppose it is also fashionable - and perhaps obligatory - to thank Opus 5.5 for collating my rants and offering amenable phrasings and critique.

items.title: LLM-Based Assistant for Dog Care Guidance
items.content: This study investigates whether domain grounding through Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and parameter-efficient fine-tuning using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) can enhance the accuracy and reliability of pet care advice generated by large language models (LLMs). We curated a dataset of breed-specific dog care information and used it to develop two systems: a RAG pipeline based on TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat-v1.0, and a fine-tuned LLaMA-3.2-1B model adapted using LoRA. Both systems were evaluated on 15 dog care questions. The RAG model achieved a perfect average score of 2.0, outperforming the fine-tuned model (mean = 1.47). Statistical analyses, including Welch's t-test, Mann-Whitney U, and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests (all p < 0.05), confirmed the significance of the performance gap. Our findings suggest that retrieval-based domain grounding leads to more accurate, consistent, and trustworthy responses than standalone fine-tuning in specialized LLM applications.
items.author: Abubakar Sadiq Shittu, Venkat Gopu, Arshita Sharma, Jacob Kennedy
items.summary: This study compares RAG (TinyLlama-1.1B) and LoRA fine-tuning (LLaMA-3.2-1B) for generating dog care advice, finding the RAG pipeline scored perfectly on 15 evaluation questions while the fine-tuned model averaged 1.47. Statistical tests confirmed the performance gap.
items.reasoning: The evaluation is very small (15 questions), uses tiny models, and confirms the well-known finding that RAG outperforms fine-tuning for domain grounding. The application domain is niche, and the methodology lacks the scale or novelty to influence research or practice beyond a classroom-project level.

items.title: Announcing RLLW: Reinforcement Learning via LessWrong
items.content:
You’ve railed against RLHF.

My job was stolen by RLVR.

Welcome to RLLW.

I think LessWrong and the blogosphere around it host the most important public conversations in the world, and there aren’t enough dedicated writers to produce the long-form content about rationality and AI we all crave. RLLW is my attempt to train a few. In the first cohort, I am working with two undergraduate apprentices, who will each write one post every two weeks.

Sam Worthington: Sam goes to Princeton and co-directs Princeton AI Alignment. He hopes to maximize his EV by getting himself into increasing amounts of trouble. He also writes here.

Jaisen Soundar: Jaisen goes to Georgia Tech and does technical AI safety research. He hopes to make a positive impact on the field through his writing.

## The first round of essays

- Green = Life − Rectangle (Sam) asks what’s up with all these rectangles everywhere and why AIs don’t seem to fit in them.
- Moderately cursed questions of AI safety (Jaisen) Explores four questions in AI safety that people think about but rarely discuss openly.

## Philosophy: Microdosing the Spirit of Inkhaven

I had planned to frame this announcement as an answer to Ben Pace’s call for better writing on LessWrong, but that call was unfortunately rebutted soundly by Ben Pace.

In this section I ramble about a couple of different things I’m trying, especially in contrast to Inkhaven. We’ll post once every two weeks for two months instead of every day for a month. More details:...

items.title: Joseph Miller Actually Tried. Is that enough?
items.content:
Last week, over 1,000 people in six countries Marched for an AI Treaty, an international day of protest organized by Stop The AI Race, with local organizers including DC AI Safety, PauseAI, and many others.

March of an AI Treaty in San Francisco (📸 Rachel Bujalski)

Then Thursday, Stop The AI Race came in support of the Ban RSI protest outside Anthropic as they IPOed (~200 people).

A couple hours after, Stop AI protesters got taken away in cuffs for blocking the doors of Anthropic, while other protesters were also handcuffed outside the Nasdaq in NYC.

Source: Mission Local. Photo by Zoe Malen

Finally, on Saturday over 1,000 people in London marched against AI Extinction.

Overall, it seems like the AI Safety movement is finally rising up to the challenge, right?

…

Right?

We now have a thousand people in London. Three years ago, the same protest had 5. This is the story of how that happened, and it’s the best example I know of what I called Actually Trying. But is that enough for humanity to survive?

Let’s find out.

# PauseAI UK

The summer of 2025 was when I first met Joseph Miller, head of PauseAI UK.

Joseph Miller - somewhere in the UK, probably

Now, contrary to other AI Safety activist movements at the time, Joseph was actively pursuing a career in AI Safety research through an (incoming) AI PhD in Oxford.

But he thought that advocating for a Pause was too important to be left to the last minute, even if it sounded weird.

Indeed, a year before I met him, he wrote:

Some AI researchers think that they should not go to protests because it is not their comparative advantage. But this is wrong, the key skill required is the ability to do something weird - to take ideas seriously and to actually try to fix important problems. The protests are currently so small that the marginal impact of an extra person showing up for a couple of hours once every few months is very large.

And indeed, this was what the UK protests in 2023 looked like:...

items.title: Thinking is Hard (for Humans)
items.content:
Cross-posted from my Substack.

## No One is Thinking about This

I started thinking about thinking in 2004, age 17, when I discovered the recorded lectures of MIT’s intro psychology course. The class devoted a single lecture to thinking, most of it about ways thinking goes wrong, like “functional fixedness” and various biases. The study of human minds seemed little interested in how thinking works, what it’s good for, how to think better. Thinking was an afterthought, simultaneously too rare to matter and too obvious to require explanation.

The same year, a new word popped up and started growing exponentially in popularity — 100x as common today as it was just 20 years ago. Overthinking. Commonly searched with: “anxiety”, “depression”, “how to stop”. Right when I became curious about thinking, everyone else decided that thinking is bad, actually. A mental illness. At best, an indulgence.

Genesis 1 describes the creation of the world: a directed and motivated process. God sees a reason — “to give light on the earth”, executes a solution — “lights in the vault of the sky”, and assesses the outcome — “it was good”. Finally, mankind is created in his image. What does “his image” mean? It’s not our kidneys (common to land vertebrates), leg bones (shared with all tetrapods), or fingernails (primates). The thing that humans and only humans have in common with the God of Genesis 1 is reason: controlling one’s thoughts in a directed, motivated way to achieve a goal. This is what thinking is, or at least what it should be when done right.

Instead, “thinking” came to mean anxious rumination. Being controlled by your thoughts, getting dragged around by them like snot on a bike tire. 20 years ago humans collectively failed to understand thinking, gave up on the problem, then declared (unthinkingly) that it’s better this way. If thinking is godlike, then rebranding anxiety as thinking is a trick worthy of the devil....
items.author: Jacob Falkovich
items.summary: A wide-ranging essay arguing that human thinking is understudied and even pathologized, tracing cultural attitudes from psychology's neglect of thinking to the rise of the term overthinking, and arguing for deliberate, directed thought. It connects historical, religious, and psychological threads to advocate for better individual thinking practices. It is a cultural/philosophical piece rather than empirical research.
items.reasoning: Well-crafted and engaging with some relevance to how humans should reason in an AI era, but it is an essay without original data, methods, or technical contributions to AI research.

items.title: The Point of Pressuring the UK Government
items.content:
This is a speech I gave at PauseAI UK's March Against AI Extinction on the 21st of November.

[Crossposted from my blog, BlueprintingHeaven.]

Most of us are not US citizens, but US AI labs threaten every non-US citizen too, so we can't just leave dealing with extinction risk from AI to America.

You can ask the US citizens to talk to their politicians for you, or you can try to talk to US politicians directly, and there are avenues for that, or you can get your government to talk to the American government, which is what PauseAI UK is trying to do.

I want to remind everyone what the point of pressuring the UK government is.

Countries do not exist in isolation from other. Geopolitics exists. If the UK made a costly signal to the US that they genuinely think advanced AI systems could kill every living thing on planet Earth, the policy experts in the US would be terrified. Countries are usually very careful and gentle with their words. A country does not tell another country "this could kill every person on Earth" for no reason. If the British government said that to Washington, serious smart people in DC and American national security will freak out and make things happen. The US government would not ignore the UK government begging for them to stop and saying that they are worried we are all going to die....
items.author: Laiba Rehman ✦ RJ
items.summary: A speech delivered at PauseAI UK's March Against AI Extinction explaining why non-US citizens should pressure their own governments, arguing that a costly signal from the UK to the US that it takes extinction risk seriously would alarm US national security and policy elites into action. The piece frames allied-government pressure as a leverage mechanism on US AI labs. It is advocacy rhetoric with a strategic theory of change.

items.title: Why do modern people ask small questions?
items.content:
Once I did a research project on how much ideas versus implementation effort is important for stuff happening. If I recall, at least part of this was looking up when ideas first appeared and when they were implemented, and inferring if the gap was short then the idea was a bigger bottleneck.

I mentioned this to my boyfriend, and he was amused at my style of research question: it sounded like it was from hundreds of years ago—these days, people usually research things like ‘for this particular species of microbe is x or y more important to its behavior in this phase?’ whereas my question was incredibly high level.

I agreed with that, but then wondered why.

One theory is that it’s actually silly to ask such high level questions—this is just too general a question to have a good answer. We didn’t know that two hundred years ago, we do now.

Another theory is that all the high level questions have been answered, so at this point in history we are filling in the gaps regarding specific microbe specifics, and everything else.

A more interesting theory he suggested is that it relates to professionalism. Science has become much more professional, and that is somehow contrary to asking questions like this. Being oriented toward ‘having a job’ is different from trying to understand the world. I liked this theory, because it fits with my broader hypothesis that professionalism is terrible.

Got any more theories?
items.author: KatjaGrace
items.summary: A reflective essay on why modern researchers tend to ask narrow, specific questions rather than the sweeping, high-level questions of earlier eras, weighing theories based on tractability, exhaustion of big questions, and the professionalization of science. The author draws on her own experience asking an old-fashioned high-level question about ideas versus implementation effort. It is an intellectual meditation on the sociology of research.
items.reasoning: Genuinely interesting and relevant to research culture, especially in fast-moving fields like AI, but it is informal speculation with no data, methods, or actionable conclusions. Low research value despite being thought-provoking.

items.title: Everyone in AI safety gets FOMO
items.content:
If you’re feeling like you should drop everything and do something else (more advocacy, more technical research, more theory research, more empirical research, etc), one thing I’d like to communicate to you is that many (all?) in AI safety feel this way or have felt this way at some point. 

Why?

- Well, the stakes are high and timelines are uncertain. So it feels like your work could be useless if you aren’t working on the precisely right thing.
- And, you’re working on unglamorous and messy things on your own end, but see the highlight reels and successes of other fields. So it can feel like you’re spinning your wheels but someone else is doing something cool.
- And, the bots are getting better, and they could be getting better at your thing!
- And, AI safety doesn’t have well-worn grooves. No one says “you are a journeyman researcher or policy person or X or Y now, you can decide your own thing”. So it will feel like you are fumbling in the dark.
- Specialisation feels lonely: you’re just working on your thing, but wow, there are so many embedded evaluators/interp people/etc. But actually, if you go specific and deep enough, you’re the only person working on your specific thing.
- In practice, specialisation may cause you to underestimate your own progress and research. You will make progress up until you hit a wall, and you may get used to your own gains, but feels acutely the places you don’t know (the more you know, the less you know).

But, for a big civilizational effort to work, people have to specialize and spend a long time doing one thing, and many groups of people have to do different things....
items.author: David Africa
items.summary: The author argues that fear of missing out is nearly universal in AI safety due to high stakes, uncertain timelines, unglamorous local work contrasted with others' highlight reels, rapidly improving AI, and the field's lack of established career grooves. The post normalizes these feelings and implicitly advises against constantly switching focus. It is peer-support commentary for the AI safety community.

items.title: What concrete mistakes did we/people make around FTX regranting?
items.content:
"I don't know about you, but I'm feeling [20]22"

I have a sense that we might be back in a period of freewheeling regranting much like 2022. I am not interested here in the FTX fraud, but I am interested in mistakes that the Future Fund and the wider community[1] made.

What were mistakes those in grantmakers and the wider community made? What were the most harmful grants made?

What could Lightcone Commons do/fund in order for this to go better?

Concrete is better if possible but please consider you are writing on the open internet and might be sharing private information.

items.title: Banana Cases
items.content:
Ages ago I saw some banana cases in the grocery store.  They seemed
like a gimmick: why would you get a piece of plastic for such a
specific use?  A decade later we have a set of three and use them
~daily.

Nora (5y) really likes bananas, and is now in kindergarten.  She wants
to bring them to school, which is great: they're tasty, reasonably
healthy, and very cheap.

(I do want to stop for a minute and gush about how through shipping
and ethylene gas management my 5yo can eat tropical fruit all through
the New England winter.  World banana production is not perfect, but
it is pretty incredible.)

Initially I was putting them in the same random set of containers we
use for storing non-hot leftovers.  These either were too small for a
banana or took up too much space in her lunchbox.  They also sealed
too well, and so let the ethylene build up and accelerate ripening.  I
remembered the banana cases, sized for a banana with vent holes for
gas exchange, and decided to get some (3 for $8).

They work well, and the bananas don't squish.  I do sometimes need to
cut off the stem for them to fit, and need to avoid unusually large
bananas.  Still, I was unreasonably dismissive of these: they solve a
real problem, and they do it well.

items.title: Scoring AI safety rally chants: results from a chant workshop
items.content:
Some friends (Logan and others) and I (Jason) attended the AI regulation rally in front of the Massachusetts State House on Saturday, Nov 14th. The event was a positive experience overall, but one aspect could have been better: the chants. In response, I ran a short workshop where other AI safety researchers and I trialed a number of chants and rated them along a few metrics. The data was compiled into a memo which I sent to AI rally organizers and am now sharing here.

## The workshop

The workshop was an hour long and had three parts: a short presentation on the theory of rallies and chants, a brainstorming session to create chants, and then actually running the chants (both ours and selected chants from recent AI rallies) which were scored along three metrics. There is a wonderful community of AI safety people in the Boston area, so for the workshop we had 8 AI safety researchers show up. We were all crammed in a small room where we loudly chanted about existential risk. It was a lot of fun, I highly recommend.

Each participant was given a bubble sheet to score each chant along three metrics: Ease, Fun, Message. I acted as the MC of the "rally", and everyone learned each chant in real time, so the process of learning each chant was included in the scoring. We would repeat each chant 4-6 times, then take 30 seconds to score it on our bubble sheets, and move on to the next chant.
